All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

derivations.claim: The adjoint $T^*$ exists by [F3]. The definition [F1] gives $\langle x|T|y\rangle_D=\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}$.
Apply [F2] with $v=y$ and $w=x$, then apply [F1] again. This gives $\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}=\langle y,T^*x\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}} =\langle T^*x|y\rangle_D$, proving the stated chain.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $z=\sum_{j<n}\langle z,e_j\rangle e_j$. Applying $T$ and using linearity, then expanding each $Te_j$ by [F2], gives $Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle f_i$.

Write $x_i=\langle x,f_i\rangle$ and $y_j=\langle y,e_j\rangle$, the coordinates from [F1]–[F2]. The image of $e_j$ under $|x\rangle\langle y|$ is $\langle e_j,y\rangle x=\overline{y_j}x$ by [F1] and [F7]. Its $i$-th coordinate is therefore $x_i\overline{y_j}$. By [F4]–[F6], these are exactly the entries of $[x]_F[y]_E^\dagger$.
The amplitude identity is the defining Dirac conversion [F3].
By [F3], the operator sum in the Statement sends every $z$ to the right-hand side of step 1.1. It therefore agrees with $T$ on every vector.

If $n=0$, then $H=0$, $T=0$, and $y=0$; if $m=0$, then $K=0$, $T=0$, and $x=0$. In either case the displayed sums and rank-one map are zero, and the amplitude identity is $0=0$. Thus all formulas include zero dimensions.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Because

$$\langle T^*Tv,v\rangle=\langle Tv,Tv\rangle\ge0$$

for every $v\in V$, and because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T$ by [[prop-adjoint-algebra]],
the operator $T^*T$ is non-negative. Let

$$|T|:=\sqrt{T^*T},$$

the unique non-negative square root from
[[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]. The **singular values**
of $T$ are the eigenvalues of $|T|$, listed with multiplicity in weakly
decreasing order.

In particular, this definition applies to endomorphisms by taking $W=V$.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, the multiset of singular values depends only on $T$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

derivations.claim: Fix an ordered basis of $H$. For endomorphisms $R,S$ of $H$ and a scalar $\alpha$, [F9] shows that the diagonal entries of $\alpha R+S$ are $\alpha R_{jj}+S_{jj}$: the $j$-th coordinate column is obtained from $(\alpha R+S)e_j=\alpha Re_j+Se_j$. Summing these entries by [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}_H(\alpha R+S)=\alpha\operatorname{tr}_H(R)+ \operatorname{tr}_H(S)$. Thus trace homogeneity and additivity used below follow from the diagonal-sum definition. The same calculation covers $H=0$ by empty sums.

Let $C:H\to K$ be any finite-dimensional linear map. If $H=0$, its operator norm is $0$ by [F5]. If $H\ne0$, choose an SVD as in [F2] with positive singular values $t_1\ge\cdots\ge t_q>0$ and orthonormal domain vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_{\dim H}$. If $q>0$, Bessel's inequality [F7] gives, for every unit vector $z$, $\|Cz\|^2=\sum_{j\le q}t_j^2|\langle z,u_j\rangle|^2\le t_1^2$, with equality at $z=u_1$. If $q=0$, the SVD says $C=0$, so every unit vector attains the value $0$. Thus the maximum in [F5] exists for every map used below, including the zero-rank case.
Choose an SVD as in [F2], with $r$ positive singular values. Then $\|A\|_1=\sum_{i<r}s_i$ by [F1]. If $r=0$, [F2] gives $A=0$ and this sum is empty.

Write the SVD domain basis as $(e_j)_{j<n}$ and its positive singular values as $s_i$ for $i<r$. By [F4], [F7], and the fact that the $j$-th diagonal entry is the $e_j$-coordinate of the image of $e_j$, $$\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)=\sum_{j<n}\langle B^*Ae_j,e_j\rangle_H=\sum_{i<r}s_i\langle B^*f_i,e_i\rangle_H=\sum_{i<r}s_i\langle f_i,Be_i\rangle_K.$$ For the last equality, [F3] gives $\langle Be_i,f_i\rangle_K=\langle e_i,B^*f_i\rangle_H$, and conjugate symmetry [F10] gives the displayed order. This is a direct endomorphism-trace calculation and uses no cyclic trace identity for maps.

Suppose $r>0$ and define $B_0:H\to K$ by $B_0z=\sum_{i<r}\langle z,e_i\rangle f_i$. By [F10], this is linear; it sends $e_i$ to $f_i$ for $i<r$ and sends the remaining basis vectors to $0$. By [F7], $\|B_0z\|^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle z,e_i\rangle|^2\le\|z\|^2$, with equality at $z=e_0$. The maximum property established in step 1.2 therefore gives $\|B_0\|=1$. Define $Cw=\sum_{i<r}\langle w,f_i\rangle e_i$. Expanding in the finite orthonormal bases using [F7] verifies $\langle B_0z,w\rangle_K=\langle z,Cw\rangle_H$, so [F3] gives $C=B_0^*$. Hence $B_0^*Ae_i=s_ie_i$ for $i<r$ and $B_0^*Ae_j=0$ for $j\ge r$. If $r=0$, set $B_0=0$.

Let $B:H\to K$ satisfy $\|B\|\le1$. By [F5] and the maximum property established in step 1.2, $\|Be_i\|\le1$ for every unit vector $e_i$; [F6] then gives $|\langle f_i,Be_i\rangle|\le1$. Applying [F8] to the sum in step 1.4 yields $|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|\le\sum_{i<r}s_i=\|A\|_1$. The same bound is immediate when $r=0$.

By [F4], [F7], and step 1.3, $\operatorname{tr}_H(B_0^*A)=\sum_{i<r}s_i=\|A\|_1$; when $r=0$, both sides are $0$. Together with step 2.2 this proves the stated maximum, including zero-dimensional spaces.

For any scalar $\alpha$, apply the maximum formula to $\alpha A$. By step 1.1, $\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*(\alpha A))=\alpha\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)$, so taking absolute values and maxima gives $\|\alpha A\|_1=|\alpha|\|A\|_1$. The definition and [F2] give $\|A\|_1\ge0$, with equality exactly when all singular values vanish, which by the SVD is exactly $A=0$.

For maps $A,D:H\to K$, every contraction $B$ satisfies $$|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*(A+D))|\le|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|+|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*D)|\le\|A\|_1+\|D\|_1$$ by the additivity from step 1.1, [F8], and step 3.1. Taking the maximum over $B$ proves $\|A+D\|_1\le\|A\|_1+\|D\|_1$. Thus the trace norm has all stated norm properties.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Because

$$\langle T^*Tv,v\rangle=\langle Tv,Tv\rangle\ge0$$

for every $v\in V$, and because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T$ by [[prop-adjoint-algebra]],
the operator $T^*T$ is non-negative. Let

$$|T|:=\sqrt{T^*T},$$

the unique non-negative square root from
[[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]. The **singular values**
of $T$ are the eigenvalues of $|T|$, listed with multiplicity in weakly
decreasing order.

In particular, this definition applies to endomorphisms by taking $W=V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

derivations.claim: If $x=0$ or $y=0$, [F1] makes $A=|x\rangle\langle y|$ the zero map. Then [F6] gives $\|A\|_1=0$, while [F2] gives $\|x\|\|y\|=0$.

Suppose $x,y\ne0$. For $z\in H$ and $w\in K$, [F1]–[F2] give $$\langle Az,w\rangle_K=\langle z,y\rangle_H\langle x,w\rangle_K =\langle z,\langle w,x\rangle_K y\rangle_H.$$ Thus the adjoint identity [F3] gives $A^*w=\langle w,x\rangle_Ky$, and therefore $A^*Az=\|x\|^2\langle z,y\rangle_H y$.

Let $e=y/\|y\|$ and put $\lambda=\|x\|^2\|y\|^2$. Step 1.2 gives $A^*Ae=\lambda e$ and $A^*Az=0$ whenever $z\perp e$. Every $z\in H$ has the decomposition $z=\langle z,e\rangle e+(z-\langle z,e\rangle e)$, whose second term is orthogonal to $e$; the two summands intersect only at $0$. Therefore $H=\operatorname{span}\{e\}\oplus e^\perp$, and $A^*A$ acts by $\lambda$ on the first summand and by $0$ on the second.

Define $R$ on the direct sum $H=\operatorname{span}\{e\}\oplus e^\perp$ by $Re=\|x\|\|y\|e$ and $Rz=0$ for $z\perp e$, extending linearly. For $z,w\in H$, put $c=\langle z,e\rangle$ and $d=\langle w,e\rangle$. Then $\langle Rz,w\rangle=\|x\|\|y\|c\overline d=\langle z,Rw\rangle$, so $R$ is self-adjoint; its eigenvalues are $\|x\|\|y\|$ on $\operatorname{span}\{e\}$ and $0$ on $e^\perp$. These eigenvalues are nonnegative, so [F5] makes $R$ non-negative. It satisfies $R^2=A^*A$ by step 2.1. Uniqueness in [F5] gives $R=|A|=\sqrt{A^*A}$. Its eigenvalues are $\|x\|\|y\|$ once and $0$ on $e^\perp$, so [F4] and [F6] give $\|A\|_1=\|x\|\|y\|$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the formula, including zero vectors and zero-dimensional spaces.

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

derivations.claim: Choose an SVD of $A$ as in [F1], with domain basis $(e_j)$ and codomain basis $(f_i)$. By [F2], $(V^*e_j)$ and $(Uf_i)$ are orthonormal bases. For every $z\in H$, [F3] gives $$UAVz=\sum_{j<r}s_j\langle Vz,e_j\rangle Uf_j =\sum_{j<r}s_j\langle z,V^*e_j\rangle Uf_j.$$ This is an SVD of $UAV$ with the same positive singular values, so [F1] gives $\|UAV\|_1=\|A\|_1$.

Let $P$ be non-negative. By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_j)$ with $Pe_j=\lambda_je_j$ and $\lambda_j\ge0$. Since $P^*=P$, $P^*P=P^2$. Computing the trace in the same basis by [F6] gives $\operatorname{tr}_H(P)=\sum_j\lambda_j=\|P\|_1$. If $H=0$, both sums are empty and equal $0$. This proves both assertions.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional complex
inner-product spaces. Then

$$\|A\|_1=\max\{\,|\operatorname{tr}_H(B^*A)|: B:H\to K\text{ linear and }\|B\|\le1\,\}.$$

Consequently, on the vector space of linear maps $H\to K$, the trace norm is
nonnegative, absolutely homogeneous, definite, and satisfies the triangle
inequality.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

For every linear map $A:H\to K$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces,

$$\|A\|_1=\operatorname{tr}_H\!\left(\sqrt{A^*A}\right).$$

Here $A^*A$ and its non-negative square root are endomorphisms of the domain
$H$; the trace is taken on $H$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

For $v\in\mathcal H$, define $X_+v=\sum_{j<n}\max(\lambda_j,0)\langle v,e_j\rangle e_j$ and $X_-v=\sum_{j<n}\max(-\lambda_j,0)\langle v,e_j\rangle e_j$. These are linear by the first-slot rule [F2] and the finite-sum definition [F9]. Their diagonal entries are real and nonnegative. If $v=\sum_j c_je_j$, then [F2] gives $\langle X_+v,v\rangle=\sum_j\max(\lambda_j,0)|c_j|^2\ge0$, and the same calculation applies to $X_-$. Thus [F3] makes both operators non-negative. Every $X_+u$ is a linear combination of basis vectors with $\lambda_j>0$, while every $X_-v$ is a linear combination of basis vectors with $\lambda_j<0$; these subsets of the orthonormal basis are orthogonal. Thus $\langle X_+u,X_-v\rangle=0$ for all $u,v$. On every $e_j$, $(X_+-X_-)e_j=\lambda_je_j=Xe_j$, hence $X=X_+-X_-$.

In this basis $X^*X=X^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_j^2$. Define $R$ by $Re_j=|\lambda_j|e_j$. Its diagonal entries are nonnegative, so [F3] makes it non-negative, and $R^2=X^*X$; uniqueness [F7] therefore gives $R=\sqrt{X^*X}$. Thus [F4]–[F5] give $\|X\|_1=\sum_j|\lambda_j|$, $\operatorname{tr}(X_+)=\sum_{\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j$, and $\operatorname{tr}(X_-)=\sum_{\lambda_j<0}(-\lambda_j)$. Their latter two sums add to $\sum_j|\lambda_j|$, proving the trace-norm identity.

If $\operatorname{tr}(X)=0$, [F5] gives $\sum_j\lambda_j=0$. Hence the sum of positive eigenvalues equals the sum of absolute values of negative eigenvalues. Step 3.1 then yields $\|X\|_1=2\operatorname{tr}(X_+)=2\operatorname{tr}(X_-)$. If $n=0$, all sums are empty and the identities still hold.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**

$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

For indices $a,b$ in the same finite index set, the **Kronecker delta** is

$$\delta_{ab}:=\begin{cases}1,&a=b,\\0,&a\ne b.\end{cases}$$

matrix whose $(r,s)$-entry is

$$(E_{ij})_{rs}:=\delta_{ri}\delta_{sj}.$$

Thus $E_{ij}$ has entry $1$ in position $(i,j)$ and entry $0$ everywhere else.
When a dimension is zero, no index of that dimension exists and there are no
matrix units of the corresponding shape.

$$[S\circ T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal D}=[S]_{\mathcal C}^{\mathcal D}[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}.$$

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

derivations.claim: If $\dim V=0$, [F1] gives $V=\{0\}$, so its only endomorphism is $D=0$. Assume henceforth $\dim V=m>0$ and choose an ordered basis.

If every entry of the matrix of $D$ were zero, [F2] would make $D$ vanish on every basis vector and hence on every vector. Thus if $D\ne0$ there are indices $i,j<m$ with matrix entry $D_{ij}\ne0$. Define $A(\sum_{k<m}a_kb_k):=a_i b_j$ using the ordered basis chosen in step 1.1. Unique coordinates [F7] make this well-defined; for scalars $\alpha,\beta$ and vectors with coordinate lists $(a_k)$ and $(c_k)$, the coordinate list of their linear combination is $(\alpha a_k+\beta c_k)$, so the formula gives $A(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha A(x)+\beta A(y)$. Thus $A$ is an endomorphism. Its matrix sends $b_i$ to $b_j$ and every other basis vector to $0$, so that matrix is $E_{ji}$.

By [F4], the matrix of $D\circ A$ is $[D][A]=[D]E_{ji}$. Row-by-column multiplication [F5] gives $([D]E_{ji})_{kk}=D_{kj}\delta_{ik}$, so every diagonal entry is $0$ except the $(i,i)$ entry, which is $D_{ij}$. By [F6], $\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)=D_{ij}\ne0$. This contradicts the hypothesis for every $A$. Therefore $D=0$, including the zero-dimensional case from step 1.1.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M,N$ be $R$-modules. The abelian group $M\otimes_RN$ has a unique $R$-module structure for which

$$r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$$

for every $r\in R$, $m\in M$, and $n\in N$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

derivations.claim: For $n=0$, the declared space is $\mathbb C$ with its usual pairing and basis $\{1\}$. For $n>0$, repeated use of [F1] and the associativity identifications in [F2] shows that the lexicographically ordered elementary product vectors form a basis of the tensor space. If one factor basis is empty, the product basis is empty and the tensor space is zero.

Use the coordinates in this product basis to define the pairing by the standard coordinate formula of [F3]. The basis gives unique coordinates by [F5], so this is a well-defined sesquilinear positive-definite pairing. It is linear first and conjugate-linear second by [F3] and [F4].

Write $x_k=\sum_{i_k}x_{k,i_k}e_{k,i_k}$ and $y_k=\sum_{i_k}y_{k,i_k}e_{k,i_k}$ in the supplied bases, using their unique coordinates [F5]. Multilinearity of elementary tensors [F6], applied one factor at a time, gives the coefficient $\prod_k x_{k,i_k}$ of each product-basis vector in $\bigotimes_k x_k$, and similarly $\prod_k y_{k,i_k}$ for $\bigotimes_k y_k$. The standard coordinate formula [F3] therefore gives $\sum_{(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})}\prod_k x_{k,i_k}\overline{y_{k,i_k}}$. Repeated finite distributivity factors this as $\prod_k\sum_{i_k}x_{k,i_k}\overline{y_{k,i_k}}$, which is the displayed product formula. For $n=0$ both expressions are $1$; if a factor has dimension $0$, the product basis is empty and both the tensor pairing and product over factor pairings are $0$.

The product formula depends only on the factor pairings. Any other supplied orthonormal bases therefore give the same pairing on elementary tensors; elementary tensors span by [F1], so sesquilinearity makes the pairings equal everywhere.

The factor permutation in the Definition sends the product basis bijectionally to the product basis in the reordered factors. Unique coordinates [F5] make its linear extension well-defined, and [F7] makes that extension linear; applying the inverse permutation to basis vectors gives the inverse linear map. For the empty list the definition is already the identity.

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary

   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

derivations.claim: At $n=0$, the domain has just the empty word and the codomain is $\{0,\ldots,2^0-1\}=\{0\}$. By [F1], its index is $0$, so the map is bijective.

Assume the result for $n$. For a word of length $n+1$, write its first bit as $b\in\{0,1\}$ and its remaining word as $y\in\{0,1\}^n$. Splitting the first term from the sum in [F1] gives $\operatorname{enc}_{n+1}(b,y)=b2^n+\operatorname{enc}_n(y)$. By the induction hypothesis, the tail index ranges bijectively over $\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}$.

If $b=0$, the resulting indices are exactly $0,\ldots,2^n-1$. If $b=1$, they are exactly $2^n,\ldots,2^{n+1}-1$. The two intervals are disjoint and their union is the full target, so equality of two encoded indices forces the first bits to agree and every target index is attained. For either fixed first bit, injectivity and surjectivity of the tail encoding give the corresponding claims for the remaining word.

By [F5], the base case and induction step prove bijectivity for all $n\ge0$. A permutation $\sigma$ of the bit positions is a bijection on words, with inverse the permutation $\sigma^{-1}$; composing it with the basis labeling in [F2] therefore permutes the basis [F3, F4].

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space. If $D:V\to V$ is linear
and $\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)=0$ for every linear map $A:V\to V$, then $D=0$.
Equivalently, the trace pairing $(D,A)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)$
has the property that its only first input pairing to zero with every second
input is $D=0$. This includes the zero space.

Let $T:U\to V$ and $S:V\to W$ be linear, with ordered bases $\mathcal B$ of
$U$, $\mathcal C$ of $V$, and $\mathcal D$ of $W$. Then

$$[S\circ T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal D}=[S]_{\mathcal C}^{\mathcal D}[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}.$$

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

The identity map of a vector space is linear. If $T:U\to V$ and $S:V\to W$
are linear maps over the same field, then $S\circ T:U\to W$ is linear.

derivations.claim: By [F8], choose ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ of $H_A$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$ of $H_B$, and set $S=\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)$. For any $T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$, [F1], [F6] and [F7] give $\operatorname{tr}(S\circ T)=\sum_{i,i'<a}\sum_{j<b} R_{(i,j),(i',j)}T_{i'i}$.

The identity $I_{H_B}$ is linear by [F9], so [F2] defines the linear map $T\otimes I_{H_B}$; its composite with $R$ is linear by [F9]. In the product basis, [F2] gives the matrix entry $T_{i'i}\delta_{j'j}$ of $T\otimes I$. By [F6] and [F7], $\operatorname{tr}(R\circ(T\otimes I))=\sum_{i,j}\sum_{i',j'}R_{(i,j),(i',j')}T_{i'i}\delta_{j'j}=\sum_{i,i',j}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}T_{i'i}$, which is the same finite sum as in step 1.1. $\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the

tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and

complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.

$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

are linear maps over the same field, then $S\circ T:U\to W$ is linear.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Write an arbitrary vector as $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha e_\alpha$ in the orthonormal product basis from [F2]. Its squared norm is $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2$. The map permutes that basis, so its image has the same coefficients in a permuted orthonormal basis and the same squared norm. Thus $P_\sigma$ is a linear isometry. For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

For every $n\ge0$, the map
$\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}$ of
[[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]] is a bijection. Any permutation of the
$n$ bit positions therefore induces a permutation of the corresponding
computational basis.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with ordered
orthonormal bases $E=(e_j)_{j<n}$ and $F=(f_i)_{i<m}$. Let $T:H\to K$ be
linear ([[def-linear-map]]), and write $T_{ij}$ for the $(i,j)$ entry of its
matrix in these bases.
Then, for every $z\in H$,

$$Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}f_i, \qquad T=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}|f_i\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

For $x\in K$ and $y\in H$, the rank-one map $|x\rangle\langle y|$ has
coordinate matrix $[x]_F[y]_E^\dagger$, where $M^\dagger=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$.
Its amplitude satisfies
$\langle x|T|y\rangle_D=\langle Ty,x\rangle_{K,\mathrm{root}}$.
All sums are empty when an index dimension is zero, and the identities include
those cases.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $I_H:H\to H$ denote the identity map $x\mapsto x$. An **effect** on $H$ is an endomorphism $E$ such that both $E$ and $I_H-E$ are non-negative in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. A **finite complete positive family** is a nonempty finite list $(E_1,\ldots,E_n)$ of non-negative endomorphisms with $\sum_{a=1}^n E_a=I_H$. The next lemma proves that every member of such a family is an effect, so the family is a finite complete effect family. This is algebraic data only; it does not assert a measurement law.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

derivations.claim: Fix $a\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. The family identity gives $I_H-E_a=\sum_{b\ne a}E_b$. For every $x\in H$, each $\langle E_bx,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real by [F2]; their finite sum is therefore nonnegative, including the empty sum $0$ when $n=1$. The sum is self-adjoint because each $E_b$ is self-adjoint and the sum is finite. Thus $I_H-E_a$ is non-negative.
Since $E_a$ is non-negative by [F1] and its complement is non-negative by step 1.1, it is an effect by the definition in [F1]. The index $a$ was arbitrary.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).
