Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $f:U\to V$ and $g:V\to\mathbb C$, where $U,V\subseteq\mathbb C$ are open. If $f$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$ and $g$ is complex differentiable at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ and

$$ (g\circ f)'(a)=g'(f(a))f'(a). $$

Let $f,g:U\to\mathbb C$ be complex differentiable at $a\in U$, and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$ (\alpha f+\beta g)'(a)=\alpha f'(a)+\beta g'(a), $$

$$ (fg)'(a)=f'(a)g(a)+f(a)g'(a). $$

If $g(a)\ne0$, then $g$ is nonzero on some neighbourhood of $a$, the reciprocal $1/g$ is complex differentiable at $a$, and

$$ (1/g)'(a)=-\frac{g'(a)}{g(a)^2},\qquad (f/g)'(a)=\frac{f'(a)g(a)-f(a)g'(a)}{g(a)^2}. $$

Every constant function has derivative $0$, and the identity function has derivative $1$.
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a domain. If $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic and $f'(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then $f$ is constant on $U$.
If $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: Put $s=\sin(\pi/6)$. Since $0<\pi/6<\pi/2$, [F8] and [F9] give $s>0$. By [F10], $s=\cos(\pi/3)=1-2s^2$, so $(2s-1)(s+1)=0$ and positivity gives $s=1/2$. By [F1], $D$ is unitarily diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ on the unit circle. Since $\det D=1$, $\lambda_1\lambda_2=1$. Choose principal angular representatives $\theta_j\in(-\pi,\pi]$ using [F7]. The norm bound and [F5] give $2|\sin(\theta_j/2)|=|\lambda_j-1|\le\rho\le1/2$, hence $|\sin(\theta_j/2)|\le1/4<1/2=\sin(\pi/6)$. Oddness and strict monotonicity in [F9] force $|\theta_j|<\pi/3$. Now [F6] gives $\theta_1+\theta_2\in2\pi\mathbb Z$; the bound on their sum forces $\theta_2=-\theta_1$.

For $|z|<1$, the scalar power series $L(z)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j+1}z^j/j$ converges absolutely by comparison with $\sum_{j\ge1}|z|^j$, so its disc of convergence contains the unit disk. By [F11], $$L'(z)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j+1}z^{j-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-z)^k=\frac1{1+z},$$ where the last equality is the finite geometric-sum identity followed by a limit. Since $1+z\ne0$ on the unit disk, [F12] gives $$\left(\frac{e^{L(z)}}{1+z}\right)'=\frac{e^{L(z)}L'(z)(1+z)-e^{L(z)}}{(1+z)^2}=0.$$ The open unit disk is convex, hence a connected open domain, so [F12] makes this quotient constant there. Its value at $0$ is $1$, and therefore $e^{L(z)}=1+z$. For $z=e^{it}-1$ with $|t|<\pi/3$, [F5], [F9], and [F10] show $|z|=2|\sin(t/2)|<1$. Thus [F6] gives $L(e^{it}-1)-it\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. This difference is continuous in $t$ by [F13], [F5], and [F8]. Dividing it by $2\pi i$ gives a continuous integer-valued real function. If it took distinct values at two points, restrict to the closed interval between them; [F14] would force it to take a noninteger value between them; hence it is constant and, at $t=0$, zero. Substitution of $z=\lambda_j-1$ now shows the matrix series diagonalizes to $i\theta_1,i\theta_2$, so exponentiating it gives $D$.

By [F2], the norm of the series is at most $\sum_{j\ge1}\rho^j/j$. The scalar identity from step 2.1 at $z=-\rho$ and [F4] identify this sum with $-\log(1-\rho)$. Since $1/j\le1$ and $\sum_{j\ge1}\rho^j=\rho/(1-\rho)\le2\rho$ for $0\le\rho\le1/2$, the claimed bound follows. The eigenvalues of $\log D$ are $i\theta_1,-i\theta_1$, so it is skew-Hermitian and has trace zero.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and write

$$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le1\}.$$

Then the following are equivalent.

1. $\overline B_X$ is compact in the norm metric ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. $X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest

derivations.claim: The ambient space $M_2(\mathbb C)$ is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$. For $U\in SU(2)$, norm preservation gives $\|U\|=1$ by [F2], so $SU(2)$ lies in the closed operator-norm unit ball. It is closed there because $U^*U=I$ and $\det U=1$ are continuous equations in the matrix entries and their conjugates. [F1] makes the closed unit ball compact; therefore its closed subset $SU(2)$ is compact.

Let $S$ be the values of finite words in $G$ and let $H=\overline S\subseteq SU(2)$. Since $S$ is closed under multiplication and matrix multiplication is continuous, $H$ is a closed semigroup. For each integer $n\ge1$, let $N_n$ be the least number of operator-norm balls of radius $1/n$ covering $SU(2)$; compactness gives such a finite cover. Fix $g\in G$. Two of $I,g,\ldots,g^{N_n}$ lie in one cover ball, say $g^r,g^s$ with $r<s$. By [F2], $\|g^{s-r}-I\|=\|(g^s-g^r)g^{-r}\|<2/n$. Let $d_n$ be the least $d\in\{1,\ldots,N_n\}$ with $\|g^d-I\|<2/n$. If $d_n=1$ for infinitely many $n$, then $g=I$ and $g^{-1}=g\in S$; otherwise $d_n\ge2$ eventually, and $g^{d_n-1}\in S$ satisfies $\|g^{d_n-1}-g^{-1}\|=\|(g^{d_n}-I)g^{-1}\|<2/n$, so $g^{-1}\in H$. This holds for every $g\in G$. Hence $H$ contains $G$ and its inverses, so it contains $\langle G\rangle$; closedness of $H$ and density of $\langle G\rangle$ give $H=SU(2)$. Therefore word values in $G$ are dense.

For each $U\in SU(2)$, density supplies a word value $g_U\in S$ with $\|U-g_U\|<\delta/2$. The open balls of radius $\delta/2$ centered at these word values cover $SU(2)$. Compactness gives a finite subcover with centers $g_1,\ldots,g_r$. Choose one finite word representing each $g_j$; the resulting list is a $\delta$-net, and the maximum of its finitely many word lengths is finite. The compactness argument supplies no effective search cutoff or certificate.

In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The displayed sign in $Y$ fixes all later orientation and rotation conventions.

derivations.claim: Taking conjugate transposes of the displayed matrices gives $X^*=X,Y^*=Y,Z^*=Z$, and their traces are all zero. Direct multiplication gives $X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I$ and $XY=iZ$, $YX=-iZ$, $YZ=iX$, $ZY=-iX$, $ZX=iY$, $XZ=-iY$. For example, $XY=\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{pmatrix}=iZ$ and $YX=\begin{pmatrix}-i&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix}=-iZ$; the remaining four products are respectively $\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}=iX$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}=-iX$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=iY$, and $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=-iY$.

Expand $(u\cdot\sigma)(v\cdot\sigma)$ bilinearly. The three diagonal terms are $(u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3)I$ by step 1.1. The paired off-diagonal terms are $i(u_2v_3-u_3v_2)X+i(u_3v_1-u_1v_3)Y+ i(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)Z$, exactly $i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma$. Put $A=i u\cdot\sigma$ and $B=i v\cdot\sigma$. Then $[A,B]=AB-BA=-(u\cdot\sigma)(v\cdot\sigma)+(v\cdot\sigma)(u\cdot\sigma)$; the vector-product formula and $v\times u=-u\times v$ give $[A,B]=-2i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma$.

A traceless Hermitian matrix has the form $\begin{pmatrix}a&b-ic\\b+ic&-a\end{pmatrix}$ with real $a,b,c$, which equals $bX+cY+aZ$. This proves the basis assertion. The product identity at $u=v$ gives $(u\cdot\sigma)^2=|u|^2I$; since $u\cdot\sigma$ is Hermitian, for every vector $x$ we have $\|(u\cdot\sigma)x\|^2=\langle (u\cdot\sigma)^2x,x\rangle =|u|^2\|x\|^2$. Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives $\|u\cdot\sigma\|=|u|$. Also $i u\cdot\sigma$ is traceless skew-Hermitian by the established matrix traces and adjoints.

For a matrix $M$, write $e^M=\sum_{j\ge0}M^j/j!$. Here
$SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. If
$D\in SU(2)$ and $\|D-I\|\le\rho\le1/2$, then the operator-norm
convergent series
$$\log D=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{j+1}(D-I)^j/j$$
satisfies $e^{\log D}=D$, is traceless and skew-Hermitian, and
$\|\log D\|\le-\log(1-\rho)\le2\rho$.

For the Pauli matrices $X,Y,Z$ in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]], the matrices
are Hermitian, traceless, and square to $I$. For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, writing
$u\cdot\sigma=u_1X+u_2Y+u_3Z$ gives
$$ (u\cdot\sigma)(v\cdot\sigma)=(u\cdot v)I+i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma.$$
Also, the Pauli triple is a real basis of the traceless Hermitian $2\times2$
matrices, $\|u\cdot\sigma\|=|u|$, and the commutator therefore satisfies
$$[iu\cdot\sigma,iv\cdot\sigma]=-2i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma.$$

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: Write $X=\log D=i v\cdot\sigma$ with $v\in\mathbb R^3$; the Pauli matrices form a real basis of the traceless skew-Hermitian $2\times2$ matrices, and [F2] gives $\|X\|=|v|$. If $v=0$, take $a=b=0$ and $V=W=I$. Otherwise set $u=v/|v|$, choose the smallest index $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ attaining $\min_i|u_i|$, and let $e_k$ be the corresponding coordinate vector. Then $w=u\times e_k$ has norm at least $\sqrt{2/3}>1/2$; put $e=w/|w|$. This is a deterministic choice with $e\perp u$. Set $a=\sqrt{|v|/2}\,e$ and $b=-\sqrt{|v|/2}\,(u\times e)$. Then $a\times b=-v/2$ and $|a|=|b|=\sqrt{|v|/2}\le\sqrt\eta$.

For every real $t$, $|\sin t|\le|t|$: it is immediate at $t=0$, and otherwise [F5] and the mean value theorem give $\sin t-\sin0=\cos(c)t$ for some $c$ between $0$ and $t$; [F4] implies $|\cos c|\le1$. Put $A=i a\cdot\sigma$, $B=i b\cdot\sigma$, $V=e^A$ and $W=e^B$. For $a\ne0$, $P=a\cdot\sigma/|a|$ is Hermitian, traceless and satisfies $P^2=I$ by [F2]; its eigenvalues are $1,-1$. Thus $e^A=I\cos|a|+iP\sin|a|$ by the power series and [F4], so it is unitary with determinant $1$ and $\|e^A-I\|=2|\sin(|a|/2)|\le|a|$. If $a=0$, $e^A=I$; the same argument applies to $B$. By [F2], $[A,B]=X$, and both distances are at most $\sqrt\eta$.

Expand $e^Ae^Be^{-A}e^{-B}$ as a sum of homogeneous terms in $A,B$. Its degree-one terms cancel, and direct multiplication of the degree-two terms gives $AB-BA=[A,B]$. By [F3], products have norm at most the product of their norms; the triangle inequality [F6] therefore bounds the sum of norms of all terms of total degree $n$ by $(4s)^n/n!$, where $s=\max(\|A\|,\|B\|)\le1/4$. Hence the degree-at-least-three remainder has norm at most $(4s)^3e^{4s}/6<32s^3$.

The exponential series and [F3] give $\|e^X-I-X\|\le\|X\|^2e^{\|X\|}/2\le2s^4e^{2s^2}\le s^3$, since $\|X\|=\|[A,B]\|\le2s^2$ and $s\le1/4$. By the triangle inequality [F6], $\|e^X-e^Ae^Be^{-A}e^{-B}\|\le33s^3\le40\eta^{3/2}$. By [F1], $e^X=D$; step 2.1 gives $[A,B]=X$, and step 3.1 controls the commutator expansion. These facts prove the claim.

The same holds for $B$. Thus the generated subgroup lies in $SU(2)$; its closure $H$ also lies there because the defining matrix equations for $SU(2)$ are closed. Continuity of multiplication and inversion makes $H$ a subgroup.

By [F1], $[A,B]=-2i(a\times b)\cdot\sigma$. Let $c=a\times b\ne0$ and $s_0=\max(\|A\|,\|B\|)$. For $|t|\le1$, multiplying the four exponential series $e^{tA}e^{tB}e^{-tA}e^{-tB}$ gives degree-one coefficient $A+B-A-B=0$ and degree-two coefficient $AB-BA=[A,B]$. Submultiplicativity bounds the sum of norms of all degree-$m$ terms by $(4s_0)^m/m!$. Hence the terms of degree at least three have norm at most $K|t|^3$, where $K=(4s_0)^3e^{4s_0}/6$. For fixed $r\ge0$, put $t=\sqrt{r/n}$. The commutator factor is $X_n=I+r[A,B]/n+R_n$ with $\|R_n\|\le Kr^{3/2}n^{-3/2}$. Set $Y_n=I+r[A,B]/n$. For fixed $r$, the norms of $X_n^k$ and $Y_n^k$ are bounded uniformly over $0\le k\le n$, because each one-step norm is at most $1+C_r/n$ for all sufficiently large $n$. The telescoping identity $X_n^n-Y_n^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}X_n^{n-1-k}(X_n-Y_n)Y_n^k$ bounds their difference by $O(n^{-1/2})$. The binomial expansion of $Y_n^n$ converges to the exponential series for $e^{r[A,B]}$: its $k$th term is bounded by $(r\|[A,B]\|)^k/k!$, a summable sequence. Swapping $A$ and $B$ gives $e^{-r[A,B]}$ for $r\ge0$. Every approximant belongs to the generated subgroup, so closedness gives $e^{s[A,B]}\in H$ for every real $s$.

The vectors $a,b,c$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^3$, since $c$ is nonzero and orthogonal to both $a$ and $b$. By [F1], every traceless skew-Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix $L$ is a real linear combination $xA+yB+z[A,B]$. For fixed matrices $S,T$, exponential-series expansion gives $e^{S/n}e^{T/n}=I+(S+T)/n+O(n^{-2})$ and $e^{(S+T)/n}=I+(S+T)/n+O(n^{-2})$. The one-step difference is $O(n^{-2})$; the norms of intermediate powers up to $n$ are bounded by $e^{\|S\|+\|T\|+1}$ for sufficiently large $n$. Telescoping therefore gives $(e^{S/n}e^{T/n})^n\to e^{S+T}$. The same estimate for three factors gives $(e^{xA/n}e^{yB/n}e^{z[A,B]/n})^n\to e^L$. Every factor lies in $H$ by step 1.1 and step 2.1, so closedness gives $e^L\in H$.

Every $U\in SU(2)$ is normal, so [F2] diagonalizes it. Its eigenvalues lie on the unit circle and their product is one, so they are $e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}$ for some real $\theta$. For the Pauli matrices $X,Y,Z$ in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]], the matrices
are Hermitian, traceless, and square to $I$. For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, writing
$u\cdot\sigma=u_1X+u_2Y+u_3Z$ gives
$$ (u\cdot\sigma)(v\cdot\sigma)=(u\cdot v)I+i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma.$$
Also, the Pauli triple is a real basis of the traceless Hermitian $2\times2$
matrices, $\|u\cdot\sigma\|=|u|$, and the commutator therefore satisfies
$$[iu\cdot\sigma,iv\cdot\sigma]=-2i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma.$$
For $\alpha\in K$, $\alpha\in\mathcal O_K$ if and only if its monic minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ lies in $\mathbb Z[X]$.
A **number field** is a finite extension $K/\mathbb Q$; write $n=[K:\mathbb Q]$.

If $\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$, then
$\{e^{2\pi i n\alpha}:n\in\mathbb Z\}$ is dense in the unit circle.

For a matrix $M$, write $e^M=\sum_{j\ge0}M^j/j!$. Write

Pauli triple, and put $A=i\,a\cdot\sigma$ and $B=i\,b\cdot\sigma$. If $H$ is
the operator-norm closure of the subgroup generated by
$\{e^{tA},e^{tB}:t\in\mathbb R\}$, then $H=SU(2)$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

A **finite gate alphabet** is a finite list of distinct labels, each assigned
one exact matrix in $SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. A
**Cauchy name** for a target $U\in SU(2)$ is a
deterministic procedure which, on unary input $1^b$, returns a rational
$2\times2$ complex matrix $Q_b$ whose real and imaginary entries differ from
the corresponding entries of $U$ by at most $2^{-b}$. The name has a stated
time bound $T(b)$. A precision request is a positive rational
$\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ in binary, using the effective encoding convention of
[[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]].

The Cauchy name specifies the exact target through all its approximants; an
individual $Q_b$ need not be unitary. An exact-real target handle and a
Cauchy-name input are distinct interfaces: the first permits ideal exact
comparisons, while a finite Turing implementation must use the second.

**Inputs:** A fixed inverse-closed dense gate package $G$ with the finite
base-net certificate $(\mathcal N_0,\eta_0,L_0)$ from
[[def-qc-inverse-closed-dense-su2-gate-set]], an exact-real target
$U\in SU(2)$, and a rational $0<\varepsilon\le\eta_0$. This is an ideal
exact-real procedure: fixed-dimensional exact matrix arithmetic, matrix
logarithm/exponential, and exact comparisons are unit-cost operations. It is
not, by this definition alone, a finite Turing algorithm.

Set $\eta_{j+1}=64\eta_j^{3/2}$ for $j\ge0$. Choose the least integer
$J\ge0$ with $\eta_J\le\varepsilon$. Define $\operatorname{Compile}(U,j)$
recursively:

1. If $j=0$, return the first word $A\in\mathcal N_0$ with
   $\|U-A\|\le\eta_0$.
2. If $j>0$, set $A=\operatorname{Compile}(U,j-1)$ and $D=UA^*$.
   If $D=I$, set $V=W=I$. Otherwise apply the Pauli-coordinate construction
   in [[lem-qc-su2-balanced-commutator]] to $D$ and $\eta_{j-1}$, obtaining
   $V,W\in SU(2)$ with $D$ approximated by $VWV^*W^*$.
3. Set $B=\operatorname{Compile}(V,j-1)$ and
   $C=\operatorname{Compile}(W,j-1)$. Return the word
   $BCB^*C^*A$. Store concatenations and inverses as a shared expression DAG;
   an inverse word is formed by reversing its label order and replacing each
   label by its listed inverse. Expanding the DAG writes the ordinary gate word.

Return $\operatorname{Compile}(U,J)$. The recursion depth is finite because
each call decreases the nonnegative integer $j$.

For a matrix $M$, write $e^M=\sum_{j\ge0}M^j/j!$. Here
$SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. If
$D\in SU(2)$ and $0\le\|D-I\|\le\eta\le1/16$, there are
$V,W\in SU(2)$ such that
$$\|V-I\|,\|W-I\|\le\sqrt\eta,\qquad \|D-VWV^*W^*\|\le40\eta^{3/2}.$$

Let $V,W,\widetilde V,\widetilde W\in SU(2)$ and $0\le\eta\le1/16$, with
$\|V-I\|,\|W-I\|\le\sqrt\eta$ and
$\|\widetilde V-V\|,\|\widetilde W-W\|\le\eta$. Then
$$\|VWV^*W^*-\widetilde V\widetilde W\widetilde V^*\widetilde W^*\|\le4\eta^{3/2}+2\eta^2\le5\eta^{3/2}.$$

Fix a positive matrix dimension $d$ and an integer $c\ge1$. A dyadic interval is a
closed interval with dyadic-rational endpoints; a complex matrix interval
stores one such interval for every real and imaginary entry. Suppose each
input is given by a Cauchy procedure which, on unary request $1^q$, returns a
rational approximation to each real and imaginary entry with error at most
$2^{-q}$ and uses $O((q+1)^c)$ bit operations. Suppose exact scalar and
matrix inputs have entries of modulus at most $3$. Each fixed algebraic real
constant is supplied by a rational polynomial and an open rational interval
with nonroot endpoints on which the polynomial has opposite endpoint signs
and exactly one real root.
When each scalar divisor
and each norm used for normalization has modulus at
least $2^{-B}$, the following routines return dyadic intervals of diameter at
most $2^{-p}$ containing the exact answer, using
$O((p+B+1)^{\max(c,3)})$ bit operations:

- any fixed finite composition of sums and products;
- quotient by a scalar whose modulus is at least $2^{-B}$;
- the nonnegative square root of a real in $[0,1]$;
- normalization $v/\|v\|_2$ of a real vector with $\|v\|_2\ge2^{-B}$;
- the matrix exponential $e^A$ when $\|A\|\le1$; and
- the matrix logarithm $\log(I+E)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j+1}E^j/j$
  when $\|E\|\le1/2$.

Here $d$ and the number of scalar operations in the fixed composition are
constants. The exponent $B$ is needed only for divisions and normalization;
the square-root routine also works at input zero. The constants in the
complexity bound may depend on the fixed dimension, routine, and Cauchy-time
constant.

For a matrix $M$, write $e^M=\sum_{j\ge0}M^j/j!$. Here
$SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. If
$D\in SU(2)$ and $\|D-I\|\le\rho\le1/2$, then the operator-norm
convergent series
$$\log D=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{j+1}(D-I)^j/j$$
satisfies $e^{\log D}=D$, is traceless and skew-Hermitian, and
$\|\log D\|\le-\log(1-\rho)\le2\rho$.

For the Pauli matrices $X,Y,Z$ in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]], the matrices
are Hermitian, traceless, and square to $I$. For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, writing
$u\cdot\sigma=u_1X+u_2Y+u_3Z$ gives
$$ (u\cdot\sigma)(v\cdot\sigma)=(u\cdot v)I+i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma.$$
Also, the Pauli triple is a real basis of the traceless Hermitian $2\times2$
matrices, $\|u\cdot\sigma\|=|u|$, and the commutator therefore satisfies
$$[iu\cdot\sigma,iv\cdot\sigma]=-2i(u\times v)\cdot\sigma.$$

Write $SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. An
**inverse-closed dense $SU(2)$ gate package** consists of a finite set
$G\subset SU(2)$ of exact matrices with finite labels such that $g^{-1}=g^*$
belongs to $G$ for each $g\in G$ and the subgroup $\langle G\rangle$ of finite
products is dense in $SU(2)$ in operator norm. A word is a finite ordered list
of labels; its value is the corresponding matrix product, and its length is
the number of labels.

For a compiler package, also fix a rational $0<\eta_0<1/4096$, a finite list
$\mathcal N_0$ of words, and an integer $L_0$ such that every $U\in SU(2)$ is
within operator-norm distance $\eta_0/4$ of the value of some word in
$\mathcal N_0$, and every listed word has length at most $L_0$. This is a
finite **base-net certificate**. Density proves that such a certificate
exists, but does not compute the list or its maximum word length.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

routine_steps.claim: Set $q_0=4096\eta_0<1$. The exact error recurrence is $\eta_{j+1}=64\eta_j^{3/2}$, so for $q_j=4096\eta_j$ we have $q_{j+1}=q_j^{3/2}$ and $\eta_j=2^{-12}q_0^{(3/2)^j}$. Choose fixed integers $K,A$ with $q_0^{(3/2)^K}<1/2$ and $2^Aq_0\ge1$. Let $j_N$ be the least integer with $(3/2)^{j_N}\ge N$ and set $J=K+j_N$. Then $q_J\le2^{-N}\le\varepsilon/2$, hence $\eta_J\le\varepsilon$. Write the encoded rational tolerance as $\varepsilon=p/q$ with positive integers $p,q$. Since $q<2^{s_\varepsilon}$ and $p\ge1$, we have $N\le s_\varepsilon+1$; binary search over integers $0,\ldots,s_\varepsilon+1$ using exact comparisons $2^N p\ge2q$ computes $N$ in time polynomial in $s_\varepsilon$. The integer $j_N$ is found by repeated rational multiplication by $3/2$; $J=O(\log N)$. Put $B=12+A\lceil(3/2)^J\rceil$, $L_J=L_0 5^J$, and $P=64(B+\lceil\log_2(L_J+1)\rceil+32)$. For every $j\le J$, $\eta_j\ge2^{-B}$; also $B=O(N)$, $\log_2(L_J+1)=O(\log N)$, and $P=O(N)$. **Inputs:** A fixed inverse-closed dense gate package $G$ with the finite
base-net certificate $(\mathcal N_0,\eta_0,L_0)$ from
[[def-qc-inverse-closed-dense-su2-gate-set]], an exact-real target
$U\in SU(2)$, and a rational $0<\varepsilon\le\eta_0$. This is an ideal
exact-real procedure: fixed-dimensional exact matrix arithmetic, matrix
logarithm/exponential, and exact comparisons are unit-cost operations. It is
not, by this definition alone, a finite Turing algorithm.

Set $\eta_{j+1}=64\eta_j^{3/2}$ for $j\ge0$. Choose the least integer
$J\ge0$ with $\eta_J\le\varepsilon$. Define $\operatorname{Compile}(U,j)$
recursively:

1. If $j=0$, return the first word $A\in\mathcal N_0$ with
   $\|U-A\|\le\eta_0$.
2. If $j>0$, set $A=\operatorname{Compile}(U,j-1)$ and $D=UA^*$.
   If $D=I$, set $V=W=I$. Otherwise apply the Pauli-coordinate construction
   in [[lem-qc-su2-balanced-commutator]] to $D$ and $\eta_{j-1}$, obtaining
   $V,W\in SU(2)$ with $D$ approximated by $VWV^*W^*$.
3. Set $B=\operatorname{Compile}(V,j-1)$ and
   $C=\operatorname{Compile}(W,j-1)$. Return the word
   $BCB^*C^*A$. Store concatenations and inverses as a shared expression DAG;
   an inverse word is formed by reversing its label order and replacing each
   label by its listed inverse. Expanding the DAG writes the ordinary gate word.

Return $\operatorname{Compile}(U,J)$. The recursion depth is finite because
each call decreases the nonnegative integer $j$.

For a matrix $M$, write $e^M=\sum_{j\ge0}M^j/j!$. Here
$SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. If
$D\in SU(2)$ and $0\le\|D-I\|\le\eta\le1/16$, there are
$V,W\in SU(2)$ such that
$$\|V-I\|,\|W-I\|\le\sqrt\eta,\qquad \|D-VWV^*W^*\|\le40\eta^{3/2}.$$

Let $V,W,\widetilde V,\widetilde W\in SU(2)$ and $0\le\eta\le1/16$, with
$\|V-I\|,\|W-I\|\le\sqrt\eta$ and
$\|\widetilde V-V\|,\|\widetilde W-W\|\le\eta$. Then
$$\|VWV^*W^*-\widetilde V\widetilde W\widetilde V^*\widetilde W^*\|\le4\eta^{3/2}+2\eta^2\le5\eta^{3/2}.$$

Write $SU(2):=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=I_2,\det M=1\}$. An
**inverse-closed dense $SU(2)$ gate package** consists of a finite set
$G\subset SU(2)$ of exact matrices with finite labels such that $g^{-1}=g^*$
belongs to $G$ for each $g\in G$ and the subgroup $\langle G\rangle$ of finite
products is dense in $SU(2)$ in operator norm. A word is a finite ordered list
of labels; its value is the corresponding matrix product, and its length is
the number of labels.

For a compiler package, also fix a rational $0<\eta_0<1/4096$, a finite list
$\mathcal N_0$ of words, and an integer $L_0$ such that every $U\in SU(2)$ is
within operator-norm distance $\eta_0/4$ of the value of some word in
$\mathcal N_0$, and every listed word has length at most $L_0$. This is a
finite **base-net certificate**. Density proves that such a certificate
exists, but does not compute the list or its maximum word length.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

For a fixed inverse-closed dense $G\subset SU(2)$ and a certified base net of
radius $0<\eta_0<64^{-2}$, the compiler of
[[alg-qc-solovay-kitaev-unitary-compiler]] returns, for
$0<\varepsilon\le\eta_0$, a word $W$ with
$\|U-W\|\le\varepsilon$. The level errors may be chosen as
$$\eta_j=64^{-2}(64^2\eta_0)^{(3/2)^j}.$$
The word length is at most $L_0 5^j$ at level $j$, hence
$O(\log^{\log_{3/2}5}(1/\varepsilon))=O(\log^{3.97}(1/\varepsilon))$.
With shared recursive words, the exact-real arithmetic count is
$O(\log^{\log_{3/2}3}(1/\varepsilon))=O(\log^{2.71}(1/\varepsilon))$;
printing the expanded word takes $O(\log^{3.97}(1/\varepsilon))$ time.
The latter are exact-real arithmetic bounds, not bit-complexity bounds.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and write

$$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le1\}.$$

Then the following are equivalent.

1. $\overline B_X$ is compact in the norm metric ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. $X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

derivations.claim: For each one-qubit factor $G_j\in U(2)$, determinant multiplicativity and $G_j^*G_j=I$ give $|\det G_j|^2=1$. Thus [F7] gives $\det G_j=e^{i\theta_j}$ for a real $\theta_j$. Put $\phi_j=\theta_j/2$ and $S_j=e^{-i\phi_j}G_j$. Then $\det S_j=e^{-2i\phi_j}\det G_j=1$ and $S_j$ is unitary, so $S_j\in SU(2)$ and $G_j=e^{i\phi_j}S_j$.

Put $h=\min(\eta_0,\varepsilon/m)>0$. Let $r$ be the least nonnegative integer with $2^{-r}\le h$ and put $\delta=2^{-r}$. Such an $r$ exists since $2^{-r}\to0$; since $h<1$, minimality gives $h/2<\delta\le h$. Thus $\delta$ is rational, satisfies $0<\delta\le\eta_0$ and $\delta\le\varepsilon/m$, and is a permitted input to the compiler in [F1]. Apply it to each $S_j$. It gives a gate word $W_j$ with $\|S_j-W_j\|\le\delta$. The phase factors $e^{i\phi_j}$ commute with all factors and multiply to one scalar for the entire circuit; after factoring it out, the exact and compiled products have the same CNOT slots and respectively $S_j$ and $W_j$ in each one-qubit slot.

First justify the full-register error at each local slot. Group its one-qubit support first and unused wires second, using the unitary wire permutation of [F10]. For a finite orthonormal basis $(e_\ell)$ of the unused register, every vector is uniquely $v=\sum_\ell v_\ell\otimes e_\ell$, and the product inner product gives $\|v\|^2=\sum_\ell\|v_\ell\|^2$. For a local difference $A$, it also gives $\|(A\otimes I)v\|^2=\sum_\ell\|Av_\ell\|^2\le\|A\|^2\sum_\ell\|v_\ell\|^2=\|A\|^2\|v\|^2$ by [F8]. Thus $\|A\otimes I\|\le\|A\|$. Conjugation by the wire permutation preserves norm, since a unitary preserves vector norms and maps the unit sphere onto itself. This includes the empty unused register. Apply this to each $S_j-W_j$ from step 2.1, giving full-register slot error at most $\delta$. Index the full ordered circuit product by $q=m+c$ slots, so the two products are $A_q\cdots A_1$ and $B_q\cdots B_1$. At a CNOT slot set $A_r=B_r$ to that exact gate; at a one-qubit slot use the exact $S_j$ and its compiled word $W_j$. Insert one factor at a time to obtain $A_q\cdots A_1-B_q\cdots B_1=\sum_{r=1}^q A_q\cdots A_{r+1}(A_r-B_r)B_{r-1}\cdots B_1$. Every surrounding factor is unitary: exact factors, compiled words, and CNOTs are all unitary. For a unitary $Q$, $\|Qv\|=\|v\|$ for every unit vector $v$, so [F8] gives $\|Q\|=1$. The operator-norm triangle inequality follows from [F8] by applying [F9] to each unit input and taking the maximum. Then [F2] bounds the product difference by the sum of the $q$ factor errors. The CNOT slots contribute zero, and the $m$ one-qubit slots each contribute at most $\delta$, giving $m\delta\le\varepsilon$. The scalar from step 2.1 is a single whole-circuit phase, proving the projective operator bound.

The unit circle is a closed subset of the closed unit ball in $\mathbb C$, so it is compact by [F6]. The continuous function $\lambda\mapsto\|U-\lambda C\|$ therefore attains its minimum at some $|\lambda|=1$. The phase from step 3.1 gives one value at most $\varepsilon$, so this minimum is also at most $\varepsilon$. By [F4], diagonalize $E$ in an orthonormal basis with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{2^k}$. Nonnegativity [F3] makes each $\lambda_i\ge0$, and $\|E\|\le1$ gives $\lambda_i\le1$ by applying the norm to a corresponding unit eigenvector. Define $E^{1/2}$ in this basis by diagonal entries $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$, which exist by [F5]. Its square is $E$, it is self-adjoint, and direct calculation on coordinates gives $\|E^{1/2}\|=\max_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\le1$. The factors $U,C$ are unitary, so [F8] gives $\|U\psi\|=\|C\psi\|=1$. The two vectors $E^{1/2}U\psi$ and $E^{1/2}\lambda C\psi$ have norms at most $1$, and their distance is at most $\varepsilon$ by step 3.1 and [F2]. The reverse triangle inequality from [F9] gives $|\|x\|-\|y\||\le\|x-y\|$ for these vectors; factoring the difference of their squared norms therefore bounds it by $(1+1)\varepsilon=2\varepsilon$. Since the scalar phase does not change a norm, this proves the event bound.

Each one-qubit word uses $O(\log^{\log_{3/2}5}(1/\delta))$ gates by [F1]. Since $1/\delta<2\max(1/\eta_0,m/\varepsilon)$ and $m/\varepsilon>2$, this is $O(\log^{\log_{3/2}5}(m/\varepsilon))$, with constants depending on the fixed base-net radius. Summing over $m$ factors and adding the $c$ exact CNOTs gives the stated count. The factorization and all replacements use the same wires, so no ancillas are introduced.

For a real angle $\theta$, define the one-qubit phase matrix $P_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})$. In control-first order define

$$CP(\theta):=C(P_\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,e^{i\theta})$$

in the ordered basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$. This is the exact controlled phase; no circuit cost or controlled access to an arbitrary black-box unitary is implied.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional target space, let $U$ be unitary on $H$, and let $|\lambda|=1$. In control-first order put
$$C(U)=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_\lambda=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $C(\lambda U)=(P_\lambda\otimes I_H)C(U)$. A scalar multiplying an entire output leaves every defined finite-POVM outcome law unchanged, whereas a scalar attached to a target matrix inside a control gives a phase on only the active control block; applying $P_{\overline\lambda}$ on the control restores the exact controlled matrix.

Fix $k\ge1$, $U\in U(2^k)$, and a real $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Suppose a supplied exact decomposition of
$U$ has $m\ge1$ one-qubit $U(2)$ factors and $c\ge0$ exact CNOT factors,

derivations.claim: On a basis vector $|ab\rangle$, the first CNOT maps it to $|a,b\oplus a\rangle$. The target phase contributes $e^{-i\theta(b\oplus a)/2}$; the second CNOT restores $|ab\rangle$; and the two final phase gates contribute $e^{i\theta(a+b)/2}$. The product is $e^{i\theta ab}$, which is $1$ on $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle$ and $e^{i\theta}$ on $|11\rangle$. This is exactly $CP_\theta$ from [F1].

Direct diagonal multiplication gives $P_\alpha=e^{i\alpha/2}R_z(\alpha)$, hence $R_z(\alpha)=e^{-i\alpha/2}P_\alpha$. Replacing $P_{-\theta/2}$ on the target contributes $e^{i\theta/4}$, while replacing each of the two $P_{\theta/2}$ gates contributes $e^{-i\theta/4}$. Their product is $e^{-i\theta/4}$, so the resulting $R_z$ circuit is $e^{-i\theta/4}CP_\theta$.

The circuit in step 1.1 is an exact factorization of the two-qubit $CP_\theta$ into three one-qubit phase gates and two CNOTs. Applying [F3] therefore gives a word $W$ and unit scalar $\mu$ with $\|CP_\theta-\mu W\|\le\varepsilon$. By [F2], $C(\mu W)=(\operatorname{diag}(1,\mu)\otimes I_4)C(W)$. If $\mu\ne1$, $\operatorname{diag}(1,\mu)$ is not a scalar on the control, so the phase is relative on the outer-control-one subspace. Thus the two-qubit projective bound alone does not certify the controlled three-qubit target.

With $\lambda_R=e^{-i\theta/4}$ from step 2.1, [F2] gives $C(\lambda_R CP_\theta)=(\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda_R)\otimes I_4) C(CP_\theta)$. Applying $P_{\theta/4}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\overline{\lambda_R})$ to the outer control restores the exact controlled target in the continuous phase-gate model.

The complete controlled target is the diagonal three-qubit matrix $D_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,1,1,1,1,e^{i\theta})$. For bits $a,b,c\in\{0,1\}$, put $p_{ab}=a\oplus b$, $p_{ac}=a\oplus c$, $p_{bc}=b\oplus c$, and $p_{abc}=a\oplus b\oplus c$. Checking the four possible Hamming weights $0,1,2,3$ makes the right side respectively $0,0,0,4$, so $4abc=a+b+c-p_{ab}-p_{ac}-p_{bc}+p_{abc}$. Apply $P_{\theta/4}$ to each single bit. To apply $P_{-\theta/4}$ to $p_{ab}$, use a CNOT with control $b$ and target $a$, apply $P_{-\theta/4}$ to wire $a$, and undo that CNOT; the target wire then again contains $a$. Use the corresponding pairs for $p_{ac}$ and $p_{bc}$. To apply $P_{\theta/4}$ to $p_{abc}$, use two CNOTs into wire $a$, apply $P_{\theta/4}$ there, and undo both CNOTs. On each basis state these circuits restore the original bits and contribute exactly the indicated signed parity phase. The resulting phase is $e^{i\theta abc}$, so this is an exact factorization of $D_\theta$ with seven one-qubit phase gates and ten CNOTs. Applying [F3] to this complete three-qubit factorization gives a projective operator approximation to $D_\theta$ itself; its scalar is global on the three-qubit block. For every integer $a$ and odd prime $p$,

$$\left(\frac ap\right)\equiv a^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.$$

For an odd prime $p$, exactly $(p-1)/2$ nonzero classes are quadratic residues modulo $p$, and exactly $(p-1)/2$ are quadratic nonresidues. Each nonzero quadratic residue has exactly two square roots modulo $p$, while each nonresidue has none.

For every prime $p$, the operations of addition and multiplication on
$\mathbb Z/p$ make it a field ([[def-field]]).

derivations.claim: Reduce $a$ modulo $p$. If $p=2$, return its residue; if $a=0$, return zero. Otherwise [F1] rejects exactly the nonsquares by testing $a^{(p-1)/2}=-1$. In the remaining case write $p-1=2^s q$ with $q$ odd and $s\ge1$. Repeatedly sample $z$ uniformly from $1,\ldots,p-1$ until $z^{(p-1)/2}=-1$. Uniform sampling is implemented by drawing $\lceil\log_2p\rceil$ bits and rejecting zero and integers at least $p$. Each draw is accepted with probability at least $1/4$, and each accepted $z$ is a nonsquare with probability $1/2$ by [F2]; thus this search has bounded expected trials and terminates almost surely.

Set $x=a^{(q+1)/2}$, $t=a^q$, $c=z^q$ and $M=s$, all modulo $p$. Then $x^2=at$, $c$ has exact multiplicative order $2^M$, and $t^{2^{M-1}}=1$ by the tests in step 1.1. While $t\ne1$, find the least $m\ge1$ with $t^{2^m}=1$ by successive squaring; it satisfies $m<M$. Put $b=c^{2^{M-m-1}}$ and replace $(x,t,c,M)$ by $(xb,tb^2,b^2,m)$. The identity $x^2=at$ is preserved. The old $t$ has order exactly $2^m$, so $t^{2^{m-1}}=-1$: in a field, the only roots of $X^2-1$ are $1,-1$ by factorization. Likewise $b^2$ has order $2^m$ and its $2^{m-1}$-st power is $-1$. Therefore the new $t$ has order dividing $2^{m-1}$, while the new $c$ has order $2^m$. The invariants are maintained and $M$ strictly decreases. After at most $s$ iterations, $t=1$ and $x^2=a$. Return $x$.

Put $B=1+\lceil\log_2p\rceil$. Every modular integer has $O(B)$ bits. Schoolbook multiplication and division use $O(B^2)$ bit operations; binary repeated squaring computes a power with $O(B)$-bit exponent in $O(B)$ modular multiplications. These bounds follow directly by forming at most $B$ shifted rows for multiplication and eliminating at most $B$ quotient digits for division. Step 1.1 uses an expected bounded number of such powers. Each of the at most $B$ iterations in step 2.1 uses at most $O(B)$ modular multiplications to find $m$ and compute $b$. Its total cost is $O(B^4)$. Initial reduction has cost polynomial in the original length of $a$ and $p$. Thus the algorithm has the asserted expected bit bound; only the nonsquare search is randomized, and its outcome never changes the correctness of the final answer.

Every $z\in D$ has exactly one canonical dyadic encoding specified in
[[def-qc-dyadic-cyclotomic-ring]].

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

derivations.claim: For $x=a+b\sqrt2\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ put $N_R(x)=|a^2-2b^2|$. For $z=A+B\omega$ with $A,B\in\mathbb Q(i)$ put $N_O(z)=|A^2-iB^2|^2=|z|^2|z^\bullet|^2$. These functions are multiplicative, positive on nonzero elements, and take positive integer values on nonzero elements of their respective rings: $A,B\in\mathbb Z[i]$ for $z\in O$, and $z z^\bullet=A^2-iB^2\in\mathbb Z[i]$. Integer norm one is equivalent to being a unit: the converse follows by multiplicativity, and the forward implication follows by taking the product of the other conjugates divided by the norm (with a sign in $R$). All coordinates of that inverse remain in the ring.

The real elements of $O$ are exactly $R$. Indeed, for $z=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2 i+a_3\omega^3$, its imaginary part is $a_2+(a_1+a_3)/\sqrt2$; irrationality of $\sqrt2$ makes this zero exactly when $a_2=0$ and $a_3=-a_1$. The real part is then $a_0+a_1\sqrt2$. A real unit of $O$ consequently is a unit of $R$, since its inverse is real too. Also $\lambda^{-1}=\sqrt2-1\in R$ and $\lambda^\bullet=-\lambda^{-1}$.

To divide in $R$, round the rational coefficients of a quotient to nearest integers. Its error $e=a+b\sqrt2$ has $|a|,|b|\le1/2$, so $N_R(e)=|a^2-2b^2|\le1/2<1$. To divide in $O$, express a quotient as $A+B\omega$ and round $A,B$ to Gaussian integers. For the errors $C,D$, $|C|^2,|D|^2\le1/2$, whence $N_O(C+D\omega)=|C^2-iD^2|^2\le(|C|^2+|D|^2)^2\le1$. If the last upper bound equals one, all four real coordinates of $C,D$ are $\pm1/2$. Then $C^2,D^2$ are purely imaginary of magnitude $1/2$, so $C^2$ and $-iD^2$ are perpendicular and the actual norm is $1/2$. Otherwise the displayed bound is already strict. Multiplicativity therefore gives a remainder of norm strictly below that of the divisor in both rings. This proves the Euclidean assertions, including ties in rounding.

If $u\in R$ is a unit, choose a sign and an integer power of $\lambda$ to make $v=\pm\lambda^j u$ lie in $[1,\lambda)$. Such a power exists because $\lambda>1$. Write $v=a+b\sqrt2$. Its signed field norm is $\pm1$, so $v^\bullet=\pm1/v$. For norm $+1$, $a=(v+1/v)/2\in[1,\sqrt2)$, hence $a=1$; the equation $a^2-2b^2=1$ forces $b=0$ and $v=1$. For norm $-1$, $a=(v-1/v)/2\in[0,1)$, hence $a=0$, incompatible with $-2b^2=-1$. This proves $u=\pm\lambda^m$. Its two embeddings are positive exactly when the sign is positive and $m$ is even. In this case $\lambda^{m/2}$ is the required real unit square root. Enumerating integer powers until the exact coefficients agree recovers $m$ in finite time. Signs and comparisons of $a+b\sqrt2$ are decided by signs of the rational coefficients and, when necessary, comparing $a^2$ and $2b^2$.

Repeated division terminates because nonzero remainder norms strictly decrease through positive integers. Back substitution expresses the gcd as a linear combination. If an irreducible $p$ does not divide $a$, the gcd of $p,a$ is a unit, so multiplying a Bezout identity by $b$ shows that $p\mid ab$ implies $p\mid b$. Thus irreducibles are prime. A nonunit has a factorization into irreducibles by induction on its norm: a proper factorization has two factors of norm at least two, each of smaller norm. The prime-divisor property and cancellation give uniqueness up to ordering and units. Divisibility is decidable by computing the quotient in the field and checking its integral coordinates; two elements are associates exactly when their quotient has integral coordinates and norm one.

Here is an explicit finite factor search, which makes the existence proof algorithmic without a primality oracle for $O$. For a nonunit $\alpha\in O$ put $M=N_O(\alpha)\ge2$ and enumerate all power-basis integer tuples with coefficients between $-(M+3)$ and $M+3$. Test whether such an element $d$ divides $\alpha$ and $1<N_O(d)<M$; any successful $d$ splits $\alpha$ into smaller-norm factors. If $\alpha$ is reducible, choose a nonunit proper divisor and multiply it by a power of the unit $\lambda$ so $1\le|d|<\lambda$. Its norm is unchanged and less than $M$, and $|d^\bullet|=\sqrt{N_O(d)}/|d|\le\sqrt M$. Recovering power-basis coefficients from the two complex embeddings gives $|a_0|,|a_2|\le(|d|+|d^\bullet|)/2$ and $|a_1|,|a_3|\le(|d|+|d^\bullet|)/\sqrt2$. They are all below $\lambda+\sqrt M<M+3$, so the list contains this normalized proper divisor. Failure of the finite search therefore certifies irreducibility. Recursing on successful factors terminates by strict norm descent, and the residual norm-one elements supply the unit.

derivations.claim: First suppose $I=[x_0,x_1]$, $J=[y_0,y_1]$ have positive lengths $\delta,\Delta$. Multiplication by the unit $\lambda^r$ on the first embedding and by $(-\lambda^{-1})^r$ on the second is a bijection of the grid solutions. Choose the integer $r$ so the new first length lies in $[\lambda^{-1},1)$, reversing the second interval's endpoints when necessary. This is done by taking an integer part of a logarithm and checking the endpoint inequalities; $P$ is unchanged. Work henceforth with the rescaled intervals. Every solution $a+b\sqrt2$ satisfies $(x_0-y_1)/(2\sqrt2)\le b\le(x_1-y_0)/(2\sqrt2)$. Enumerate the integers in this interval. For each $b$, the interval $[x_0-b\sqrt2,x_1-b\sqrt2]$ has length less than one, so its least integer is the only possible $a$; retain it only if both grid inequalities hold. No solution is duplicated or missed. The number of $b$ proposals is at most $1+(\delta+\Delta)/(2\sqrt2)=O(1+P)$ because $\lambda^{-1}\le\delta<1$ and $\Delta=P/\delta$. The integer endpoints and the affine formula for $b$ give random access to proposals.

Any pair of intervals whose length product is at least $\lambda^3$ contains a solution. Indeed, rescale as above, this time putting the first length in $[\lambda,\lambda^2)$; the second length is then greater than or equal to $\lambda$. For the two interval centers $x,y$, round $(x+y)/2$ and $(x-y)/(2\sqrt2)$ to their nearest integers $a,b$. Both errors $|a+b\sqrt2-x|$ and $|a-b\sqrt2-y|$ are at most $(1+\sqrt2)/2=\lambda/2$, so the rounded point satisfies both constraints. If $P\ge4\lambda^3$, put $q=\lfloor P/(2\lambda^3)\rfloor$. Divide $I$ into $q$ equal cells and use the concentric closed half of each cell. Each resulting interval paired with $J$ has length product $P/(2q)\ge\lambda^3$. Their disjointness gives $q$ distinct solutions, and $q\ge P/(4\lambda^3)$. Consequently the proposal bound in step 1.1 is $O(N+1)$, including the case $P<4\lambda^3$.

If $I$ is a singleton and $J$ has length $\Delta$, replace $I$ temporarily by the concentric interval of length $1/(\Delta+1)$ and test the original equality when filtering proposals. The product is at most one, so step 1.1 gives only constantly many proposals and contains all original solutions. Treat a singleton $J$ symmetrically; if both are singletons, enlarge both to length $1/2$. Empty intervals need no work. For all cases, restore the inverse unit scaling on retained points. Thus the asserted finite list and counting estimates hold without an unbounded search for a witness or a free floor oracle.

The absolute value at both endpoints is less than $5/7$: use $1-1/\lambda<3/5$, $\sqrt2<10/7$, and $\lambda^{1/5}<6/5$. The remaining term is below $(4/15)(6/5)^2=48/125$, so $S'/S<25/49+48/125<9/10$.

Put $R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$\lambda=1+\sqrt2$. Both rings are norm-Euclidean domains and hence unique
factorization domains with effective gcd and associate tests. There is a
terminating finite-search algorithm factoring every nonzero element of $O$
into primes and a unit. The units of $R$ are exactly $\pm\lambda^j$
($j\in\mathbb Z$); a unit is positive at both real embeddings if and only
if it is a square of a unit of $R$. These assertions include effective square
root recovery. No polynomial runtime bound is asserted for finite-search
factorization.

derivations.claim: For any $t\in D$, both $t^\dagger t=|t|^2$ and $(t^\dagger t)^\bullet=|t^\bullet|^2$ are nonnegative. If either real embedding of $\xi$ is negative, reject. The signs are decidable by rational arithmetic and squaring the rational coefficients of $a+b\sqrt2$ after checking their signs. If either embedding is zero, injectivity of that embedding implies $\xi=0$, and the output $t=0$ suffices. Thus the remaining case has both embeddings strictly positive. Choose $r$ by clearing the powers of two in the two coefficients of $\xi$; multiplication by the positive rational square $4^r$ preserves their signs.

Put $\delta=1+\omega$ and $\lambda=1+\sqrt2$. Direct multiplication gives $N_O(\delta)=2$, $\delta^\dagger=\omega^{-1}\delta$, and $\delta^4=2i\lambda^2$. Norm two makes $\delta$ irreducible, hence prime by [F1]. As $i$ and $\lambda$ are units, the last identity shows that $2$ has just the prime associate class of $\delta$, with multiplicity four. Every element $w\in D$ has a unique-factorization valuation $v_\pi(w)\in\mathbb Z$ at each prime associate class of $O$, obtained from its integral numerator minus the valuations of its power-of-two denominator; only $v_\delta(w)$ can be negative. Conjugation acts on these valuations by permuting the prime classes, since it is a ring automorphism. In particular, for a fixed class, $v_\pi(w^\dagger w)=2v_\pi(w)$.

If $w^\dagger w=\eta\in O$ for $w\in D$, then $2v_\delta(w)=v_\delta(\eta)\ge0$, so all valuations of $w$ are nonnegative and $w\in O$. To see the last implication without any assumption on units of $D$, write $w=a/2^m$ with $a\in O$; its only possible denominator class is $\delta$, and the valuation inequality says $\delta^{4m}\mid a$, hence $2^m\mid a$. Consequently a solution to $t^\dagger t=\xi$ gives an integral solution $w=2^r t$ to $w^\dagger w=\eta$. Every conjugation-fixed prime exponent of $\eta$ must therefore be even. Conversely an integral solution for $\eta$ gives a solution for $\xi$ by division by $2^r$. This proves both necessity of the parity test and completeness of the denominator-clearing reduction.

Factor nonzero $\eta$ by the finite algorithm of [F1]. Determine conjugation orbits by conjugating each factor and testing associates; $\eta^\dagger=\eta$ and uniqueness of prime factorization imply that both classes in every two-element orbit occur with the same exponent. This is also an effective prime splitting test: each factor is assigned either to a fixed class or to a pair of distinct conjugate classes; no unproved classification by rational primes modulo eight is required. If a fixed exponent is odd, reject as justified in step 2.1. Otherwise, for each fixed class of exponent $2h$ choose its displayed prime to power $h$, and for each pair of exponent $m$ choose one displayed prime to power $m$. Let $s$ be the product of these choices, with empty product one. Then $s^\dagger s$ and $\eta$ have exactly the same prime-class exponents.

Their quotient $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$ is a unit of $O$ by unique factorization, and is real. Its inverse is real too, so it is a unit of $R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ by [F1]. Both embeddings of $s^\dagger s$ are strictly positive, as are those of $\eta$, so both embeddings of $e$ are positive. The unit-square construction of [F1] therefore returns $v\in R$ with $v^2=e$. Because $v^\dagger=v$, $(vs)^\dagger(vs)=e s^\dagger s=\eta$, and division by $2^r$ gives the claimed $t$. All loops terminate: denominator clearing is finite, factorization terminates, associate tests are exact, the factor list is finite, and square-root recovery terminates for a positive real unit. Together with the rejection cases and necessity this proves the entire decision and construction claim.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Let $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$ and
$D_+=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]\subseteq\mathbb R$. For every $z\in D$, its
complex-conjugate norm satisfies $z^\dagger z\in D_+$. More precisely, if
$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r$ is its canonical encoding,
then
$$z^\dagger z=\frac{P+\sqrt2Q}{2^{2r}},\quad P=\sum_{j=0}^3a_j^2,\quad Q=a_0(a_1-a_3)+a_2(a_1+a_3).$$

derivations.claim: The two inequalities $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$, together with their complex conjugates, give $|\sigma_j(u)|\le1$ for all four embeddings $j=1,3,5,7$; these are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite by [F2]. If $k=-m<0$, the definition of $k$ gives $x=(\sqrt2)^k u=(\sqrt2)^{-m}u\in O$, so $u=(\sqrt2)^m x$. Thus $|\sigma_j(x)|\le2^{-m/2}$ for every $j$. By [F3], $x\bar x=P+\sqrt2Q$ with $P,Q\in\mathbb Z$. Since $\bullet$ negates $\sqrt2$ and commutes with conjugation, the product of all four embeddings is $\prod_{j=1,3,5,7}\sigma_j(x)=(x\bar x)(x^\bullet\overline{x^\bullet})=(P+\sqrt2Q)(P-\sqrt2Q)=P^2-2Q^2$. It is a nonzero integer because $x\ne0$ and each embedding is injective. Its modulus is at most $2^{-2m}<1$, a contradiction. This proves $k\ge0$.

For $k\ge0$, set $a=(\sqrt2)^ku\in O$. Then $|\sigma_j(a)|\le2^{k/2}$ for every $j$. Fourier inversion in the power basis gives $a_r=\frac14\sum_{j\in\{1,3,5,7\}}\sigma_j(a)\omega^{-jr}$: expanding the sum, the coefficient of $a_s$ is $\frac14\sum_{j\text{ odd}}\omega^{j(s-r)}$, which equals $1$ for $s=r$ and $0$ for distinct $r,s\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Therefore $|a_r|\le\frac14\sum_j|\sigma_j(a)|\le2^{k/2}$. Since $a_r$ is an integer, it lies in the stated finite interval.

For $x=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3\in O$, multiplication by
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ has coefficient vector
$(b-d,a+c,b+d,c-a)$. Consequently $\sqrt2$ divides $x$ in $O$ exactly when
$a\equiv c$ and $b\equiv d\pmod2$. Also,

$$x\bar x=P+\sqrt2Q,\qquad P=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2,\quad Q=a(b-d)+c(b+d),$$

and $2$ divides $x\bar x$ in $O$ exactly when $\sqrt2$ divides $x$.

derivations.claim: Put $s=\operatorname{sde}(z)$ and $x=(\sqrt2)^s z\in O$. Minimality of $s$ implies $\sqrt2\nmid x$, since otherwise $x=\sqrt2 y$ with $y\in O$ would make $(\sqrt2)^{s-1}z=y\in O$.

Write $x=a+b\omega+c\omega^2+d\omega^3$ and set $A=a+c$, $B=b+d$. By [F1], $\sqrt2\nmid x$ means $(A,B)$ is not $(0,0)$ modulo $2$. The two congruences $P\equiv A+B$ and $Q\equiv AB$ show that $P,Q$ are not both even: among the three nonzero pairs $(A,B)\in\{0,1\}^2$, the pair $(A+B,AB)$ is never $(0,0)$. For $P+\sqrt2Q$, divisibility by $(\sqrt2)^2=2$ is equivalent to both coefficients $P,Q$ being even. Hence $x\bar x$ is divisible by $\sqrt2$ at most once.

Let $m\in\{0,1\}$ be the number of factors $\sqrt2$ dividing $x\bar x$; write $x\bar x=(\sqrt2)^m y$ with $y\in O$ and $\sqrt2\nmid y$. Since $|z|^2=(x\bar x)/(\sqrt2)^{2s}$, its least denominator exponent is $2s-m$: multiplying by that power gives $y$, while any smaller exponent leaves a denominator because $\sqrt2\nmid y$. Thus $\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)=2s-m$.
The hypothesis gives $2s-m\le3$ and $m\le1$, so $2s\le4$ and $s\le2$.

With ordinary binary integers, schoolbook arithmetic and independent unbiased random bits, its expected bit cost is polynomial in the input length; after reducing $a$ modulo $p$, it is $O((1+\log p)^4)$. [[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

For nonzero $z\in D$, define
$\operatorname{sde}(z)=\min\{k\in\mathbb Z:(\sqrt2)^kz\in O\}$; exponents may
be negative. Set $\operatorname{sde}(0)=-\infty$. For a matrix $U$, the
denominator statistic used in the synthesis statements below is
$\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)$, the exponent of the squared modulus of its
upper-left entry. The base regime in this convention is exponent at most $3$.

Let $\bullet$ be the automorphism of $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$ defined in
[[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], so $\omega^\bullet=-\omega=\omega^5$,
and let $u\in D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|u|\le1$ and $|u^\bullet|\le1$. Then $k=\operatorname{sde}(u)\ge0$. If
$a=(\sqrt2)^ku=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$, then

$$|a_j|\le2^{k/2}\quad(0\le j\le3).$$

Thus for each fixed $k$ only finitely many coefficient vectors can occur; the
integer search may be restricted to
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

derivations.claim: Write $q=1+\sqrt2$ and $C=(1+\sqrt2)/2$. For any integer $m$, the unit (using $q^{-1}=\sqrt2-1$ for negative $m$) $\lambda=q^m\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ satisfies $|\lambda^\bullet|=\lambda^{-1}$. For arbitrary real $x,y$, solve the two real linear equations $\lambda(a+\sqrt2 b)=x$ and $\lambda^\bullet(a-\sqrt2 b)=y$ for real $a,b$ and round each to an integer by [F3]. The resulting $\alpha\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ satisfies $|\alpha-x|\le C\lambda$ and $|\alpha^\bullet-y|\le C\lambda^{-1}$. Applying this independently to real and imaginary coordinates gives, for arbitrary complex centers $z,w$, a $v\in O$ such that $|v-z|\le\sqrt2 C\lambda$ and $|v^\bullet-w|\le\sqrt2 C\lambda^{-1}$.

Set $s=2^{k/2}$. Choose the integer $m$ so that $4\sqrt2 C/(sR)\le\lambda<4q\sqrt2 C/(sR)$. If $s^2rR\ge128$, then $32C^2q=56+40\sqrt2<128$ implies $\sqrt2 C\lambda<sr/4$, while $\sqrt2 C\lambda^{-1}\le sR/4$. Apply step 1.1 to centers of disks in $sA$ and $(\sqrt2)^{k\bullet}B$; the latter disk has radius $sR$, since $|(\sqrt2)^{k\bullet}|=s$. Both $v$ and $v+\lambda$ lie in the first disk: their errors are bounded by $sr/4$ and $sr/4+\lambda<sr/4+sr/(4\sqrt2 C)<sr$. Their bullet images likewise lie in the second disk, since the corresponding errors are at most $sR/4$ and $sR/4+sR/(4\sqrt2 C)<sR$. Dividing by $(\sqrt2)^k$ gives two distinct simultaneous grid points.

Put $\delta=\varepsilon^2/2$. The disk centered at $(1-\delta/2)e^{-i\theta/2}$ with radius $r=\delta/2=\varepsilon^2/4$ lies in the unit disk and in the half plane $\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\delta$ by the triangle inequality. Take this as the disk in $A$ and the full unit disk as $B$. Since $2^Kr\ge128$, step 2.1 gives two candidates of exponent at most $K$. Every candidate is nonzero because its displayed real part is positive; [F2] therefore gives nonnegative exponents and finitely many candidates through each fixed exponent. In particular $k_2\le K$.

If $u\ne v$ are grid points of exponent at most $k_2$, then for every integer $\ell\ge0$ the $2^\ell+1$ points $w_h=(h/2^\ell)u+(1-h/2^\ell)v$, $0\le h\le2^\ell$, are distinct. They have exponent at most $k_2+2\ell$, and both their original and bullet images lie in the required convex regions, because rational coefficients are fixed by $\bullet$. Thus the grid is infinite. Together with finite layers this proves the existence of its stated enumeration, and taking $\ell=\lceil\log_2 j\rceil$ gives the exponent bound.

derivations.claim: Put $\delta=1+\omega$ and $q=1+\sqrt2$. Direct multiplication gives $\delta^2=q\sqrt2\omega$, $\delta^4=2q^2i$, and $\delta^{-1}=(1-\omega+\omega^2-\omega^3)/2$. Since $q^{-1}=\sqrt2-1\in O$, these identities give $D=O[\delta^{-1}]$. Choose the least integer $h\ge0$ such that $u=x/\delta^h$ with $x=a\omega^3+b\omega^2+c\omega+d\in O$. Multiplying $x$ by the displayed inverse of $\delta$ shows that $x/\delta\in O$ exactly when $a+b+c+d$ is even: each numerator coefficient is a signed sum of the four coefficients, and all four sums have the same parity. Thus if $h>0$, this sum is odd.

If $h=0$, the two disk conditions give $|x|^2+|x^\bullet|^2=2(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)\le2$. Consequently $x=0$ or $x=\pm\omega^j$ for $0\le j\le3$. If $h=1$, the same identity and $|\delta|^2+|\delta^\bullet|^2=4$ give $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2\le2$; its parity is odd by minimality, so it equals $1$. Then $x$ is again a root of unity, contradicting $|u^\bullet|^2=1/(2-\sqrt2)>1$. Thus the cases $h\le1$ give only $u=0$ (where $n=1$) and the eight roots of unity (where $n=0$).

For $h\ge2$, multiplication gives $x^\dagger x=A+B\sqrt2$, where $A=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ and $B=cd+bc+ab-da$. The odd sum of coefficients makes $A$ odd; also $B\equiv(a+c)(b+d)\equiv0\pmod2$ since the two factors have opposite parity. Write $(\delta^\dagger\delta)^h=(2+\sqrt2)^h=C+D\sqrt2$. Both $C,D$ are even, since $(2+\sqrt2)^2=6+4\sqrt2$. It follows that $\xi=(X+Y\sqrt2)/(2+\sqrt2)^h$, with $X=C-A$ odd and $Y=D-B$ even. Taking real conjugates gives $\xi^\bullet\xi=(X^2-2Y^2)/2^h$. Its numerator is $1\pmod8$, hence odd, so this denominator is already minimal. This proves the residue assertion; nonnegativity follows from $0\le\xi,\xi^\bullet\le1$.

For nonzero $u$, write $u=v/(\sqrt2)^k$, $v\in O$. Then $\xi=(2^k-v^\dagger v)/2^k$, and $2^k-v^\dagger v\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ by the same multiplication as in step 3.1. Therefore $2^{2k}\xi^\bullet\xi$ is an integer, whence $\ell\le2k$. The inequality $0\le\xi^\bullet\xi\le1$ now yields $n\le2^\ell\le4^k$.

citations.quote: Put $\lambda=1+\sqrt2$. For bounded closed real intervals $I,J$, let $N$ count $\alpha\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ with $\alpha\in I$, $\alpha^\bullet\in J$, and put $P=|I||J|$. There is an explicit finite proposal list containing every solution once, with constant work per proposal, of length $O(N+1)$. If both lengths are positive its length is $O(P+1)$, and $N\ge P/(4\lambda^3)$ when $P\ge4\lambda^3$. The list has constant-size random-access data. Empty intervals give empty lists; singleton intervals are also allowed. Floor operations are specified as integer-part operations, and their comparison cost is charged separately, rather than assumed constant.

Let $E,F$ be ellipses in $\mathbb R^2$, specified by their centers and positive definite symmetric matrices. Normalize their matrices separately to determinant one, obtaining $D_0,\Delta_0$. Suppose the eigenvalues of both normalized matrices lie in $[H^{-1},H]$, $H\ge2$. There is a constructive real linear map $G$ such that $G\mathbb Z[\omega]=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, $\det G=\pm1$, $(Gu)^\bullet=G^\bullet u^\bullet$, and both $G(E)$ and $G^\bullet(F)$ have area at least $1/6$ of their axis-aligned bounding-box area. It uses $O(\log H)$ matrix/arithmetic/logarithm/exponentiation operations and $O(\log H)$ integer-part operations. All real quantities to which integer parts are applied have magnitude $H^{O(1)}$, so implementing those parts by comparisons and binary search costs $O((\log H)^2)$ operations overall. The entries of $G,G^\bullet$ have magnitude $H^{O(1)}$.
