derivations.claim: The ring $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$ has exactly four residue classes modulo $\sqrt2 O$, represented by $0,1,\omega,1+\omega$. Indeed $\sqrt2\omega=1+i$ and $\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ imply $i\equiv1$, $\omega^3\equiv\omega$, and $2\equiv0$. Conversely the coefficient map $a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3\mapsto(a_0+a_2,a_1+a_3)\bmod2$ annihilates every multiple of $\sqrt2$: multiplying by $\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ gives even sums in both coordinates. Thus those four residues are distinct and exhaustive. Consequently for $k\ge1$ the three chosen affine subproblems describe precisely the elements of least exponent $k$. For $k=0$, the algorithm scans all $81$ coefficient tuples in $\{-1,0,1\}^4$; [F3] bounds every nonzero grid candidate in this layer by that box, and zero fails the cap because $1-\varepsilon^2/2>0$. The two further cosets $\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]+i\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ and its translate by $\omega$ partition $O$: expand a power-basis element's real and imaginary parts and separate the parity of $a_1+a_3$. Thus all affine subproblems are disjoint. The lattice bijection [F2] and the exact filters preserve every solution, while the emitted set suppresses revisits. The exhaustive background scan makes every finite layer terminate for every sequence of random bits.

The cap is sandwiched between $E$ and its concentric $1/8$-dilate. In coordinates $u=xw+y iw$, cap points have $1-h\le x\le1$ and $y^2\le2h$, so $(x-(1-h/2))^2/h^2+y^2/(4h)\le1/4+1/2<1$. Conversely the $1/8$-ellipse lies in $|x-(1-h/2)|\le h/8$, $|y|\le\sqrt h/4$, hence $x\ge1-h$ and $x^2+y^2\le(1-3h/8)^2+h/16<1$ for $0<h<1/8$. The normalized outer ellipse eigenvalues are $2/\sqrt h$ and $\sqrt h/2$, within $[H^{-1},H]$ for $H=4/\varepsilon$; the disk matrix is the identity. Therefore [F2] applies with $\log H=O(L)$. For a final normalized ellipse matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $b^2\le15$, its centered bounding box has half-widths $\sqrt d,\sqrt a$. At its box scaled by $1/8$, the quadratic form is at most $2(ad+|b|\sqrt{ad})/64\le1$, since $ad=1+b^2\le16$. Each transformed cap therefore contains its outer ellipse's bounding box scaled concentrically by $1/64$, and the same weaker bound holds for the transformed disk. Affine shifts, negative scalar dilations, and coset translations preserve these inclusions.

At $k=0$ the direct coefficient scan has at most $81$ proposals, hence $M=O(N+1)$ for the number $N$ of layer solutions. For $k\ge1$, consider one of the at most six subproblems. If $P_x,P_y\ge T$, the two inner axis rectangles from step 1.2 supply independent coordinate grid problems with length products $P_x/64^2$ and $P_y/64^2$. Both exceed $4\lambda^3$, so [F1] gives at least $cP_x$ and $cP_y$ solutions, with a fixed $c>0$. Their Cartesian product lies inside both true constraints, giving $N_{\rm sub}\ge c^2P_xP_y$. The two outer one-dimensional proposal lengths are $O(P_x+1)$ and $O(P_y+1)$, so their product is $O(N_{\rm sub})$. If one coordinate product is below $T$, its entire proposal list and filtered coordinate list have bounded length by [F1]. Each remaining exact slice gives $O(N_x+1)$ proposals by the same result, including singleton slices. Summing over the constantly many coordinate solutions gives $O(N_{\rm sub}+1)$ proposals. Combining the at most six disjoint subproblems proves $M=O(N+1)$. In particular an empty layer has only constantly many proposals; no exponentially large lower-denominator list is generated.

The bound [F2] on $G$ and the affine scalings $2^{k/2}$ bounds all outer centers and widths above by $\exp(O(k+L))$. A nonzero outer width is bounded below by $\exp(-O(k+L))$, by the ellipse eigenvalue bounds and $\det G=\pm1$. Thus the integer parts in outer one-dimensional preprocessing cost $O(k+L)$ comparisons each. There are only constantly many exact slice intervals in the small-coordinate branch. A positive slice can have arbitrarily small width, so the algorithm pads it before the [F1] normalization: replace a slice width $\delta$ smaller than $1/(\Delta+1)$ by that value, keeping its center and filtering the original slice. Its product is at most one and it creates constantly many proposals. Otherwise $\delta\ge1/(\Delta+1)$, so both positive widths used for normalization are at least $\exp(-O(k+L))$, since $\Delta$ is bounded by the outer width. The same padding handles singleton slices, and an empty slice is skipped. In either branch the [F1] unit-rescaling exponents are $O(k+L)$, all floor operands have magnitude $\exp(O(k+L))$, and the earlier $O(N_x+1)$ bound is retained. Root and line-intersection calculations use boundedly many source arithmetic operations; sign decisions are charged exact comparisons. Finally $M=O(N+1)$ and [F3] give $\log(M+1)=O(k+1)$, so each random proposal attempt uses $O(k+1)$ random bits and is accepted with probability at least $1/2$. A balanced comparison tree on exact coefficient tuples handles the emitted set in $O(\log(N+2))=O(k+1)$ comparisons per visit. Thus each proposal visit and all layer preprocessing cost $\operatorname{poly}(k+L)$ in expectation, with polynomial moments.

Every actual solution occupies exactly one proposal index. For $N\ge1$, after $s<N$ distinct solutions have been drawn, an independent random attempt produces a new solution with probability at least $(N-s)/(2M)$. Ignoring the background scan can only delay obtaining $j$ solutions. The expected number of random draws to obtain them is at most $\sum_{s<j}2M/(N-s)\le2C(N+1)\sum_{s<j}1/(N-s)\le4Cj\sum_{t=1}^j1/t$, since $N/(N-s)\le j/(j-s)$ for $N\ge j$. This is $O(j(1+\log j))$. Moreover each waiting time is dominated by a geometric variable with success probability $1/(4C(s+1))$, whose $r$th moment is $O_r((s+1)^r)$: sum its geometric tail, or bound the sum by the integral of $r x^{r-1}\exp(-x/(4C(s+1)))$. The inequality $(\sum_{s<j}x_s)^r\le j^{r-1}\sum_{s<j}x_s^r$ gives the stated $O_r(j^{2r})$ draw-moment bound. Each random draw adds only one background visit. Independently, after at most $M$ such pairs the deterministic scan ends the layer, bounding complete-layer work by $O((N+1)\operatorname{poly}(k+L))$. Combining these estimates with step 3.1 proves all complexity claims. They control prefixes as well as complete output sizes, so they do not hide a whole-layer precomputation before the first candidate.

The sequential background guarantees finite completion for every bit sequence, and M=O(N+1) controls empty layers. No bit-time or worst-case-delay claim for arbitrary reals. Let $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ and let $u_1,u_2,\ldots$ be the distinct points in
$\mathcal G=\{u\in D:|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1,\ \operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2\}$,
ordered by nondecreasing least denominator exponent $k_j$.
Put $K=\lceil\log_2(512/\varepsilon^2)\rceil$. Then this sequence is infinite,
$k_2\le K$, and
$$k_j\le k_2+2\lceil\log_2 j\rceil\qquad(j\ge1).$$
More generally, if two bounded convex plane regions $A,B$ contain disks of
radii $r,R>0$, the simultaneous grid
$\{u\in(\sqrt2)^{-k}O:u\in A,\ u^\bullet\in B\}$ has at least two points
whenever $2^k rR\ge128$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose constants $a\ge1$ and $b>0$, with $a=O(k_2+1)$, so that $p_j\ge1/(a+b\ln j)$ for all $j\ge1$. The assumed joint-failure bound and $1-x\le e^{-x}$ imply $\Pr(J>j)\le\prod_{h=1}^j(1-p_h)\le\exp(-j/(a+b\ln j))$. This upper bound tends to zero, which proves almost sure finiteness.

For $j\ge a$, put $x=j/a\ge1$. Since $\ln a\le a$ and $\ln x\le2\sqrt x$, one has $a+b\ln j\le(1+3b)a\sqrt x$. Hence $\Pr(J>j)\le\exp(-\sqrt{j/a}/(1+3b))$ for $j\ge a$. For an integer-valued positive random variable, summing the identity $J^r=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}((j+1)^r-j^r)$ and using nonnegative sums gives $\mathbb E[J^r]=\sum_{j\ge0}((j+1)^r-j^r)\Pr(J>j)$. The part $j<a$ is $O(a^r)$. The remaining part is bounded by a constant times $\sum_{j\ge a}(j+1)^{r-1}e^{-\sqrt{j/a}/(1+3b)}=O(a^r)$: comparison with the integral and substitution $y=\sqrt{t/a}$ reduce it to $a^r\int_1^\infty y^{2r-1}e^{-y/(1+3b)}\,dy$, which is finite by repeated integration by parts. This proves all the moment bounds.

The elementary tangent bound $\ln x\le\ln\mu+(x-\mu)/\mu$ for $x,\mu>0$, with $\mu=\mathbb E[J]$, gives $\mathbb E[\log_2J]\le\log_2\mathbb E[J]=O(1+\log(k_2+1))$. Finally $\log J\le J$, and expansion of $J(1+k_2+J)^d$ reduces its expectation to the finitely many moments in step 2.1; these are polynomial in $k_2+1$. The stated bounds in $\varepsilon$ follow from [F1].

For nonzero $z\in D$, define
$\operatorname{sde}(z)=\min\{k\in\mathbb Z:(\sqrt2)^kz\in O\}$; exponents may
be negative. Set $\operatorname{sde}(0)=-\infty$. For a matrix $U$, the
denominator statistic used in the synthesis statements below is
$\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)$, the exponent of the squared modulus of its
upper-left entry. The base regime in this convention is exponent at most $3$.

derivations.claim: Replace $Y$ by $iXZ$, and move all $X$ factors to the right using $XT^r=\omega^rT^{-r}X$ and $XH=HZ$. Combine adjacent diagonal powers. For an even interior exponent, use $H^2=I$, $HT^4H=X$, $HT^2H=\omega T^{-2}HT^{-2}$, or $HT^6H=\omega^{-1}T^2HT^2$. Each replacement strictly decreases the H count and introduces only free diagonal Clifford or Pauli factors. Repeat until all interior exponents are odd. Combining powers never increases the number of odd powers, since the parity of a sum is at most the sum of the parities. Thus both counts never increase. Exact scalar exponents are updated modulo $8$. A stack of diagonal blocks and H symbols implements this reduction in linear time in the input word length: each interior even-block replacement removes at least one H symbol and requires only bounded local stack updates.

For a unit column $(u,v)^T$, set $x=2\operatorname{Re}(\bar uv)$, $y=2\operatorname{Im}(\bar uv)$, $z=|u|^2-|v|^2$. Direct matrix multiplication gives the H action $(x,y,z)\mapsto(z,-y,x)$ and the $T^r$ action $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x\cos(r\pi/4)-y\sin(r\pi/4),x\sin(r\pi/4)+y\cos(r\pi/4),z)$. For odd $r$, its sine and cosine are independently signed $1/\sqrt2$. The rightmost $T^cX^e$ starts the column at $(0,0,(-1)^e)$, and the leftmost $T^a$ does not change the final $z$.

Ignore these endpoint factors temporarily. After one H the triple is $(\pm1,0,0)$. After two H gates with an odd intervening power it is $(0,\pm1/\sqrt2,\pm1/\sqrt2)$. After three it has $x=\pm1/\sqrt2$, $y=\pm1/2$, $z=\pm1/2$, so the respective least exponents are $1,2,2$. If two nonzero elements have unequal least exponents, their sum and difference have exponent equal to the larger one: scale by that larger power; one summand is primitive modulo $\sqrt2O$ and the other is divisible by $\sqrt2$, so their sum cannot be divisible. Inductively, after $h\ge3$ H gates the exponents of $(x,y,z)$ are $(h-2,h-1,h-1)$. Indeed an odd rotation makes both new transverse coordinates have exponent $h$, and H makes the new exponents $(h-1,h,h)$. The same transition from the displayed two-H triple establishes the induction base.

Since $|u|^2=(1+z)/2$, the positive exponent $h-1$ of $z$ for $h\ge2$ gives exponent $h+1$ for $|u|^2$ by the same primitive-numerator argument. For one H, $z=0$ and $|u|^2=1/2$ has exponent $2$; for zero H the column is a basis vector. Thus the squared-entry exponent distinguishes every possible reduced H count, including $0,1$. Any competing word reduces by step 1.1 without increasing H count, and its squared-entry exponent is unchanged by scalar phase. Its reduced H count therefore equals that of the given reduced word. This proves H minimality.

derivations.claim: By [F7], determinant is a homomorphism on $G$, and [F2] places its image in the finite group $\mu_8$. Therefore its kernel $G_1=\{W\in G:\det W=1\}$ has finite index in $G$. Let $\pi:U(2)\to PU(2)$ be the quotient map. Then $\pi(G_1)$ has finite index in $\pi(G)$, and [F1] makes $\pi(G)$ dense. Its closure $\overline{\pi(G_1)}$ is consequently a closed finite-index subgroup of $PU(2)$: the dense group $\pi(G)$ is a finite union of cosets of $\pi(G_1)$, so its closure is the same finite union of the corresponding closed cosets of $\overline{\pi(G_1)}$. Every projective class has an $SU(2)$ representative: write $\det Q=e^{i\phi}$ using [F8] and multiply $Q$ by $\lambda=e^{-i\phi/2}$. Every $SU(2)$ matrix has eigenvalues $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$; [F4] diagonalizes it and the path $s\mapsto S\operatorname{diag}(e^{is\alpha}, e^{-is\alpha})S^*$ joins it to $I$. Thus $SU(2)$, and hence its continuous image $PU(2)$, is connected. The complement of a finite-index closed subgroup is a finite union of its closed cosets, so that subgroup is also open. Since $PU(2)$ is connected, its only nonempty clopen subgroup is $PU(2)$ itself; hence $\overline{\pi(G_1)}=PU(2)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ and, by the density just proved, a word $W\in G_1$ and a scalar $|\lambda|=1$ with $\|W-\lambda R\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\delta$. Write the columns of $W$ and $R$ as $w_1,w_2$ and $r_1,r_2$. Multilinearity [F5] gives $\det W-\det(\lambda R)=\det(w_1-\lambda r_1,w_2) +\det(\lambda r_1,w_2-\lambda r_2)$. For $x=(x_1,x_2)^T$ and $y=(y_1,y_2)^T$, expanding both sides gives $|\det(x,y)|^2=\|x\|^2\|y\|^2-|\langle x,y\rangle|^2 =|x_1|^2|y_2|^2+|x_2|^2|y_1|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(x_1y_2\bar x_2\bar y_1) \le\|x\|^2\|y\|^2$. Since the columns are unit vectors and each column difference has norm less than $\delta$ by [F6], $|1-\lambda^2|\le2\delta$.

Put $a=|\lambda-1|$ and $b=|\lambda+1|$. Then $a^2+b^2=4$ and $ab=|1-\lambda^2|\le2\delta$. Since $\max(a,b)\ge\sqrt2$ from $a^2+b^2=4$, we have $\min(a,b)=ab/\max(a,b)\le\sqrt2\,\delta$. Choose $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ attaining this minimum. By the triangle inequality and $\|R\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1$, $\|W-\sigma R\|_{\mathrm{op}}< (1+\sqrt2)\delta$. The scalar $-I$ is a word in $G$: direct multiplication gives $$X=HZH=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad XZ=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad (XZ)^2=-I.$$ Thus $\sigma W\in G_1$, and $\|\sigma W-R\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|W-\sigma R\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is less than $(1+\sqrt2)\delta$. Because $\det(-I)=1$ and $\det W=1$, this scalar correction leaves the determinant equal to $1$. Choosing $\delta<\varepsilon/(1+\sqrt2)$ proves the claim.

derivations.claim: Put $\Delta=R_z(\theta)^*U$. It is unitary and has determinant $1$, so [F2] diagonalizes it. Its eigenvalues $\lambda,\mu$ have modulus one by unitarity and satisfy $\lambda\mu=1$ by the determinant, hence $\mu=\bar\lambda$. By [F4], write $\lambda=e^{it}$ with $t\in[0,2\pi)$; if $t>\pi$, swap $\lambda,\mu$ and put $\alpha=2\pi-t$, while if $t\le\pi$ put $\alpha=t$. Thus the eigenvalues are $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$ for some $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$. From the displayed matrices, $\operatorname{tr}\Delta=e^{i\theta/2}u+e^{-i\theta/2}\bar u =2\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$. Hence $\cos\alpha= \operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$.

Left multiplication by $R_z(\theta)^*$ preserves vector norms, so [F3] gives $\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|I-\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Let $S$ be a unitary diagonalizer of $\Delta$ from [F2]; conjugation by $S$ preserves the operator norm by [F3]. Using [F4] then gives $\|I-\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2 =\max(|1-e^{i\alpha}|^2,|1-e^{-i\alpha}|^2) =2-2\cos\alpha =2-2\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)$. Input two data bits $a,b$ and a third clean work bit $t=0$. On the ordered
register $(a,b,t)$, apply the following chronological word:

1. $H_t$.
2. $\operatorname{CNOT}_{b,t},T_t^\dagger,\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,t},T_t,
   \operatorname{CNOT}_{b,t},T_t^\dagger,\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,t}$.
3. $T_b,T_t,H_t$.
4. $\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,b},T_a,T_b^\dagger,\operatorname{CNOT}_{a,b}$.
5. $T_t$.
6. Apply the same 15-gate word from steps 1–4 again.

The 15-gate word in steps 1–4 is the specified three-wire block. The output
is the complete three-wire circuit, with no implicit fourth wire.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix

$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$

$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Let $n\ge r\ge1$, let $w=(w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1})$ be an ordered tuple of distinct wires in $[n]$, and let $U:\mathcal Q_r\to\mathcal Q_r$ be unitary. There is a unique unitary $\widetilde U_w:\mathcal Q_n\to\mathcal Q_n$ that applies $U$ to the ordered wires $w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1}$ and acts as the identity on the other wires.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Let $D$ be a finite ordered quantum register and let $A$ be an ordered register of $k\ge0$ ancilla qubits, with Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_D$ and $\mathcal H_A$. Write $|0_A\rangle=|0^k\rangle$, including $|0_A\rangle=1$ when $k=0$. Let $U$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$ and let $V$ be a unitary on $\mathcal H_D$.

The register $A$ is a **clean ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when
$$
U(|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|0_A\rangle
$$
for every vector $|\psi\rangle_D$. Thus the data operation is independent of the input vector and all clean wires return exactly to zero.

The register $A$ is a **dirty ancilla register for $U$ and $V$** when the operator identity $U=V\otimes I_A$ holds on $\mathcal H_D\otimes\mathcal H_A$. Equivalently, every product input $|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$ is mapped to $V|\psi\rangle_D\otimes|\eta\rangle_A$, with the same $V$ for every data and ancilla vector. This requires exact restoration of an arbitrary, initially unknown ancilla state and forbids residual data–ancilla correlation.

These are exact contracts for the complete subroutine. A temporary intermediate alteration of an ancilla is permitted if the full unitary satisfies the stated identity.

$$
T|a,b,t\rangle=|a,b,t\oplus ab\rangle,
$$

$$
F|0,a,b\rangle=|0,a,b\rangle,\qquad F|1,a,b\rangle=|1,b,a\rangle.
$$

Wire order is exactly the order displayed; the first two wires of $T$ are controls and the third is its target, while the first wire of $F$ is its control and the other two are conditionally swapped. derivations.claim: Fix the controls $a,b$ and let $q$ be the target bit immediately after the first $H_t$. The seven phase gates in [F1] contribute exponent $E_{a,b}(q)=-(q\oplus b)+(q\oplus a\oplus b)-(q\oplus a)+b+q\pmod8$. For $(a,b)=00,01,10,11$, the pairs $(E(0),E(1))$ are respectively $(0,0),(1,1),(0,0),(7,3)$. Conjugating these diagonal phases by the final $H_t$ therefore gives, for the four control values, $I,\omega I,I,\omega^7X$ on the target. The last CNOT–$T_a$–$T_b^\dagger$–CNOT block contributes data phase $\omega^{a-(a\oplus b)}$, which is $1,\omega^{-1},1,\omega$ in the same order. The combined action is exactly $|a,b,t\rangle\mapsto|a,b,t\oplus ab\rangle$ with phase $1$ in all eight cases, proving the displayed word is Toffoli in the sense of [F7]. By [F3,F4], these basis actions give the denotational matrix of the displayed chronological circuit.

Starting with $t=0$, the first Toffoli sends $|a,b,0\rangle$ to $|a,b,ab\rangle$. The middle $T_t$ multiplies this vector by $\omega^{ab}$; applying the Toffoli action [F7] again gives target $ab\oplus ab=0$. Thus the full circuit sends each basis vector to $\omega^{ab}|a,b,0\rangle$. The matrix product is the chronological circuit action by [F3,F4].

Every vector on data and a finite-dimensional reference with a clean ancilla has the finite expansion $\sum_{a,b,r}c_{abr}|a,b,r\rangle|0\rangle$. derivations.claim: By [F6], the two one-wire embeddings are $H\otimes I_2,I_2\otimes H$ and the corresponding tensor embeddings for $T,T^\dagger,S,S^\dagger,X,Y,Z$ and scalar phases. CNOT is a single transposition of $|10\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$, so its determinant is $-1=\omega^4$. Thus every primitive determinant is an even power of $\omega$; [F4,F7] make the determinant of a finite circuit product an even power as well.

The target has determinant $\det C(T)=\omega$. Exact equality contradicts step 1.1. If a two-wire circuit $V$ equals $\lambda C(T)$ for a unit scalar $\lambda$ as in [F8], then its $(0,0)$ entry is $\lambda$, so [F1] gives $\lambda\in D$; unitarity gives $\lambda\bar\lambda=1$, so [F2] gives $\lambda=\omega^j$. Every exact one-qubit Clifford+T matrix word, including a free scalar
Clifford phase $\omega^j I$, has determinant in
$\{\omega^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For square matrices $U,V$ of the same size, write $U\sim_{\mathrm{phase}}V$ when $U=\lambda V$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $|\lambda|=1$. This relation is kept distinct from exact matrix equality.

For $\theta\in\mathbb R$ set
$R_z(\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\theta/2},e^{i\theta/2})$. Given
$\varepsilon>0$, the on-the-nose ancilla-free approximation problem is to
find a finite one-qubit Clifford+T word $U$ such that

$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon,$$

and minimize the number of occurrences of $T$ or $T^\dagger$; the $T$-count
of a word is this integer. An overall scalar Clifford phase $\omega^j I$,
viewed under [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence]], is free in the resource
count but remains part of the exact matrix used in the displayed norm
inequality. Thus changing the representative can change feasibility even
when it leaves T-count unchanged. No workspace wire is
permitted. The operator norm is the finite-dimensional norm from
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

This defines a mathematical optimization problem for exact real inputs
$(\theta,\varepsilon)$. It does not specify a bit representation or assert a
Turing algorithm for arbitrary real input.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional target space, let $U$ be unitary on $H$, and let $|\lambda|=1$. In control-first order put
$$C(U)=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_\lambda=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $C(\lambda U)=(P_\lambda\otimes I_H)C(U)$. A scalar multiplying an entire output leaves every defined finite-POVM outcome law unchanged, whereas a scalar attached to a target matrix inside a control gives a phase on only the active control block; applying $P_{\overline\lambda}$ on the control restores the exact controlled matrix.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

derivations.claim: Write $\det U=\omega^k$ by [F1], and set $V=e^{-ik\pi/8}R^*U$. Since $\det R=1$, [F4] gives $\det V=e^{-ik\pi/4}\omega^k=1$. The unitary $V$ is normal, so [F2] diagonalizes it. Its two eigenvalues have product $1$ and modulus $1$, hence are $e^{i\phi},e^{-i\phi}$ for some $\phi$ by [F9]; consequently $\operatorname{tr}V=2\cos\phi$ is real. Choose $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ such that $W=\sigma V$ has nonnegative trace. Since $-1=e^{i8\pi/8}$, $W=e^{in\pi/8}R^*U$ for an integer $n$, and $W$ is unitary with determinant $1$.

Since $W\in SU(2)$, its eigenvalues are a unit scalar and its conjugate; by [F9] write them $e^{it},e^{-it}$ and, swapping them if needed, choose $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$ with eigenvalues $e^{i\alpha},e^{-i\alpha}$. Then $\operatorname{tr}W=2\cos\alpha\ge0$; [F10,F11] imply $\alpha\le\pi/2$. For any unit scalar $\mu$, choose its angle $t\in[0,2\pi)$ by [F9] and set $\psi=t$ if $t\le\pi$, or $\psi=t-2\pi$ otherwise. Thus $\psi\in[-\pi,\pi]$. By [F2] and [F3], $\|I-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|1-e^{i\alpha}|$ and $\|I-\mu W\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max\{|1-e^{i(\psi+\alpha)}|,|1-e^{i(\psi-\alpha)}|\}$. If $\psi\ge0$, put $t=\psi+\alpha\in[\alpha,3\pi/2]$. For $t\le\pi$, $\sin(t/2)\ge\sin(\alpha/2)$ by [F10]; for $t\ge\pi$, sine decreases on $[\pi/2,3\pi/2]$, so $\sin(t/2)\ge\sin(3\pi/4)$. By [F11,F12], $\sin(3\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/4)=1/\sqrt2$, and $\alpha/2\le\pi/4$ gives $\sin(\alpha/2)\le1/\sqrt2$ by [F10]. If $\psi\le0$, apply the same bound to $t=|\psi|+\alpha$ from the second eigenvalue. By [F9,F10], $|1-e^{ix}|=2|\sin(x/2)|$ and these bounds imply $\|I-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|I-\mu W\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

Left multiplication by $R$ preserves operator norm, since it preserves the norm of every vector in the maximum [F3]. As $W=e^{in\pi/8}R^*U$, step 2.1 implies $\|R-e^{in\pi/8}U\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|I-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|R-\lambda U\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Write $n=2q+r$ with $r\in\{0,1\}$. Then $e^{in\pi/8}=\omega^q e^{ir\pi/8}$. Since $\omega^q$ is a free scalar Clifford phase in [F6], moving it between the explicit scalar and the representative leaves the projective T-count unchanged. Thus the two phase representatives are $e^{ir\pi/8}\in\{1,e^{i\pi/8}\}$, proving the reduction.

In the control-first basis [F8], direct block multiplication gives $C(\lambda U)=\operatorname{diag}(I,\lambda U)=(\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)\otimes I)C(U)$, in agreement with the supplier identity [F7]. The first factor is generally not a global scalar on the joint control-target system, so replacing $U$ by $\lambda U$ under control requires this relative phase correction.

$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ has coefficient vector

$$x\bar x=P+\sqrt2Q,\qquad P=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2,\quad Q=a(b-d)+c(b+d),$$

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.
If $z\in D$ and $z\bar z=1$, then $z=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$.

derivations.claim: For a nonzero real element $P+\sqrt2Q\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, define $\nu(P+\sqrt2Q)$ as the largest $r\ge0$ for which $(\sqrt2)^r$ divides it in $O$. This maximum exists: divisibility by $(\sqrt2)^{2q}=2^q$ forces both integer coefficients $P,Q$ to be divisible by $2^q$, which cannot hold for arbitrarily large $q$ unless the element is zero. If $y=(\sqrt2)^j y_0$ with $\sqrt2\nmid y_0$, then the definition of sde gives $\operatorname{sde}(y/(\sqrt2)^r)=r-j$.

Applying each embedding of $K$ to $|u|^2+|v|^2=1$ preserves the identity by [F6]; hence every embedding of each entry has modulus at most $1$. Since $s>3$, $u
e0$. If $v=0$, then $|u|^2=1$ and $s=0$, a contradiction, so $v
e0$ as well. Let $r_u=\operatorname{sde}(u)$ and $r_v=\operatorname{sde}(v)$. From [F2] and $s>3$, $r_u\ge2$. More generally, if $\max(r_u,r_v)\ge1$ and the exponents differ, the same argument below gives a contradiction. If $r_u>r_v$, set $x=(\sqrt2)^{r_u}u$ and $y=(\sqrt2)^{r_v}v$. Then $x ar x+2^{r_u-r_v}y ar y=2^{r_u}$; the right side and second term lie in $2O$, so $x ar x\in2O$. Write $x=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$. By [F3], $x ar x=P+\sqrt2Q$ with $P=\sum a_j^2$ and $Q=a_0(a_1-a_3)+a_2(a_1+a_3)$. If $P,Q$ are both even, then $a_0+a_2$ and $a_1+a_3$ have equal parity because $P\equiv(a_0+a_2)+(a_1+a_3)\pmod2$, while $Q\equiv(a_0+a_2)(a_1+a_3)\pmod2$ forces both even. Then [F3] gives $\sqrt2\mid x$, contradicting the minimality of $r_u$. Since $x ar x\in2O$ would make both $P,Q$ even in the power basis, this is impossible. If $r_v>r_u$, interchange $u,v$ and use the same calculation with the larger exponent. Thus $r_u=r_v=:r$. Write $x=(\sqrt2)^ru$ and $y=(\sqrt2)^rv$. Their minimal exponents make both primitive with respect to $\sqrt2$. Let $G$ be the group of exact one-qubit Clifford+T matrix words, and let
$SU(2)=\{U\in U(2):\det U=1\}$. For every $R\in SU(2)$ and every
$\varepsilon>0$, some $W\in G$ satisfies $\det W=1$ and
$\|R-W\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon$.

Set $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$, $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and
$D=O[1/2]=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The relation $\omega^4=-1$ reduces every
element of $O$ to four integer coefficients in the power basis
$1,\omega,\omega^2,\omega^3$. The canonical dyadic encoding of a nonzero
$z\in D$ is

$$z=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/2^r,$$

where $r\ge0$ is least and, if $r>0$, the four integers are not all even.
Zero is encoded with $r=0$ and all four coefficients zero. Arithmetic is exact:
multiply polynomials, reduce with $\omega^4=-1$, combine denominators, and
remove the common power of $2$ from the coefficients. The integral-basis
supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-ring-of-integers]] and the proof of
[[lem-qc-dyadic-coefficient-encoding]] justify existence and uniqueness.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$, where $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The class $[5]_8$ is a
unit modulo $8$, so the cyclotomic Galois group supplier
[[cor-the-galois-group-of-a-rational-cyclotomic-field]] gives the unique
$\mathbb Q$-automorphism $\bullet$ with
$\omega^\bullet=\omega^5=-\omega$. It fixes $i=\omega^2$ and sends
$\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ to $-\sqrt2$. Complex conjugation and $\bullet$
commute, as is checked on the generator $\omega$. The four embeddings of $K$
are the identity, complex conjugation, $\bullet$, and their composite,
because the Galois group consists of the four maps $\omega\mapsto\omega^j$
for $j=1,3,5,7$. Since $\bullet$ fixes $1/2$ and maps $\omega$ into
$\mathbb Z[\omega]$, it preserves $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$.

This is the nontrivial real-conjugation embedding used in the scaled-grid
conditions; it is distinct from complex conjugation.

Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, and
$$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}\in SU(2).$$
Then
$$\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2,F3], the entries of $T,T^\dagger$ lie in $D$. Also $\sqrt2=\omega-\omega^3$ and $1/\sqrt2=(\omega-\omega^3)/2$, so every entry of $H$ lies in $D$. The ring $D$ is closed under complex conjugation because $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}=\omega^7\in D$. Apply [F1] to $R_z(\theta)\in SU(2)$ and choose an exact word $U$ with $\det U=1$ and $\|R_z(\theta)-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\varepsilon$. Every entry of $U$ lies in $D$ because each generator has entries in $D$ and products of matrices over a subring remain over that subring. Let the first column be $(u,t)^T$. It is a unit vector; its orthogonal unit vector $(-\bar t,\bar u)^T$ is therefore the second column up to a unit scalar $\lambda$. The determinant of the resulting matrix is $\lambda$, so $\det U=1$ forces $\lambda=1$. Hence $U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\bar t\\t&\bar u\end{pmatrix}$ and $t^\dagger t=1-u^\dagger u$.

Applying $\bullet$ to $U^*U=I$ preserves products and fixes $I$; [F4] also makes it commute with the adjoint. Thus $U^\bullet$ is unitary, and its first-column norm gives $|u^\bullet|^2+|t^\bullet|^2=1$. The original first column similarly gives $|u|^2+|t|^2=1$, so $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$.

The strict approximation in step 1.1 and [F5] imply $\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)>1-\varepsilon^2/2$, hence the required weak inequality. Together with step 1.1 this gives a grid candidate and an exact solution of its norm equation.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.
There is a unique $\gamma\in(0,2)$ with $\cos\gamma=0$. It is the smallest positive zero of cosine.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Suppose $\varepsilon<c$ and put $A=V R_z(\theta)^*$. The matrix $A$ is unitary. By [F2] it has an orthonormal eigenbasis. For a nonzero eigenvector $v$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$, norm preservation gives $|\lambda|\,\|v\|=\|Av\|=\|v\|$, so $|\lambda|=1$; by [F11] write the two eigenvalues as $e^{i\phi_1},e^{i\phi_2}$ with $\phi_j\in[-\pi,\pi]$. Unitary multiplication preserves [F3], and the norm of a diagonal matrix is the largest modulus of its entries, so $|1-e^{i\phi_j}|\le\varepsilon<c$. Since $|1-e^{ix}|=2|\sin(x/2)|$ by [F10]. Since $|\phi_j|/2\in[0,\pi/2]$, [F12] gives $|\sin(\phi_j/2)|=\sin(|\phi_j|/2)$ and $\sin0=0$; [F9] makes this strictly increasing in $|\phi_j|$. Thus $|1-e^{i\phi_j}|<c$ implies $|\phi_j|<\pi/8$. Hence $|\phi_1+\phi_2|<\pi/4$. By [F1,F6] and $\det R_z(\theta)=1$, $e^{i(\phi_1+\phi_2)}=\det A=\det V=\omega^j$. The only eighth root with an argument strictly between $-\pi/4$ and $\pi/4$ is $1$; thus $\det V=1$.

Suppose $\varepsilon\ge c$. Set $q=\lfloor2\theta/\pi+1/2\rfloor$ by [F8]. Then $q-1/2\le2\theta/\pi<q+1/2$, so $|q\pi/4-\theta/2|\le\pi/8$. Set $C=\omega^{-q}S^q=\operatorname{diag}(\omega^{-q},\omega^q)$. It is a Clifford matrix with determinant one and T-count zero by [F4]. The two diagonal entries of $R_z(\theta)-C$ have the same modulus $|1-e^{i(q\pi/4-\theta/2)}|\le 2\sin(\pi/16)=c$ by [F9, F10], and $c\le\varepsilon$ by the case hypothesis. To check the domain used here, [F13] gives $0<\pi/16<\pi/2$; [F9, F12] give $0\le\sin(\pi/16)$, and [F14] gives $\sin(\pi/16)\le\pi/16$. Thus $c=2\sin(\pi/16)\le\pi/8<1/2$. [F3] therefore gives the required error bound. At equality $\varepsilon=c$ the weak inequality still holds.

For $\varepsilon<c$, step 1.1 says every feasible matrix already has determinant one. For $\varepsilon\ge c$, step 1.2 attains T-count zero, which is minimal by nonnegativity [F5]. The feasible set is nonempty by [F7], applied with error smaller than $\varepsilon$. Its T-counts form a nonempty subset of the nonnegative integers, hence have a least element attained by a feasible word. Thus restricting to determinant-one matrices never changes this attained minimum.

citations.quote:
Fix $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$ and $D=\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. Use the automorphism
$\bullet$ from [[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], which sends
$\omega$ to $-\omega=\omega^5$ and fixes $i$. Let $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ and
$\theta\in\mathbb R$. The scaled grid for this input is

$$\mathcal G(\theta,\varepsilon)=\{u\in D:\ |u|\le1,\ |u^\bullet|\le1,\ \operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta/2}u)\ge1-\varepsilon^2/2\}.$$

The default iterator is [[alg-qc-rz-efficient-scaled-grid-iterator]], with
$w=e^{-i\theta/2}$. It emits every candidate once in increasing least
$k=\operatorname{sde}(u)$, with randomized order within each layer and
finite layer completion for every random-bit sequence. Its expected prefix
cost and all fixed prefix moments are proved in
[[thm-qc-rz-efficient-scaled-grid-enumeration]].

A complete finite-search alternative uses lexicographic power-basis
coefficients within each layer. For each $k\ge0$, write
$u=(a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3)/(\sqrt2)^k$ with least exponent
$k$; the finite coefficient bound is
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$, proved in
[[lem-qc-cyclotomic-scaled-grid-finiteness]]. Test the three displayed
conditions exactly. This defines a finite candidate list for each $k$.

For a candidate $u$, put
$\xi=1-u^\dagger u=1-|u|^2\in D_+=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]$, using
[[lem-qc-dyadic-cyclotomic-conjugate-norm]]. For scalars, $z^\dagger=\bar z$.
Write
$\xi^\bullet\xi=n/2^\ell$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ and least $\ell\ge0$; compute
it by writing $\xi=a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Z[1/2]$ and multiplying
$(a-b\sqrt2)(a+b\sqrt2)=a^2-2b^2$. The two disk conditions give
$\xi,\xi^\bullet\ge0$, so $n\ge0$; if $\xi\ne0$, injectivity of $\bullet$
gives $n>0$.
The complete norm-equation subprocedure receives $\xi$ and, if $n\ne0$, a prime
factorization of $n$. It must decide whether some $t\in D$ satisfies
$t^\dagger t=\xi$, return an exact such $t$ if one exists, and otherwise return
`NO_SOLUTION`. If $\xi=0$, it returns $t=0$. A bounded factorization attempt
may return `FACTOR_TIMEOUT`; that result skips this candidate and is not a
proof of `NO_SOLUTION`.

### Factored norm-equation subprocedure

When the supplied integer factorization is available, use the efficient
construction in [[thm-qc-factored-cyclotomic-norm-equation-efficient]].
Clear the denominator by $\eta=4^r\xi$, taking the least nonnegative
$r$ for which $\eta\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$. For each rational prime in its
known norm factorization, recover its real prime generators using
$\gcd(p,\sqrt2-b)$ when $b^2=2\pmod p$ exists, and otherwise retain
$p$. Split these into cyclotomic prime generators by the displayed modular
roots of $-1$ or $-2$ and cyclotomic gcds; retain the inert generators and
include $\delta=1+\omega$ over $2$. Recover the exponents in
$\eta$ by exact division, allocate them under complex conjugation as below,
and recover the real unit by multiplying by $1+\sqrt2$ or its inverse
until its positive embedding lies in $[1,1+\sqrt2)$.
The cited construction specifies all residue-class branches and its
randomized modular square-root subroutine; balance gcd remainders by real
units as there. It returns an exact solution or `NO_SOLUTION` and has
expected polynomial bit cost in the explicit algebraic input size. For a
grid candidate of exponent $k$, this is polynomial in $k+1$.

### Calibrated bounded prime attempts

In bounded mode no prime recognition oracle is used. For candidate exponent
$k$, use the fixed calibrated polynomial
$$P(k)=2^{200}(k+1)^{20}$$
from [[thm-qc-factored-cyclotomic-norm-equation-efficient]]. If $n=0$,
return $t=0$. If $n=1$, run the complete efficient construction with the
empty odd-prime factor list; its remaining powers of two are known.

For $n>1$, execute the factored construction prospectively, using the
single factor hint $n^1$, for at most $2P(k)$ of its elementary binary
operations. This is an attempt, not a claim that $n$ is prime. Instrument
all loops, including random sampling, with this counter. Guard every partial
operation: check divisors for zero and obtain modular inverses by the
integer extended Euclidean algorithm, aborting if the gcd is not one.
Impossible order/root searches, malformed outputs, negative solver outcomes,
failed inverses, and work-cap interruptions all end the attempt with
`FACTOR_TIMEOUT`, never with a claim of `NO_SOLUTION`.

Before accepting any prospective output, reduce its rational power-basis
coefficients and check $t^\dagger t=\xi$ exactly. Accept only when that
equality holds; otherwise return `FACTOR_TIMEOUT`. Watchdog, guard and final
certificate costs are charged; they are polynomial in $k+1+P(k)$ even on
composite inputs. The solver-work counter bounds every intermediate bit
string by its input length plus $2P(k)$, so certification cannot hide an
unbounded output cost. Use fresh independent random bits at each candidate.

After the capped prime attempt fails, return FACTOR_TIMEOUT for this
candidate and continue to the next grid candidate. Bounded mode makes no
additional factoring attempt and takes no factor-suggestion procedure or
additional factor-attempt budget as input. Complete oracle mode instead
supplies a valid full factorization and runs the complete efficient solver
without this cap.

### Complete finite-search alternative

Use the complete terminating construction of
[[thm-qc-cyclotomic-norm-equation-decision]]. Explicitly, after the zero
case choose the least integer $r\ge0$ clearing the coefficient denominators so that
$\eta=4^r\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$. Factor $\eta$ in
$O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$ by the finite divisor search in
[[lem-qc-cyclotomic-euclidean-factorization-and-units]]. Group the prime
associate classes under $\dagger$. If any fixed class has odd exponent,
return `NO_SOLUTION`. Otherwise form $s$ by allocating half each fixed
exponent, and all of the common exponent to one class from each conjugate
pair. Compute the positive real unit $e=\eta/(s^\dagger s)$, recover
$v\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ with $v^2=e$ by the unit construction, and return
$t=vs/2^r$. Every computation here uses exact power-basis arithmetic.

The supplied integer factorization is retained as an admissible input for
implementations using rational-prime splitting. The finite-search mode above
does not need it and has no asserted polynomial runtime. In bounded mode,
FACTOR_TIMEOUT skips the current candidate and never changes the complete
subprocedure's NO_SOLUTION criterion.

### Comparison contract

The grid comparisons involve the supplied real parameters $\theta$ and
$\varepsilon$. Their exact comparison interface is part of the outer
real-input contract. It is independent of the algebraic norm solver, whose
sign, equality, divisibility and associate tests are all exact and terminating.

Put $R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$, $O=\mathbb Z[\omega]$, and $D=O[1/2]$, with $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. Given $\xi\in R[1/2]$ and a valid complete rational-prime factorization of the nonzero numerator $n$ in the reduced fraction $\xi^\bullet\xi=n/2^\ell$, there is an exact randomized algorithm returning $t\in D$ with $t^\dagger t=\xi$, or correctly reporting that no such $t$ exists. Zero input requires no factorization. The algorithm terminates almost surely and has expected bit cost polynomial in the total binary length $L$ of the explicitly encoded rational coefficients of $\xi$ and the supplied factorization. Denominators are ordinary binary integers, not compressed exponent encodings. The algorithm does not compute or verify rational primality of the promised prime factors.

In particular, suppose $0\le\xi,\xi^\bullet\le1$, and $k$ is the least nonnegative integer with $(\sqrt2)^k\xi\in R$. Given the factorization of $n$, the expected cost, including exact solution recovery or a correct negative answer, is polynomial in $k+1$ when $\xi$ is supplied in reduced coefficient form. For a grid candidate $u\in D$ with least $\sqrt2$-denominator exponent $h$, its residual $\xi=1-u^\dagger u$ has least exponent at most $2h$. Under the same embedding bounds, $n\le4^h$ and the residual solver has expected cost polynomial in $h+1$. The unrestricted cost includes the bit length of the coefficients, rather than depending on $\log n$ alone.

For the stated grid residual with $n$ prime, or $n\in\{0,1\}$, a concrete schoolbook implementation of this algorithm has expected bit cost at most $P(h)=2^{200}(h+1)^{20}$. This explicit bound includes input reading in reduced coefficient form and exact verification of a returned solution. Bit cost counts Boolean operations and bit reads/writes on binary arrays; multi-bit arithmetic is performed by the schoolbook loops detailed below. It gives a numerical cap for interrupted attempts; it makes no correctness or termination assertion about calling prime-specific branches with a composite integer falsely presented as prime.

Let $u\in D$ satisfy $|u|,|u^\bullet|\le1$, put
$\xi=1-u^\dagger u$, and write $\xi^\bullet\xi=n/2^\ell$ with
$n\in\mathbb Z$ and least $\ell\ge0$. Then $n\ge0$, and either $n=0$ or
$n\equiv1\pmod8$. If $u\ne0$ has least square-root-of-two denominator
exponent $k$, then $n\le4^k$.

Let $\xi\in\mathbb Z[\sqrt2,1/2]$ be positive at both real embeddings.
If $\xi^\bullet\xi=p/2^\ell$ with $\ell\ge0$ and a rational prime
$p\equiv1\pmod8$, then $t^\dagger t=\xi$ has a solution in
$\mathbb Z[\omega,1/2]$. The complete finite-time norm solver returns a
solution on every such input. The same conclusion holds when
$\xi^\bullet\xi=1/2^\ell$. No runtime bound is implied.

derivations.claim: The exact certificate check in [F1] is a comparison of the four rational power-basis coefficients of $t^\dagger t$ and $\xi$. Equality of these coefficients is equality in the field, so acceptance always proves the required equation. On a composite input no field property of a proposed residue quotient and no `NO_SOLUTION` message is used as evidence: a failed operation, negative outcome, or work-cap interruption causes only a skip.

The construction is interrupted after $B=2\lceil P(k)\rceil$ binary operations, regardless of whether its proposed prime factor was valid. Every generated bit string then has length bounded by the input length plus $B$. The grid-input bound of [F2] makes its input length polynomial in $k+1$. A fixed-degree rational-coefficient multiplication and equality check therefore takes polynomial work in $k+1+B$, by schoolbook integer multiplication and division. Since $B$ is a specified polynomial, total work including exact certification is polynomial on every input.

If $n$ is prime, the proposed one-factor factorization is valid, and [F3,F4] make its norm equation solvable. Let $T\ge0$ be the binary work of the uncapped construction on this input. By the calibrated bound [F2], $\mathbb E[T]\le P(k)$. The elementary inequality $T\ge B\,\mathbf1_{\{T>B\}}$ gives $\Pr(T>B)\le\mathbb E[T]/B\le1/2$. Whenever $T\le B$, [F2] returns an exact solution and step 1.1 accepts it. Thus success probability is at least $1/2$. The zero case is explicit in [F1], and [F4] plus the complete factored empty-list branch gives the numerator-one case.

Condition first on all arithmetic data $\mathcal D$. Each call is then a deterministic function of its own input and its fresh solver bits, so its success events are independent under this conditional probability. By step 2.2 its conditional success probability is at least $I_i/2$; this also holds for the immediate zero/unit branches. Consequently $\Pr(J>j\mid\mathcal D)\le\prod_{i=1}^j(1-I_i/2)$. Average this inequality over $\mathcal D$. The indicators, rather than the successful-call events, are independent in the stated model; hence $\mathbb E[\prod_{i=1}^j(1-I_i/2)]=\prod_{i=1}^j(1-p_i/2)$. The lower bounds on $p_i$ give the displayed joint-failure estimate. Correlated numerical inputs can correlate the unconditional call successes, but cannot invalidate this estimate.

risk_review.notes: Checked all four proof steps against the full capped-solver Definition and reviewed calibrated P(k), prime-numerator solvability and residue suppliers. Exact coefficient verification makes acceptance sound even for composites; all failed/undefined/capped branches skip, never certify unsolvability. Watchdog bounds string lengths and final certification is polynomial in k+P(k), hence polynomial in k on every input. For an actual prime the supplied factor is valid, expected cost <=P and Markov at 2P gives success >=1/2. Zero and numerator-one branches are complete. Conditioning on all arithmetic data fixes primality and leaves fresh solver streams independent; conditional failure <=product(1−I_i/2), whose average factors by the modelled indicator independence. No unconditional solver-success independence is asserted. This is explicitly an ideal arithmetic model, not a primality theorem for fixed inputs. No defect found.

Every finite circuit on $n$ ordered wires using only the matrices in
[[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]] has all matrix entries in $D$.

If $U=\begin{pmatrix}u&b\\v&d\end{pmatrix}$ is a $2\times2$ unitary with
entries in $D$, then for some $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$,

$$U=\begin{pmatrix}u&-\omega^j\bar v\\v&\omega^j\bar u\end{pmatrix},\qquad |u|^2+|v|^2=1.$$

Let $(u,v)^T$ be a unit vector with entries in $D$, and put
$s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)$. If $s>3$, then some $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ has

$$\operatorname{sde}\!\left(\left|\frac{u+\omega^{-k}v}{\sqrt2}\right|^2\right)=s-1.$$

Moreover, every such unit column with $s\le3$ is prepared exactly from
$|0\rangle$ by a word in $H,T,T^\dagger$. A complete coefficient-and-word
table for the finite base set is recorded at
`research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
If $z\in D$ and $z\bar z=1$, then $z=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$.

derivations.claim: If $U$ is a finite Clifford+T circuit matrix, [F1] puts all its entries in $D$.

Conversely, let $U\in U(2)$ have entries in $D$. By [F2] its first column $(u,v)^T$ is a normalized column. Apply the descent in [F3] repeatedly while $s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)>3$. Each step replaces the current matrix $M$ by $HT^{-k}M$ and decreases the nonnegative integer $s$ by exactly one; hence after finitely many steps the first column lies in the base regime.

By [F3], the base column has a word $W_0$ with $W_0|0\rangle=(u_0,v_0)^T$. Reversing each descent step by prepending its recorded $T^kH$ gives a word $W$ with first column equal to the original $(u,v)^T$. The unitary $W^*U$ has first column $(1,0)^T$, so orthogonality of its columns makes it $\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ for a unit scalar $\lambda$. Its entries lie in $D$, since $W,U$ have entries in that ring. Therefore [F4] gives $\lambda=\omega^j$, and $U=WT^j$ is a finite Clifford+T word.
Both implications are proved. The proof constructs the converse word with only exact coefficient operations and the finite base lookup; no approximation, ancilla, or multi-qubit inference is used.

Use $G=\{H,T,T^\dagger,S,S^\dagger,X,Y,Z\}$ and allow scalar phases $\omega^qI$. Only $H$ contributes to the H count; only $T,T^\dagger$ contribute to the T count. Every word can be rewritten, with its exact scalar retained, as

$$\omega^q T^a H T^{b_1}H\cdots H T^{b_{h-1}}H T^c X^e,$$

where all $b_i$ are odd, exponents are read modulo $8$, and $e\in\{0,1\}$. For $h=0$ interpret this as $\omega^qT^aX^e$. The rewriting never increases either resource count. Each odd power uses one T gate and even powers use none. A reduced word with $h\ge2$ has $\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)=h+1$; with $h=1$ the exponent is $2$, and with $h=0$ the squared entry is $0$ or $1$. Consequently reduced words minimize H count among all words for the same matrix up to global phase.

Input a $2\times2$ matrix $U$ as four canonical elements of $D$. Perform the
following exact procedure.

1. Test $U^*U=I$ by rational coefficient arithmetic. If it fails, return
   `INVALID`.
2. Set $M=U$ and an empty list $K$. While
   $s=\operatorname{sde}(|M_{00}|^2)>3$, test $k=0,1,2,3$ in that order and
   choose the first for which
$\operatorname{sde}(|(HT^{-k}M)_{00}|^2)=s-1$. Append $k$ to $K$ and replace
$M$ by $HT^{-k}M$.
3. Look up the first column of $M$ in the complete base-column table at
   `research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
   Let $W_0$ be its stored H/T preparation word. Compute
   $W_0^*M=\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ exactly and find $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$
   with $\lambda=\omega^j$.
4. If $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ in reduction order, form the exact matrix-word
factorization
$$U=(T^{k_1}H)\cdots(T^{k_r}H)W_0T^j.$$
For the chronological output, emit $T^j$ first, then the stored chronological
gate list for $W_0$, then for $i=r,r-1,\ldots,1$ emit $H$ followed by
$T^{k_i}$. The QC09 semantics put later gates on the left, so this list has the
displayed matrix product.
5. Reduce this word by the exact stack rewriting in
   [[lem-qc-hadamard-reduced-word-denominators]]: move Pauli $X$ factors to
   the right, combine diagonal powers modulo eight, and replace each
   $HT^{2r}H$ by its zero- or one-H Clifford expression until all interior
   diagonal powers are odd. Retain the scalar phase $\omega^qI$ produced by
   these identities in the exact output. Emit even powers as $S,Z$ factors
   and odd powers as one $T$ or $T^\dagger$ with free $S,Z$ factors, then
   return the reduced factors in reverse order as the chronological list.

The denominator descent and table completeness are the mathematical
properties in [[lem-qc-clifford-t-denominator-descent-and-base]] and
[[thm-qc-single-qubit-exact-clifford-t-characterization]]. The finite lookup
table uses exact rational coefficients; no numerical equality tolerance is
used.

Let $(u,v)^T$ be a unit vector with entries in $D$, and put
$s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)$. If $s>3$, then some $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ has

$$\operatorname{sde}\!\left(\left|\frac{u+\omega^{-k}v}{\sqrt2}\right|^2\right)=s-1.$$

Moreover, every such unit column with $s\le3$ is prepared exactly from
$|0\rangle$ by a word in $H,T,T^\dagger$. A complete coefficient-and-word
table for the finite base set is recorded at
`research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.

Let $\bullet$ be the automorphism of $K=\mathbb Q(\omega)$ defined in
[[def-qc-cyclotomic-bullet-automorphism]], so $\omega^\bullet=-\omega=\omega^5$,
and let $u\in D\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|u|\le1$ and $|u^\bullet|\le1$. Then $k=\operatorname{sde}(u)\ge0$. If
$a=(\sqrt2)^ku=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3$, then

$$|a_j|\le2^{k/2}\quad(0\le j\le3).$$

Thus for each fixed $k$ only finitely many coefficient vectors can occur; the
integer search may be restricted to
$|a_j|\le\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$.

For nonzero $z\in D$, write $s=\operatorname{sde}(z)$. There is
$m\in\{0,1\}$ such that
$\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)=2s-m$. In particular, if
$\operatorname{sde}(|z|^2)\le3$, then $\operatorname{sde}(z)\le2$.

derivations.claim: By [F2,F3], before the final reduction the compiler has an exact word for $U$. By [F1] its final reduced word is exact and H-optimal, and $n\ge4$ makes its H count $h=n-1$. Write its endpoint exponents $a,c$ and its trailing Pauli factor $X^e$ as in [F1]. Each of the $h-1$ odd interior powers costs one T, so its T count is $h-1+p(a)+p(c)$, where $p(r)=r\bmod2\in\{0,1\}$.

Every Clifford block generated by $H,S,X,Y,Z$ reduces by [F1] to at most one H: all diagonal exponents remain even during that reduction. Splitting any word containing $t$ T gates into $t+1$ Clifford blocks therefore proves $h(V)\le t(V)+1$ for every represented $V$. This argument applies to $T^\dagger$ equally.

There are $n-3$ descent iterations and a constant-size base lookup. Each trial uses boundedly many coefficient additions, sign permutations, multiplications by fixed ring constants, and denominator tests. At every iteration all embeddings of the current unitary remain unitary, so all embedded entries have modulus at most one. For a positive squared-entry exponent, the complementary squared norm has the same exponent: subtracting its primitive numerator from the positive power of $\sqrt2$ leaves it primitive. Thus [F5] bounds every entry exponent by $(n+1)/2$; the base regime is bounded by [F3]. By [F4] all numerator coefficients have $O(n+1)$ bits. Denominator tests need no integer multiplication: for $x=a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3\ne0$, let $m$ be the minimum of the binary trailing-zero counts of its nonzero coefficients, and put $y=x/2^m$. Its $\sqrt2$-valuation is $2m+\delta$, where $\delta=1$ exactly when both opposite-coefficient sums of $y$ are even. Indeed $y$ is not divisible by $2$, so it can contain at most one factor $\sqrt2$. For the resulting primitive numerator $z$, its norm has zero or one factor $\sqrt2$ by [F5]; this factor occurs exactly when $\sum z_i$ is even, since the rational coefficient of $z\bar z$ is $\sum z_i^2$. These parity and trailing-zero scans take $O(n+1)$ bit operations. Every descent trial therefore costs $O(n+1)$ bits and boundedly many ring operations, with coefficient valuations counted as linear binary scans.

Choose $\ell$ and $j$ with $a+\ell$ and $c-j$ odd. Then $HT^\ell UT^jH$ has an odd-interior reduced word with $h+2$ H gates: commute $X^e$ past $T^jH$ using the identities in [F1], which changes only the sign of $j$ and adds a free terminal $Z$ when $e=1$. Its H count is therefore minimal. Conversely if either parity condition fails, the adjacent even-interior pair reduces, giving strictly fewer than $h+2$ H gates. Thus the extension condition is equivalent to $p(\ell)=1-p(a)$ and $p(j)=1-p(c)$.

Apply step 1.2 to the extended matrix $V=HT^\ell UT^jH$. Multiplication by these endpoint factors gives $t(V)\le t(U)+p(\ell)+p(j)$, while $h(V)=h+2$ gives $t(V)\ge h+1$. Consequently $t(U)\ge h+1-p(\ell)-p(j)=h-1+p(a)+p(c)$. Step 1.1 attains this bound, proving simultaneous optimality and both formulas. The same argument proves the endpoint formula for every reduced word with at least one H, since its extension still has at least three H gates and [F1] applies.

The initial word has $O(n+1)$ gates and its stack reduction is linear by [F1], retaining only exponents modulo eight and a scalar exponent modulo eight. The preceding bounds give $O(n+1)$ ring operations and $O((n+1)^2)$ bit operations overall. Any word's total H/T count is at least $h(U)=n-1$; the output has $h+t\le2h+1=O(n+1)$ by step 1.1. Hence $n+1=\Theta(n_{\rm opt}+1)$, proving the claimed bounds.

citations.quote:
Input a $2\times2$ matrix $U$ as four canonical elements of $D$. Perform the
following exact procedure.

1. Test $U^*U=I$ by rational coefficient arithmetic. If it fails, return
   `INVALID`.
2. Set $M=U$ and an empty list $K$. While
   $s=\operatorname{sde}(|M_{00}|^2)>3$, test $k=0,1,2,3$ in that order and
   choose the first for which
$\operatorname{sde}(|(HT^{-k}M)_{00}|^2)=s-1$. Append $k$ to $K$ and replace
$M$ by $HT^{-k}M$.
3. Look up the first column of $M$ in the complete base-column table at
   `research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
   Let $W_0$ be its stored H/T preparation word. Compute
   $W_0^*M=\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ exactly and find $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$
   with $\lambda=\omega^j$.
4. If $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ in reduction order, form the exact matrix-word
factorization
$$U=(T^{k_1}H)\cdots(T^{k_r}H)W_0T^j.$$
For the chronological output, emit $T^j$ first, then the stored chronological
gate list for $W_0$, then for $i=r,r-1,\ldots,1$ emit $H$ followed by
$T^{k_i}$. The QC09 semantics put later gates on the left, so this list has the
displayed matrix product.
5. Reduce this word by the exact stack rewriting in
   [[lem-qc-hadamard-reduced-word-denominators]]: move Pauli $X$ factors to
   the right, combine diagonal powers modulo eight, and replace each
   $HT^{2r}H$ by its zero- or one-H Clifford expression until all interior
   diagonal powers are odd. Retain the scalar phase $\omega^qI$ produced by
   these identities in the exact output. Emit even powers as $S,Z$ factors
   and odd powers as one $T$ or $T^\dagger$ with free $S,Z$ factors, then
   return the reduced factors in reverse order as the chronological list.

The denominator descent and table completeness are the mathematical
properties in [[lem-qc-clifford-t-denominator-descent-and-base]] and
[[thm-qc-single-qubit-exact-clifford-t-characterization]]. The finite lookup
table uses exact rational coefficients; no numerical equality tolerance is
used.

Let $(u,v)^T$ be a unit vector with entries in $D$, and put
$s=\operatorname{sde}(|u|^2)$. If $s>3$, then some $k\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ has

$$\operatorname{sde}\!\left(\left|\frac{u+\omega^{-k}v}{\sqrt2}\right|^2\right)=s-1.$$

Moreover, every such unit column with $s\le3$ is prepared exactly from
$|0\rangle$ by a word in $H,T,T^\dagger$. A complete coefficient-and-word
table for the finite base set is recorded at
`research/quantum-computing-algorithms-60-2026-10-15-batch-13-finite-certificates.json`.
If $z\in D$ and $z\bar z=1$, then $z=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}$.

For nonzero $z\in D$, define
$\operatorname{sde}(z)=\min\{k\in\mathbb Z:(\sqrt2)^kz\in O\}$; exponents may
be negative. Set $\operatorname{sde}(0)=-\infty$. For a matrix $U$, the
denominator statistic used in the synthesis statements below is
$\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)$, the exponent of the squared modulus of its
upper-left entry. The base regime in this convention is exponent at most $3$.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Use $G=\{H,T,T^\dagger,S,S^\dagger,X,Y,Z\}$ and allow scalar phases $\omega^qI$. Only $H$ contributes to the H count; only $T,T^\dagger$ contribute to the T count. Every word can be rewritten, with its exact scalar retained, as

$$\omega^q T^a H T^{b_1}H\cdots H T^{b_{h-1}}H T^c X^e,$$

where all $b_i$ are odd, exponents are read modulo $8$, and $e\in\{0,1\}$. For $h=0$ interpret this as $\omega^qT^aX^e$. The rewriting never increases either resource count. Each odd power uses one T gate and even powers use none. A reduced word with $h\ge2$ has $\operatorname{sde}(|U_{00}|^2)=h+1$; with $h=1$ the exponent is $2$, and with $h=0$ the squared entry is $0$ or $1$. Consequently reduced words minimize H count among all words for the same matrix up to global phase.

derivations.claim: Initially $U=I\cdot M$ with $M=U$. If a loop iteration records $k$ and sets $M'=HT^{-k}M$, then $M=T^kHM'$. Therefore, after $r$ reductions, the recorded sequence $K=(k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ satisfies $U=(T^{k_1}H)\cdots(T^{k_r}H)M$.

At every iteration, $M$ remains unitary with entries in $D$, since the matrices in [F5] are unitary over $D$. If its exponent exceeds $3$, [F2] ensures that the finite search over $k=0,1,2,3$ finds a value reducing that integer exponent by exactly one. Thus the loop terminates after finitely many iterations with exponent at most $3$.

Let $W_0$ be the table word for the first column of the terminal $M$. Then $W_0^*M$ is unitary with first column $(1,0)^T$, hence is $\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda)$ for a unit scalar $\lambda$. Its entries lie in $D$, so [F3] gives $\lambda=\omega^j$ for some $j\in\{0,\ldots,7\}$. Consequently $M=W_0T^j$.

Substituting this identity into step 1.1 yields exactly the matrix factorization returned in [F1]. The algorithm emits its factors from right to left as a chronological gate list; [F6] says later gates multiply on the left, so that list has the displayed matrix. The final reduction preserves this matrix by [F7], including its scalar factor. Hence the returned word implements $U$ exactly.
