Fix the explicit complete transition-table coding specified below. There are two distinct fixed finite-alphabet probabilistic interpreters, one for the sequential access profile and one for the erased-index head-access-only random-access profile. Each interpreter simulates valid descriptions $e$ with input $x$ and an external binary clock $b$, reproducing exactly the source acceptance or rejection reached in at most $b$ source transitions and rejecting nonhalting expiry. The simulated fair-bit distribution is exact. Writing $n=|x|$ and $L=|e|+1$, there are absolute constants $C,d$ such that each simulation takes time
$$ C L^d\bigl(n+(b+1)\log^d(n+b+L+2)\bigr). $$
For the index-only profile, jump addresses are written on one-way sequential write-only index tapes erased after use; the older nonerasing delimited-head profile is a distinct profile and is not covered by this index-only assertion. The fixed interpreter has a fixed finite physical head count even when the described source head count varies. Malformed descriptions halt rejecting. This is a time simulation; no preservation of the source's simultaneous space bound is asserted.

In particular, for each fixed polynomially bounded time-constructible $T(n)\ge n$ and fixed $c$, descriptions of length at most $c\log(n+2)$ are simulated in either one fixed declared profile in $O(T(n)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n+2))$ time, including the clock constructor. Arbitrary superpolynomial clocks retain the general displayed bound rather than this specialization.

Use fixed finite-control fair-bit probabilistic machines with read-only binary input followed by blanks and a fixed finite number of work tapes and heads, with a finite explicit transition-table code. Each nonhalting transition consumes one independent fair bit as in [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. Fix one access profile for each complexity class.

In the **sequential** profile, heads move locally by at most one cell per transition. In the **erased-index head-access** profile, use the head-access mechanism of the final 2012 Van Melkebeek–Watson model: a zero-initialized binary classical work tape, a fixed finite number of input/work heads, and classical finite control. Each head may move left, right, stay, or jump in one transition to an address computed on a designated one-way sequential-access write-only index tape. Index tapes are initially empty, writing each bit is charged to the ordinary transition count, and an index tape is erased after each use. The original input tape is read-only and contains the input followed by blanks. If coincident work heads make an operation undefined, omit that work-tape operation in the transition. All heads start at the left boundary; left motion there clamps at zero.

The **published VMW derived basis restriction**, denoted the **basis** profile, also permits the classical basis action of the source's native coherent input query. On a contiguous block $[l,r]$ of a specified binary work tape, the first $r-l$ bits give the binary input index $i$ in most-significant-first order and the last cell holds $b$; the query replaces only $b$ by $b\mathbin\oplus x_i$, using zero on invalid input indices. Both endpoints are freshly emitted on erased index tapes. The native query costs one transition, as in the published quantum model. The input indices are $1,\ldots,n$, with $x_0=0$; the empty address word denotes zero, and reversed endpoints cause omission of the query. Allow a fixed finite number of binary work tapes, local operations of fixed finite arity, and native queries on any specified tape: this is the fixed finite product of these classical basis operations, permitting separate path-simulation rows. This is an explicit locally defined comparison model derived from the quantum operations. The source does not separately state a formal classical block-query machine definition, and no equivalence with the index-only profile is assumed. The clocked-normalization lemma proves the required time-only simulation into that profile for clocks at least the input length; no general sublinear-time equivalence is asserted.

For historical comparison, the **preprint-delimited VMW profile** retains the 2007 preprint convention: a jump reads the address written between two classical work-tape heads, without the final paper's write-only erased index tapes. This is a separately named profile. No equivalence or preservation of time/space bounds between the preprint-delimited and published profiles is asserted. Results proved below for the published profile do not establish their extension to the preprint-delimited profile.

Time is the maximum number of transitions on every branch. Sequential space counts distinct visited work cells. Erased-index and basis space use the maximum address of every work cell accessed on any branch, including the highest endpoint of every native basis-query block; read-only input and index tapes are not counted in this maximum-address measure. The preprint-delimited space convention is likewise its maximum visited work-head address. For a fixed profile, $\mathrm{PrTIME}(t)$ uses strict acceptance probability greater than $1/2$ on members and at most $1/2$ on nonmembers; $\mathrm{PrTISP}(t,s)$ adds the stated space bound. Subscripts $\mathrm{seq}$, $\mathrm{index}$, $\mathrm{basis}$, and $\mathrm{preprint}$ distinguish the four profiles. An exact classical oracle is deterministic; writing its queries and returning from them are charged, and total query-string length is at most the outer running time.

For either $P\in\{\mathrm{seq},\mathrm{basis}\}$, define $\mathrm{LCH}_{P,1}=\mathrm{PrTIME}_P(n)$ and $\mathrm{LCH}_{P,j+1}=\mathrm{PrTIME}_P(n)^{\mathrm{LCH}_{P,j}}$. Oracle queries are exact and all fair-bit branches belong to the outer machine. An omitted profile in an item must be fixed explicitly by that item's hypotheses; profiles are never silently identified.

A $\mathrm{MajSAT}$ formula has a fixed finite set of Boolean variables and is accepted when at least half of assignments satisfy it. A $\mathrm{MajMajSAT}$ formula has two disjoint ordered variable blocks and is accepted when at least half of outer assignments leave a residual formula true on at least half of inner assignments. Use a common explicit plain-formula encoding for MajSAT. MajMajSAT accepts this same plain encoding with one implicit fresh unused outer variable and all formula variables in the inner block; it also accepts a separately tagged encoding with the two variable blocks explicitly listed. Thus every plain MajSAT instance embeds identically, bit for bit, into MajMajSAT with unchanged truth value. The unused outer variable is part of the decoded fixed finite variable set. Concretely, use distinct fixed tags for plain and partitioned inputs, a unary declaration of the number of variables, fixed-width variable indices, and prefix-encoded binary AND/OR and unary NOT gates (with constant tokens). The partitioned form also gives the outer-block split; variables are renamed into block order. Plain-format validity is checked by one pending-subexpression counter, variable-range checks and a scan of the declared fields, using $O(n\,\mathrm{polylog}\,n)$ time and $O(\log n)$ workspace. These conventions do not alter either at-least-half threshold. Malformed encodings are rejected by both problems.

derivations.claim: First construct and justify the only balancing procedure used below. An insertion-only AVL tree is a binary search tree with each node storing its key, two child pointers, a parent pointer, height, subtree size and optional OR aggregate. Set the height of an empty subtree to zero. Maintain that the two child heights differ by at most one. A tree of height $h$ has at least $N_h$ nodes, where $N_0=0$, $N_1=1$ and $N_h\ge1+N_{h-1}+N_{h-2}$. For $h\ge2$ this implies $N_h+1\ge2(N_{h-2}+1)$, since the minimum sizes are nondecreasing. Induction therefore gives $N_h+1\ge2^{\lfloor h/2\rfloor}$, so $h\le2\log_2(N_h+1)+1$. Consequently the invariant implies logarithmic root-to-node paths, without any distributional assumption on keys.

Search by the ordinary ordered comparisons. An absent key is inserted as a leaf at the null child where search ends. Retrace its ancestor path, recomputing height, subtree size, and OR aggregate from each node's two children and its own value. Until the first unbalanced ancestor, each subtree height increases by at most one; these metadata updates are required whether or not a rotation occurs. If no ancestor is unbalanced, the height invariant already holds. Otherwise let $z$ be the lowest unbalanced ancestor. Suppose its left height has become two greater than its right height; the opposite case is the left/right reflection. Let $y$ be its left child. The child $y$ cannot have equal child heights: if its new child heights were $t,t$, one child would be unchanged at $t$, so its old maximum child height would already have been $t$ and its own height would not have increased. Thus the new child heights of $y$ differ by one. If $y$ is left-heavy, write the heights of its left subtree, its right subtree and $z$'s right subtree as $t+1,t,t$. Rotate right at $z$, making $y$ the root of this local subtree. Its right child is now $z$, whose two child heights are $t,t$, hence whose height is $t+1$; $y$'s two child heights are both $t+1$, hence its height is $t+2$. Recompute the fields of the rotated nodes bottom-up, then continue the metadata updates above the repaired subtree. All local balances are valid. The old pre-insertion subtree at $z$ also had height $t+2$, so this restores that old height. [step 1.1, construct]

In the remaining left-heavy case, $y$ is right-heavy. Let $w$ be $y$'s right child. Write the heights of $y$'s left subtree and $z$'s right subtree as $t,t$. The two child subtrees of $w$ have heights each at most $t$, at least $t-1$ when nonempty as required by AVL balance, and maximum $t$. Rotate left at $y$, then right at $z$, making $w$ the local root. Its left child $y$ now has child heights $t$ and at most $t$ differing by at most one, hence height $t+1$; its right child $z$ has the analogous heights and also height $t+1$. The root $w$ has height $t+2$, again the old pre-insertion height at $z$. This also covers $t=0$, where the relevant empty children have height zero. The right-heavy cases are exact reflections. Rotations preserve the in-order key sequence: the single rotation changes $((A,y,B),z,C)$ to $(A,y,(B,z,C))$, and the double rotation changes $((A,y,(B,w,C)),z,D)$ to $((A,y,B),w,(C,z,D))$. All nodes retain their stable identities, while a constant number of child/parent pointers change. After this first repair the subtree's old height is restored, so higher ancestors cannot acquire a new imbalance. Recompute height, size and OR first on the lower rotated nodes, then their new root, and then along the remaining ancestor path. Thus search and insertion use $O(\log(N+2))$ node operations, and maintain all stated fields. This proves the needed AVL result locally; no deletions will be used.

For each virtual binary work tape keep an **outer** insertion-only AVL tree whose keys are canonical numerical block prefixes $P$ in the representation $a=PB+r$, $0\le r<B$. Each outer node has a permanent compact block ID equal to its stable allocation ID. Store a canonical binary prefix word and its length at that node. To compare a freshly supplied prefix of length $A'$ with a stored prefix, first compare their lengths, which are short integers. If unequal this decides numerical order; if equal compare their $A'$ bits lexicographically. Each comparison costs $O(A'+\log H+\log L)$ elementary short-address/bit operations, including access to the stored key. Search/insertion makes $O(\log(N+2))$ such comparisons by step 1.1 and step 2.1 and step 3.1. Only head-jump or query-endpoint registration requires such a fresh-key search. As in [F1], on every registration also register $P-1$ if nonnegative and $P+1$, whose canonical words can be formed by ordinary scans in $O(A'+1)$ work. The sum of all these key lengths is $L^{O(1)}(b+1)$ by fresh-index charging in [F1]; duplicate keys are not stored twice. This bounds all long-prefix reading and key comparison costs by $L^{O(1)}(b+1)\mathrm{polylog}\,H$. Initial prefix zero and its neighbor one add only fixed keys per virtual tape.

Every outer node owns an **inner** insertion-only AVL tree of all offsets so far accessed in that block. Its keys are $s$-bit offsets; its node stores the current binary cell value. Keep nodes even when their value becomes zero, so deletion is unnecessary. The inner subtree OR is the OR of its nodes' cell values. The outer node's own OR is its inner root's OR, or zero for an empty inner tree; its subtree OR combines its own OR and the two outer child subtree ORs. A new cell is initially zero, and then receives any prescribed write. Each source local operation accesses only $L^{O(1)}$ cells. A query will access at most $k+1$ individual cells in addition to its range-OR operation below. Hence the number of inner nodes is at most $L^{O(1)}(b+1)(k+1)$. Searching/inserting an offset costs $O(\log(N+2))$ comparisons of $s$-bit keys. A bit-value change recomputes OR along its inner ancestor path and then along its owning outer node's ancestor path; rotations maintain the same aggregates by step 3.1. Thus one short-offset access/write costs $L^{O(1)}\mathrm{polylog}\,H$ physical work. Unregistered prefixes and absent offsets represent zero cells.

The parent pointers and subtree sizes allow numerical comparisons of **already registered** block IDs without rereading their possibly long keys. Compute the in-order rank of a known node $v$ as its left-subtree size plus one, then ascend to the root, adding one plus the ancestor's left-subtree size whenever the current node is that ancestor's right child. Every node visited contributes exactly the keys preceding $v$ that lie in the corresponding ancestor piece, so the result is the exact one-based numerical rank. This uses $O(\log(N+2))$ short-record operations by step 1.1. Stable node IDs and current parent/size fields remain valid after rotations. No insertion occurs while the ranks of one operation are being used. Two compact cell addresses are compared by these outer ranks and then their short offsets. Local head moves use the same three cached adjacent-prefix IDs as [F1]: between source jumps a head travels at most $b<B$ cells, so cannot leave those three blocks. In particular repeated crossings of a block boundary cost only short-offset arithmetic and cached-ID selection. They never incur another long-prefix comparison.

Prove the range-OR procedure explicitly. In an AVL tree whose nodes have in-order ranks, sizes and OR aggregates, the OR of a contiguous rank interval is obtainable in $O(\log(N+2))$ node visits. At a subtree, its root rank and child rank intervals are computed from a carried starting rank and the left size. If a subtree's whole rank interval is inside the query interval, use its stored aggregate; if disjoint, skip it; otherwise recurse on the intersecting children and include the root's own value if its rank is in the interval. At each depth only subtrees containing one of the two query boundaries can require recursion: at most two partially intersected subtrees, together with at most a constant number of their fully included/disjoint children. Thus total visits are $O(\text{height}+1)$. Inner offset trees use ordinary $s$-bit key comparisons to locate offset bounds, with the same procedure or the corresponding two boundary paths. For a source address interval $[a,c)$, if both endpoints have the same block ID, query that inner offset interval. If their block IDs differ, OR the suffix of the left inner tree, the prefix of the right inner tree, and the outer subtree range strictly between their numerical ranks. Registered endpoint prefixes exist by registration, even if their inner trees are empty. All untouched cells contribute zero. This computes exactly the OR of every source work bit in $[a,c)$, including arbitrarily large gaps of unvisited zero cells, in $L^{O(1)}\mathrm{polylog}\,H$ work.

Realize the data structures in the index-only target by the fixed physical protocol in [F1]. Source index words occupy separate $b+1$-cell reserved regions; arithmetic reservation does not scan them. Store the long prefix words in append-allocated arrays. Allocate each outer/inner node as a fixed-width binary record with short child/parent pointers, height/size, current bit or inner-root pointer, and OR fields. The outer-node count and total long-key length are $L^{O(1)}(b+1)$; the inner-node count is $L^{O(1)}(b+1)\log H$. All record lengths are $L^{O(1)}\log H$, so the largest physical address is $L^{O(1)}(b+1)\log^{O(1)}H$. Select a padded pointer width $q=K(s+\lceil\log_2 L\rceil+1)$ for a sufficiently large absolute $K$; the preceding bound is smaller than $2^q$. Every pointer, height, size and low-offset arithmetic operand fits in polynomially many $q$-bit fields. A constant number of fixed physical heads, reserved scratch regions, emitted short erased input/work indices and ordinary local scans implements each elementary node or array-bit operation in $L^{O(1)}\mathrm{polylog}\,H$ transitions, as in [F1]. No extra physical head per source head, arbitrary alphabet extension, unit-cost large-integer operation, or long uncharged address is used.

On a source basis query, consume and register the two fresh endpoint index words, with their neighboring prefixes, as in step 4.1. Save the answer bit at address $v$. Starting from endpoint $v$, take at most $k$ virtual predecessor steps, stopping at $u$. Each predecessor uses only short-offset arithmetic and the cached three-prefix neighborhood of $v$, because $k\le b<B$ for $n\ge1$; when $n=0$, $k=0$ and no predecessor step is needed. Record the encountered bits, in reverse order, to obtain the last $\min(k,v-u)$ address bits. Comparisons with $u$ use compact ranks/offsets from step 5.2, not long key strings. Let $p$ be the position reached, namely $\max(u,v-k)$. Query range-OR on $[u,p)$ using step 6.1. If that OR is one, some address bit more significant than the last $k$ bits is nonzero, so the query address is at least $2^k>n$ and the answer must stay unchanged. If it is zero, the entire numerical input address is the recorded low word, padded with leading zeros to $k$ bits. Compare that short integer $i$ with $1$ and $n$. Outside $1\le i\le n$, leave the answer unchanged; inside this range, emit the physical input address for bit $i$ (subtract one, then add any fixed paired-input encoding offset) on the index-only target's ordinary input index tape, make the native classical input read, and XOR the retrieved input bit into the saved answer cell. In the empty-address case $u=v$, the low word is zero and $x_0=0$ as specified. This exactly implements $Q_x$ on all basis work configurations, while never invoking a block query in the target. The source address register can be reused indefinitely; each operation uses aggregates and short accesses rather than rescanning that register.

The charged long-prefix operations total $L^{O(1)}(b+1)\mathrm{polylog}\,H$ by step 4.1. Each source transition additionally uses $L^{O(1)}\mathrm{polylog}\,H$ for finite-table lookup, short head updates, collisions, ordinary cell reads/writes, and at most one fixed finite number of basis queries. A basis query contributes at most $k=O(\log(b+2))$ short cell accesses, a constant number of rank/range-OR operations, and a short emitted input index, all bounded by the same type of polylogarithmic factor. Multiply by the short-record physical cost from step 6.2, add the $O(n)$ input-length scan and polynomial code initialization, and enlarge the absolute exponent $d$ to obtain the theorem's bound. The same allocation bound proves the asserted time-scale maximum address. This is solely a time normalization; the dictionary need not respect a smaller original source space bound.

Use [F1]'s external-clock driver: test halting before expiry, consume one designated fresh fair bit for the next source table, save the complete source instructions, and apply their operations with the source's simultaneous-action and collision conventions. Ordinary source operations are exact by [F1] and the compact numerical address/value invariants; a source block query is exact by step 7.1. Induction reproduces the entire source basis configuration after each simulated transition. All added dictionary, balancing, rank, OR and input-read work is deterministic. Ignoring physical fair bits except the designated source choices therefore preserves every consumed source prefix's probability $2^{-j}$; summing disjoint terminal prefixes preserves acceptance, rejection and timeout probabilities exactly. A halt on transition $b$ is reported, and nonhalting expiry rejects.

For descriptions of length $O(\log(n+2))$ and fixed polynomially bounded clocks $b=T(n)\ge n$, both $L$ and $\log H$ are polylogarithmic in $n+2$, so step 8.1 gives $O(T(n)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n+2))$ time. A fixed deterministic clock constructor can first be simulated by the already proved index-only external-clock interpreter with doubling budgets, as in the combined clocked candidate, with total time $O(T(n)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n+2))$. The resulting index-only target is included in the basis-query profile. Thus the time-hierarchy diagonal can use this normalized interpreter in the basis-query profile, and Cook-style trace encodings can use its bounded-address index-only computation. This does not identify sublinear-time basis-query and index-only classes, and transports no original source-space bound.

Use fixed finite-control fair-bit probabilistic machines with read-only binary input followed by blanks and a fixed finite number of work tapes and heads, with a finite explicit transition-table code. Each nonhalting transition consumes one independent fair bit as in [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. Fix one access profile for each complexity class.

In the **sequential** profile, heads move locally by at most one cell per transition. In the **erased-index head-access** profile, use the head-access mechanism of the final 2012 Van Melkebeek–Watson model: a zero-initialized binary classical work tape, a fixed finite number of input/work heads, and classical finite control. Each head may move left, right, stay, or jump in one transition to an address computed on a designated one-way sequential-access write-only index tape. Index tapes are initially empty, writing each bit is charged to the ordinary transition count, and an index tape is erased after each use. The original input tape is read-only and contains the input followed by blanks. If coincident work heads make an operation undefined, omit that work-tape operation in the transition. All heads start at the left boundary; left motion there clamps at zero.

The **published VMW derived basis restriction**, denoted the **basis** profile, also permits the classical basis action of the source's native coherent input query. On a contiguous block $[l,r]$ of a specified binary work tape, the first $r-l$ bits give the binary input index $i$ in most-significant-first order and the last cell holds $b$; the query replaces only $b$ by $b\mathbin\oplus x_i$, using zero on invalid input indices. Both endpoints are freshly emitted on erased index tapes. The native query costs one transition, as in the published quantum model. The input indices are $1,\ldots,n$, with $x_0=0$; the empty address word denotes zero, and reversed endpoints cause omission of the query. Allow a fixed finite number of binary work tapes, local operations of fixed finite arity, and native queries on any specified tape: this is the fixed finite product of these classical basis operations, permitting separate path-simulation rows. This is an explicit locally defined comparison model derived from the quantum operations. The source does not separately state a formal classical block-query machine definition, and no equivalence with the index-only profile is assumed. The clocked-normalization lemma proves the required time-only simulation into that profile for clocks at least the input length; no general sublinear-time equivalence is asserted.

For historical comparison, the **preprint-delimited VMW profile** retains the 2007 preprint convention: a jump reads the address written between two classical work-tape heads, without the final paper's write-only erased index tapes. This is a separately named profile. No equivalence or preservation of time/space bounds between the preprint-delimited and published profiles is asserted. Results proved below for the published profile do not establish their extension to the preprint-delimited profile.

Time is the maximum number of transitions on every branch. Sequential space counts distinct visited work cells. Erased-index and basis space use the maximum address of every work cell accessed on any branch, including the highest endpoint of every native basis-query block; read-only input and index tapes are not counted in this maximum-address measure. The preprint-delimited space convention is likewise its maximum visited work-head address. For a fixed profile, $\mathrm{PrTIME}(t)$ uses strict acceptance probability greater than $1/2$ on members and at most $1/2$ on nonmembers; $\mathrm{PrTISP}(t,s)$ adds the stated space bound. Subscripts $\mathrm{seq}$, $\mathrm{index}$, $\mathrm{basis}$, and $\mathrm{preprint}$ distinguish the four profiles. An exact classical oracle is deterministic; writing its queries and returning from them are charged, and total query-string length is at most the outer running time.

For either $P\in\{\mathrm{seq},\mathrm{basis}\}$, define $\mathrm{LCH}_{P,1}=\mathrm{PrTIME}_P(n)$ and $\mathrm{LCH}_{P,j+1}=\mathrm{PrTIME}_P(n)^{\mathrm{LCH}_{P,j}}$. Oracle queries are exact and all fair-bit branches belong to the outer machine. An omitted profile in an item must be fixed explicitly by that item's hypotheses; profiles are never silently identified.

A $\mathrm{MajSAT}$ formula has a fixed finite set of Boolean variables and is accepted when at least half of assignments satisfy it. A $\mathrm{MajMajSAT}$ formula has two disjoint ordered variable blocks and is accepted when at least half of outer assignments leave a residual formula true on at least half of inner assignments. Use a common explicit plain-formula encoding for MajSAT. MajMajSAT accepts this same plain encoding with one implicit fresh unused outer variable and all formula variables in the inner block; it also accepts a separately tagged encoding with the two variable blocks explicitly listed. Thus every plain MajSAT instance embeds identically, bit for bit, into MajMajSAT with unchanged truth value. The unused outer variable is part of the decoded fixed finite variable set. Concretely, use distinct fixed tags for plain and partitioned inputs, a unary declaration of the number of variables, fixed-width variable indices, and prefix-encoded binary AND/OR and unary NOT gates (with constant tokens). The partitioned form also gives the outer-block split; variables are renamed into block order. Plain-format validity is checked by one pending-subexpression counter, variable-range checks and a scan of the declared fields, using $O(n\,\mathrm{polylog}\,n)$ time and $O(\log n)$ workspace. These conventions do not alter either at-least-half threshold. Malformed encodings are rejected by both problems.

derivations.claim: Store each simulated binary work tape unchanged on a physical binary tape, initially zero, and maintain its fixed finite head addresses with $O(\log(n+2))$-bit counters. Since all work accesses are below $M$, every valid work-head/index endpoint value is bounded by $M$. Accumulate a freshly emitted source index bit by shift-and-append, saturating work indices at $M$ and ordinary input-head indices at $N+T+1$. A work overflow cannot be used on the promised run; appending bits cannot undo it. An overflowing input jump remains outside the input for every remaining local step, so a FAR marker returns blank until the next jump. Index lengths and emitted contents are unread except on use; these numeric summaries and resets therefore implement exactly their observable effects. Each counter operation, short physical index emission, head read/write and input-position comparison costs polylogarithmic time and logarithmic workspace. Physical input-head read at position $i<N$ calls the generator of $y_i(x)$, using charged short erased indices for its source-input reads. Outside that range it returns blank.

For each simulated work tape keep a second zero-initialized binary tape containing the heap representation of a complete binary OR tree with $M$ leaves. Leaf $M+a$ stores work bit $a$ for $0\le a<M$, and internal node $j$ stores the OR of nodes $2j,2j+1$. Initially every value is zero, matching the source; no initialization sweep is needed. When work bit $a$ changes, update its leaf and ascend through $\lfloor j/2\rfloor$ to the root, recomputing each OR from its two children. At most $1+\log_2M$ nodes are visited; every address is below $2M$ and takes $O(\log(n+2))$ bits to emit. Thus an update costs polylogarithmic time with only a fixed number of logarithmic counters. The invariant follows inductively because only ancestors of the changed leaf can change. Arbitrarily many zero cells require no explicit allocation or stored pointers.

The OR of work interval $[l,r)$ is found in at most $2\log_2M+2$ tree-node reads. Start with $L=M+l$, $R=M+r$. If $L$ is odd include node $L$ and increment $L$; if $R$ is odd decrement $R$ and include that node. Replace both by their integer halves and repeat until equal. At each stage the included fringe nodes are disjoint, and the remaining uncovered interval is the union of the complete sibling pairs between the updated endpoints; halving replaces precisely those pairs by their parents. Induction proves that the included nodes partition exactly the original leaf interval. Each level includes at most two nodes, and there are at most $1+\log_2M$ levels. Their stored OR is therefore exactly the requested range OR. The procedure uses logarithmic counters and polylogarithmic time.

Implement a native source query with $u\le v$ as follows. Put $k=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil$, and inspect the last $\min(k,v-u)$ address bits immediately before $v$, using short physical addresses. Let $p=\max(u,v-k)$. Query the tree OR of $[u,p)$. If it is one, the binary input address is at least $2^k>N$, so the native query leaves its answer unchanged. Otherwise the entire numerical address is the inspected low word, padded with leading zeros to $k$ bits. For $1\le i\le N$, generate $y_{i-1}(x)$ and XOR it into work bit $v$, then update that tape's OR tree as in step 2.1. For an invalid index leave the answer unchanged. The empty address gives zero and hence no change, and reversed endpoints are omitted as specified by [F1]. Only $O(\log(n+2))$ work-bit reads, a range-OR query, one generator call and one update are needed. Every accessed physical work/tree address is $O(M)$, and only logarithmic scratch is used. The source address word can be reused indefinitely; the maintained tree avoids rescanning its long high part.

Ordinary source local operations change only a fixed finite number of bits, so apply step 2.1 to each changed bit after taking the source's simultaneous reads and respecting its collision rule. Source input queries are exact by step 1.1 and step 4.1, and all head/index transitions are exact by step 1.1. Induction on the source clock therefore gives the identical source configurations and branch outcomes, with the harmless FAR summary of permanently blank input positions. The simulator takes exactly one designated independent fair bit per source transition and ignores all its other physical fair bits; each source choice prefix has its original mass $2^{-j}$. All auxiliary work is deterministic, so outcomes and acceptance probabilities are identical. At most a polylogarithmic amount of work is done per transition, plus the initial $O(n)$ input-length setup. Source work and OR trees have extent $O(M)$ on fixed finitely many tapes, and every generator/counter needs $O(\log(n+2))$ workspace. These are exactly the claimed time and space bounds.

derivations.claim: Two-word addition has the following constant-depth Boolean construction. For $d$-bit words $a,b$, put $g_j=a_j\wedge b_j$ and $p_j=a_j\vee b_j$. The carry entering bit $k>0$ is $$c_k=\bigvee_{0\le j<k}\left(g_j\wedge\bigwedge_{j<t<k}p_t\right),\qquad c_0=0.$$ A carry is generated by two ones, propagated through positions with at least one one, and killed by two zeros; this proves the formula. The output bit is the XOR of $a_k,b_k,c_k$, computed by its constant-size Boolean truth table, with the final carry appended. These formulas have constant depth and polynomial size, and predecessor tests use equality and order on their bit-position addresses.

For $m\ge2$, let $\ell=\lceil\log_2m\rceil$, let $b$ be the least power of two at least $\ell$, and put $B=2^b$. Then $m\le B\le m^2$. Split each input into consecutive $b$-bit blocks and pad the last block with zeros. For block $q$, define $$S_q=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{r=0}^{b-1}2^r x_{i,qb+r}.$$ Its upper bound is $C=m(B-1)$, polynomial in $mw$.

To compute all bits of $S_q$, pad the row domain to a power of two $M_0\ge m$ with $M_0<2m$. Create a rectangular set of distinct copy gates $(i,r,t)$ with $0\le i<M_0$, $0\le r<b$, and $0\le t<B$. Gates with $i\ge m$ or $t\ge2^r$ are zero; otherwise they copy $x_{i,qb+r}$. There are $D=M_0bB$ slots, a power of two polynomial in $mw$, and exactly $S_q$ slots are true. For each $1\le h\le D$, feed these slots and $D+1$ distinct constant slots to a MAJ gate, with exactly $D-h+1$ constant slots equal to one. Its odd fan-in is $2D+1$, so under either convention for majority it tests $S_q+(D-h+1)\ge D+1$, equivalently $S_q\ge h$. Write this output as $T_{q,h}$ and set $T_{q,0}=1$, $T_{q,D+1}=0$. Then $E_{q,h}=T_{q,h}\wedge\neg T_{q,h+1}$ tests $S_q=h$, and bit $u$ of $S_q$ is the OR of $E_{q,h}$ over the indices $h$ having bit $u$ equal to one. The depth is constant and the size polynomial.

Write $S_q=r_q+Bv_q$. Since $r_q<B$ and $v_q<m\le B$, form two words: $R$ has block $q$ equal to $r_q$, and $V$ has block $q+1$ equal to $v_q$ and block zero zero. These bits are direct selections from the bits computed in step 2.1. The blocks do not overlap within either word, and $$\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}x_i=\sum_q S_q B^q=R+V.$$ Apply step 1.1 once to $R,V$. This is a constant number of constant-depth stages of polynomial total size.

We verify uniformity explicitly. Use fixed-length tuples with a constant number of $O(\log(mw+2))$-bit fields for gate type, block, row, within-block bit, copy, threshold, output-bit and constant-slot indices. All predecessor predicates in step 1.1 and step 1.2 and step 2.1 and step 3.1 use equality, order, the bit predicate on $h$, $t<2^r$, the constant-slot test $u<D-h+1$, and $j=qb+r$. Since $b$ is a power of two, the last relation is a shift and concatenation. The exponent of the power of two $D=M_0bB$ is the sum of the corresponding bit-length exponents. Testing $t<2^r$ compares $r$ with the highest nonzero bit position of $t$. Determine the field widths and $b$ from the binary dimensions and perform these tests by a constant number of linear scans, additions, subtractions, shifts and comparisons of $O(\log(mw+2))$-bit words. Each gate-type or predecessor query takes $O(\log(mw+2))$ time on the random-access uniformity machine; no general multiplication of two varying address fields is used. Dimensions and coordinate domains are padded to powers of two, and positions outside the actual input bounds are constant zero. For $m=1$, copy the input word. Finally $\sum_i x_i<m2^w\le2^{w+\lceil\log_2m\rceil}$, so the retained output width is exactly the one in the Statement.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

derivations.claim: Choose $x\in O$ and $r>0$ with the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)\subseteq O$. Put $s=r/(2\sqrt m)>0$ and let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^m[x_j-s/2,x_j+s/2]$. For every $y\in Q$, $\|y-x\|_2\le\sqrt m\,s/2=r/4<r$, so $Q\subseteq O$ and $\operatorname{vol}(Q)=s^m>0$.

Suppose $O$ were null. By [F1], with $\varepsilon=s^m/4$ there is a sequence of closed cubes $C_i$ covering $Q$ whose side lengths $\ell_i\ge0$ have $\sum_i\ell_i^m\le s^m/4$. For each $i\ge0$, set $\delta_i=\min\{1,\,s^m2^{-i-5}/(3^m(1+\ell_i)^{m-1})\}$ and enlarge $C_i$ concentrically to an open cube $C_i'$ of side $\ell_i+2\delta_i$. By [F6] and $\delta_i\le1$, $0\le\Delta_i:=(\ell_i+2\delta_i)^m-\ell_i^m\le d_i:=s^m2^{-i-5}$. For every $N\ge0$, induction using the finite-sum recursion gives $\sum_{i<N}d_i=s^m(1-2^{-N})/16\le s^m/16$. Thus every partial sum of the nonnegative enlarged-cost sequence $b_i=(\ell_i+2\delta_i)^m=\ell_i^m+\Delta_i$ satisfies $\sum_{i<N}b_i\le s^m/4+s^m/16=5s^m/16$, by [F4] and [F5]. A second application of [F5] gives a convergent total enlarged-cost series with sum at most $5s^m/16<s^m/2$.

The open cubes $C_i'$ cover the closed box $Q$, so [F2] gives a finite subcover $C_{i_1}',\ldots,C_{i_t}'$. Order its indices increasingly and take $N$ larger than the largest one. By [F4], the subcover's total cost is at most $\sum_{i<N}b_i$, which is at most $5s^m/16<s^m/2$ by step 2.1.

Write $\overline{C_i'}$ for the closed cube with the same center and side as $C_i'$, so $\operatorname{vol}(\overline{C_i'})=b_i$. Cut $Q$ and these finitely many closed covering cubes at all their coordinate endpoints. The positive-side grid cells inside $Q$ partition it; the interior of each cell lies in one covering cube because no covering-cube boundary crosses the cell. Assign each cell to the least index of a covering cube containing its interior. By finite cut-additivity from [F3], the assigned cells for each cube have total volume at most that closed cube's volume, while all cells sum to $\operatorname{vol}(Q)=s^m$. Thus $s^m\le\sum_{j=1}^t\operatorname{vol}(\overline{C_{i_j}'})<s^m/2$, a contradiction. Therefore $O$ is not null.

citations.quote:
Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the
plane of pairs of naturals is countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

The bijection is exhibited, not merely asserted to exist. Define $2^m$ by
recursion on $m$ ([[thm-recursion]]) by $2^0 = 1$ and $2^{\sigma(m)} = 2^m + 2^m$,
and set

$$J(m,n) = 2^m \cdot \sigma(n + n), \qquad \text{that is} \qquad J(m,n) = 2^m(2n+1).$$

Then $J$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, and $\sigma$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, so $\sigma^{-1} \circ J$ is a bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. What makes $J$ bijective is the
decomposition of a nonzero natural into a power of two times an odd number,
existence and uniqueness both.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

**Addition** $+ : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by
recursion on the second argument: for each fixed $m \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$m + 0 = m, \qquad m + \sigma(n) = \sigma(m + n).$$

For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, define the **order** by

$$m \le n \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{N}\ (m + k = n),$$

and the **strict order** by $m < n \iff (m \le n \text{ and } m \neq n)$, using
addition ([[def-nat-addition]]).
The relation $\le$ on $\mathbb{N}$, where $m \le n \iff \exists k\ (m + k = n)$ ([[def-nat-order]]), is a linear (total) order: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, and total.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

derivations.claim: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be compact and null, and let $\eta>0$. If $K=\varnothing$, the empty family covers it. Otherwise [F1] gives a countable closed-cube cover $(C_j)$ with total volume at most $\eta/8$. Write $C_j=\prod_{r<m}[a_{jr},a_{jr}+\ell_j]$ and let $x_{jr}=a_{jr}+\ell_j/2$ be its center coordinates. Set $\delta_j=\min\{1,\eta2^{-j-5}/(3^m(1+\ell_j)^{m-1})\}$ and let $C'_j=\prod_{r<m}(x_{jr}-(\ell_j+2\delta_j)/2,x_{jr}+(\ell_j+2\delta_j)/2)$, an open concentric enlargement. By [F11], $(\ell_j+2\delta_j)^m-\ell_j^m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\iota\binom mr\ell_j^{m-r}(2\delta_j)^r\le\delta_j(1+\ell_j)^{m-1}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\iota\binom mr2^r<3^m\delta_j(1+\ell_j)^{m-1}\le\eta2^{-j-5}$, because $\delta_j^r\le\delta_j$, $\ell_j^{m-r}\le(1+\ell_j)^{m-1}$ and $\sum_{r=1}^m\iota\binom mr2^r=3^m-1$. Define the covering cost of an open cube of side $s$ to be $s^m$; this agrees with [F5] for its closed counterpart. Put $d_j=\eta2^{-j-5}$ and $b_j=(\ell_j+2\delta_j)^m=\ell_j^m+\Delta_j$, where $0\le\Delta_j\le d_j$. For every $N\ge0$, induction using [F9] gives $\sum_{j<N}d_j=\eta(1-2^{-N})/16\le\eta/16$: the formula is $0$ at $N=0$, and the successor step adds $\eta2^{-N-5}$. By [F7], the original nonnegative volume series has every partial sum at most $\eta/8$. Finite-sum additivity and monotonicity [F10] therefore give $\sum_{j<N}b_j\le\eta/8+\sum_{j<N}d_j\le3\eta/16$ for every $N$. Since $b_j\ge0$, [F7] gives a convergent total covering-cost series with sum at most $3\eta/16<\eta/4$. The open cubes cover $K$, and compactness [F2] gives a finite subcover.

Order the finite subcover by its original indices and write $L_r$ and $x_r$ for the side and center of its $r$th open cube. Its finite total cost is at most the partial sum of $(b_j)$ through its largest original index, hence at most $3\eta/16<\eta/4$ by [F7, F10, step 1.1]. The finite polynomial sum $\sum_r(L_r+\zeta)^m$ is continuous at $\zeta=0$, so choose $\zeta>0$ for which it is less than $\sum_rL_r^m+\eta/8<3\eta/8$. By [F4], choose rational $q_r$ with $L_r<q_r<L_r+\zeta$ and a rational center $y_r\in\mathbb Q^m$ whose coordinates differ from $x_r$ by less than $(q_r-L_r)/4$. The closed rational cube of side $q_r$ centered at $y_r$ contains the open cube of side $L_r$ centered at $x_r$, since each coordinate displacement is less than $L_r/2+(q_r-L_r)/4<q_r/2$. These finitely many rational cubes cover $K$, and their total volume is less than $3\eta/8<\eta/2$ by [F5].

Fix a bijection $\nu:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q$ and a pairing bijection $\pi:\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N$ from [F3]. A list of $t$ rational cubes is determined by $(m+1)t$ rationals: its side and its $m$ center coordinates for each cube. Encode a tuple $(a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1})\in\mathbb N^r$ recursively by $c_0=0$ and $c_{r+1}(a_0,\ldots,a_r)=\pi(a_0,c_r(a_1,\ldots,a_r))$. Since $\pi$ and $\nu$ are injective, pairing the list length $t$ with the code of its $(m+1)t$ rational coordinates gives an injection from all finite rational cube lists into $\mathbb N$. For each natural code, use its unique list preimage if it has one, and otherwise use the empty list; this defines an enumeration $(\mathcal C_s)_{s\ge0}$ that includes every list. By step 2.1, every compact null $K$ has at least one enumerated list covering it with total volume less than $\eta/2$. The set of qualifying codes is nonempty, so it has a least member by [F6]. The least-code rule assigns a unique cover to each pair $(K,\eta)$ without choosing from an arbitrary family.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $i\ge0$, apply the unique rule of step 3.1 to $(K_i,\eta_i)$ with $\eta_i=\varepsilon2^{-i-1}$. Let $t_i$ be the finite length of its selected list, whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon2^{-i-2}$. Define $N_0=0$ and $N_{i+1}=N_i+t_i$ recursively as in [F8]. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, if $N_i\le n<N_{i+1}$ for some $i$, take the cube at position $n-N_i$ in the $i$th list; otherwise take the degenerate zero-side cube at the origin. The half-open index intervals are disjoint: if $i<j$, then $N_{i+1}\le N_j$, so no $n$ lies in both. Each cube of the $i$th list, at position $j<t_i$, occurs at index $N_i+j$; thus every selected list occurs in the sequence.

Any finite initial segment meets only finitely many blocks. If it meets none, its total volume is zero. Otherwise, its finite set of block indices has a largest member $r$: scan the finite list and retain the larger at each comparison using the linear order in [F8]. Each partial block costs at most its full-list bound from step 4.1. By [F9], the budget sum $B_r=\sum_{i=0}^{r}\varepsilon2^{-i-2}$ satisfies $B_0=\varepsilon/4=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-1})$ and $B_{r+1}=B_r+\varepsilon2^{-r-3}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-r-1})+\varepsilon2^{-r-3}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-r-2})$. So induction gives $B_r=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-r-1})<\varepsilon/2$. Thus every partial sum of the nonnegative volume series is at most $\varepsilon/2$, and [F7] gives convergence with total at most $\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$. The sequence covers $\bigcup_iK_i$, so [F1] shows that this union is null. Since every selected list is assigned by the unique least-code rule of step 3.1, the proof uses no choice principle.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 handles K=empty using the empty finite cover, whose total cost is zero.
Step 1.1 admits zero-side cubes in the initial null cover and enlarges each by a positive delta_j before compactness.
Steps 4.1-5.1 cover a one-term sequence of compact null sets; the resulting cover has total volume below epsilon.
Step 1.1 handles an empty set and degenerate input cubes, while the positive enlargement gives open cubes for the finite subcover.
Step 2.1 replaces the finite open subcover by closed rational cubes that contain it, so boundary points remain covered.
Steps 3.1-5.1 use the least qualifying rational-cover code and a fixed sequence construction, avoiding a countable choice of covers.

For an integer $D\ge1$ and unit vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^D$, write $[u]$ and $[v]$ for their pure-state rays and define the projective chord distance by

$$d_{\mathrm{ch}}([u],[v])=\inf_{|\lambda|=1}\|u-\lambda v\|_2.$$

Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the norm induced by the root inner product, which is linear in its first argument. The infimum is over unit complex scalars, so it removes only the common phase of a state vector. The companion lemma [[lem-qc-projective-chord-distance-formula]] evaluates this infimum, proves it is attained, gives the closed formula, and proves independence from the chosen unit representatives.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Two nonzero vectors $x,y\in H$ represent the same **ray** when $y=\alpha x$ for some nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb C$. A **pure state** is such a ray. If $u$ is a unit representative, its associated operator is $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$, with the bra, ket and outer-product convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. The theorem [[thm-qc-ray-projector-well-defined-and-bijective]] proves that this operator is a rank-one orthogonal projection independent of the chosen unit representative, so it is the operator representative of the pure state.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Put $c=\langle v,u\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$. For every $|\lambda|=1$, expand by [F2]: $\|u-\lambda v\|_2^2=2-\overline\lambda\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}-\lambda\langle v,u\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}=2-2\operatorname{Re}(\lambda c)$.

If $c=0$, the real part is zero for every unit $\lambda$; if $c\ne0$, choose $\lambda=\overline c/|c|$, giving $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda c)=|c|$. Since $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda c)\le|c|$ for every unit $\lambda$, this phase attains the infimum in [F1]; the value is $\sqrt{2-2|c|}$, a real nonnegative number by [F4].

Replacing $u$ and $v$ by unit scalar multiples changes $\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$ by a unit scalar, so its modulus and the displayed value do not change. Since the infimum is attained, it is zero exactly when a minimizing phase satisfies $u=\lambda v$, which is exactly equality of the represented rays by [F3].

boundaries.reason: The Statement is conditional on a given pair of unit vectors, not an empty-family assertion.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 treats c=0 directly: every phase gives squared distance 2 and the formula gives sqrt(2).
At |c|=1, Cauchy–Schwarz equality and step 3.1 identify the vectors as the same ray, whose distance is zero.
The argument includes D=1 and collinear unit vectors; step 3.1 reduces zero distance exactly to phase proportionality.
Fact F4 and step 2.1 bound |c| between 0 and 1, so the square root is real at both overlap endpoints.
Step 2.1 gives an explicit minimizing phase: any unit phase when c=0 and conjugate(c)/|c| otherwise.
The forward implication from zero distance to the same ray follows from attainment in step 3.1.
The reverse implication follows because same-ray unit representatives differ by a unit phase, which makes the infimum zero in step 3.1.

risk_review.notes: All three steps independently checked with the linear-first root pairing: expansion uses c=<v,u>, minimizing phase is conjugate(c)/|c|, c=0 is handled, Cauchy-Schwarz makes the radical nonnegative. Independent unit rescaling preserves modulus; attained zero distance is exactly equality of rays. No defect or edit.

For an integer $D\ge1$, let $\mathbb{CP}^{D-1}$ be the quotient of $\mathbb C^D\setminus\{0\}$ by $z\sim w$ when $w=\lambda z$ for a nonzero complex scalar $\lambda$. Give $\mathbb C^D\setminus\{0\}$ its usual Euclidean topology and the quotient the topology in which a subset is open exactly when its inverse image is open. Every nonzero ray has a unit representative, and two unit representatives of one ray differ by a unit scalar, so this is the pure-state ray space of [[def-qc-pure-state-and-ray]].

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,D-1\}$ define the standard patch $U_j=\{[z]\in\mathbb{CP}^{D-1}:z_j\ne0\}$ and the candidate coordinate map $\phi_j([z])=(z_i/z_j)_{i\ne j}$, with the coordinates kept in increasing original index order. Its candidate inverse sends $w\in\mathbb C^{D-1}$ to the ray of the vector with $j$th coordinate $1$ and other coordinates given by $w$ in that same order. [[thm-qc-projective-chart-dimension]] proves these are smooth charts, computes their real dimension, and notes that a single standard patch omits part of projective space when $D\ge2$.

derivations.claim: If $[z]\in U_j$, multiplying $z$ by any nonzero complex scalar leaves every ratio $z_i/z_j$ unchanged, so $\phi_j$ is well-defined on rays. The representative $z/z_j$ has $j$th coordinate $1$ and all other coordinates equal to those ratios, so the stated inverse sends $\phi_j([z])$ back to $[z]$.

Conversely, applying $\phi_j$ to the inverse representative with $j$th coordinate $1$ returns each entry of $w$; hence the two maps are inverse bijections. The composite of $\phi_j$ with the quotient map is given by continuous coordinate ratios on $\mathbb C^D\setminus\{0\}$, so $\phi_j$ is continuous by the defining quotient topology. The inverse is the quotient map composed with the continuous representative map $w\mapsto e_j+\sum_{i\ne j}w_i e_i$, hence is continuous.

Let $\pi:\mathbb C^D\setminus\{0\}	o\mathbb{CP}^{D-1}$ be the quotient map. Then $\pi^{-1}(U_j)=\{z:z_j
e0\}$ is Euclidean open, so $U_j$ is open by the quotient topology. On $U_j\cap U_k$ with $j
e k$, write $w=\phi_j([z])$. Then $w_k

e j,k$. Conversely, $w_k=1/w'_j$ and $w_i=w'_i/w'_j$ for $i
e j,k$. These rational maps are smooth as real maps on their open coordinate domains, so the charts are compatible and form a smooth atlas.

The patches cover every ray because a nonzero vector has at least one nonzero coordinate. If $D\ge2$, choose $k\ne j$; the ray of the basis vector $e_k$ has $j$th coordinate zero and is not in $U_j$, so each fixed standard patch is proper. For D=1, C^{D-1}=C^0 is a point and the unique patch is the whole ray space; step 4.1 restricts properness to D>=2.
Step 3.1 has no distinct-index transition when D=1; the one-chart atlas remains valid.
Step 3.1 uses only overlaps where w_k is nonzero, so reciprocal transition formulas are defined on precisely their domains.
The patch cover in step 4.1 follows by taking any nonzero coordinate of each nonzero representative; the index set is finite.
The chart-to-inverse identity is verified in step 1.1 and inverse-to-chart identity in step 2.1.
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 verify both inverse identities, including the reverse map-to-coordinate identity.
