**The order of a finite group.** Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) whose
underlying set is finite ([[def-countable]]), so that $G \approx n$ for some
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]). That natural number is unique: if
$G \approx n$ and $G \approx n'$ then $n \approx n'$, since $\approx$ is
symmetric and transitive, and then $n = n'$ by claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. The
**order of $G$** is that unique natural number, written $|G|$. A group is
**infinite** when its underlying set is not finite, and $|G|$ is then not
defined.

**The order of an element.** Let $G$ be any group and $g \in G$, with natural
powers as in [[def-group-power]]. Put

$$S_g \;:=\; \{\, k \in \mathbb{N} \;:\; k \ge 1 \text{ and } g^{k} = e \,\} \;\subseteq\; \mathbb{N}.$$

- If $S_g \ne \varnothing$, the **order of $g$** is its least element,

  $$\operatorname{ord}(g) \;:=\; \min S_g \;\in\; \mathbb{N},$$

  which exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]):
  every nonempty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ has a least element, and that element is
  unique, being $\le$ every element of $S_g$ and a member of it. We then say $g$
  has **finite order**.
- If $S_g = \varnothing$ we say $g$ has **infinite order** and write
  $\operatorname{ord}(g) = \infty$, where $\infty$ is a symbol reserved for this
  case and is not a natural number. No arithmetic is performed with it here.

By construction $\operatorname{ord}(g) \ge 1$ whenever it is finite, and
$\operatorname{ord}(g) = 1$ exactly when $g = e$, since $g^{1} = g$.

**Every element of a finite group has finite order.** If $G$ is finite then
$S_g \ne \varnothing$ for every $g \in G$, by [[lem-order-of-element-exists]], so
$\operatorname{ord}(g)$ is a natural number.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]), written **additively**: its
operation is written $+$, its identity is written $0$, and its underlying set is
finite. Let $\mathbb C^{\times}$ be the group of units of the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]), that
is, the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.

An **additive character** of $G$ is a group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]])

$$\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb C^{\times},\qquad \chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\,\chi(y)\quad(x,y\in G).$$

Write $\widehat G$ for the set of all additive characters of $G$. Since $G$ and
$\mathbb C^{\times}$ are groups, every additive character automatically
satisfies $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(-x)=\chi(x)^{-1}$
([[lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties]]), so multiplicativity is the whole
requirement.

**This is not the representation-theoretic character.** The word "character"
already names the function $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ attached to
a finite-dimensional complex representation $V$ of $G$
([[def-character-of-a-complex-representation]],
[[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). That
function need not be multiplicative — only for a one-dimensional representation
is it a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^{\times}$ — and the next item proves the
precise bridge: the additive characters of a finite abelian group are exactly
the characters of its one-dimensional complex representations, and exactly its
irreducible ones.

**Well-definedness.** $\widehat G$ is defined as a set of functions
$G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$, so the definition itself selects nothing. In
particular it chooses no decomposition of $G$, no enumeration of $G$, and no
isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$, and it asserts nothing here about a group
structure on $\widehat G$; the dictionary proved in the next item records what
structure there is.

Let $G$ and $G'$ be groups with identities $e$ and $e'$, and let $f : G \to G'$
be a group homomorphism ([[def-group-homomorphism]]), so $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ for
all $x, y \in G$. Then:

1. $f(e) = e'$;
2. $f(g^{-1}) = f(g)^{-1}$ for every $g \in G$;
3. $f(g^{n}) = f(g)^{n}$ for every $g \in G$ and every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, powers
   being those of [[def-group-power]].

For **monoid** homomorphisms the analogue of claim 1 is false, so preservation of
the identity has to be part of the definition: the map $u : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$
with $u(x) = 0$ for every $x$ satisfies $u(xy) = u(x)u(y)$ for the multiplicative
monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot,1)$, yet $u(1) = 0 \ne 1$.

Write $\iota_{\mathbb R}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]]. If $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $z=re^{i\theta}\ne0$, its $n$ distinct roots are
$$r^{1/n}\exp\!\left(i\frac{\theta+2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right),\qquad k\in\mathbb N,\quad 0\le k<n.$$
For $z=0$, the only $n$th root is $0$. Thus the $n$th roots of unity are precisely $\exp\!\left(i\frac{2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right)$ for $k\in\mathbb N$ with $0\le k<n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], [[cor-complex-de-moivre-formula]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]], [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[def-complex-integer-powers]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

derivations.claim: Put $n:=\operatorname{ord}(x)\ge1$. By [F1] and [F3], $\chi(x)^n=\chi(nx)=\chi(0)=1$, with $\chi(0)=1$ by [F2].
By [F4], $\chi(x)=\exp(2\pi i k/n)$ for some $0\le k<n$. Therefore [F5] gives $|\chi(x)|=1$. The argument includes $x=0$, for which $n=1$ and $\chi(0)=1$.

citations.quote:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]), written **additively**: its
operation is written $+$, its identity is written $0$, and its underlying set is
finite. Let $\mathbb C^{\times}$ be the group of units of the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]), that
is, the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.

An **additive character** of $G$ is a group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]])

$$\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb C^{\times},\qquad \chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\,\chi(y)\quad(x,y\in G).$$

Write $\widehat G$ for the set of all additive characters of $G$. Since $G$ and
$\mathbb C^{\times}$ are groups, every additive character automatically
satisfies $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(-x)=\chi(x)^{-1}$
([[lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties]]), so multiplicativity is the whole
requirement.

**This is not the representation-theoretic character.** The word "character"
already names the function $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ attached to
a finite-dimensional complex representation $V$ of $G$
([[def-character-of-a-complex-representation]],
[[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). That
function need not be multiplicative — only for a one-dimensional representation
is it a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^{\times}$ — and the next item proves the
precise bridge: the additive characters of a finite abelian group are exactly
the characters of its one-dimensional complex representations, and exactly its
irreducible ones.

**Well-definedness.** $\widehat G$ is defined as a set of functions
$G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$, so the definition itself selects nothing. In
particular it chooses no decomposition of $G$, no enumeration of $G$, and no
isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$, and it asserts nothing here about a group
structure on $\widehat G$; the dictionary proved in the next item records what
structure there is.

Let $G$ and $G'$ be groups with identities $e$ and $e'$, and let $f : G \to G'$
be a group homomorphism ([[def-group-homomorphism]]), so $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ for
all $x, y \in G$. Then:

1. $f(e) = e'$;
2. $f(g^{-1}) = f(g)^{-1}$ for every $g \in G$;
3. $f(g^{n}) = f(g)^{n}$ for every $g \in G$ and every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, powers
   being those of [[def-group-power]].

For **monoid** homomorphisms the analogue of claim 1 is false, so preservation of
the identity has to be part of the definition: the map $u : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$
with $u(x) = 0$ for every $x$ satisfies $u(xy) = u(x)u(y)$ for the multiplicative
monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot,1)$, yet $u(1) = 0 \ne 1$.

Write $\iota_{\mathbb R}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]]. If $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $z=re^{i\theta}\ne0$, its $n$ distinct roots are
$$r^{1/n}\exp\!\left(i\frac{\theta+2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right),\qquad k\in\mathbb N,\quad 0\le k<n.$$
For $z=0$, the only $n$th root is $0$. Thus the $n$th roots of unity are precisely $\exp\!\left(i\frac{2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right)$ for $k\in\mathbb N$ with $0\le k<n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], [[cor-complex-de-moivre-formula]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]], [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[def-complex-integer-powers]].

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]) written additively. Its set of additive characters is
$$\widehat G:=\{\chi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}:\chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\chi(y)\text{ for all }x,y\in G\},$$
where an additive character is the group homomorphism of [[def-additive-character-of-a-finite-abelian-group]]. For $\chi,\psi\in\widehat G$, define their pointwise product by $(\chi\psi)(x):=\chi(x)\psi(x)$. The constant-one function is denoted $1$, and the pointwise inverse is $\chi^{-1}(x):=\chi(x)^{-1}$.

This specifies a set and operations. The later theorem `thm-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual-is-finite-abelian-group` proves that these operations make $\widehat G$ a finite abelian group; no isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$ is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: If $\chi\in\widehat{C_n}$ as defined in [F4], then $\chi(g)^n=\chi(ng)=\chi(0)=1$ by [F1] and the given relation $ng=0$, so evaluation at $g$ maps this character set into the set in [F3]. Every element is $jg$ by [F2], and [F1] gives $\chi(jg)=\chi(g)^j$; thus evaluation at $g$ is injective.

Conversely, for each $n$th root of unity $z$, define $\chi_z(jg):=z^j$ for $j\in\mathbb Z$. If $jg=kg$, [F2] gives $j-k=qn$ for some integer $q$, so $z^j=z^k(z^n)^q=z^k$ by [F3, F5]; hence the value is well defined. Also $\chi_z(jg+kg)=z^{j+k}=\chi_z(jg)\chi_z(kg)$ by [F5], so $\chi_z$ is an additive character in [F4], and $\chi_z(g)=z$.

Steps 1.1 and 1.2 make evaluation at $g$ a bijection from the character set [F4] to the $n$ distinct roots in [F3]. This also covers $n=1$: the quotient is trivial and the sole root is $1$. Therefore $|\widehat{C_n}|=n$.

citations.quote: For every finite abelian group $G$ there is a unique list $$1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_r$$ such that $G\cong C_{n_1}\times\cdots\times C_{n_r}$. Moreover $|G|=n_1\cdots n_r$. The trivial group corresponds to the empty list and empty product.

Let $G_1,\ldots,G_r$ be finite abelian groups and let $P=G_1\times\cdots\times G_r$ be their recursively parenthesized external direct product. By convention, $P$ is the trivial group when $r=0$. Restriction to the coordinate factors gives a bijection
$$\widehat P\longrightarrow\widehat{G_1}\times\cdots\times\widehat{G_r}.$$
Its inverse sends $(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r)$ to $\chi(g_1,\ldots,g_r)=\prod_{i=1}^r\chi_i(g_i)$. For $r=0$, both sides are singletons.

Write $C_n=\langle g\rangle$ additively, so $jg$ denotes the sum of $j$ copies of $g$ and $ng=0$. If $C_n$ has order $n\ge1$, then its set $\widehat{C_n}$ of additive characters has cardinality $n$. Each character is uniquely determined by $\chi(g)$, and the possible values are exactly the $n$ distinct complex $n$th roots of unity. For each such root $z$, the corresponding character is $\chi_z(jg)=z^j$ for every $j\in\mathbb Z$.

If $G$ and $H$ are finite groups, then their external direct product is finite
and has order $|G\times H|=|G|\,|H|$.

Group isomorphisms, automorphisms and the set $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$.

An **isomorphism** $f:G\to H$ is a bijective group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).  When
$G=H$, it is an **automorphism** of $G$.  Write

$$\operatorname{Aut}(G):=\{f:G\to G:f\text{ is an automorphism}\}.$$

**The order of a finite group.** Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) whose
underlying set is finite ([[def-countable]]), so that $G \approx n$ for some
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]). That natural number is unique: if
$G \approx n$ and $G \approx n'$ then $n \approx n'$, since $\approx$ is
symmetric and transitive, and then $n = n'$ by claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. The
**order of $G$** is that unique natural number, written $|G|$. A group is
**infinite** when its underlying set is not finite, and $|G|$ is then not
defined.

**The order of an element.** Let $G$ be any group and $g \in G$, with natural
powers as in [[def-group-power]]. Put

$$S_g \;:=\; \{\, k \in \mathbb{N} \;:\; k \ge 1 \text{ and } g^{k} = e \,\} \;\subseteq\; \mathbb{N}.$$

- If $S_g \ne \varnothing$, the **order of $g$** is its least element,

  $$\operatorname{ord}(g) \;:=\; \min S_g \;\in\; \mathbb{N},$$

  which exists by the well-ordering principle ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]):
  every nonempty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ has a least element, and that element is
  unique, being $\le$ every element of $S_g$ and a member of it. We then say $g$
  has **finite order**.
- If $S_g = \varnothing$ we say $g$ has **infinite order** and write
  $\operatorname{ord}(g) = \infty$, where $\infty$ is a symbol reserved for this
  case and is not a natural number. No arithmetic is performed with it here.

By construction $\operatorname{ord}(g) \ge 1$ whenever it is finite, and
$\operatorname{ord}(g) = 1$ exactly when $g = e$, since $g^{1} = g$.

**Every element of a finite group has finite order.** If $G$ is finite then
$S_g \ne \varnothing$ for every $g \in G$, by [[lem-order-of-element-exists]], so
$\operatorname{ord}(g)$ is a natural number.

The inverse of a bijective group homomorphism is a group homomorphism.

If $f:G\to H$ is a bijective group homomorphism, then its set-theoretic inverse
$f^{-1}:H\to G$ is a group homomorphism.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]) written additively. Its set of additive characters is
$$\widehat G:=\{\chi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}:\chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\chi(y)\text{ for all }x,y\in G\},$$
where an additive character is the group homomorphism of [[def-additive-character-of-a-finite-abelian-group]]. For $\chi,\psi\in\widehat G$, define their pointwise product by $(\chi\psi)(x):=\chi(x)\psi(x)$. The constant-one function is denoted $1$, and the pointwise inverse is $\chi^{-1}(x):=\chi(x)^{-1}$.

This specifies a set and operations. The later theorem `thm-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual-is-finite-abelian-group` proves that these operations make $\widehat G$ a finite abelian group; no isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$ is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: If the invariant-factor list is empty, [F1] identifies $G$ with the trivial group, which is cyclic of order $1$. By [F3] it has one character and one element, so $|\widehat G|=|G|=1$ for the character set in [F8].

Otherwise fix one isomorphism $\varphi:G\to P$, where $P=C_{n_1}\times\cdots\times C_{n_r}$ is the finite iterated product. By [F6] and [F7], both $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are group homomorphisms. Thus $\chi\mapsto\chi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\psi\mapsto\psi\circ\varphi$ preserve the character sets in [F8] and are inverse bijections between $\widehat G$ and $\widehat P$.

By [F2], $\widehat P$ is in bijection with $\prod_i\widehat{C_{n_i}}$. Each factor has $n_i$ elements by [F3], and repeated application of [F5] to the finite Cartesian products gives $|\widehat P|=\prod_i n_i$.
The same repeated product-order formula gives $|P|=\prod_i n_i$ by [F4]; the isomorphism in step 1.2 preserves finite cardinality by [F6]. Hence $|G|=\prod_i n_i=|\widehat G|$.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]) written additively. Its set of additive characters is
$$\widehat G:=\{\chi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}:\chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\chi(y)\text{ for all }x,y\in G\},$$
where an additive character is the group homomorphism of [[def-additive-character-of-a-finite-abelian-group]]. For $\chi,\psi\in\widehat G$, define their pointwise product by $(\chi\psi)(x):=\chi(x)\psi(x)$. The constant-one function is denoted $1$, and the pointwise inverse is $\chi^{-1}(x):=\chi(x)^{-1}$.

This specifies a set and operations. The later theorem `thm-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual-is-finite-abelian-group` proves that these operations make $\widehat G$ a finite abelian group; no isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$ is part of this definition.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]), written **additively**: its
operation is written $+$, its identity is written $0$, and its underlying set is
finite. Let $\mathbb C^{\times}$ be the group of units of the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]), that
is, the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.

An **additive character** of $G$ is a group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]])

$$\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb C^{\times},\qquad \chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\,\chi(y)\quad(x,y\in G).$$

Write $\widehat G$ for the set of all additive characters of $G$. Since $G$ and
$\mathbb C^{\times}$ are groups, every additive character automatically
satisfies $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(-x)=\chi(x)^{-1}$
([[lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties]]), so multiplicativity is the whole
requirement.

**This is not the representation-theoretic character.** The word "character"
already names the function $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ attached to
a finite-dimensional complex representation $V$ of $G$
([[def-character-of-a-complex-representation]],
[[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). That
function need not be multiplicative — only for a one-dimensional representation
is it a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^{\times}$ — and the next item proves the
precise bridge: the additive characters of a finite abelian group are exactly
the characters of its one-dimensional complex representations, and exactly its
irreducible ones.

**Well-definedness.** $\widehat G$ is defined as a set of functions
$G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$, so the definition itself selects nothing. In
particular it chooses no decomposition of $G$, no enumeration of $G$, and no
isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$, and it asserts nothing here about a group
structure on $\widehat G$; the dictionary proved in the next item records what
structure there is.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $G$ and $G'$ be groups with identities $e$ and $e'$, and let $f : G \to G'$
be a group homomorphism ([[def-group-homomorphism]]), so $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ for
all $x, y \in G$. Then:

1. $f(e) = e'$;
2. $f(g^{-1}) = f(g)^{-1}$ for every $g \in G$;
3. $f(g^{n}) = f(g)^{n}$ for every $g \in G$ and every $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, powers
   being those of [[def-group-power]].

For **monoid** homomorphisms the analogue of claim 1 is false, so preservation of
the identity has to be part of the definition: the map $u : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$
with $u(x) = 0$ for every $x$ satisfies $u(xy) = u(x)u(y)$ for the multiplicative
monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot,1)$, yet $u(1) = 0 \ne 1$.

If $G$ is a finite abelian group with invariant-factor decomposition $G\cong C_{n_1}\times\cdots\times C_{n_r}$, then $|\widehat G|=\prod_i n_i=|G|$. The empty product is allowed: it represents the trivial group and has value $1$. This is a finite-set cardinality assertion; it does not choose an isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$.

derivations.claim: For $\chi,\psi\in\widehat G$, $x,y\in G$, and pointwise product as in [F1], $(\chi\psi)(x+y)=\chi(x)\chi(y)\psi(x)\psi(y)=\chi(x)\psi(x)\chi(y)\psi(y)$ by commutativity in [F2]. Thus $\chi\psi$ is again a homomorphism. The constant-one function is a homomorphism because it sends every sum to $1\cdot1=1$; [F3] also confirms each character takes the identity to $1$.

The pointwise inverse is a homomorphism because $(\chi(x+y))^{-1}=(\chi(x)\chi(y))^{-1}=\chi(x)^{-1}\chi(y)^{-1}$ in the abelian group $\mathbb C^{\times}$. Associativity and commutativity of pointwise product, its identity law, and the inverse laws follow by evaluating at each $x$ and using the corresponding laws in [F2]. Hence $\widehat G$ is an abelian group.
The dual is finite by [F4], and its order is $|G|$ by the same result. Thus it is a finite abelian group of the asserted order.

citations.quote: For every finite abelian group $G$ there is a unique list $$1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_r$$ such that $G\cong C_{n_1}\times\cdots\times C_{n_r}$. Moreover $|G|=n_1\cdots n_r$. The trivial group corresponds to the empty list and empty product.

Let $G_1,\ldots,G_r$ be finite abelian groups and let $P=G_1\times\cdots\times G_r$ be their recursively parenthesized external direct product. By convention, $P$ is the trivial group when $r=0$. Restriction to the coordinate factors gives a bijection
$$\widehat P\longrightarrow\widehat{G_1}\times\cdots\times\widehat{G_r}.$$
Its inverse sends $(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r)$ to $\chi(g_1,\ldots,g_r)=\prod_{i=1}^r\chi_i(g_i)$. For $r=0$, both sides are singletons.

Write $C_n=\langle g\rangle$ additively, so $jg$ denotes the sum of $j$ copies of $g$ and $ng=0$. If $C_n$ has order $n\ge1$, then its set $\widehat{C_n}$ of additive characters has cardinality $n$. Each character is uniquely determined by $\chi(g)$, and the possible values are exactly the $n$ distinct complex $n$th roots of unity. For each such root $z$, the corresponding character is $\chi_z(jg)=z^j$ for every $j\in\mathbb Z$.

Write $\iota_{\mathbb R}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]]. If $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $z=re^{i\theta}\ne0$, its $n$ distinct roots are
$$r^{1/n}\exp\!\left(i\frac{\theta+2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right),\qquad k\in\mathbb N,\quad 0\le k<n.$$
For $z=0$, the only $n$th root is $0$. Thus the $n$th roots of unity are precisely $\exp\!\left(i\frac{2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right)$ for $k\in\mathbb N$ with $0\le k<n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], [[cor-complex-de-moivre-formula]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]], [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[def-complex-integer-powers]].
If $G$ is a finite abelian group, $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$ is an additive character, and $x\in G$, then $|\chi(x)|=1$.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Group isomorphisms, automorphisms and the set $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$.

An **isomorphism** $f:G\to H$ is a bijective group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).  When
$G=H$, it is an **automorphism** of $G$.  Write

$$\operatorname{Aut}(G):=\{f:G\to G:f\text{ is an automorphism}\}.$$

The inverse of a bijective group homomorphism is a group homomorphism.

If $f:G\to H$ is a bijective group homomorphism, then its set-theoretic inverse
$f^{-1}:H\to G$ is a group homomorphism.

derivations.claim: If $G$ is trivial, every additive character sends its identity to $1$ by [F7], so [F10] makes the character set a singleton; the sum is $1=|G|$ and the formula holds. Otherwise fix an invariant-factor isomorphism $\varphi:G\to P=\prod_i C_{n_i}$ from [F1]. By [F8] and [F9], composition with $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ gives inverse bijections of the character sets [F10], taking $x,y$ to $a=\varphi(x),b=\varphi(y)$. Thus it suffices to compute the sum for $P$.

In each cyclic factor write $a_i=r_i g_i$ and $b_i=s_i g_i$, with $0\le r_i,s_i<n_i$. By [F3] and [F7], a character whose value on $g_i$ is $\omega_{n_i}^k$ has values $\omega_{n_i}^{kr_i}$ and $\omega_{n_i}^{ks_i}$ on $a_i$ and $b_i$. By [F4], $|\omega_{n_i}|=1$, so $\overline{\omega_{n_i}^{ks_i}}=\omega_{n_i}^{-ks_i}$. The character-indexed sum in this coordinate is therefore $\sum_{k=0}^{n_i-1}\omega_{n_i}^{k(r_i-s_i)}$. If $r_i=s_i$ modulo $n_i$, this equals $n_i$. Otherwise $q:=\omega_{n_i}^{r_i-s_i}\ne1$ by distinctness of the roots in [F3], and $q^{n_i}=1$, so $\sum_{k=0}^{n_i-1}q^k=(1-q^{n_i})/(1-q)=0$ by the geometric-sum identity. For $n_i=1$ the first case applies and the sum is $1$.

Under the product-character bijection, finite-sum factorization [F5] makes the sum over $\widehat P$ the product of these cyclic sums. It is therefore $\prod_i n_i$ exactly when every coordinate of $a$ equals the corresponding coordinate of $b$, and is zero otherwise.
The coordinate map $\varphi$ is injective, so all coordinates agree exactly when $x=y$; and [F1] gives $|G|=|P|=\prod_i n_i$. The empty product case was handled in step 1.1. This proves the formula.

citations.quote: Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.

Let $G$ be a group and let $N\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}G$ be a normal subgroup
([[def-normal-subgroup]]). The **quotient group**, or **factor group**, $G/N$
has the left cosets

$$G/N:=\{gN:g\in G\}$$

as its elements ([[def-coset]], [[def-index]]), with product

$$ (gN)(hN):=ghN.$$

Independence of the chosen representatives is proved in
[[thm-coset-multiplication-well-defined-iff-normal]], and the group axioms are
proved in [[thm-quotient-group-laws]].

Let $N\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}G$. The left cosets form a group $G/N$ under

$$ (gN)(hN)=ghN.$$

Its identity is $N=eN$, and the inverse of $gN$ is $g^{-1}N$.

Let $H\le G$. The **left coset set** is

$$G/H:=\{gH:g\in G\}.$$

By [[lem-coset-partition]], its elements are exactly the blocks of the coset
partition of $G$. The **index** of $H$ in $G$ is

$$[G:H]:=|G/H|$$

when $G/H$ is finite, with finite cardinality as in
[[def-finite-cardinality]]. If $G/H$ is not finite, write $[G:H]=\infty$.
Here $\infty$ is a symbol, not a natural number, and no arithmetic with it is
defined.

The right coset set has the same finite or infinite size because
[[lem-left-and-right-cosets-equinumerous]] gives an explicit bijection between
the two coset sets. Thus the index does not depend on choosing left rather than
right cosets.
If $G$ is abelian and $N\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}G$, then $G/N$ is abelian.

Let $H\le G$ and let $a,b,x\in G$. Then

$$x\in aH\iff a^{-1}x\in H,$$

and

$$aH=bH\iff a^{-1}b\in H.$$

The corresponding right-coset criterion is $Ha=Hb$ if and only if
$ab^{-1}\in H$.

The empty product is allowed: it represents the trivial group and has value $1$. This is a finite-set cardinality assertion; it does not choose an isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$.

Let $G$ be a finite group and $H\le G$. Then

$$|G|=[G:H]\,|H|.$$

Consequently, under the canonical embedding $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$,
$\iota(|H|)$ divides $\iota(|G|)$.

Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  ([[def-binary-operation]]);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it ([[def-identity-element]]), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ ([[def-invertible-element]]). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

For any subset $K\subseteq\widehat G$ (in particular, for any subgroup once $\widehat G$ has been proved to be a group), define
$$K^{\perp}:=\{g\in G:\chi(g)=1\text{ for every }\chi\in K\}.$$
The pairing is evaluation, and the same convention is used in both directions. `lem-qa-finite-abelian-annihilators-are-subgroups` proves that these sets are subgroups when the input is a subgroup.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the quotient is defined; [F2] gives its group law, and [F3] makes $Q:=G/H$ finite abelian. Finiteness also follows from the finite coset partition in [F6].

Let $\pi:G\to Q$ be $\pi(g)=g+H$. The quotient law in [F2] gives $\pi(g+g')=(g+H)+(g'+H)=\pi(g)+\pi(g')$, so $\pi$ is a homomorphism. For $h\in H$, $\pi(h)=H$, the identity coset; every character sends the identity to $1$. Thus for $\psi\in\widehat Q$, $\psi\circ\pi$ is a character by [F8] and is trivial on $H$, so [F9] shows inflation maps $\widehat Q$ into $H^\perp$.

For $\chi\in H^\perp$, define $\widetilde\chi(g+H):=\chi(g)$. If $g+H=g'+H$, [F4] gives $g'-g\in H$, hence $\chi(g')=\chi(g)\chi(g'-g)=\chi(g)$; so $\widetilde\chi$ is well defined. For cosets $g+H,g'+H$, the quotient law [F2] gives $\widetilde\chi((g+H)+(g'+H))=\chi(g+g')=\chi(g)\chi(g')$, so $\widetilde\chi$ is a character of $Q$.

For every $g\in G$, $(\widetilde\chi\circ\pi)(g)=\widetilde\chi(g+H)=\chi(g)$; for every $\psi\in\widehat Q$ and coset $g+H$, descent of its inflation returns $\widetilde{(\psi\circ\pi)}(g+H)=(\psi\circ\pi)(g)=\psi(g+H)$. Thus inflation and descent are inverse bijections. By [F5], $|H^\perp|=|\widehat Q|=|Q|$, and by [F2], $|Q|=[G:H]$.
Lagrange [F6] gives $|G|=[G:H]|H|$. Combining with step 2.1 gives $|H^\perp|\,|H|=|G|$, and division by the positive integer $|H|$ from [F7] gives $|H^\perp|=|G|/|H|$.

citations.quote: For a finite abelian group $G$, the pointwise product, constant-one identity and pointwise inverse on $\widehat G$ make it a finite abelian group. Its order is $|\widehat G|=|G|$.

Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  ([[def-binary-operation]]);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it ([[def-identity-element]]), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ ([[def-invertible-element]]). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]), written **additively**: its
operation is written $+$, its identity is written $0$, and its underlying set is
finite. Let $\mathbb C^{\times}$ be the group of units of the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]), that
is, the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.

An **additive character** of $G$ is a group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]])

$$\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb C^{\times},\qquad \chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\,\chi(y)\quad(x,y\in G).$$

Write $\widehat G$ for the set of all additive characters of $G$. Since $G$ and
$\mathbb C^{\times}$ are groups, every additive character automatically
satisfies $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(-x)=\chi(x)^{-1}$
([[lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties]]), so multiplicativity is the whole
requirement.

**This is not the representation-theoretic character.** The word "character"
already names the function $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ attached to
a finite-dimensional complex representation $V$ of $G$
([[def-character-of-a-complex-representation]],
[[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). That
function need not be multiplicative — only for a one-dimensional representation
is it a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^{\times}$ — and the next item proves the
precise bridge: the additive characters of a finite abelian group are exactly
the characters of its one-dimensional complex representations, and exactly its
irreducible ones.

**Well-definedness.** $\widehat G$ is defined as a set of functions
$G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$, so the definition itself selects nothing. In
particular it chooses no decomposition of $G$, no enumeration of $G$, and no
isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$, and it asserts nothing here about a group
structure on $\widehat G$; the dictionary proved in the next item records what
structure there is.

derivations.claim: The trivial character is in $H^\perp$. If $\chi,\psi\in H^\perp$ and $h\in H$, then $(\chi\psi)(h)=\chi(h)\psi(h)=1$, and $\chi^{-1}(h)=\chi(h)^{-1}=1$. Thus $H^\perp$ contains the identity and is closed under pointwise product and inverse in the group $\widehat G$.

The identity $0$ of $G$ lies in $K^\perp$ by [F3]. If $g,h\in K^\perp$, then for every $\chi\in K$, $\chi(g+h)=\chi(g)\chi(h)=1$ and $\chi(-g)=\chi(g)^{-1}=1$. Therefore $K^\perp$ is closed under addition and inverses in $G$.
By the subgroup criterion in [F2], steps 1.1 and 1.2 show respectively that $H^\perp\le\widehat G$ and $K^\perp\le G$.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and $\widehat G$ its character dual ([[def-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual]]), which is finite with $|\widehat G|=|G|$ ([[thm-qa-finite-abelian-dual-has-same-cardinality]]). Put $N:=|G|$ and $N_{\mathbb R}:=\iota_{\mathbb R}(N)$ its canonical real image ([[def-order-in-a-group]], [[def-canonical-natural]]). Since $G$ contains its identity, $N\ge1$, and hence $N_{\mathbb R}>0$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). Its rational power $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}$ is therefore well defined ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

For $f\in\mathbb C^G$, define $F_Gf\in\mathbb C^{\widehat G}$ by
$$ (F_Gf)(\chi):=N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad \chi\in\widehat G. $$
Here $\mathbb C^X$ is the space of all functions $X\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]]) and the sum is the finite sum in $\mathbb C$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). This fixes the negative-character sign and uses the same factor $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}$ in both directions. Unitarity is proved separately; it is not part of this definition.

If $G$ is a finite abelian group with invariant-factor decomposition $G\cong C_{n_1}\times\cdots\times C_{n_r}$, then $|\widehat G|=\prod_i n_i=|G|$. The empty product is allowed: it represents the trivial group and has value $1$. This is a finite-set cardinality assertion; it does not choose an isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and let $\chi,\psi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$ be
additive characters of $G$
([[def-additive-character-of-a-finite-abelian-group]]). Then
$$\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g)\,\overline{\psi(g)} =\begin{cases}1&\chi=\psi,\\ 0&\chi\ne\psi,\end{cases}$$
the sum being the finite sum over $G$ of complex-valued terms
([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). In particular, if $\chi$ is not the
trivial additive character then $\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g)=0$. The normalized inner
product is linear in its first argument, exactly as on the published
representation-character page
([[def-standard-inner-product-on-complex-class-functions]]).

For a finite abelian group $G$ and $x,y\in G$,
$$\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\chi(x)\overline{\chi(y)}=\begin{cases}|G|,&x=y,\\0,&x\ne y.\end{cases}$$
This is orthogonality of the columns indexed by group elements. It is proved from cyclic root sums and is not inferred from row orthogonality.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the transform acts on a function $f$ by the coefficient formula defining $U$. By [F2], its row and column index sets have equal finite cardinality, so $U$ is square.

For $x,y\in G$, the $(x,y)$ entry of $U^*U$ is $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\chi(x)\overline{\chi(y)}$, because [F6] gives $(N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2})^2=N_{\mathbb R}^{-1}$. By [F4], this is $1$ when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise, exactly the entry of $I_G$. Hence $U^*U=I_G$.

For $\chi,\psi\in\widehat G$, the $(\chi,\psi)$ entry of $UU^*$ is $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1}\sum_{x\in G}\overline{\chi(x)}\psi(x)$. By [F6] and [F3], this is $1$ when $\chi=\psi$ and $0$ otherwise, exactly the entry of $I_{\widehat G}$. Hence $UU^*=I_{\widehat G}$.

By [F1], the action of this coefficient matrix on the function values of any $f\in\mathbb C^G$ is exactly $F_Gf$. The two identities in steps 1.2 and 1.3 therefore prove the asserted unitarity of the transform as defined here.

[[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). That
function need not be multiplicative — only for a one-dimensional representation
is it a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^{\times}$ — and the next item proves the
precise bridge: the additive characters of a finite abelian group are exactly
the characters of its one-dimensional complex representations, and exactly its
irreducible ones.

**Well-definedness.** $\widehat G$ is defined as a set of functions
$G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$, so the definition itself selects nothing. In
particular it chooses no decomposition of $G$, no enumeration of $G$, and no
isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$, and it asserts nothing here about a group
structure on $\widehat G$; the dictionary proved in the next item records what
structure there is.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

citations.quote: For a finite abelian group $G$, the pointwise product, constant-one identity and pointwise inverse on $\widehat G$ make it a finite abelian group. Its order is $|\widehat G|=|G|$.

If $G$ is a finite abelian group with invariant-factor decomposition $G\cong C_{n_1}\times\cdots\times C_{n_r}$, then $|\widehat G|=\prod_i n_i=|G|$. The empty product is allowed: it represents the trivial group and has value $1$. This is a finite-set cardinality assertion; it does not choose an isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$.

For every finite abelian group $G$ there is a unique list $$1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_r$$ such that $G\cong C_{n_1}\times\cdots\times C_{n_r}$. Moreover $|G|=n_1\cdots n_r$. The trivial group corresponds to the empty list and empty product.

Let $G_1,\ldots,G_r$ be finite abelian groups and let $P=G_1\times\cdots\times G_r$ be their recursively parenthesized external direct product. By convention, $P$ is the trivial group when $r=0$. Restriction to the coordinate factors gives a bijection
$$\widehat P\longrightarrow\widehat{G_1}\times\cdots\times\widehat{G_r}.$$
Its inverse sends $(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r)$ to $\chi(g_1,\ldots,g_r)=\prod_{i=1}^r\chi_i(g_i)$. For $r=0$, both sides are singletons.

Write $C_n=\langle g\rangle$ additively, so $jg$ denotes the sum of $j$ copies of $g$ and $ng=0$. If $C_n$ has order $n\ge1$, then its set $\widehat{C_n}$ of additive characters has cardinality $n$. Each character is uniquely determined by $\chi(g)$, and the possible values are exactly the $n$ distinct complex $n$th roots of unity. For each such root $z$, the corresponding character is $\chi_z(jg)=z^j$ for every $j\in\mathbb Z$.

Write $\iota_{\mathbb R}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]]. If $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $z=re^{i\theta}\ne0$, its $n$ distinct roots are
$$r^{1/n}\exp\!\left(i\frac{\theta+2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right),\qquad k\in\mathbb N,\quad 0\le k<n.$$
For $z=0$, the only $n$th root is $0$. Thus the $n$th roots of unity are precisely $\exp\!\left(i\frac{2\pi\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)}{\iota_{\mathbb R}(n)}\right)$ for $k\in\mathbb N$ with $0\le k<n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], [[cor-complex-de-moivre-formula]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]], [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[def-complex-integer-powers]].

Let $A$ be a finite set ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then:

1. $B$ is finite;
2. $\lvert B\rvert \le \lvert A\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]);
3. $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ if and only if $B = A$;
4. every injection $f : A \to A$ is a bijection, and every surjection
   $f : A \to A$ is a bijection.

Clause 3 is the finite form of the Dedekind statement: a finite set is not
equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. Clause 4 is its working form, and
**finiteness is exactly the hypothesis that fails in general**: the successor map
is an injection of $\mathbb{N}$ into itself that is not surjective, which is the
false statement recorded on this page's companion.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

Group isomorphisms, automorphisms and the set $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$.

An **isomorphism** $f:G\to H$ is a bijective group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).  When
$G=H$, it is an **automorphism** of $G$.  Write

$$\operatorname{Aut}(G):=\{f:G\to G:f\text{ is an automorphism}\}.$$

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]) written additively. Its set of additive characters is
$$\widehat G:=\{\chi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}:\chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\chi(y)\text{ for all }x,y\in G\},$$
where an additive character is the group homomorphism of [[def-additive-character-of-a-finite-abelian-group]]. For $\chi,\psi\in\widehat G$, define their pointwise product by $(\chi\psi)(x):=\chi(x)\psi(x)$. The constant-one function is denoted $1$, and the pointwise inverse is $\chi^{-1}(x):=\chi(x)^{-1}$.

This specifies a set and operations. The later theorem `thm-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual-is-finite-abelian-group` proves that these operations make $\widehat G$ a finite abelian group; no isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$ is part of this definition.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group ([[def-group]]), written **additively**: its
operation is written $+$, its identity is written $0$, and its underlying set is
finite. Let $\mathbb C^{\times}$ be the group of units of the field $\mathbb C$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[lem-ring-units-form-a-group]]), that
is, the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication.

An **additive character** of $G$ is a group homomorphism
([[def-group-homomorphism]])

$$\chi:G\longrightarrow\mathbb C^{\times},\qquad \chi(x+y)=\chi(x)\,\chi(y)\quad(x,y\in G).$$

Write $\widehat G$ for the set of all additive characters of $G$. Since $G$ and
$\mathbb C^{\times}$ are groups, every additive character automatically
satisfies $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(-x)=\chi(x)^{-1}$
([[lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties]]), so multiplicativity is the whole
requirement.

**This is not the representation-theoretic character.** The word "character"
already names the function $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ attached to
a finite-dimensional complex representation $V$ of $G$
([[def-character-of-a-complex-representation]],
[[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). That
function need not be multiplicative — only for a one-dimensional representation
is it a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^{\times}$ — and the next item proves the
precise bridge: the additive characters of a finite abelian group are exactly
the characters of its one-dimensional complex representations, and exactly its
irreducible ones.

**Well-definedness.** $\widehat G$ is defined as a set of functions
$G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$, so the definition itself selects nothing. In
particular it chooses no decomposition of $G$, no enumeration of $G$, and no
isomorphism $G\cong\widehat G$, and it asserts nothing here about a group
structure on $\widehat G$; the dictionary proved in the next item records what
structure there is.

derivations.claim: For each $g\in G$, evaluation on the dual group [F7] is a character: if $\chi,\psi\in\widehat G$, then $\operatorname{ev}(g)(\chi\psi)=\chi(g)\psi(g)=\operatorname{ev}(g)(\chi)\operatorname{ev}(g)(\psi)$. Thus $\operatorname{ev}(g)\in\widehat{\widehat G}$.

If $G$ is nontrivial, fix the isomorphism $\varphi:G\to\prod_i C_{n_i}$ from [F3]. For any nonzero $g$, some coordinate is $\varphi(g)_j=[m]$ with $1\le m<n_j$. In the product, the character trivial on every coordinate except $j$, with generator value $\omega_{n_j}$ on that factor, exists by [F4]. Its composite $\chi$ with $\varphi$ is a character of $G$ and satisfies $\chi(g)=\omega_{n_j}^m\ne1$, because the listed $n_j$ roots are distinct and $m$ is nonzero modulo $n_j$. Thus every nonzero element is detected by a character. The trivial-group case has no nonzero element and satisfies this statement vacuously.

Evaluation is a homomorphism from $G$ to the pointwise group $\widehat{\widehat G}$, since for every $\chi$, $\operatorname{ev}(g+h)(\chi)=\chi(g+h)=\chi(g)\chi(h)=(\operatorname{ev}(g)\operatorname{ev}(h))(\chi)$.

If $\operatorname{ev}(g)=\operatorname{ev}(h)$, then for every $\chi\in\widehat G$, [F7] and [F8] give $\chi(g-h)=\chi(g)\chi(h)^{-1}=1$. If $g-h\ne0$, step 1.2 supplies a character with $\chi(g-h)\ne1$, a contradiction. Hence $g=h$ and evaluation is injective.

By [F2], $|\widehat G|=|G|$ and, applying [F2] to the finite abelian group $\widehat G$ from [F1], $|\widehat{\widehat G}|=|\widehat G|$. Thus the finite domain and codomain of the injective map in step 2.2 have equal cardinality.

The image of $\operatorname{ev}$ is a subset of $\widehat{\widehat G}$ with the same finite cardinality as that codomain, because $\operatorname{ev}$ is injective. By [F5] the image is the whole codomain, so $\operatorname{ev}$ is bijective. Together with step 2.1 and the definition [F6], it is a group isomorphism.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and $\widehat G$ its character dual ([[def-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual]]), which is finite with $|\widehat G|=|G|$ ([[thm-qa-finite-abelian-dual-has-same-cardinality]]). Put $N:=|G|$ and $N_{\mathbb R}:=\iota_{\mathbb R}(N)$ its canonical real image ([[def-order-in-a-group]], [[def-canonical-natural]]). Since $G$ contains its identity, $N\ge1$, and hence $N_{\mathbb R}>0$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). Its rational power $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}$ is therefore well defined ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

For $f\in\mathbb C^G$, define $F_Gf\in\mathbb C^{\widehat G}$ by
$$ (F_Gf)(\chi):=N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad \chi\in\widehat G. $$
Here $\mathbb C^X$ is the space of all functions $X\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]]) and the sum is the finite sum in $\mathbb C$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). This fixes the negative-character sign and uses the same factor $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}$ in both directions. Unitarity is proved separately; it is not part of this definition.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group with character dual $\widehat G$ ([[def-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual]]). For a subgroup $H\le G$ ([[def-subgroup]]), define its character annihilator by
$$H^{\perp}:=\{\chi\in\widehat G:\chi(h)=1\text{ for every }h\in H\}.$$
For any subset $K\subseteq\widehat G$ (in particular, for any subgroup once $\widehat G$ has been proved to be a group), define
$$K^{\perp}:=\{g\in G:\chi(g)=1\text{ for every }\chi\in K\}.$$
The pairing is evaluation, and the same convention is used in both directions. `lem-qa-finite-abelian-annihilators-are-subgroups` proves that these sets are subgroups when the input is a subgroup.

For a subgroup $H\le G$ of a finite abelian group, restriction and inflation identify $H^\perp$ with the character dual of $G/H$. Consequently
$$|H^\perp|=|G/H|=[G:H]=\frac{|G|}{|H|},\qquad |H^\perp|\,|H|=|G|.$$
The quotient convention is left cosets, with additive notation.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and let $\chi,\psi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$ be
additive characters of $G$
([[def-additive-character-of-a-finite-abelian-group]]). Then
$$\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g)\,\overline{\psi(g)} =\begin{cases}1&\chi=\psi,\\ 0&\chi\ne\psi,\end{cases}$$
the sum being the finite sum over $G$ of complex-valued terms
([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). In particular, if $\chi$ is not the
trivial additive character then $\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g)=0$. The normalized inner
product is linear in its first argument, exactly as on the published
representation-character page
([[def-standard-inner-product-on-complex-class-functions]]).
If $G$ is a finite abelian group, $\chi:G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$ is an additive character, and $x\in G$, then $|\chi(x)|=1$.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$, and let $m, p \in \mathbb{Z}$ and
$n, q \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n, q \ge 1$ satisfy $m/n = p/q$ in $\mathbb{Q}$
([[def-rationals]]). Then

$$\big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m} = \big(a^{1/q}\big)^{p}.$$

Consequently the value $a^{r}$ of [[def-rational-power]] depends only on the
rational $r$ and not on the representative $m/n$ chosen for it, so
[[def-rational-power]] really does define a function
$(a, r) \mapsto a^{r}$ on $\{a > 0\} \times \mathbb{Q}$. The same conclusion
holds in the supplementary case $a = 0$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]), where
every representative gives the value $0$.

Let $N_{\mathbb R}$ be the canonical positive real image of $|G|$ from [[def-qa-normalized-finite-abelian-fourier-transform]]. Define the finite coefficient matrix $U$, with rows indexed by $\widehat G$ and columns by $G$, by
$$U_{\chi,x}=N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad \chi\in\widehat G,\ x\in G.$$
It is square and satisfies $U^*U=I_G$ and $UU^*=I_{\widehat G}$, where $U^*$ is the conjugate transpose and $I_X$ is the identity matrix indexed by $X$, with $(I_X)_{x,y}=1$ when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise. These two identities are the meaning of “unitary” here.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and $\widehat G$ its character dual ([[def-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual]]), which is finite with $|\widehat G|=|G|$ ([[thm-qa-finite-abelian-dual-has-same-cardinality]]). Put $N:=|G|$ and $N_{\mathbb R}:=\iota_{\mathbb R}(N)$ its canonical real image ([[def-order-in-a-group]], [[def-canonical-natural]]). Since $G$ contains its identity, $N\ge1$, and hence $N_{\mathbb R}>0$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]). Its rational power $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}$ is therefore well defined ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

For $f\in\mathbb C^G$, define $F_Gf\in\mathbb C^{\widehat G}$ by
$$ (F_Gf)(\chi):=N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad \chi\in\widehat G. $$
Here $\mathbb C^X$ is the space of all functions $X\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-function-space]]) and the sum is the finite sum in $\mathbb C$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). This fixes the negative-character sign and uses the same factor $N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}$ in both directions. Unitarity is proved separately; it is not part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Write $F_Gf=Uf$ in the point-mass coordinate bases. From [F1], $U^*$ is a two-sided inverse of $U$, so $f=U^*(F_Gf)$.

The $x$ coordinate of $U^*(F_Gf)$ is $\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\overline{U_{\chi,x}}(F_Gf)(\chi)$. By [F2], $\overline{U_{\chi,x}}=N_{\mathbb R}^{-1/2}\chi(x)$, which gives exactly the displayed formula.

For a finite abelian group $G$, give $\widehat G$ its pointwise multiplication. Its dual $\widehat{\widehat G}$ consists of functions $\Phi:\widehat G\to\mathbb C^{\times}$ satisfying $\Phi(\chi\psi)=\Phi(\chi)\Phi(\psi)$. The evaluation map
$$\operatorname{ev}:G\longrightarrow\widehat{\widehat G},\qquad \operatorname{ev}(g)(\chi):=\chi(g),$$
is a group isomorphism. The map itself is canonical; a decomposition into cyclic factors is used only to prove it is injective.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group with character dual $\widehat G$ ([[def-qa-finite-abelian-character-dual]]). For a subgroup $H\le G$ ([[def-subgroup]]), define its character annihilator by
$$H^{\perp}:=\{\chi\in\widehat G:\chi(h)=1\text{ for every }h\in H\}.$$
For any subset $K\subseteq\widehat G$ (in particular, for any subgroup once $\widehat G$ has been proved to be a group), define
$$K^{\perp}:=\{g\in G:\chi(g)=1\text{ for every }\chi\in K\}.$$
The pairing is evaluation, and the same convention is used in both directions. `lem-qa-finite-abelian-annihilators-are-subgroups` proves that these sets are subgroups when the input is a subgroup.
For a finite abelian group $G$, the pointwise product, constant-one identity and pointwise inverse on $\widehat G$ make it a finite abelian group. Its order is $|\widehat G|=|G|$.
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group. For every subgroup $H\le G$, $H^\perp$ is a subgroup of $\widehat G$. For every subgroup $K\le\widehat G$, $K^\perp$ is a subgroup of $G$.

For a subgroup $H\le G$ of a finite abelian group, restriction and inflation identify $H^\perp$ with the character dual of $G/H$. Consequently
$$|H^\perp|=|G/H|=[G:H]=\frac{|G|}{|H|},\qquad |H^\perp|\,|H|=|G|.$$
The quotient convention is left cosets, with additive notation.

Let $A$ be a finite set ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then:

1. $B$ is finite;
2. $\lvert B\rvert \le \lvert A\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]);
3. $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ if and only if $B = A$;
4. every injection $f : A \to A$ is a bijection, and every surjection
   $f : A \to A$ is a bijection.

Clause 3 is the finite form of the Dedekind statement: a finite set is not
equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. Clause 4 is its working form, and
**finiteness is exactly the hypothesis that fails in general**: the successor map
is an injection of $\mathbb{N}$ into itself that is not surjective, which is the
false statement recorded on this page's companion.

Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  ([[def-binary-operation]]);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it ([[def-identity-element]]), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ ([[def-invertible-element]]). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

derivations.claim: Put $A:=(H^\perp)^{\perp_{\widehat G}}=\{\Phi\in\widehat{\widehat G}:\Phi(\chi)=1\text{ for every }\chi\in H^\perp\}$, the character annihilator of the subgroup $H^\perp$ inside the group $\widehat G$. If $h\in H$, every $\chi\in H^\perp$ has $\chi(h)=1$ by [F2], so $\operatorname{ev}(h)(\chi)=1$ for every such $\chi$ and $\operatorname{ev}(h)\in A$. Thus $\operatorname{ev}(H)\subseteq A$.

By [F3], $H^\perp$ is a subgroup of the finite abelian group $\widehat G$; [F6] gives $|H^\perp|\ge1$. Applying [F4] to $G,H$ and then to $\widehat G,H^\perp$ gives $|H^\perp||H|=|G|$ and $|A||H^\perp|=|\widehat G|=|G|$, the last equality following from [F1]. Cancellation gives $|A|=|H|$. The injective evaluation isomorphism [F1] gives $|\operatorname{ev}(H)|=|H|$; with step 1.1, the finite-subset result [F5] yields $A=\operatorname{ev}(H)$.

By definition [F2], $g\in(H^\perp)^\perp$ exactly when $\chi(g)=1$ for every $\chi\in H^\perp$, which is exactly when $\operatorname{ev}(g)\in A$. Since step 2.1 proves $A=\operatorname{ev}(H)$ and [F1] makes evaluation injective, its preimage is $H$; hence $(H^\perp)^\perp=H$.
