For a finite Boolean query problem (N,D,f), all matrices below are indexed by the same fixed ordering of D. For i∈[N], define the input-mismatch matrix
$$(\Delta_i)_{xy}:=\mathbf 1[x_i\ne y_i].$$
For same-size matrices define the entrywise product $(A\circ B)_{xy}:=A_{xy}B_{xy}$. Define the same-output mask $F_{xy}:=\mathbf 1[f(x)=f(y)]$ and the all-ones matrix $J_{xy}:=1$. Thus $J-F$ is the opposite-output mask.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Fix distributions $p_x(i)\ge0$ with $\sum_i p_x(i)=1$ for each x, and let $\eta=\min_{f(x)\ne f(y)}\sum_{i:x_i\ne y_i}\sqrt{p_x(i)p_y(i)}>0$. Let $\Gamma\ge0$ be an admissible nonzero matrix. By [F4], choose a real orthonormal eigenbasis of the symmetric matrix $\Gamma$; thus $\|\Gamma\|=\max_j|\lambda_j|=\max_{\|z\|=1}|z^{\mathsf T}\Gamma z|$ and $\lambda_{\max}(\Gamma)=\max_{\|z\|=1}z^{\mathsf T}\Gamma z$. For every real unit z, entrywise nonnegativity gives $|z^{\mathsf T}\Gamma z|\le |z|^{\mathsf T}\Gamma|z|\le\lambda_{\max}(\Gamma)$. Since $\Gamma$ is nonzero admissible, it has a positive off-diagonal entry, so a vector supported equally on that pair has positive Rayleigh quotient and $\lambda_{\max}(\Gamma)>0$. Hence $\|\Gamma\|=\lambda_{\max}(\Gamma)$. If v is a unit top eigenvector, then $|v|$ is a nonnegative unit vector with $|v|^{\mathsf T}\Gamma|v|\ge v^{\mathsf T}\Gamma v=\lambda_{\max}(\Gamma)$, so equality holds and $\delta:=|v|$ is also a top eigenvector.

For every cross-output pair the mismatch overlap is at least η; all coefficients Γ_xy δ_xδ_y are nonnegative. Therefore η||Γ||≤Σ_{x,y}Γ_xyδ_xδ_yΣ_iΔ_i(x,y)√(p_x(i)p_y(i)) =Σ_i s_i^T(Γ∘Δ_i)s_i, where (s_i)_x=δ_x√p_x(i).

By Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] and the induced norm definition [F3], each summand is at most ||Γ∘Δ_i||·||s_i||². Summing gives at most max_i||Γ∘Δ_i||·Σ_iΣ_xδ_x²p_x(i)=max_i||Γ∘Δ_i||, because every p_x is a probability distribution and ||δ||=1. Divide by η and the positive denominator to obtain the claimed upper certificate for Γ; maximizing over Γ proves Adv(f)≤1/η.

For a finite matrix A indexed by D×D and Boolean masks Δ={Δ_i}_{i=1}^N, define
$$
\gamma_2(A\mid\Delta):=\inf \max\!\left\{\max_{x\in D}\sum_i\|u_{x,i}\|^2,\ \max_{y\in D}\sum_i\|v_{y,i}\|^2\right\},
$$
where the infimum is over finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and vector families satisfying
$$A_{xy}=\sum_i(\Delta_i)_{xy}\langle u_{x,i}|v_{y,i}\rangle_D\quad(x,y\in D).$$
Set the value to $+\infty$ if no such families exist. Every feasible family may be taken in dimension at most $2|D|$ for each i.

For the Boolean mismatch masks, $\gamma_2(A\mid\Delta)<\infty$ if and only if $A_{xx}=0$ for every x. Whenever finite, the infimum is attained by finite vector families. A minimizing family can be taken in dimension at most $2|D|$ for each coordinate i.

For a nonconstant finite Boolean query problem define
$$\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f):= \max_{\substack{\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{D\times D},\ \Gamma=\Gamma^{\mathsf T},\ \Gamma\ne0\\ \Gamma\circ F=0}} \frac{\|\Gamma\|}{\max_{i\in[N]}\|\Gamma\circ\Delta_i\|}.$$
Negative entries are allowed. The denominator is positive and the maximum is finite and attained by [[lem-qa-16-general-adversary-finite-and-attained]]. For constant f set $\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)=0$. The **nonnegative adversary value** $\operatorname{Adv}(f)$ is the same maximum with the additional constraint $\Gamma_{xy}\ge0$ for all x,y; it is also set to zero for constant f.

For every finite nonconstant partial Boolean function $f:D\to\{0,1\}$,
$$\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)=\min_{\{v_{x,i}\}}\max\{C_0,C_1\},\qquad C_b:=\max_{x:f(x)=b}\sum_i\|v_{x,i}\|^2.$$
The vectors lie in a common finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and satisfy, for all distinct $x,y$,
$$\sum_{i:x_i\ne y_i}\langle v_{x,i}|v_{y,i}\rangle_D=\mathbf1[f(x)\ne f(y)].$$
The minimum is attained. If only opposite-output constraints are initially required, tensoring each vector with $|x_i\oplus f(x)\rangle$ imposes the equal-output zero constraints without changing costs or cross-output values.
If $A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ are positive semidefinite, then their entrywise product $A\circ B$, defined by $(A\circ B)_{jk}=A_{jk}B_{jk}$, is positive semidefinite.

derivations.claim: For A=J−F, the defining factorization equations for γ₂(A|Δ) are exactly Σ_{i:x_i≠y_i}⟨u_{x,i}|v_{y,i}⟩=1 for opposite outputs and 0 for equal outputs. The target has zero diagonal, so [F2] gives a finite attained value.

The dual-vector theorem [F4] gives the minimum of precisely these equations and the same maximum row/column squared-norm cost. Its single-family form has cost max{C_0,C_1}. Assigning u_{x,i}=w_{x,i} and v_{y,i}=w_{y,i} for every input gives a factorization of identical cost, while the dual-vector proof constructs the single family by taking the row family on D_0 and the column family on D_1, then applying the Boolean output-label code. Therefore the two minima coincide and equal Adv±(f).

In the equivalent cross-output-only formulation, tensoring by the two-code label yields equal-output zeros while preserving cross-output constraints. The associated label Gram matrix is PSD, and [F5] confirms its entrywise product with each original Gram matrix is PSD; thus this equivalent realization remains a valid finite Gram factorization with unchanged vector norms. The Boolean output alphabet makes the label inner product exactly 1 on required cross-output mismatches and 0 on same-output mismatches, so there is no output-size loss factor.

$$W_t=\sum_{x,y\in D}\Gamma_{xy}\alpha_x\alpha_y\langle\psi_x^t|\psi_y^t\rangle_D,$$
where α is a real unit eigenvector of Γ with eigenvalue of magnitude ||Γ||. Then |W_0|=||Γ|| and
$$|W_T|\le 2\sqrt{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}\,\|\Gamma\|.$$

In a standard XOR bit-query algorithm, one oracle call changes the progress $W_t$ of [[lem-qa-16-adversary-progress-endpoints]] by at most
$$|W_{t+1}-W_t|\le2\max_{i\in[N]}\|\Gamma\circ\Delta_i\|.$$

Fix an integer N≥1, a nonempty finite set D⊆{0,1}^N, and a Boolean function f:D→{0,1}. A Boolean query problem is the tuple (N,D,f) with input x∈D and standard XOR oracle
$$O_x|i,b,w\rangle=|i,b\oplus x_i,w\rangle\quad (i\in[N],\ b\in\{0,1\}).$$
For 0≤ε<1/2, Q_ε(f) is the least worst-case number of these oracle calls of an algorithm outputting f(x) with probability at least 1−ε for every x∈D. The input promise does not restrict the oracle address. Only query calls are counted here; no gate-efficiency assertion is part of this definition.

For a $T$-query quantum algorithm [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] at input length $n$, its **worst-case quantum query cost** is the maximum number of designated oracle calls over all promised instances in $P_n$ and all measurement branches. When $P_n$ is empty, define this cost to be $0$. For nonempty $P_n$, a finite circuit and finite branch sets ensure that this maximum exists; a solver whose branch counts are not uniformly bounded has infinite worst-case query cost. An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

In the pure query model, ordinary gates outside the oracle calls are uncharged by the query coordinate. If a task also reports gate, preparation, measurement, or classical costs, those are separate coordinates. Bounded-error query cost uses the same worst-case maximum; its success threshold is the per-instance condition in [[def-qa-bounded-error-promise-correctness]], not an average over oracle inputs.

Negative entries are allowed. The denominator is positive and the maximum is finite and attained by [[lem-qa-16-general-adversary-finite-and-attained]]. derivations.claim: Fix a nonconstant f and an algorithm with per-input error at most ε, as in the parameterized definition [F3]. For any admissible real symmetric Γ, [F6] applied to its complexification gives an eigenvalue of modulus ||Γ||; the eigenvalue is real, and real or imaginary part of a corresponding eigenvector is a nonzero real eigenvector, so choose a real unit principal eigenvector α. Put D_Γ=max_i||Γ∘Δ_i||. Between queries the algorithm's input-independent unitaries preserve all pairwise inner products, so they do not change W. For T queries, [F2] and the triangle inequality give |W_T−W_0|≤2T D_Γ.
By [F1], ||Γ||=|W_0|≤|W_T|+|W_T−W_0|≤(2√(ε(1−ε)))||Γ||+2T D_Γ. Since ε<1/2, rearrangement yields T≥(1/2−√(ε(1−ε)))||Γ||/D_Γ.
The inequality holds for every admissible Γ. Taking the attained maximum ratio from [F5] gives Q_ε(f)≥(1/2−√(ε(1−ε)))Adv±(f). For constant f the empty algorithm is exact and both sides are zero.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For a nonconstant finite Boolean query problem define
$$\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f):= \max_{\substack{\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{D\times D},\ \Gamma=\Gamma^{\mathsf T},\ \Gamma\ne0\\ \Gamma\circ F=0}} \frac{\|\Gamma\|}{\max_{i\in[N]}\|\Gamma\circ\Delta_i\|}.$$
Negative entries are allowed. The denominator is positive and the maximum is finite and attained by [[lem-qa-16-general-adversary-finite-and-attained]]. For constant f set $\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)=0$. The **nonnegative adversary value** $\operatorname{Adv}(f)$ is the same maximum with the additional constraint $\Gamma_{xy}\ge0$ for all x,y; it is also set to zero for constant f.

For nonconstant f let
$$\operatorname{Adv}(f):= \max_{\substack{\Gamma=\Gamma^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{D\times D},\ \Gamma\ne0,\ \Gamma\circ F=0\\ \Gamma_{xy}\ge0\ \forall x,y}} \frac{\|\Gamma\|}{\max_i\|\Gamma\circ\Delta_i\|}.$$
Set $\operatorname{Adv}(f)=0$ if f is constant. This is the nonnegative-weight adversary bound under exactly the same masks and query normalization as $\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)$.

For a finite Boolean query problem (N,D,f), all matrices below are indexed by the same fixed ordering of D. For i∈[N], define the input-mismatch matrix
$$(\Delta_i)_{xy}:=\mathbf 1[x_i\ne y_i].$$
For same-size matrices define the entrywise product $(A\circ B)_{xy}:=A_{xy}B_{xy}$. Define the same-output mask $F_{xy}:=\mathbf 1[f(x)=f(y)]$ and the all-ones matrix $J_{xy}:=1$. Thus $J-F$ is the opposite-output mask.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Fix an integer N≥1, a nonempty finite set D⊆{0,1}^N, and a Boolean function f:D→{0,1}. A Boolean query problem is the tuple (N,D,f) with input x∈D and standard XOR oracle
$$O_x|i,b,w\rangle=|i,b\oplus x_i,w\rangle\quad (i\in[N],\ b\in\{0,1\}).$$
For 0≤ε<1/2, Q_ε(f) is the least worst-case number of these oracle calls of an algorithm outputting f(x) with probability at least 1−ε for every x∈D. The input promise does not restrict the oracle address. Only query calls are counted here; no gate-efficiency assertion is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Let f:D_f→{0,1} be a nonconstant Boolean function on N bits and g:D_g→{0,1} a nonconstant Boolean function on m bits. The composed partial function h=f∘g^N has domain D_h={ (x_1,…,x_N)∈D_g^N : (g(x_1),…,g(x_N))∈D_f }. This domain is nonempty: choose one z∈D_f and fixed preimages in D_g of 0 and 1, which exist because g is nonconstant, then lift the coordinates of z blockwise. Choose optimal matrices Γ_f,Γ_g normalized so max_i||Γ_f∘Δ_i||=max_j||Γ_g∘Δ_j||=1; write a=||Γ_g||=Adv±(g).

Decompose each adversary matrix by output classes, Γ_g=[[0,B_g],[B_g^T,0]]. For a,b∈{0,1}, let G^{ab} be the (a,b) block of Γ_g when a≠b and let G^{aa}=a I on D_g^a. For x,y∈D_h put \tilde x=(g(x_1),…,g(x_N)) and define (Γ_h)_{xy}=(Γ_f)_{\tilde x,\tilde y}\prod_{j=1}^N G^{\tilde x_j,\tilde y_j}_{x_j,y_j}. This matrix is real symmetric and vanishes whenever h(x)=h(y); if Γ_f,Γ_g are entrywise nonnegative, so is Γ_h.

By [F4,F5], choose a singular-vector basis of the cross block B_g. Pair its positive singular vectors across the two output classes, and pair equal numbers of left and right null vectors with singular value zero. If the null-space dimensions differ, each leftover null vector is a one-dimensional component supported on just one output class; its equal-output patch is aI and its cross-output action is zero. For a paired singular value s≤a, the four restrictions G^{00},G^{01},G^{10},G^{11} act as a times C_s=[[1,s/a],[s/a,1]], which is positive semidefinite with unit diagonal. A leftover singleton is represented by C_0=diag(1,0) or diag(0,1), a positive semidefinite matrix with diagonal entries at most one. For each tuple of child components, the corresponding invariant subspace is indexed by the compatible outer output labels b∈D_f, and the restriction of Γ_h is a^N times the compression of Γ_f∘C, where C_{b,b′} is the product of the selected two-output factors. The tensor-product factor C is positive semidefinite with diagonal entries at most one. Write C_{b,b′}=⟨c_b|c_{b′}⟩ with ||c_b||≤1; then V|b⟩=|b⟩⊗|c_b⟩ is a contraction and V^*(Γ_f⊗I)V=Γ_f∘C, so ||Γ_f∘C||≤||Γ_f||. The SVD components span every child input space, proving ||Γ_h||≤||Γ_f||a^N.

Choose top singular pairs (u_f,v_f) and (u_g,v_g) for the cross blocks of Γ_f and Γ_g. The bipartite block form makes α_f=(u_f,v_f)/√2 and α_g=(u_g,v_g)/√2 eigenvectors with eigenvalues ||Γ_f|| and a. For a fixed outer output tuple b, each child factor G^{b_j,b′_j} sends the restricted α_g component in class b′_j to a times the corresponding component in class b_j, whether b_j=b′_j (the patched aI block) or b_j≠b′_j (the singular-vector equation for B_g). Substitution in the definition of Γ_h therefore shows α_h(x)=α_f(tilde x)∏_jα_g(x_j) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue ||Γ_f||a^N. Together with step 2.1 this gives ||Γ_h||=||Γ_f||a^N.

Fix an input bit q in block j and put d=||Γ_g∘Δ_q||. If d=0, then every entry of Γ_g∘Δ_q is zero, the equal-output patch dI is zero, and the masked composed block is zero. Suppose d>0. In Γ_h∘Δ_{j,q}, if the outer block outputs agree at j, its factor Γ_f∘Δ_j is zero; equivalently, the patched equal-output child block is diagonal in x_j and is killed by the inner mismatch Δ_q. If the outer outputs differ at j, the child cross block is exactly the corresponding block of Γ_g∘Δ_q. Thus the masked composite has the same entrywise construction as step 1.2 with outer matrix Γ_f∘Δ_j, child j cross block from Γ_g∘Δ_q patched by dI on equal-output blocks, and every other child patched by aI. Repeating the invariant-subspace and correlation-compression argument of step 2.1 bounds its norm by ||Γ_f∘Δ_j|| d a^{N−1}. The paired, zero-singular, and singleton components are handled as in step 2.1; the outer and inner filtered norms are at most one by normalization, so ||Γ_h∘Δ_{j,q}||≤a^{N−1}.

Therefore max_{j,q}||Γ_h∘Δ_{j,q}||≤a^{N-1}, while ||Γ_h||=Adv±(f)a^N by step 3.1. Its ratio is at least Adv±(f)a, proving Adv±(f∘g^N)≥Adv±(f)Adv±(g). If Γ_f and Γ_g are nonnegative, step 1.2 makes Γ_h nonnegative, so the identical argument proves Adv(f∘g^N)≥Adv(f)Adv(g). If either function is constant, the asserted lower bound is the trivial zero bound.

**Inputs.** A finite nonconstant Boolean function $f:D\to\{0,1\}$ on $N\ge1$ input bits and a supplied finite dual-vector certificate $\{v_{x,i}\}$ in a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$, meaning that for every distinct $x,y\in D$,
$$\sum_{i:x_i\ne y_i}\langle v_{x,i}|v_{y,i}\rangle_D=\mathbf1[f(x)\ne f(y)].$$
Its class costs $C_b:=\max_{x:f(x)=b}\sum_i\|v_{x,i}\|^2$ satisfy $C_0,C_1\le A$ for a supplied bound $A\ge1$. The declared standard XOR input oracle is available. The input-independent controlled witness-span reflection specified below is a nonoracle operation in this query model; no efficient gate implementation for it is assumed.

**Output.** A Boolean estimate of $f(x)$ for the promised input $x\in D$.

**Instructions.** Use the finite work space
$$\mathcal H=\operatorname{span}\{|start\rangle\}\oplus(\mathbb C^N\otimes V\otimes\mathbb C^2).$$
Here the address basis is $|i\rangle=e_{i-1}$ for $i\in[N]$, and $|start\rangle$ is a specified unit vector orthogonal to the query summand.
The witness family is classical instance data used to specify a subspace, not an input-dependent state preparation. Define
$$\nu_x=1+\frac1{2A}\sum_i\|v_{x,i}\|^2,\qquad |\psi_x\rangle=\nu_x^{-1/2}\left(|start\rangle+\frac1{\sqrt{2A}}\sum_i|i\rangle|v_{x,i}\rangle|x_i\rangle\right).$$
Let $\Delta$ project onto the span of all $|\psi_y\rangle$ with $f(y)=1$, and let
$$\Pi_x=|start\rangle\langle start|+\sum_{i=1}^N|i\rangle\langle i|\otimes I_V\otimes|x_i\rangle\langle x_i|$$
project onto $|start\rangle$ plus query states whose response is $x_i$. Form the exact ordered product
$$U_x=(2\Pi_x-I)(2\Delta-I).$$

Choose $M=2^m$ as the least power of two satisfying $M\ge512A$. Initialize the data register to $|start\rangle$ and apply the coherent QPE gate list followed by its projective readout on $U_x$. Implement controlled $U_x$ in chronological order by controlled $(2\Delta-I)$, then controlled $(2\Pi_x-I)$, retaining both plus-on-range signs. Repeat that complete controlled circuit $2^j$ times for the required power $U_x^{2^j}$ at each $j=0,\ldots,m-1$. Each controlled input-dependent reflection is the two-unconditional-query consistency-reflection circuit of [[alg-qa-16-controlled-consistency-reflection]]. For the measured phase label $y$, return $1$ exactly when $y=0$ and return $0$ otherwise. No gate-complexity bound is asserted for the input-independent reflection about the full witness span or the remaining nonoracle gates.

Let H be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, Π and Δ orthogonal projections on H, R_Π=2Π-I and R_Δ=2Δ-I, and U=R_ΠR_Δ. For 0≤ω≤π, let E_ω be the spectral projection of U onto eigenvalues e^{iφ} whose principal arguments satisfy |φ|≤ω. If Δw=0, then
$$\|E_\omega\Pi w\|\le \frac{\omega}{2}\|w\|.$$

Let $m\ge1$, $Q=2^m$, and $\theta\in[0,1)$. Every nearest grid label $y$ has $P_\theta(y)\ge4/\pi^2$. For any $\eta\in\mathbb R$ with $K=\lfloor Q\eta\rfloor\ge2$,
$$\Pr_{y\sim P_\theta}\!\left[d_{\mathbb T}(\theta-y/Q)\ge\eta\right]\le\frac1{2(K-1)}.$$
If $Q\theta$ is an integer $t$, then $P_\theta(t)=1$ and all other labels have probability $0$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

For every finite nonconstant partial Boolean function $f:D\to\{0,1\}$,
$$\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)=\min_{\{v_{x,i}\}}\max\{C_0,C_1\},\qquad C_b:=\max_{x:f(x)=b}\sum_i\|v_{x,i}\|^2.$$
The vectors lie in a common finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and satisfy, for all distinct $x,y$,
$$\sum_{i:x_i\ne y_i}\langle v_{x,i}|v_{y,i}\rangle_D=\mathbf1[f(x)\ne f(y)].$$
The minimum is attained. If only opposite-output constraints are initially required, tensoring each vector with $|x_i\oplus f(x)\rangle$ imposes the equal-output zero constraints without changing costs or cross-output values.
If f is nonconstant, then $\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\ge1$. In particular the finite optimal adversary value A used by the reflection evaluator may be taken with A≥1.

**Inputs.** A Boolean query problem with $N\ge1$, promised input $x\in D$ accessed by its standard XOR oracle, a finite work space $K$, a one-bit control $c$, and a data register with orthogonal decomposition
$$\mathcal H=\operatorname{span}\{|start\rangle\}\oplus(\mathbb C^N\otimes K\otimes\mathbb C^2),$$
where the address basis is $|i\rangle=e_{i-1}$ for $i\in[N]$ and $|start\rangle$ is a specified unit vector orthogonal to the query summand,
and one clean scratch bit $u=0$. Fix a known address $i_0\in[N]$. Define the consistency sum
$$\Pi_x=|start\rangle\langle start|+\sum_{i=1}^N|i\rangle\langle i|\otimes I_K\otimes|x_i\rangle\langle x_i|.$$

**Output.** A gate list for the controlled plus-on-range reflection $2\Pi_x-I$ on the data register, returning the scratch bit to zero.

**Instructions.** In query mode route address $i$ to the oracle and use $u$ as its target. In start mode route the oracle address to the fixed $i_0$ and apply a Hadamard to $u$, so its query target is $|+\rangle$. Make one unconditional standard XOR oracle call. Apply phase $-1$ exactly when $c=1$, the mode is query, and the response bit $z$ differs from $u$; disable this phase on start and when $c=0$. Make a second unconditional XOR call with the same address routing. In start mode apply the Hadamard to $u$ again. Return the data and control registers and the scratch. No controlled unknown-oracle call is invoked.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. Fix the two signs

$$R_\Pi:=2\Pi-I,\qquad S_\Pi:=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi.$$

Thus $R_\Pi$ acts as $+I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and $-I$ on $\ker\Pi$; $S_\Pi$ reverses those signs. They are not interchangeable inside a controlled block. For a unit vector $\psi$, the rank-one reflection is $R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I$ with the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An access model counts a direct reflection as one primitive call only when that call is explicitly declared. Controlled reflection access is a separate declaration. If $|0\rangle$ is a specified unit input in the same space $H$, the state is prepared as $\psi=U|0\rangle$ for a declared unitary $U$, and a reflection is implemented by conjugating $R_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I$, the construction is $UR_0U^\dagger$ and its cost must include the calls to $U$, $R_0$, and $U^\dagger$. A state vector or matrix description alone implies neither an efficient reflection nor inverse access.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in the first argument. For nonzero $x\in H$, put $u=x/\|x\|$. If $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ has $|\lambda|=1$, then $u$ and $\lambda u$ determine the same rank-one density operator. Consequently, for every finite POVM $(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ on $H$, each defined outcome probability satisfies

$$\operatorname{tr}(|u\rangle\langle u|E_a)=\operatorname{tr}(|\lambda u\rangle\langle\lambda u|E_a).$$

The unnormalized vector $x$ itself gives $\operatorname{tr}(|x\rangle\langle x|)=\|x\|^2$ and is not a density operator when $\|x\|\ne1$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and $U:H\to H$ a unitary. Let $\theta\in\mathbb R$, and suppose the model separately grants controlled access to both $U$ and $e^{i\theta}U$. There is a normalized eigenvector $\phi$ with $U\phi=\mu\phi$ and $|\mu|=1$. Let $C=Q_2=\mathbb C^2$ be the control qubit with ordered computational basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$; define $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and prepare $(|0\rangle+\overline\mu|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ with target $\phi$. The two joint effects are $E_\pm=|\pm\rangle\langle\pm|\otimes I_H$. The $E_+$ outcome has probability $1$ after $C(U)$ and $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ after $C(e^{i\theta}U)$. Thus the two controlled maps give different outcome laws exactly when $\theta\notin2\pi\mathbb Z$; when $\theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the controlled maps coincide. This is a mathematical witness; it does not assert that controlled access or the witness-state preparation is free.

**Input.** An integer $m\ge1$; an $m$-qubit phase register; a finite-dimensional system register $H$; a unitary $U:H\to H$; a unit eigenvector $\psi$ with promised phase $\theta\in[0,1)$; and one of the forward access capabilities in [[def-qa-eigenphase-estimation-model]].

**Output.** A classical label $y\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$ and its phase estimate $y/Q$, where $Q=2^m$.

**Instructions.**

1. Initialize the phase register in $|0^m\rangle$ and the system register in $\psi$.
2. Apply the Hadamard $H=(X+Z)/\sqrt2$ of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] to each phase wire. This prepares $Q^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{Q-1}|x\rangle\otimes\psi$ in the declared big-endian order.
3. For $j=0,\ldots,m-1$, apply the supplied controlled $U^{2^j}$ to control wire $q_{m-1-j}$ and the system. Under single controlled-unitary access, implement that operation with $2^j$ sequential calls to $C(U)$, as specified by the access model.
4. Apply the inverse of the positive-sign exact binary QFT circuit of [[def-qa-cyclic-quantum-fourier-transform]] and [[thm-qa-exact-binary-qft-circuit-correct]]. $$D_h=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\in D_g^N:(g(x_1),\ldots,g(x_N))\in D_f\},\qquad h=f\circ g^N.$$

$$\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(h)\ge\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(g),\qquad \operatorname{Adv}(h)\ge\operatorname{Adv}(f)\operatorname{Adv}(g).$$

For a nonconstant finite Boolean query problem (N,D,f), let each p_x be a probability distribution on [N]. If

Thus every composition domain is nonempty and both adversary bounds in [F2] apply. The signed matrix in [F1] and repeated composition in [F2] give $\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f^{(k)})\ge\operatorname{Adv}^{\pm}(f)^k>(2.511486)^k$.

The base coordinate distributions in [F1] have mismatch overlap at least η=2/5. If P_X^{(k)} is a distribution over the 4^k input coordinates with cross-output overlap at least η^k, define for an input X=(X_1,…,X_4) to f^{(k+1)} P_X^{(k+1)}(j,r)=p_{\tilde X}(j)P_{X_j}^{(k)}(r),\quad \tilde X_j=f^{(k)}(X_j). Summing those j gives total overlap at least η·η^k=η^{k+1}; normalization follows by multiplying two probability distributions.

$$\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P):=1-\|P|_{H_0}\|_{2,\pi}.$$

The norm of the restriction to the zero subspace is $0$ by [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]], so a one-state chain has absolute gap $1$. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is built into this definition: a reducible chain with a nonconstant stationary vector in $H_0$ can have gap $0$, and a periodic chain can have gap $0$ because of an eigenvalue $-1$. The eigenvalue form of the definition is proved in [[thm-qa-17-absolute-gap-eigenvalue-characterization]].

For a finite reversible chain $(X,P,\pi)$, equip $\mathbb C^X$ with $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_x\pi_x f_x\overline{g_x}$. Then $P$ is self-adjoint for this inner product, and the mean-zero subspace

$$H_0:=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}=\{f:\langle f,\mathbf 1\rangle_\pi=0\}$$

is invariant under $P$. The restriction $P|_{H_0}$ is therefore a well-defined endomorphism and is self-adjoint for the restricted inner product.

Let $(X,P,\pi)$ be a finite reversible chain and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$. Define $\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2:=\sum_x\pi_x|f_x|^2$ and $(Pf)_x:=\sum_yP_{xy}f_y$. Then

$$\|Pf\|_{2,\pi}^2\le\|f\|_{2,\pi}^2,$$

so $P$ is a contraction on the finite weighted inner-product space $L^2(X,\pi)$. Detailed balance is not needed for this inequality beyond the stated stationary-law hypotheses.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

$$U:=S R_A,\qquad W:=U^2=(S R_A S)R_A=(2S\Pi S-I)(2\Pi-I).$$

An endomorphism $P$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace if and only if

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]],

[[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]). The intermediate value
theorem therefore makes its restricted image exactly $[-1,1]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]). Likewise, cosine is continuous and strictly
decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, with endpoint values $1$ and $-1$, so its restricted
image is $[-1,1]$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]],
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-intermediate-value]]).
Their principal inverses are denoted

$$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$

and are characterised by

$$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$

The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse
sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions.
Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the sets $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{im}T$ are
linear subspaces. Moreover, $T$ is injective if and only if $\ker T=\{0_V\}$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

derivations.claim: If $X=\varnothing$, then $\mathbb C^X=\mathbb C^{X\times X}=\{0\}$, so there are no eigenvalues and the claims are vacuous. Assume now $X\ne\varnothing$. By [F1] and [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $(v_j)$ of the self-adjoint $D$, with real eigenvalues $\lambda_j\in[-1,1]$; the bound follows from $\|D\|\le1$.

For distinct basis vectors $v_j,v_k$, the spans $\operatorname{span}\{Tv_j,STv_j\}$ and $\operatorname{span}\{Tv_k,STv_k\}$ are orthogonal: the $T$-images and their swapped images pair to $\langle v_j,v_k\rangle=0$, while the cross pairings equal $\langle v_j,Dv_k\rangle=\lambda_k\langle v_j,v_k\rangle=0$. These spans together generate $A+B$, where $A=\operatorname{ran}T$ and $B=\operatorname{ran}(ST)$.

Fix an eigenvalue $\lambda_j\in(-1,1)$ and its plane basis $a=Tv_j,b=STv_j$. By [F2], the matrix of $U$ in the ordered basis $(a,b)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\lambda_j\end{pmatrix}$, so its characteristic equation is $z^2-2\lambda_jz+1=0$. Its roots are $z=\lambda_j\pm i\sqrt{1-\lambda_j^2}$; each root has eigenvector $(1,-z)$ in these coordinates, and the roots are distinct because $|\lambda_j|<1$. Put $\theta_j=\arccos\lambda_j\in(0,\pi)$. By [F7], $\cos\theta_j=\lambda_j$. If $0<\theta_j\le\pi/2$, strict increase from $\sin0=0$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ gives $\sin\theta_j>0$; if $\pi/2<\theta_j<\pi$, strict decrease to $\sin\pi=0$ on $[\pi/2,\pi]$ gives the same. These monotonicity and endpoint facts are [F12] and [F14]. Then [F8] and uniqueness in [F9] yield $\sin\theta_j=\sqrt{1-\lambda_j^2}$. [F10] identifies the roots as $\exp(\pm i\theta_j)$, and [F11] squares them to $\exp(\pm2i\theta_j)$ for $W=U^2$.

If $\lambda_j=\pm1$, [F2] gives $STv_j=\lambda_jTv_j$, so the corresponding line contributes the single eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ to $U$ and $+1$ to $W$. This counts one endpoint eigenvalue per eigendirection, not two coincident plane eigenvalues.

Let $H=A+B$, the sum of the images of $T$ and $ST$ as identified by [F15]; both are subspaces by [F13], so their sum is a subspace. By [F6], $\mathbb C^{X\times X}=H\oplus K$ with $K=H^\perp$. Since $K\subseteq A^\perp$, [F3] gives $U|_K=-S|_K$. The swap preserves $K$: for $a\in A$ and $w\in K$, $\langle a,Sw\rangle=\langle Sa,w\rangle=0$ because $Sa\in B$, and for $b\in B$ and $w\in K$, $\langle b,Sw\rangle=\langle Sb,w\rangle=0$ because $Sb\in A$.

On $K$, $S^2=I$, so each $w\in K$ decomposes as $(w+Sw)/2+(w-Sw)/2$; these summands lie in $K$ by step 3.1 and satisfy $S(w+Sw)=w+Sw$ and $S(w-Sw)=-(w-Sw)$. Thus $U=-S$ has eigenvalues only $\pm1$ on $K$, and $W=U^2$ is identity there. Combining this with steps 2.2–2.3 gives the complete eigenvalue multiset, including repeated eigenvalues and any overlap of endpoint values with the complement. No irreducibility, aperiodicity, or choice principle is used.

For a nonempty finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$, a **row-preparation access model** supplies an explicit bijection $\eta:X\to\{0,\ldots,|X|-1\}$; write $\kappa_x$ for the image of $x$ under this bijection. Every ket $|x\rangle$ below denotes the basis vector $|\kappa_x\rangle$. The model supplies a finite work register $W$ with a specified clean unit vector $|0_W\rangle$ and a unitary $V_P$ on the ordered register product $\mathbb C^X\otimes\mathbb C^X\otimes W$ satisfying

$$V_P\bigl(|x\rangle\otimes|0\rangle\otimes|0_W\rangle\bigr)=\left(|x\rangle\otimes\sum_y\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle\right)\otimes|0_W\rangle\qquad(x\in X).$$

The state encoding and its description are part of the supplied circuit interface and are included in the circuit description or uniform generator. The model separately declares access and costs for the forward call $V_P$, inverse call $V_P^*$, controlled $V_P$, controlled $V_P^*$, a direct range-reflection call, controlled range-reflection access, the clean-state reflection $R_0$, controlled $R_0$, the swap on the first two registers, and controlled swap access. The clean-state reflection is

$$R_0:=2\bigl(I_X\otimes|0,0_W\rangle\langle0,0_W|\bigr)-I,$$

where the second register and work register are in their specified clean states. When range reflection is implemented from row preparation, the supplied circuit word is $V_PR_0V_P^*$; the access-cost theorem proves that on the clean-work subspace it realizes the logical reflection $2TT^*-I$. The swap acts as $S$ on the first two registers and as the identity on $W$.

Query calls, gate counts, circuit-description bits, uniform-generation time, and precision are separate cost coordinates. A controlled walk implemented factor by factor needs controlled access to each constituent, including the preparation calls, $R_0$, and the swap. A matrix $P$ by itself supplies none of these circuits or efficient costs. For a family of encoded chains, a uniform circuit family is an additional explicit input, not a consequence of the finite matrix definition.

For the finite row-stochastic kernel and row-preparation map of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]], let $\Pi:=TT^*$, the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{ran}(T)$, and choose the reflection sign

$$R_A:=2\Pi-I.$$

With $S$ the two-register swap, define the one-reflection Szegedy step and its square by

$$U:=S R_A,\qquad W:=U^2=(S R_A S)R_A=(2S\Pi S-I)(2\Pi-I).$$

Products act right to left. This fixes $U$ and $W$ as different operators. Algebraically, if $Uv=\mu v$, then $Wv=\mu^2v$ on the same vector. The other common reflection sign is $I-2\Pi=-R_A$ and is not interchangeable inside a controlled operation.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

For a finite-dimensional unitary $U$, **inverse access** is the explicitly granted operation $U^\dagger=U^{-1}$. Its availability and query or gate charge are recorded separately from forward access, including any controlled access in [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. For a chronological sequence of length $k\ge0$ that applies $U_1$ first and $U_k$ last, the total operator is $W=U_k\cdots U_1$ when $k>0$ and $W=I_H$ when $k=0$. For $k>0$, the inverse sequence applies $U_k^\dagger$ first, then $U_{k-1}^\dagger$, down to $U_1^\dagger$; for $k=0$ it is the empty sequence.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

An endomorphism $P$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace if and only if

$$P^2=P\qquad\text{and}\qquad P^*=P.$$

In that case it is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}P$, along $\ker P=(\operatorname{im}P)^\perp$. The cases $P=0$ and $P=I$ are included.

derivations.claim:
By [F3], $T^*T=I$, so $\Pi:=TT^*$ is idempotent; [F8] gives $\Pi^*=\Pi$, and [F9] identifies it as the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{ran}T$ (it maps into $\operatorname{ran}T$ and fixes every $Tv$). Let $J:\mathbb C^X\to\mathbb C^X\otimes\mathbb C^X\otimes W$ send $|x\rangle$ to $|x,0,0_W\rangle$. The orthonormal product basis [F7] makes $J$ an isometry and gives $JJ^*=I_X\otimes|0,0_W\rangle\langle0,0_W|$. By [F1], $V_PJ=T\otimes|0_W\rangle$. Hence, using [F5] and unitarity of $V_P$,
$$V_PR_0V_P^*=2(V_PJ)(V_PJ)^*-I=2\bigl(TT^*\otimes|0_W\rangle\langle0_W|\bigr)-I.$$
For any logical state $h\in\mathbb C^{X\times X}$, this operator sends $h\otimes|0_W\rangle$ to $(2TT^*-I)h\otimes|0_W\rangle=R_Ah\otimes|0_W\rangle$. The extended swap sends $h\otimes|0_W\rangle$ to $Sh\otimes|0_W\rangle$. Thus the word $SV_PR_0V_P^*$ restricts to $SR_A=U$ and returns the work register to its clean state.

Reading $SV_PR_0V_P^*$ from right to left applies one $V_P^*$ call, one $R_0$, one $V_P$ call, and one swap. The inverse and forward preparation, reflection and swap costs are therefore each charged once in this implementation.

In the factorwise controlled implementation, replace each factor in step 2.1 by its control-first block. By [F4], their product is the controlled full word: the control-zero block is identity and the control-one block is $SV_PR_0V_P^*$. It uses controlled $V_P^*$, $R_0$, $V_P$, and $S$, with each declared cost charged separately; without one of these capabilities this particular construction is unavailable.

By [F2], $W=U^2$ is two successive $U$ steps, and step 1.1 shows the work state is clean again after each step. Thus exactly two copies of the step counts in step 2.1 implement $W$. The resource coordinates remain separate by [F6].

citations.quote:
A **finite row-stochastic kernel** is a finite set $X$ and a matrix $P=(P_{xy})_{x,y\in X}$ with $P_{xy}\in[0,1]$ and

$$\sum_{y\in X}P_{xy}=1\qquad(x\in X).$$

The row convention is $P_{xy}=\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)$: distributions are row vectors and one transition sends $\mu$ to $\mu P$. If $X=\varnothing$, the row conditions are vacuous and there is no probability distribution on $X$. No stationary distribution, reversibility, irreducibility, aperiodicity, or efficient circuit access is part of this definition.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

For a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$, let $\mathbb C^X$ and $\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ carry the standard orthonormal label and ordered-product bases. If $X\ne\varnothing$, these coordinate spaces are implemented as two ordered registers; if $X=\varnothing$, they are zero spaces and every map below is the unique zero-dimensional map. Define the row-preparation linear map $T:\mathbb C^X\to\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ and the swap $S$ on basis vectors by

A **finite row-stochastic kernel** is a finite set $X$ and a matrix $P=(P_{xy})_{x,y\in X}$ with $P_{xy}\in[0,1]$ and

$$\sum_{y\in X}P_{xy}=1\qquad(x\in X).$$

The row convention is $P_{xy}=\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)$: distributions are row vectors and one transition sends $\mu$ to $\mu P$. If $X=\varnothing$, the row conditions are vacuous and there is no probability distribution on $X$. No stationary distribution, reversibility, irreducibility, aperiodicity, or efficient circuit access is part of this definition.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $p$ be the transition matrix of a countable state space $E$
([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]), so that
$p(x,y)\ge0$ and $\sum_{y\in E}p(x,y)=1$ for every $x\in E$. A **state measure**
is a function $\mu:E\to[0,+\infty)$ with $\mu(x)<+\infty$ for every $x$; it is
**nonzero** when $\mu(x)>0$ for at least one $x$. Such a measure $\mu$ is
**reversible** for $p$, and $\mu$ satisfies **detailed balance** for $p$, when

$$\mu(x)\,p(x,y)=\mu(y)\,p(y,x)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in E .$$

If in addition $\sum_{x\in E}\mu(x)=1$, then $\mu$ is a **reversible
probability distribution** for $p$.

Because each value $\mu(x)$ is finite and each transition entry lies in $[0,1]$,
every product $\mu(x)p(x,y)$ is a well-defined element of $[0,+\infty)$; the
identity is between nonnegative numbers and involves no subtraction of infinite
quantities. Every entry $p(x,x)$ satisfies the identity trivially, including
when $\mu(x)=0$. A state with $\mu(x)=0$ may have $p(x,\cdot)$ arbitrary; the
identity then forces $\mu(y)p(y,x)=0$ for all $y$, so no flow from the positive
support of $\mu$ enters $x$. The definition imposes no irreducibility,
aperiodicity or normalization hypothesis, and a nonzero reversible measure may
have infinite total mass; normalization to total mass one is stated separately.
The reversal interpretation of detailed balance is given by
[[thm-time-reversal-of-a-stationary-markov-chain]], and the lemma
[[lem-detailed-balance-implies-invariance]] shows that a reversible measure is
invariant even when its total mass is infinite.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

A **finite reversible Markov chain** is a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$ together with a supplied probability vector $\pi=(\pi_x)_{x\in X}$ such that $\pi_x>0$ for every $x$, $\sum_x\pi_x=1$, $\pi P=\pi$, and

$$\pi_xP_{xy}=\pi_yP_{yx}\qquad(x,y\in X).$$

The stationary law and detailed balance are explicit input hypotheses; the definition does not invoke a theorem that produces a stationary law. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is assumed. In particular, a periodic reversible chain is included.

For $x\in E$, let

$$R_x:=\{n\in\mathbb N:n\ge1\text{ and }p^{(n)}(x,x)>0\}.$$

If $R_x=\varnothing$, set $d(x):=0$. If $R_x\ne\varnothing$, define $d(x)$ to be the greatest positive integer dividing every element of $R_x$ (the gcd convention of [[def-common-divisor-and-gcd]]). This greatest divisor exists: fix one $t\in R_x$; every common positive divisor of $R_x$ is a divisor of $t$, so the set of such divisors is a nonempty finite subset of the positive divisors of $t$, and therefore has a greatest element. The set being maximized is intrinsic to $R_x$, so the result is independent of the auxiliary $t$. Only positive return times enter; $p^{(0)}(x,x)=1$ does not force $d(x)=1$.

For a finite reversible chain $(X,P,\pi)$, let $H_0=\{f:\sum_x\pi_xf_x=0\}$ with the weighted inner product from [[lem-qa-17-reversible-transition-self-adjoint-on-l2-pi]]. Define its **absolute spectral gap** by

$$\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P):=1-\|P|_{H_0}\|_{2,\pi}.$$

The norm of the restriction to the zero subspace is $0$ by [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]], so a one-state chain has absolute gap $1$. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is built into this definition: a reducible chain with a nonconstant stationary vector in $H_0$ can have gap $0$, and a periodic chain can have gap $0$ because of an eigenvalue $-1$. The eigenvalue form of the definition is proved in [[thm-qa-17-absolute-gap-eigenvalue-characterization]].

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

derivations.claim: Both rows of $P$ sum to one, $\pi P=\pi$, and $\pi_0P_{01}=\pi_1P_{10}=1/2$; the diagonal detailed-balance equations are automatic. Hence $(X,P,\pi)$ is a finite reversible chain.
Starting from either state, a return occurs exactly at positive even times, so the return-time set is $\{2,4,6,\ldots\}$ and its gcd is $2$. The chain is period two.

The constant vector $\mathbf1=(1,1)$ has eigenvalue $1$, while $h=(1,-1)$ spans $H_0$ and satisfies $Ph=-h$. Thus the restriction to $H_0$ has norm $1$, so [F3] gives $\delta_{\mathrm{abs}}(P)=0$. The eigenvalues of $P$ are exactly $1$ and $-1$.

A **finite reversible Markov chain** is a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$ together with a supplied probability vector $\pi=(\pi_x)_{x\in X}$ such that $\pi_x>0$ for every $x$, $\sum_x\pi_x=1$, $\pi P=\pi$, and

$$\pi_xP_{xy}=\pi_yP_{yx}\qquad(x,y\in X).$$

The stationary law and detailed balance are explicit input hypotheses; the definition does not invoke a theorem that produces a stationary law. No irreducibility or aperiodicity is assumed. In particular, a periodic reversible chain is included.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

For a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$, let $\mathbb C^X$ and $\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ carry the standard orthonormal label and ordered-product bases. If $X\ne\varnothing$, these coordinate spaces are implemented as two ordered registers; if $X=\varnothing$, they are zero spaces and every map below is the unique zero-dimensional map. Define the row-preparation linear map $T:\mathbb C^X\to\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ and the swap $S$ on basis vectors by

$$T|x\rangle=|x\rangle\otimes\sum_{y\in X}\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle,\qquad S|x,y\rangle=|y,x\rangle.$$

Every scalar square root is the unique nonnegative real root. Define the **discriminant** by $D:=T^*ST$, using the adjoint characterized by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$ for the root inner product, which is linear in its first argument. The row-preparation map is an isometry; its complete verification is [[thm-qa-17-discriminant-self-adjoint]]. This is the general row-stochastic construction and assumes no reversibility.

For the finite row-stochastic kernel and row-preparation map of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]], let $\Pi:=TT^*$, the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{ran}(T)$, and choose the reflection sign

$$R_A:=2\Pi-I.$$

With $S$ the two-register swap, define the one-reflection Szegedy step and its square by

$$U:=S R_A,\qquad W:=U^2=(S R_A S)R_A=(2S\Pi S-I)(2\Pi-I).$$

Products act right to left. This fixes $U$ and $W$ as different operators. Algebraically, if $Uv=\mu v$, then $Wv=\mu^2v$ on the same vector. The other common reflection sign is $I-2\Pi=-R_A$ and is not interchangeable inside a controlled operation.

For any eigenpair $Dv=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ and $\lambda\in[-1,1]$, put $a:=Tv$ and $b:=STv$. Then $\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}$ is invariant under $U$, and

$$U a=b,\qquad U b=-a+2\lambda b.$$

All eigenvalues of $D$ satisfy the displayed interval hypothesis by [[thm-qa-17-discriminant-self-adjoint]]. If $\lambda=1$ or $\lambda=-1$, then $b=\lambda a$ and the span is one-dimensional. If $-1<\lambda<1$, the two vectors are linearly independent and the invariant subspace is two-dimensional.

For the projection $\Pi=TT^*$ onto $A=\operatorname{ran}(T)$, the operators $R_A=2\Pi-I$ and $S$ are self-adjoint involutions. Hence $U=SR_A$ and $W=U^2$ are unitary. On $A^\perp$, $\Pi=0$ and therefore $U=-S$.

Let $D=T^*ST$ be the discriminant of a finite row-stochastic kernel and let $U=S(2TT^*-I)$ and $W=U^2$. For every eigenvalue $\lambda\in(-1,1)$ of $D$, counted with multiplicity, its invariant planes contribute eigenvalues

$$\exp(i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }U,\qquad \exp(2i\arccos\lambda),\ \exp(-2i\arccos\lambda)\quad\text{for }W.$$

For each eigendirection with $\lambda=1$ (respectively $\lambda=-1$), the plane collapses to a line on which $U$ acts as $+I$ (respectively $-I$), so $W$ acts as $+I$. On the remaining subspace $K=(\operatorname{ran}T+\operatorname{ran}(ST))^\perp$, $U=-S$ and its eigenvalues lie in $\{+1,-1\}$; therefore all eigenvalues of $W$ there are $+1$. If $X=\varnothing$, both spaces are zero and the statements about eigenvalues are vacuous.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the sets $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{im}T$ are
linear subspaces. Moreover, $T$ is injective if and only if $\ker T=\{0_V\}$.

For a linear subspace $W$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) of an inner product space $V$, using the preceding notion of orthogonality ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]), its **orthogonal complement** is

$$W^\perp:=\{v\in V:\langle v,w\rangle=0\text{ for every }w\in W\}.$$

This is a linear subspace: $0\in W^\perp$, and linearity in the first argument shows that $au+bv\in W^\perp$ whenever $u,v\in W^\perp$ and $a,b$ are scalars. One has $V^\perp=\{0\}$ by positive definiteness and $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Since $P_a$ is symmetric and has nonnegative entries, [F2] gives $D=P_a$. The vectors $u_+=(1,1)$ and $u_-=(1,-1)$ form a basis with $Du_+=u_+$ and $Du_-=(1-2a)u_-$.

At $a=0$, $T|0\rangle=|00\rangle$ and $T|1\rangle=|11\rangle$, so $A=B=\operatorname{span}\{|00\rangle,|11\rangle\}$. On $A$, $R_A=2TT^*-I$ is $+I$ and $S=I$, so $U=+I$. On $K=\operatorname{span}\{|01\rangle,|10\rangle\}$, [F6] gives $U=-S$, whose eigenvectors $|01\rangle+|10\rangle$ and $|01\rangle-|10\rangle$ have eigenvalues $-1$ and $+1$. Hence $\sigma(U)=\{1,1,1,-1\}$ and $W=I$ has four eigenvalues $+1$.

At $a=1$, $T|0\rangle=|01\rangle$ and $T|1\rangle=|10\rangle$, so $A=B=\operatorname{span}\{|01\rangle,|10\rangle\}$. On $A$, $R_A=+I$ and $U=S$, with eigenvalues $+1,-1$. On $K=\operatorname{span}\{|00\rangle,|11\rangle\}$, $S=I$, so [F6] gives $U=-I$. Thus $\sigma(U)=\{1,-1,-1,-1\}$ and $W=I$ has four eigenvalues $+1$.

Suppose $0<a<1$ and set $\lambda=1-2a\in(-1,1)$ and $\theta=\arccos\lambda\in(0,\pi)$. By [F7], the $u_+$ endpoint line contributes $+1$ to $U$ and $W$, and the $u_-$ invariant plane contributes $e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}$ to $U$ and $e^{2i\theta},e^{-2i\theta}$ to $W$.

Under the hypothesis of step 2.1, put $r=\sqrt{1-a}$ and $s=\sqrt a$. Let $A=\operatorname{im}T$ and $B=\operatorname{im}(ST)$; these are subspaces by [F9]–[F10]. A **finite row-stochastic kernel** is a finite set $X$ and a matrix $P=(P_{xy})_{x,y\in X}$ with $P_{xy}\in[0,1]$ and

$$\sum_{y\in X}P_{xy}=1\qquad(x\in X).$$

The row convention is $P_{xy}=\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)$: distributions are row vectors and one transition sends $\mu$ to $\mu P$. If $X=\varnothing$, the row conditions are vacuous and there is no probability distribution on $X$. No stationary distribution, reversibility, irreducibility, aperiodicity, or efficient circuit access is part of this definition.

For a finite row-stochastic kernel $(X,P)$, let $\mathbb C^X$ and $\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ carry the standard orthonormal label and ordered-product bases. If $X\ne\varnothing$, these coordinate spaces are implemented as two ordered registers; if $X=\varnothing$, they are zero spaces and every map below is the unique zero-dimensional map. Define the row-preparation linear map $T:\mathbb C^X\to\mathbb C^{X\times X}$ and the swap $S$ on basis vectors by

$$T|x\rangle=|x\rangle\otimes\sum_{y\in X}\sqrt{P_{xy}}|y\rangle,\qquad S|x,y\rangle=|y,x\rangle.$$

Every scalar square root is the unique nonnegative real root. Define the **discriminant** by $D:=T^*ST$, using the adjoint characterized by $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$ for the root inner product, which is linear in its first argument. The row-preparation map is an isometry; its complete verification is [[thm-qa-17-discriminant-self-adjoint]]. This is the general row-stochastic construction and assumes no reversibility.

For every finite row-stochastic kernel, the map $T$ of [[def-qa-17-szegedy-transition-isometry]] satisfies $T^*T=I$ and is an isometry, and the matrix entries of $D=T^*ST$ are

$$D_{xy}=\sqrt{P_{xy}P_{yx}}.$$

Hence $D$ is real symmetric, self-adjoint, and $\|D\|\le1$. If $(X,P,\pi)$ is also finite reversible, then

$$D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt\pi)\,P\,\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt\pi).$$

Every eigenvalue of $D$ is real and belongs to $[-1,1]$. The empty state set has the zero endomorphism and empty spectrum; the similarity assertion is only made when a positive stationary probability vector is supplied.

For $x,y\in U$, $P'_{xy}=P_{xy}$ and $P'_{yx}=P_{yx}=P_{xy}$, so [F2] gives $D(P')_{xy}=P_{xy}$. If $x,y\in\mathcal M$, the product $P'_{xy}P'_{yx}$ is $1$ exactly when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise, giving the identity block. If exactly one of $x,y$ is marked, the transition from the marked state to the unmarked state is zero, so $D(P')_{xy}=0$. These three disjoint cases give the displayed direct sum.

$$T^*=T,$$

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Summing over $x$ and using symmetry, so that every column sum is also $1$, yields $\|Qz\|^2\le\|z\|^2$. Since $Q$ is self-adjoint by its real symmetric matrix and [F4], [F3] gives a real orthonormal eigenbasis; the contraction inequality forces every eigenvalue of $Q$ into $[-1,1]$. Thus $P=(I+Q)/2$ is self-adjoint with spectrum in $[0,1]$. Its row sums are $1$, so $P\mathbf u=\mathbf u$.

If $U=\varnothing$, then $P_U=0$ and the conclusion follows from [F5]. Otherwise choose a unit vector $z$ supported on $U$ and write $z=\alpha\mathbf u+v$ with $v\perp\mathbf u$. [F6] applied to $\langle z,\mathbf u\rangle=\langle z,\Pi_U\mathbf u\rangle$ gives $|\alpha|^2\le\|\Pi_U\mathbf u\|^2=|U|/n=1-\varepsilon$, so $\|v\|^2=1-|\alpha|^2$.

The orthogonal complement $\mathbf u^\perp$ is invariant under $P$ by self-adjointness and $P\mathbf u=\mathbf u$. Its eigenvalues are at most $1-\delta$ by the stated second-eigenvalue hypothesis. Therefore $\langle z,Pz\rangle=|\alpha|^2+\langle v,Pv\rangle\le |\alpha|^2+(1-\delta)\|v\|^2\le1-\delta\varepsilon$.

The compression $P_U$ is positive semidefinite because $\langle z,P_Uz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle\ge0$ for every vector supported on $U$, by the nonnegative spectrum in step 1.1. It is self-adjoint, so its operator norm is its largest eigenvalue; equivalently it is the maximum of its unit-vector Rayleigh quotients. Step 2.1 bounds each such quotient by $1-\delta\varepsilon$, proving the result.

$$\|P_U\|\le 1-\delta\varepsilon.$$

Let $X$ be the finite state set, $P$ its row-transition matrix, $\mathcal M\subseteq X$ the marked set, $U=X\setminus\mathcal M$, and $P_{UU}$ the principal submatrix indexed by $U$. For an initial probability row vector $\mu$, the **hitting-time survival law** is

$$\Pr_\mu(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t):=\mu_U P_{UU}^{\,t}\mathbf 1_U,\qquad t\in\mathbb N_0,$$

where $\mu_U$ is the restriction of $\mu$ to $U$ and $\mathbf 1_U$ is the all-ones column vector on $U$. This is the finite sum of probabilities of all length-$t$ paths that remain in $U$; it does not require a path-space construction. For $U=\varnothing$ the right side is $0$; for $\mathcal M=\varnothing$ it is $1$.

The hitting time $\tau_{\mathcal M}:=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\in\mathcal M\}$ is the $\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$-valued variable determined by this survival law. Its extended expectation is $\mathbb E_\mu\tau_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{t\ge0}\Pr_\mu(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t)$, and a constant-success hitting bound is a specified integer $t$ for which $\Pr_\mu(\tau_{\mathcal M}\le t)$ is bounded below by a positive constant. These resource conventions are kept separate.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Let $u_U=|U|^{-1/2}\mathbf1_U$. For the uniform initial law on $U$, [F2] gives $\Pr(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t)=\langle u_U,P_{UU}^{\,t}u_U\rangle$. Since $P_{UU}$ is positive semidefinite, it has eigenvalues in $[0,1-\delta\varepsilon]$ by [F1]; its $t$th power therefore has operator norm at most $(1-\delta\varepsilon)^t$. [F3] and $\|u_U\|=1$ prove the survival bound, including $t=0$.

Put $a=\delta\varepsilon$. For $0<a<1$, the nonnegative-integer tail formula in [F2] and the finite geometric partial sums give $\mathbb E\tau_{\mathcal M}=\sum_{t\ge0}\Pr(\tau_{\mathcal M}>t)\le\sum_{t\ge0}(1-a)^t=1/a$. For the constant-success bound choose $t=\lceil1/a\rceil$. Since $(1-a)(1+a)=1-a^2\le1$, we have $1-a\le(1+a)^{-1}$; the finite binomial expansion gives $(1+a)^t\ge1+ta\ge2$. Hence $(1-a)^t\le(1+a)^{-t}\le1/2$. If $a=1$, step 1.1 gives zero no-hit probability for every $t\ge1$, so one step suffices. The case $\mathcal M=X$ is immediate from the definition.
