citations.quote:
**Input:** An integer $n\ge0$, an ordered $n$-qubit register initialized to
$e_{0^n}$, and a Hamiltonian-access contract for
$$A_n:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}X_j,$$
where $X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$X_j:=I_2^{\otimes j}\otimes X\otimes I_2^{\otimes(n-j-1)}$ is its tensor-map
extension acting on factor $j$ and as the identity on every other factor, by
[[def-qc-tensor-map]]. The contract must explicitly
supply either the whole operation $U_{A_n}(\pi/2)$ or the $n$ local operations
$U_{X_j}(\pi/2)$ in the declared ordered tensor factors. The local-operation option requests each one-qubit evolution separately; its
equivalence to the whole evolution is proved by the correctness argument and
is not assumed here. This contract does not make arbitrary matrix exponentiation free. Every supplied query, gate, description-bit,
and synthesis cost is recorded under
[[def-qa-19-hamiltonian-access-cost-model]] and
[[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]].

**Procedure:** If the whole operation is supplied, apply $U_{A_n}(\pi/2)$ once.
If the local operations are supplied, apply $U_{X_j}(\pi/2)$ once for each
$j=0,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order. Then perform the computational-basis
projective measurement and return the observed $n$-bit word. For $n=0$, the
sum is empty, the register is the one-dimensional empty tensor product, the
evolution is the identity, and the output word is empty. For every $n$, the
operation and readout costs come from the declared access and circuit models;
the matrix formula alone supplies no implementation or cost.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

In this page a **Hamiltonian** is a self-adjoint endomorphism $H$ of a
finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

The second expression uses the finite spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]. If $V$ is the zero
space, the spectrum is empty and the empty sum is the unique endomorphism,
which is also the identity on $V$. This definition specifies a mathematical
unitary from a finite matrix; it makes no claim that the operation has an
efficient circuit or a free access cost.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $V$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let
$(e_y)_{y\in Y}$ be a finite orthonormal basis, and let $\phi\in V$ be a unit
vector. Measuring the pure state $[\phi]$ by the projective measurement onto
the basis lines outputs $y\in Y$ with probability
$$p_\phi(y)=|\langle \phi,e_y\rangle|^2,\qquad \sum_{y\in Y}p_\phi(y)=1.$$
In particular, for self-adjoint $H:V\to V$, real $t$, and unit $\psi$, the
walk output $\phi=U_H(t)\psi$ is unit and
$p_t(y)=|\langle U_H(t)\psi,e_y\rangle|^2$. For an initial vertex $e_x$, the
probability of observing vertex $y$ is $|\langle U_H(t)e_x,e_y\rangle|^2$.

For every integer $n\ge0$, the algorithm
[[alg-qa-19-hypercube-state-transfer]] evolves the initial vector $e_{0^n}$
to
$$U_{A_n}(\pi/2)e_{0^n}=(-i)^n e_{1^n}.$$
Consequently its computational-basis measurement outputs $1^n$ with
probability one, including the empty word when $n=0$.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim: Put $f_+=(e_0+e_1)/\sqrt2$ and $f_-=(e_0-e_1)/\sqrt2$. By [F2]–[F4] they form an orthonormal basis, and direct multiplication gives $Xf_+=f_+$ and $Xf_-=-f_-$. By [F5], $U_X(t)$ acts on these vectors by $e^{-it}$ and $e^{it}$. On $f_+$, $\cos t\,I-i\sin t\,X$ acts by $\cos t-i\sin t=e^{-it}$; on $f_-$ it acts by $\cos t+i\sin t=e^{it}$, using [F6]–[F7]. Thus the two maps agree on a basis. At $t=\pi/2$, [F8] yields $U_X(\pi/2)=-iX$, so $U_X(\pi/2)e_0=-i e_1$.

The displayed matrix for $A_2$ follows by applying $X\otimes I+I\otimes X$ to each of the four basis vectors in [F2] using the tensor-map action [F11]. The four vectors $f_+\otimes f_+$, $f_+\otimes f_-$, $f_-\otimes f_+$, and $f_-\otimes f_-$ form a basis by [F2]–[F3]. On $f_\epsilon\otimes f_\eta$ with $\epsilon,\eta\in\{1,-1\}$, $A_2$ has eigenvalue $\epsilon+\eta$; [F5]–[F6] give evolution coefficient $e^{-i\pi(\epsilon+\eta)/2}=e^{-i\pi\epsilon/2}e^{-i\pi\eta/2}$, which is exactly the coefficient of $U_X(\pi/2)\otimes U_X(\pi/2)$ by [F11]. The operators therefore agree on a basis, and step 1.1 gives $U_{A_2}(\pi/2)=-X\otimes X$. Hence $U_{A_2}(\pi/2)e_{00}=-e_{11}$.

In the $n=1$ case, step 1.1 gives outcome $1$ amplitude $-i$; in the $n=2$ case, step 2.1 gives outcome $11$ amplitude $-1$. Both have squared modulus $1$, so [F9] gives the opposite-corner outcome with probability one in each case. These calculations are the $n=1,2$ instances of [F10].

**Inputs:** An integer $N\ge2$, an integer $m\ge\lceil\log_2N\rceil$, an
injective label encoding $\mathsf{enc}:[N]\to\{0,1\}^m$, and the corresponding
$m$-qubit register. Its **active subspace** is
$S:=\operatorname{span}\{e_{\mathsf{enc}(x)}:x\in[N]\}$; bit strings outside the
image of $\mathsf{enc}$ are unused labels. The marked label $w\in[N]$ is available
through the declared oracle/access model, not as an inspected classical value.

On $S$, define the complete-graph adjacency by
$$A e_{\mathsf{enc}(x)}:=\sum_{y\in[N],\,y\ne x}e_{\mathsf{enc}(y)},$$
and extend $A$ by zero on $S^\perp$. Define
$P_wz:=\langle z,e_{\mathsf{enc}(w)}\rangle e_{\mathsf{enc}(w)}$ on the full register and
the self-adjoint generator $H:=-A/N-P_w$.

The input also supplies:

- a state-preparation circuit $A_s$ whose label-register output from the
  specified zero input is the pure state
  $e_s:=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in[N]}e_{\mathsf{enc}(x)}$; if its implementation uses
  workspace, the model states its initialization, final state, and separate
  query, gate, and description-bit costs;
- the total Boolean function $f_w:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}$ defined by
  $f_w(\mathsf{enc}(x))=1$ exactly when $x=w$ and $f_w(z)=0$ on every unused label,
  together with the full unitary XOR-oracle access and its cost from
  [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]]; and
- a Hamiltonian-access contract that supplies either the ideal $U_H(t)$ or a
  unitary simulator $V_{H,t,\rho}$ with a supplied certificate
  $\|V_{H,t,\rho}-U_H(t)\|_{\rm op}\le\rho$, including all query, gate,
  description-bit, precision, and classical-construction costs.

The function oracle does not itself supply the continuous-time operation
$U_H(t)$: any conversion from its marked predicate to evolution under $P_w$,
and any simulation of the adjacency term, must be separately declared and
charged under [[def-qa-19-hamiltonian-access-cost-model]].

**Procedure:** Prepare $e_s$, apply the supplied ideal evolution or simulator
for $t=\pi\sqrt N/2$, and measure the register in its computational basis
using [[def-qc-projective-measurement]]. Decode a measured string in the image
of $\mathsf{enc}$ to its label and return it; return `FAIL` on an unused string. If
$N=2^n$ and $\mathsf{enc}$ is the standard $n$-bit encoding, the supplied preparation
may be $A_s=H^{\otimes n}$ by
[[lem-qa-19-hadamard-uniform-state-preparation]]; charge $n$ gates when $H$
is primitive and the declared synthesis costs otherwise. For arbitrary $N$,
$A_s$ is a supplied, charged input. No query, gate, or runtime bound follows from
the finite matrix description alone.

Let $V$ be a finite vertex set with a fixed order and let
$w:V\times V\to[0,\infty)$ be symmetric. Self-loops are allowed and their
weight is counted once in each row sum. On $\mathbb C^V$ with ordered basis
$(e_v)_{v\in V}$, define the weighted adjacency matrix by
$A_{uv}=w(u,v)$, the degree $d(v)=\sum_{u\in V}w(v,u)$, and
$D_{vv}=d(v)$ with all off-diagonal entries zero. The **positive Laplacian**
is $L_+=D-A$; the other common sign convention is $L_-=A-D=-L_+$. A walk
generator records the chosen edge weights, loop convention, basis order, and
one of these signs. It is not a discrete transition matrix.

When every $d(v)>0$, the **normalized adjacency** is the separately defined
matrix $A_{\rm norm}=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}$. No normalized-adjacency operation is
defined here at zero-degree vertices. The matrices $A,D,L_+,L_-$ are Hermitian:
$A_{vu}=w(v,u)=w(u,v)=\overline{A_{uv}}$ and $D$ is real diagonal. Under
the positive-degree condition, $D^{-1/2}$ is also real diagonal, so
$A_{\rm norm}^*=A_{\rm norm}$. A zero-vertex graph gives the zero coordinate
space and empty matrices; a quantum-walk input separately requires a
normalized state, so it has no instance on that space.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a

For $|r\rangle$, each summand $A|x\rangle$ contains $|w\rangle$ once, so its $|w\rangle$ coefficient is $\sqrt{N-1}$; for each unmarked $y$, the sum contains $|y\rangle$ once for each $x\ne y,w$, hence $N-2$ times. For a term-list input $H=\sum_{j=1}^m H_j$, a real time $h$, and the announced order $1,\ldots,m$, define
$$S_1(h):=e^{-ihH_1}e^{-ihH_2}\cdots e^{-ihH_m}.$$
Operator products are written in their ordinary left-to-right algebraic order, so the rightmost factor acts first on a vector. For an integer $r\ge1$, the $r$-step first-order approximation at time $t$ is $S_1(t/r)^r$. Each exponential is the finite-matrix evolution of [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]]; this definition does not identify the product with $e^{-itH}$ when terms fail to commute.

Let $H$ be a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex
inner-product space $V$. For real $t,s$, the evolution from
[[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]] satisfies
$$U_H(0)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t)^*U_H(t)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t+s)=U_H(t)U_H(s),\qquad \frac{d}{dt}U_H(t)=-iHU_H(t).$$
Moreover, $U_H$ is the unique differentiable map $Y:\mathbb R\to
\operatorname{End}(V)$ satisfying $Y'(t)=-iHY(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_V$.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: If $V=\{0\}$, every endomorphism is the unique zero map and both sides of the theorem are zero. Otherwise, for self-adjoint $H_1,H_2$, put $A=-iH_1$ and $B=-iH_2$. For $h\ge0$ define $F(s)=e^{(h-s)(A+B)}e^{sA}e^{sB}$ for $0\le s\le h$. Its endpoints are $F(0)=e^{h(A+B)}$ and $F(h)=e^{hA}e^{hB}$. Differentiating the three finite-matrix evolutions using [F2] and the entrywise product rule gives $F'(s)=e^{(h-s)(A+B)}(e^{sA}B-Be^{sA})e^{sB}$.

For fixed $s\ge0$, differentiating $e^{uA}Be^{(s-u)A}$ for $0\le u\le s$ and integrating yields $e^{sA}B-Be^{sA}=\int_0^s e^{uA}[A,B]e^{(s-u)A}\,du$. For unitaries $R,S$, [F2] and [F4] give $\|R\|=\|S\|=\|R^{-1}\|=\|S^{-1}\|=1$; [F3] applied to $RXS$ and then to $R^{-1}(RXS)S^{-1}$ gives $\|RXS\|=\|X\|$. Thus the unitary factors in the integrands and in [step 1.1] give $\|F'(s)\|\le s\|[A,B]\|$. Integrating from $0$ to $h$ gives $\|e^{h(A+B)}-e^{hA}e^{hB}\|\le h^2\|[A,B]\|/2$. For $h<0$ apply the same result to $-A,-B$ and $|h|$; since $[A,B]=-[H_1,H_2]$, the bound is $h^2\|[H_1,H_2]\|/2$ for all real $h$.

Put $A_j=-iH_j$. For $k=1,\ldots,m$, let $P_k=e^{hA_1}\cdots e^{hA_k}$ and $T_k=e^{h\sum_{j=1}^kA_j}$. Adding and subtracting $e^{h\sum_{j<k}A_j}e^{hA_k}$ and applying the two-term estimate in [step 2.1] gives $\|T_k-P_k\|\le\|T_{k-1}-P_{k-1}\|+\frac{h^2}{2}\|[\sum_{j<k}A_j,A_k]\|$. Linearity gives $[\sum_{j<k}A_j,A_k]=\sum_{j<k}[A_j,A_k]$, and $[A_j,A_k]=-[H_j,H_k]$; the triangle inequality from [F4] bounds this norm by $\sum_{j<k}\|[H_j,H_k]\|$. Right multiplication by $e^{hA_k}$ preserves the norm by the unitary norm argument in [step 2.1]. Starting with $T_1=P_1$ and iterating proves the local $m$-term bound $\|e^{-ihH}-S_1(h)\|\le\frac{h^2}{2}\sum_{j<k}\|[H_j,H_k]\|$.

Set $h=t/r$. The identity $S^r-U^r=\sum_{\ell=0}^{r-1}S^{r-1-\ell}(S-U)U^\ell$ writes the difference as $r$ terms. The unitary norm argument in [step 2.1] bounds each term by $\|S_1(h)-U_H(h)\|$, so [step 3.1] gives $\|S_1(h)^r-U_H(h)^r\|\le\frac{t^2}{2r}\sum_{j<k}\|[H_j,H_k]\|$. By [F2], $U_H(h)^r=U_H(t)$.

derivations.claim: The claim is immediate on the zero-dimensional space, so assume $V\ne\{0\}$. Write $A_j=-iH_j$, $A=\sum_jA_j$, $P(h)=S_2(h)$, and $Q(h)=U_H(h)$. Every factor is unitary by [F1], and the palindromic word gives $P(-h)=P(h)^{-1}$; also $Q(-h)=Q(h)^{-1}$. Differentiating the factors at zero, the two occurrences with coefficient $1/2$ contribute a total coefficient $1$ for each $A_j$, so $P(0)=Q(0)=I$ and $P'(0)=Q'(0)=A$.

Let $E(h)=P(h)-Q(h)$. Smoothness follows by repeatedly differentiating the constant-generator identity in [F1]. Thus $E(h)=Ch^2+O(h^3)$ for some endomorphism $C$ by [L1]. The inverse identities in step 1.1 give $E(-h)=P(h)^{-1}-Q(h)^{-1}=-P(h)^{-1}E(h)Q(h)^{-1}$. Since both inverse factors equal $I+O(h)$, comparing degree-two coefficients yields $C=-C$, hence $C=0$. Therefore $P$ and $Q$ have matching Taylor coefficients through degree two.

Write $P(h)=F_1(h)\cdots F_{2m-1}(h)$ in its displayed order, with $F_\ell(h)=e^{c_\ell h A_{j_\ell}}$ and the coefficients $c_\ell$ equal to the half-step palindrome in [F2]. Repeated product differentiation and [F1] give $\|P'''(h)\|\le(\sum_\ell |c_\ell|\|H_{j_\ell}\|)^3=M^3$: each $j<m$ occurs twice with coefficient $1/2$, and $j=m$ occurs once with coefficient $1$. Also $Q'''(h)=A^3Q(h)$. For a unit vector $v$, the vector triangle inequality gives $\|Av\|\le\sum_j\|H_jv\|\le\sum_j\|H_j\|=M$, so [F4] yields $\|A\|\le M$. Then [F3], [F4], and unitarity give $\|Q'''(h)\|\le M^3$. The integral Taylor remainder after degree two therefore gives $\|P(h)-Q(h)\|\le(2M^3)|h|^3/3!=M^3|h|^3/3$.

Expand $P(h)^r-Q(h)^r$ by telescoping. The definition [F4] and submultiplicativity [F3] show that unitary factors preserve the norm, so its norm is at most $rM^3|h|^3/3$ by [step 3.1]. With $h=t/r$, this is $|t|^3M^3/(3r^2)$; [F1] gives $Q(h)^r=U_H(t)$.

**Input:** A finite term-list access input with $H=\sum_{j=1}^m H_j$, a finite time code $t$ in the expression language of [[def-qa-20-term-list-access-model]], a rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, a certified rational $C_2\ge0$ satisfying $C_2\ge\sum_{1\le j<\ell\le m}\|[H_j,H_\ell]\|$, and a supplied certified rational upper bound $R\ge0$ satisfying $R\ge t^2C_2/\epsilon$. For $t\ne0$, put $r=\max\{1,\lceil R\rceil\}$ and $h=t/r$; the access declarations must supply each term call at this exact signed code $h$, with its implementation and costs. A call may be directly supported at $h$ or supplied by separately declared inverse or time-reversed access, with that route's own costs. When $t\ne0$, every approximate call must have a certified error, and the sum of those errors over all $rm$ calls must be at most $\epsilon/2$. The time-code and call conventions are those of [[def-qa-20-term-list-access-model]].

**Output:** The composed unitary circuit for the declared product order, together with its query, gate, ancilla, coefficient-bit, description-bit, and classical-generation cost record.

**Instructions:**

1. Compare the exact value of the supplied time code with $0$. If it is $0$, return the identity circuit.
2. Otherwise set $r=\max\{1,\lceil R\rceil\}$ using rational arithmetic and set $h=t/r$ as a supported finite expression code.
3. For each of exactly $r$ repetitions, execute the declared term calls chronologically in order $m,m-1,\ldots,1$. By [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]], later executed gates multiply on the left. The ideal exact-call operator for one repetition is therefore $e^{-ihH_1}\cdots e^{-ihH_m}$ of [[def-qa-20-first-order-product-formula]]; with supplied implementations the actual operator is $V_1(h)\cdots V_m(h)$, with the declared call errors accumulated separately. If the call at $h$ is supplied through inverse or time-reversed access, use that separately declared route and its cost and error record; do not infer it from forward access alone.
4. Keep circuit-generation, coefficient, and all oracle costs in their separate declared coordinates. When $t\ne0$ and calls are approximate, retain their per-call error records; admissibility requires their sum over all $rm$ calls to be at most $\epsilon/2$.

The procedure makes no claim that the required term calls or their uniform generator exist for an arbitrary matrix.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $H_1,\ldots,H_m$ be self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V$ with $m\ge1$, and set $H=\sum_{j=1}^mH_j$. For every real $t$ and integer $r\ge1$,
$$\left\|S_1(t/r)^r-U_H(t)\right\|\le\frac{t^2}{2r}\sum_{1\le j<k\le m}\|[H_j,H_k]\|,$$
where $S_1$ has the fixed order of [[def-qa-20-first-order-product-formula]] and $U_H(t)=e^{-itH}$ is the finite-matrix evolution of [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]].

A **term-list access input** consists of an integer $m\ge1$, finite-dimensional self-adjoint endomorphisms $H_1,\ldots,H_m$ on one stated register, and the exact target $H=\sum_{j=1}^m H_j$. A supported time code is a finite expression whose leaves are rational numbers or symbols $\rho_q$ denoting the unique positive real root of $x^q=4$ for an odd integer $q\ge1$; [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] gives a unique nonnegative root; it is positive because $0^q=0\ne4$. Internal operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division by a nonzero expression. Its exact real value and bit length are recorded. These codes include rational times and every coefficient-scaled rational time in the finite Suzuki recursion.

For each $j$, the input declares which time codes are supported and supplies either the exact operation $e^{-isH_j}$ or a full-list uniform circuit generator, in the sense of [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], that returns a unitary $V_j(s)$ together with a certified error $\eta_j(s)\ge0$ satisfying $\|V_j(s)-e^{-isH_j}\|\le\eta_j(s)$. If a circuit uses auxiliary registers, it supplies the exact clean or dirty contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]] so that its induced operation $V_j(s)$ on the target is well-defined: clean registers start and return to zero for every target input, and dirty registers are acted on by the identity. The operator-norm error is measured on the induced target operation. The provider specifies how each supported code is passed to the generator and records its actual description length and generation time; no polynomial bound is inferred. This is an explicit access promise, not a claim that every matrix has such a family.

For each supported call the input records its named-oracle query counts, gate count, ancillary wires, description bits, coefficient bits, and classical generation cost. Costs of composing the calls into a full product and generating that product are separately recorded as $Q_{\rm wrap}$ and $G_{\rm wrap}$. A controlled form is available only when separately declared as the block operation of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. Inverse access to a call is available only when separately declared under [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]], with its own cost and error record. Forward access implies neither capability. The term list supplies no promise that any operation or coefficient computation is free.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner

**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest

derivations.claim: If $t=0$, the algorithm returns the identity and the exact evolution is also the identity. Otherwise $r=\max\{1,\lceil R\rceil\}\ge R\ge t^2C_2/\epsilon$. Since $C_2$ bounds the commutator sum, [F2] gives exact product error at most $t^2C_2/(2r)\le\epsilon/2$.

Replace the exact term calls one at a time by their supplied unitary implementations. For unitaries, the definition [F5] and submultiplicativity [F4] show that left and right multiplication preserve operator norm. Thus a telescoping expansion of the two products bounds the operator-norm change by the sum of the individual call errors. The input certificate in [F1] makes this total at most $\epsilon/2$. The triangle inequality with step 1.1 gives total error at most $\epsilon$.

For $t\ne0$, each of the $m$ term circuits occurs once in each of $r$ repetitions, so their query and gate totals are $r\sum_jq_j$ and $r\sum_jg_j$. For the announced term order $1,\ldots,m$ and real $h$, define the palindromic product
$$S_2(h):=e^{-ihH_1/2}e^{-ihH_2/2}\cdots e^{-ihH_{m-1}/2}e^{-ihH_m}e^{-ihH_{m-1}/2}\cdots e^{-ihH_2/2}e^{-ihH_1/2}.$$
For $m=1$ this is just $e^{-ihH_1}$. The $r$-step approximation is $S_2(t/r)^r$, with $r\ge1$. A written product acts right-to-left, as in [[def-qa-20-first-order-product-formula]]. Every term call and any signed-time implementation cost must be declared by [[def-qa-20-term-list-access-model]].

**Input:** Integers $k,r\ge1$, a finite time code $t$ in the expression language of [[def-qa-20-term-list-access-model]], and a finite term-list access input.

**Admissible conditions:** If $t\ne0$, for every term occurrence $e^{-i c_\nu tH_{j_\nu}/r}$ in the fully expanded segment, the access input supports that exact signed time code for term $H_{j_\nu}$ and declares its implementation, per-call costs, and any approximation-error record. The call may be supplied directly at the signed code or through separately declared inverse or time-reversed access with its own cost and error record. This condition includes the half-time calls in the base formula and every signed central call in the recursion.

**Output:** The finite product circuit and its declared query, gate, ancilla, coefficient-bit, description-bit, and classical-generation costs.

**Instructions:**

1. Compare the exact value of the supplied time code with $0$. If it is $0$, return the identity. Otherwise begin with $S_2(h)$ from [[def-qa-20-symmetric-second-order-formula]], where $h=t/r$.
2. For each $j=2,\ldots,k$, let $\rho_{2j-1}$ be the unique nonnegative root of $x^{2j-1}=4$ from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]; it is positive since $0^{2j-1}\ne4$. Put $p_j=(4-\rho_{2j-1})^{-1}$, and recursively replace the current even-order formula $S_{2j-2}(h)$ by
$$S_{2j}(h):=S_{2j-2}(p_jh)^2S_{2j-2}((1-4p_j)h)S_{2j-2}(p_jh)^2.$$
3. Recursively expand one segment until only the term exponentials remain, retaining their displayed operator order. For exactly $r$ repetitions, execute the factors of each expanded segment chronologically in the reverse of their displayed operator order. Since later executed gates multiply on the left by [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]], the exact-call operator is $S_{2k}(t/r)^r$. If calls are approximate, execute their supplied unitary implementations in that same chronological order and retain the per-call error records; the displayed $S_{2k}$ remains the ideal exact-call word.
4. For each central coefficient $1-4p_j$, use the implementation declared for that actual signed call time. For $q=2j-1\ge3$, let $\rho_q$ be the positive root of $\rho_q^q=4$. It is positive, and $\rho_q<4$: otherwise monotonicity of positive integer powers ([[lem-power-monotone]]) would give $\rho_q^q\ge4^q>4$, a contradiction. Hence $4-\rho_q>0$, $p_j=(4-\rho_q)^{-1}>1/4$, and $1-4p_j<0$. Thus the central coefficient is negative; the actual call time is this coefficient times the current recursive time argument. Use the resulting signed code, which may be positive or negative, with its directly supported implementation or separately declared inverse or time-reversed access. Charge exact coefficient descriptions and classical generation separately.

The recursion is finite because $j$ increases only from $2$ through $k$, and each expansion makes five calls to the preceding formula. No asymptotic error or cost guarantee is part of this procedure definition.

Let $H$ be a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex
inner-product space $V$. For real $t,s$, the evolution from
[[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]] satisfies
$$U_H(0)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t)^*U_H(t)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t+s)=U_H(t)U_H(s),\qquad \frac{d}{dt}U_H(t)=-iHU_H(t).$$
Moreover, $U_H$ is the unique differentiable map $Y:\mathbb R\to
\operatorname{End}(V)$ satisfying $Y'(t)=-iHY(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_V$.

In this page a **Hamiltonian** is a self-adjoint endomorphism $H$ of a
finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

The second expression uses the finite spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]. If $V$ is the zero
space, the spectrum is empty and the empty sum is the unique endomorphism,
which is also the identity on $V$. This definition specifies a mathematical
unitary from a finite matrix; it makes no claim that the operation has an
efficient circuit or a free access cost.

A **term-list access input** consists of an integer $m\ge1$, finite-dimensional self-adjoint endomorphisms $H_1,\ldots,H_m$ on one stated register, and the exact target $H=\sum_{j=1}^m H_j$. Internal operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division by a nonzero expression. Its exact real value and bit length are recorded. These codes include rational times and every coefficient-scaled rational time in the finite Suzuki recursion.

For each $j$, the input declares which time codes are supported and supplies either the exact operation $e^{-isH_j}$ or a full-list uniform circuit generator, in the sense of [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], that returns a unitary $V_j(s)$ together with a certified error $\eta_j(s)\ge0$ satisfying $\|V_j(s)-e^{-isH_j}\|\le\eta_j(s)$. The operator-norm error is measured on the induced target operation. The provider specifies how each supported code is passed to the generator and records its actual description length and generation time; no polynomial bound is inferred. This is an explicit access promise, not a claim that every matrix has such a family.

For each supported call the input records its named-oracle query counts, gate count, ancillary wires, description bits, coefficient bits, and classical generation cost. Costs of composing the calls into a full product and generating that product are separately recorded as $Q_{\rm wrap}$ and $G_{\rm wrap}$. A controlled form is available only when separately declared as the block operation of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. Inverse access to a call is available only when separately declared under [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]], with its own cost and error record. Forward access implies neither capability. Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]), let
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with powers as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. **Signs.** If $a \ge 0$ then $a^n \ge 0$, and if $a > 0$ then $a^n > 0$.
2. **Strict monotonicity in the base.** If $0 \le a < b$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n < b^n$. Consequently, for $a, b \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$: $a < b \iff a^n < b^n$ and $a \le b \iff a^n \le b^n$, and $x \mapsto x^n$ is injective on $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with the base.** If $a \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a \ge 1$; if $a > 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a > 1$; and if $0 \le a \le 1$ then $a^n \le 1$.
4. **Monotonicity in the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^m < a^n$ whenever $m < n$ in $\mathbb{N}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^n = 1$ for all $n$; and if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^m > a^n$ whenever $m < n$.

derivations.claim: Put $A_j=-iH_j$ and $A=\sum_jA_j$. The base word $S_2(h)$ is palindromic by [F1], so [F3] gives $S_2(-h)=S_2(h)^{-1}$; the same identity holds for $U(h)$ by [F3] and [F4]. Its derivative at zero is $A$, because the two half-time occurrences of every outer $A_j$ sum to one full occurrence, while the middle term occurs once. Also $U(0)=S_2(0)=I$. By [L2], $E(h)=S_2(h)-U(h)=Ch^2+O(h^3)$ for some matrix $C$. The inverse identities imply $E(-h)=-S_2(h)^{-1}E(h)U(h)^{-1}$; comparing degree-two terms gives $C=-C$, hence $C=0$. Thus $E(h)=O(h^3)$, proving the base order-two claim as well as the symmetry base case.

Fix $j\ge2$ and assume as the induction hypothesis [ih] that $S_{2j-2}(-h)=S_{2j-2}(h)^{-1}$ and that $S_{2j-2}$ agrees with $U$ through degree $2j-2$. Put $q=2j-1$, $p=p_j$, and $c=1-4p$. By [L2] and Taylor's theorem, $S_{2j-2}(h)-U(h)=Eh^q+O(h^{q+1})$. By [F6], the unique nonnegative root $\rho_q$ with $\rho_q^q=4$ exists; it is positive because zero has zero $q$-th power. Since $q\ge3$, [F7] gives $\rho_q<4$: otherwise $\rho_q^q\ge4^q>4$, contradicting $\rho_q^q=4$. Thus $p=(4-\rho_q)^{-1}>1/4$ and $c=1-4p=-\rho_qp<0$. The five scaled copies in [F2] have leading error coefficients $p^qE,p^qE,c^qE,p^qE,p^qE$. Their other factors equal $I+O(h)$, so multiplying an error term by those factors changes it only by $O(h^{q+1})$. The ideal factors $U(ph)^2U(ch)U(ph)^2$ equal $U((4p+c)h)=U(h)$ by [F3]. The coefficient $c$ is an expression in the rational and positive-root tokens of [F5], so the signed call has a finite exact code. Hence the coefficient of $h^q$ in $S_{2j}(h)-U(h)$ is $(4p^q+c^q)E$. Since $c=-\rho_qp$ and $\rho_q^q=4$, $c^q=-4p^q$, so this coefficient vanishes and the difference is $O(h^{q+1})=O(h^{2j})$.

Let $A(h)=S_{2j-2}(ph)$ and $B(h)=S_{2j-2}(ch)$. The recursive word is $A(h)A(h)B(h)A(h)A(h)$. The induction hypothesis in step 1.2 gives inverse symmetry for $A$ and $B$; reversing the five factors shows $S_{2j}(-h)=S_{2j}(h)^{-1}$. Also $U(-h)=U(h)^{-1}$. By step 1.2 and [L2], write $S_{2j}(h)-U(h)=Dh^{2j}+O(h^{2j+1})$. The inverse identity gives $Dh^{2j}=-Dh^{2j}+O(h^{2j+1})$, hence $D=0$ and the difference is $O(h^{2j+1})$. Therefore $S_{2j}$ agrees with $U$ through degree $2j$ and has inverse symmetry. Together with the base case in step 1.1, induction proves both claims for every finite $k$.

For a term-list input $H=\sum_{j=1}^m H_j$, a real time $h$, and the announced order $1,\ldots,m$, define
$$S_1(h):=e^{-ihH_1}e^{-ihH_2}\cdots e^{-ihH_m}.$$
Operator products are written in their ordinary left-to-right algebraic order, so the rightmost factor acts first on a vector. For an integer $r\ge1$, the $r$-step first-order approximation at time $t$ is $S_1(t/r)^r$. Each exponential is the finite-matrix evolution of [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]]; this definition does not identify the product with $e^{-itH}$ when terms fail to commute.

Let $H$ be a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex
inner-product space $V$. For real $t,s$, the evolution from
[[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]] satisfies
$$U_H(0)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t)^*U_H(t)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t+s)=U_H(t)U_H(s),\qquad \frac{d}{dt}U_H(t)=-iHU_H(t).$$
Moreover, $U_H$ is the unique differentiable map $Y:\mathbb R\to
\operatorname{End}(V)$ satisfying $Y'(t)=-iHY(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_V$.

derivations.claim: Put $A=-iH_1$ and $B=-iH_2$, so $AB=BA$. Define $Y(s)=e^{sA}e^{sB}$. By [F2] and the product rule, $Y'(s)=Ae^{sA}e^{sB}+e^{sA}Be^{sB}=(A+B)Y(s)$, where commutation lets $B$ pass through $e^{sA}$. Also $Y(0)=I$.
The unique solution of $Z'=(A+B)Z$, $Z(0)=I$, is $U_{H_1+H_2}(s)$ by [F2]. Hence $Y(h)=U_{H_1+H_2}(h)$ for every real $h$, which proves the one-step identity in [F1].
Taking $h=t/r$ and composing the exact identity $r$ times gives $S_1(t/r)^r=U_{H_1+H_2}(t/r)^r=U_{H_1+H_2}(t)$ by the group law in [F2] and the product definition [F1].

Fix $N\ge1$, a sparsity bound $d\ge1$, an integer $b\ge1$, and an injective code $\mathrm{enc}:C\to\{0,1\}^b$ for a finite set $C\subset\mathbb C$ containing $0$ and closed under conjugation. Put $w=\lceil\log_2N\rceil$ and $v=\lceil\log_2d\rceil$, identify $[N]$ with the first $N$ strings in $\{0,1\}^w$, and regard any remaining strings as invalid labels. A valid $w$-bit index is zero-extended to $w+1$ bits. Let $H=(H_{xy})_{x,y\in[N]}$ be Hermitian, have entries in $C$, and have at most $d$ nonzero entries in every row. For each valid row $x$, list its nonzero column indices in increasing order. Define the total location function $f_H(x,\ell)$ to be the $\ell$-th listed index for a valid slot $0\le\ell<d$ when that slot exists, and a distinguished sentinel otherwise. Invalid row labels and invalid slot labels also return the sentinel. Encode the sentinel by a fixed $(w+1)$-bit word outside the valid index codes. Define the total value function $g_H(x,y)$ to return $\mathrm{enc}(H_{xy})$ on valid labels and $\mathrm{enc}(0)$ on invalid labels. All label widths and codes are part of the finite input description.

The **row-location oracle** and **entry-value oracle** are the coherent XOR maps $O_{f_H}|x,\ell,z\rangle=|x,\ell,z\oplus f_H(x,\ell)\rangle$ and $O_{g_H}|x,y,z\rangle=|x,y,z\oplus g_H(x,y)\rangle$, where the output target has respectively $w+1$ and $b$ bits. The slot register has $v$ bits; all unused slot strings are invalid and use the sentinel. These are total Boolean-function oracles on every bitstring basis input. They are instances of [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], whose justified-by supplier proves unitarity and involutivity for arbitrary total functions. Each named call and any separately granted controlled or inverse call is charged under [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. This exact-code model describes the decoded matrix $H$; approximating a different target matrix requires a separate bound on the matrix difference. Row and value access alone does not supply a term list or term-evolution circuits.

A **term-list access input** consists of an integer $m\ge1$, finite-dimensional self-adjoint endomorphisms $H_1,\ldots,H_m$ on one stated register, and the exact target $H=\sum_{j=1}^m H_j$. A supported time code is a finite expression whose leaves are rational numbers or symbols $\rho_q$ denoting the unique positive real root of $x^q=4$ for an odd integer $q\ge1$; [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] gives a unique nonnegative root; it is positive because $0^q=0\ne4$. Internal operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division by a nonzero expression. Its exact real value and bit length are recorded. These codes include rational times and every coefficient-scaled rational time in the finite Suzuki recursion.

For each $j$, the input declares which time codes are supported and supplies either the exact operation $e^{-isH_j}$ or a full-list uniform circuit generator, in the sense of [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], that returns a unitary $V_j(s)$ together with a certified error $\eta_j(s)\ge0$ satisfying $\|V_j(s)-e^{-isH_j}\|\le\eta_j(s)$. If a circuit uses auxiliary registers, it supplies the exact clean or dirty contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]] so that its induced operation $V_j(s)$ on the target is well-defined: clean registers start and return to zero for every target input, and dirty registers are acted on by the identity. The operator-norm error is measured on the induced target operation. The provider specifies how each supported code is passed to the generator and records its actual description length and generation time; no polynomial bound is inferred. This is an explicit access promise, not a claim that every matrix has such a family.

For each supported call the input records its named-oracle query counts, gate count, ancillary wires, description bits, coefficient bits, and classical generation cost. Costs of composing the calls into a full product and generating that product are separately recorded as $Q_{\rm wrap}$ and $G_{\rm wrap}$. A controlled form is available only when separately declared as the block operation of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. Inverse access to a call is available only when separately declared under [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]], with its own cost and error record. Forward access implies neither capability. The term list supplies no promise that any operation or coefficient computation is free.

derivations.claim: Fix $N=2^n$, equip $\mathbb C^N$ with its standard inner product, and let $|x\rangle$ denote its standard basis. For any function $f:[N]\to\{-1,+1\}$ define $H_f=\sum_{x=1}^N f(x)|x\rangle\langle x|$. This diagonal matrix is Hermitian and each row has exactly one nonzero entry; the row-location oracle returns $x$ at the nonzero slot, and the entry-value oracle returns $f(x)$ on the diagonal query $(x,x)$. Thus the input is $1$-sparse in [F1].

The canonical ordered rank-one list is $H_f=\sum_{x=1}^N f(x)|x\rangle\langle x|$, with $N$ terms, and is determined by $(f(1),\ldots,f(N))$. There are $2^N$ such lists but only $2^N-1$ binary strings of length less than $N$, so any lossless binary encoding has a worst-case length of at least $N$ bits. If a deterministic exact recovery procedure makes fewer than $N$ classical row-value queries, some row $x$ is unqueried; changing only $f(x)$ preserves every reply in its transcript but changes the canonical list, so that transcript cannot determine the list for both inputs.

Since $N=2^n$, this canonical list's description and exact classical recovery costs grow exponentially in the index length $n$. The sparse model supplies only the row/value calls by [F1], whereas the term-list model additionally requires the list and term-evolution access by [F2]; those extra promises therefore cannot be inferred from the sparse interface. No lower bound for every possible alternative decomposition, quantum query procedure, or circuit implementation is asserted.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $H_1,\ldots,H_m$ be self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V$ with $m\ge1$, and set $H=\sum_{j=1}^mH_j$. For every real $t$ and integer $r\ge1$,
$$\left\|S_1(t/r)^r-U_H(t)\right\|\le\frac{t^2}{2r}\sum_{1\le j<k\le m}\|[H_j,H_k]\|,$$
where $S_1$ has the fixed order of [[def-qa-20-first-order-product-formula]] and $U_H(t)=e^{-itH}$ is the finite-matrix evolution of [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]].

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: In the standard inner product, direct conjugate transpose gives $X^*=X$ and $Z^*=Z$. Matrix multiplication gives $XZ=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=-iY$ and $ZX=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=iY$. Therefore $[X,Z]=XZ-ZX=-2iY$.
The same matrices give $Y^*Y=I_2$. Hence [F2] and [F3] give $\|Y\|=1$, and scalar homogeneity of the operator norm yields $\|[X,Z]\|=2$.
Substituting $H_1=X$, $H_2=Z$ and $\|[X,Z]\|=2$ into [F1] gives $\|S_1(t/r)^r-U_{X+Z}(t)\|\le(t^2/(2r))2=t^2/r$. For the exact finite boundary $t=0$, both evolutions are $I_2$ and the error is zero.

For $H_1=\lambda X$ and $H_2=Z-\lambda X$, both terms are Hermitian and their sum is $Z$. Direct multiplication gives $Z^*Z=I_2$, and [F2]–[F3] give $\|Z\|=1$. Bilinearity and $[X,X]=0$ give $[H_1,H_2]=\lambda[X,Z]$, whose norm is $2\lambda$ by [step 2.1] and $\lambda\ge0$. Thus [F1] gives the sufficient certificate $\lambda t^2/r$. To make this particular bound at most $\epsilon$ requires $r\ge\lambda t^2/\epsilon$ when $t\ne0$. This quantity is unbounded as $\lambda$ grows while the total matrix and its norm stay fixed; it shows that this error certificate cannot choose a uniform $r$ from $\|H\|$ and $\epsilon$ alone. It is not a lower bound on the actual simulation error.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

For every linear map $A:H\to K$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces,

$$\|A\|_1=\operatorname{tr}_H\!\left(\sqrt{A^*A}\right).$$

Here $A^*A$ and its non-negative square root are endomorphisms of the domain
$H$; the trace is taken on $H$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

derivations.claim: Put $c:=\langle u|v\rangle_D$ and $s:=\sqrt{1-|c|^2}$. By [F3], $0\le s\le1$. If $s=0$, equality in Cauchy–Schwarz makes $v$ a unit scalar multiple of $u$, so $P_v=P_u$ and $D(P_u,P_v)=0$.

Suppose $s>0$ and set $e:=(v-cu)/s$. The Dirac convention makes $\langle u|e\rangle_D=0$, and direct expansion gives $\|e\|=1$. In the orthonormal basis $(u,e)$ of their span, $P_u-P_v$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}s^2&-cs\\-\overline c\,s&-s^2\end{pmatrix}$; it is zero on the orthogonal complement. This Hermitian matrix has trace $0$ and determinant $-s^2$, hence eigenvalues $s,-s$. By [F4]–[F6], $\|P_u-P_v\|_1=2s$, so $D(P_u,P_v)=s$.
For either case, $\|u-v\|^2=2-2\operatorname{Re}c\ge2(1-|c|)$, while $s^2=(1-|c|)(1+|c|)\le2(1-|c|)$. Thus $D(P_u,P_v)=s\le\|u-v\|$, including the $s=0$ case from step 1.1.

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

derivations.claim: If either tensor factor is zero-dimensional, then $X=0$ and the claimed inequality follows from the empty coordinate sum in [F4]; assume both factors are nonzero for the rest of the proof. For any Hermitian $Z$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, [F3] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_i)$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. The adjoint identity [F11] and conjugate symmetry make $\lambda_i=\langle Ze_i,e_i\rangle=\langle e_i,Ze_i\rangle=\overline{\lambda_i}$, so each $\lambda_i$ is real. For every Hermitian $Y$ with $\|Y\|\le1$, [F12] gives $\operatorname{tr}(ZY)=\sum_i\lambda_i\langle Ye_i,e_i\rangle_{\rm root}$. Again [F11] makes each diagonal entry real, and [F8]–[F9] put it in $[-1,1]$. Thus $|\operatorname{tr}(ZY)|\le\sum_i|\lambda_i|=\|Z\|_1$: in the eigenbasis, $Z^\dagger Z$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i^2$, so [F2] its nonnegative square root has eigenvalues $|\lambda_i|$, and [F1], [F2], [F12] give the trace norm sum. Equality is attained by the Hermitian contraction acting by $\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_i)$ on each $e_i$ (and by $0$ when $\lambda_i=0$). Hence $\|Z\|_1=\sup_{Y=Y^\dagger,\ \|Y\|\le1}|\operatorname{tr}(ZY)|$.

Formula [F4] shows $\operatorname{Tr}_E X$ is Hermitian: transposing and conjugating its $(i,i')$ entry gives $\sum_j\overline{X_{(i',j),(i,j)}}=\sum_jX_{(i,j),(i',j)}$. If $Y=Y^\dagger$ and $\|Y\|\le1$, choose an orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $H_E$ by [F10] and write arbitrary $\xi=\sum_jx_j\otimes f_j$ and $\zeta=\sum_jy_j\otimes f_j$. The product inner product and tensor-map action [F6]–[F7] give $\langle(Y\otimes I_E)\xi,\zeta\rangle=\sum_j\langle Yx_j,y_j\rangle=\sum_j\langle x_j,Yy_j\rangle=\langle\xi,(Y\otimes I_E)\zeta\rangle$ by self-adjointness and [F11], so $Y\otimes I_E$ is Hermitian. Also [F6]–[F8] give $\|(Y\otimes I_E)\xi\|^2=\sum_j\|Yx_j\|^2\le\sum_j\|x_j\|^2=\|\xi\|^2$, so $\|Y\otimes I_E\|\le1$.

For the remaining nonzero-factor case, apply the variational identity in step 1.1 to $\operatorname{Tr}_E X$. For each allowed $Y$, [F5] and step 1.2 give $|\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_E X)Y)|=|\operatorname{tr}(X(Y\otimes I_E))|\le\|X\|_1$, using step 1.1 for the Hermitian contraction $Y\otimes I_E$. Taking the supremum proves the claimed inequality.

citations.quote: Let $A$ be a finite register with distinguished unit computational-basis vector $|0_A\rangle$ (unit by [[thm-qc-computational-basis-orthonormal]]), let $S$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and define the isometry $J:S\to A\otimes S$ by $Jx=|0_A\rangle\otimes x$. The product inner product makes $J$ an isometry; [[lem-qc-linear-isometry-adjoint-identities]] gives $J^\dagger J=I_S$, and [[thm-qc-isometric-encoding-projector]] makes $\Pi_0:=JJ^\dagger$ the orthogonal projection onto its image. On elementary tensors this is $|0_A\rangle\langle0_A|\otimes I_S$ by the convention of [[def-qc-tensor-map]]. For a unit vector $\phi\in A\otimes S$, define its zero-branch vector $q:=J^\dagger\phi$, zero-branch weight $p_0:=\|q\|^2$, and complementary-branch weight $p_\perp:=\|(I-\Pi_0)\phi\|^2$. When $p_0>0$, the conditional system vector is $q/\sqrt{p_0}$; when $p_0=0$, no conditional vector is assigned. This definition fixes only the clean-ancilla two-outcome branch rule used on this page; it makes no physical realization claim.

finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is

indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces and let
$V:H\to K$ be a linear isometry. Then $V^\dagger V=I_H$. If $V$ is also
surjective, then $VV^\dagger=I_K$.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

derivations.claim: From the product inner product [F2] and unit norm [F5], $\|Jx\|^2=\langle |0_A\rangle\otimes x,|0_A\rangle\otimes x\rangle=\|x\|^2$ for every $x$, so $J$ is an isometry by its definition in [F3]. Therefore $J^\dagger J=I_S$ by [F3]. It follows that $\Pi_0=JJ^\dagger$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, $\Pi_0\phi=Jq$, and $\phi=\Pi_0\phi+(I-\Pi_0)\phi$.

The two summands are orthogonal because $\Pi_0(I-\Pi_0)=0$ and $\Pi_0^\dagger=\Pi_0$. Expanding their squared norm by [F4] gives $1=\|\phi\|^2=\|\Pi_0\phi\|^2+\|(I-\Pi_0)\phi\|^2=\|q\|^2+p_\perp=p_0+p_\perp$. Both summands are nonnegative, so each lies in $[0,1]$.

If $p_0>0$, then $\|q/\sqrt{p_0}\|^2=p_0/p_0=1$. If $p_0=0$, definiteness of the inner-product norm gives $q=0$, so normalization is undefined and the definition correctly assigns no conditional vector.

derivations.claim: Write $\beta_j=\sqrt{|c_j|/\alpha}$ and $\omega_j=c_j/|c_j|$ for $c_j\ne0$ (take $\omega_j=1$ when $c_j=0$). PREPARE gives $e^{i\theta}\sum_{j<m}\beta_j|j,0_{\rm work}\rangle$ from the all-zero ancilla. After SELECT, the $j$th component is $e^{i\theta}\beta_j|j,0_{\rm work}\rangle\otimes\omega_jV_j\psi$. The all-zero matrix element of PREPARE$^\dagger$ on $|j,0_{\rm work}\rangle$ is $e^{-i\theta}\beta_j$ by [F1], so the global phase cancels and $J^\dagger WJ\psi=\sum_j\beta_j^2\omega_jV_j\psi=M\psi/\alpha$. If $\|M\psi\|>0$, division of the branch vector by its norm gives $M\psi/\|M\psi\|$. If $M\psi=0$, the weight is zero and [F4] forbids assigning a normalized conditional vector to that branch.

Let $H=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_jV_j$ on a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, with $m\ge1$, real $a_j$ and Hermitian unitaries $V_j$, and put $\Lambda=\sum_j|a_j|$. For real $h$ and integer $K\ge0$, define
$$M_K(h):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{(-ihH)^k}{k!}.$$
Its ordered product-term LCU list has one empty tuple for $k=0$, with coefficient $1$ and unitary $I$, and for each $1\le k\le K$ and ordered tuple $(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ has coefficient
$$c_{k,\mathbf j}:=\frac{(-i)^k h^k a_{j_1}\cdots a_{j_k}}{k!}$$
and unitary $V_{j_1}\cdots V_{j_k}$. Distinct tuples remain distinct entries even if their product unitaries coincide. The absolute coefficient sum of this listed representation is
$$s_K(h):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{(\Lambda|h|)^k}{k!}.$$

Whenever $s_K(h)\le2$, append two distinct identity entries with coefficients $+q$ and $-q$, where $q=(2-s_K(h))/2$. They leave the represented matrix unchanged and raise the listed absolute coefficient sum to exactly $2$. If $q=0$, the zero-weight entries may be retained with zero preparation amplitude or omitted. The polynomial, coefficient phases, ordered tuple index, and any numerical precision used to generate them are part of the finite input/access record; no term product, coefficient table, PREPARE circuit, or SELECT circuit is free.

In this page a **Hamiltonian** is a self-adjoint endomorphism $H$ of a
finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

The second expression uses the finite spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]. If $V$ is the zero
space, the spectrum is empty and the empty sum is the unique endomorphism,
which is also the identity on $V$. This definition specifies a mathematical
unitary from a finite matrix; it makes no claim that the operation has an
efficient circuit or a free access cost.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $H$ with eigenvalues $\lambda$. For a unit eigenvector $u_\lambda$, $|\lambda|=\|Hu_\lambda\|=\|\sum_j a_jV_ju_\lambda\|\le\sum_j|a_j|\|V_ju_\lambda\|=\Lambda$ by [F2]–[F4]. On this basis, [L1] and [L2] make the difference diagonal with scalar entries $\sum_{k=0}^K(-ih\lambda)^k/k!-\exp(-ih\lambda)$.
Since $x\ge0$, the finite Taylor coefficient sum obeys $0\le s_K=\sum_{k=0}^Kx^k/k!\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!=e^x$ by [L1] and [F5]. If $x\le\ln2$, [F7] gives $s_K\le e^x\le2$.

Put $n=K+1$. The absolute scalar-series tail at eigenvalue $\lambda$ is at most $\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}(|h||\lambda|)^k/k!$. Writing $k=n+j$ and using $(n+j)!\ge n!j!$ bounds this by $(|h||\lambda|)^n/n!\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(|h||\lambda|)^j/j!=e^{|h||\lambda|}(|h||\lambda|)^n/n!$ by [F5]–[F6]. If the diagonal error has entries $d_i$ in the eigenbasis and $z=\sum_i z_i u_i$, then its squared output norm is $\sum_i|d_i|^2|z_i|^2\le(\max_i|d_i|)^2\|z\|^2$; an eigenbasis vector attaining the finite maximum gives equality in the operator norm [F4]. Hence the operator norm is $\max_i|d_i|$. Since $0\le|h||\lambda_i|\le x$, the monotonicity of $e^u$ and $u^n$ on nonnegative reals gives $e^{|h||\lambda_i|}|h|^n|\lambda_i|^n/n!\le e^xx^n/n!$. Taking the maximum proves the stated tail bound.

Assume $x\le\ln2$, so $e^x\le2$ by [F7]. Let $L=\ln(1/\eta)$. The exponential series gives $2<e<3$: its first two terms sum to $2$, while $1/k!\le2^{-(k-1)}$ for $k\ge2$, with strict inequality for $k\ge3$, so the remaining sum is less than $1$. Thus $\exp(0)=1<2<\exp(1)=e$ by [F5], and the strict increase and inverse relation in [F7] give $0<\ln2<1$. If $L<1$, $n=10$ gives $2x^{10}/10!<2/10!<1/3<e^{-1}<\eta$. If $L\ge1$, take $n=\lceil16eL/\ln(e+L)\rceil$. For $z\ge1$, $g(z)=\sqrt z-\ln z$ has derivative $g'(z)=(\sqrt z-2)/(2z)$, so it decreases up to $z=4$ and increases thereafter. Since $e>2$, $\exp(2)=e^2>4$, hence $\ln4<2$ by [F7]; thus $g(z)\ge g(4)=2-\ln4>0$. Also $e+L<4L$. Therefore $$\frac ne\ge\frac{16L}{\ln(e+L)}\ge\frac{16L}{\sqrt{e+L}}>4\sqrt{e+L},$$ so $\ln(n/e)>\tfrac12\ln(e+L)$. Hence $n\ln(n/e)\ge8eL\ge L+\ln4$, using $e>2$, $L\ge1$, and $\ln4<2$. For the factorial estimate, monotonicity of $\ln s$ gives $\ln(n!)=\sum_{k=1}^n\ln k\ge\int_1^n\ln s\,ds=n\ln n-n+1$, so $n!\ge(n/e)^n\ge e^{L+\ln4}=4/\eta$. Since $e^xx^n/n!\le2/n!$, this choice gives a tail at most $\eta/2\le\eta$. In both cases $n=O(1+L/\ln(e+L))$. Since $\ln(e+e^L)\le L+\ln2\le e+L$, this is also $O(1+L/\ln\ln(e+e^L))$, the displayed order after changing logarithm bases. Hence $K=n-1$ has the stated order.
