This is the efficient numerical variant explicitly authorized by OP0/OP1; the complete exact/complete numerical modes retain their own root schedule. Its cost coordinate charges rational field arithmetic, including exact integer arithmetic on loop indices, rational comparisons, and exact input-coefficient comparisons. In particular, each integer midpoint division by $2$ in a bounded binary search is charged. Exact input-coefficient equality/order tests are explicitly ideal charged resources; coefficient encoding/access and implementation, including any algebraic refinement or minimal-polynomial conversion, are separate costs. It asserts no Turing or bit-time bound.

`ROUND-QSP(p,d,δ)` receives a real coefficient polynomial of degree at most $d$, parity $d\bmod 2$, with $|p|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, and rational $\delta>0$. Put $\tau=\min(\delta,8)$. Initialize $L=0$ and increment it until $2^{-L}\le\tau/[64(d+1)]$. Set $a=(1-\tau/16)p$. Set $A=1$ if $d=0$ and $A=(d+1)d^d$ if $d\ge1$. For each permitted coefficient $y$ of $a$, set the integer $M=(A+2)2^L$, initialize $lo=-M$ and $hi=M+1$, and repeat while $hi-lo>1$: set $k=\lfloor(lo+hi)/2\rfloor$, compare $y$ with $k2^{-L}$, and set $lo=k$ if $k2^{-L}\le y$, otherwise set $hi=k$. Let $k=lo$. If $y=k2^{-L}$, set this rounded coefficient to that mesh value; otherwise compare $y$ with $(k+\tfrac12)2^{-L}$ and choose the nearer of $k2^{-L}$ and $(k+1)2^{-L}$, taking the lower point in a tie. Keep all other coefficients zero. For $d=0$ the only permitted coefficient is the constant coefficient and this same search rounds it; no interpolation is used. Return the resulting dyadic polynomial $h$ and the integer polynomial obtained from $1-h^2$ by multiplying by $2^{2L}$.

`GRID-ROOTS(P,b)` receives a nonzero rational real polynomial $P$ and $b\ge1$. If $P$ is constant, return the empty root list. Otherwise let $n=\deg P\ge1$. First divide every coefficient by the nonzero leading coefficient, using rational field operations. Only then clear the denominators of these monic coefficient ratios and remove integer content. Compute integer gcds by Euclidean division, obtaining each quotient by bounded integer binary search rather than a free floor primitive. Use the square-free reduction, winding count, multiplicity test and real Sturm counts of [[alg-qa-23-polynomial-root-isolation]], with the following bounded search and rational sign implementations.

At any coordinate interval $(u,v)$, set $N=100(n+1)$, where $n=\deg P$. Choose the least dyadic denominator $D=2^k$ for which the middle third contains at least $N+1$ consecutive grid points $j/D$. Take its first $N$ points. For outer half-widths use intervals $(B,B+1)$, with $B=2+\max_{j<n}|a_j/a_n|$ rounded upward to an integer; the search need not start at zero. Test all pairs of the two $N$-point sets in lexicographic order, using precisely the existing root-free-boundary, nonzero-vertex-imaginary-part, and nonzero-edge-imaginary-polynomial tests. Use the first admissible pair. If none exists return `INTERNAL_ERROR`. For subdivision use the two parent coordinate intervals and their middle thirds, so every child width is at most $2/3$ of its parent width. This bounded search replaces the unbounded global dyadic-pair enumeration only in this numerical alternate.

Implement each edge sign $R(\alpha)$, where $I(\alpha)=0$, by rational root isolation of the square-free part of $RI$ (omit a nonzero constant factor, and handle $R\equiv0$ separately). Use Sturm counts of $I$ and $R$ in each product-root isolator to identify the $I$-roots; retain only those with $I$-count one and $R$-count zero, refining as needed. Use a rational sample therein for the sign of $R$. Boundary root-freeness ensures that $\alpha$ is not a common root. Endpoint roots are tested and factored out before open-interval Sturm counting. The sign change of $I$ at $\alpha$ is its pair of rational endpoint signs. For sign refinement avoid roots of $RI$ when choosing cuts. The one-dimensional Sturm subdivisions use the first nonroot among $N$ dyadic grid points in the middle third, with the same bounded-grid rule. Euclidean gcd, division, and negative-remainder Sturm chains use exact rational field operations. Stop and return isolators by the original diameter/count rule.

For every nonzero rational or exact-algebraic complex polynomial $p$ and integer $b\ge1$, under the exact algebraic operation model declared in [[alg-qa-23-polynomial-root-isolation]], the algorithm terminates and returns pairwise-disjoint open rational rectangles of Euclidean diameter at most $2^{-b}$, each containing exactly one distinct root and together containing every root. Each rectangle carries the algebraic root descriptor and the original multiplicity. The supplied `REALROOTS` and `SIGNCERT` routines also terminate and return the stated exact real-root and interval-sign certificates. No bit-complexity bound is asserted.

Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an ordered subfield and let $f\in K[t]$ be nonconstant and square-free, where **square-free means** $\gcd(f,f')=1$. Put $f_0=f$, $f_1=f'$, and, while the next remainder is nonzero, set $f_{j+1}=-\operatorname{rem}(f_{j-1},f_j)$. For $x\in K$, let $V(x)$ be the number of sign changes in $(f_0(x),\ldots,f_m(x))$ after deleting zero entries, where $f_m$ is the last nonzero member. If $a,b\in K$, $a<b$, and $f(a)f(b)\ne0$, then the number of distinct real roots of $f$ in $(a,b)$ is $V(a)-V(b)$.

By [[prop-vandermonde-square-is-symmetric]] and [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-symmetric-polynomials]], there is a unique polynomial $D_n\in\mathbb Z[T_1,\ldots,T_n]$ such that

$$\Delta_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)^2=D_n(e_1,\ldots,e_n).$$

For a monic polynomial

$$f(t)=t^n+a_1t^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n$$

over a commutative ring, its **discriminant** is

$$\operatorname{Disc}(f):=D_n(-a_1,a_2,\ldots,(-1)^na_n).$$

Equivalently, in any algebra in which $f$ splits with roots $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n$, this coefficient expression evaluates to $\Delta_n(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)^2$. The definition therefore depends only on the coefficients and not on a choice or ordering of roots. For a monic constant polynomial, $\operatorname{Disc}(1)=1$.

Let $F$ be a field and let $f\in F[t]$ be monic of degree $n$. In a splitting field write

$$f(t)=\prod_{i=1}^n(t-\alpha_i).$$

Then

$$\operatorname{Disc}(f)=\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2.$$

Moreover, $\operatorname{Disc}(f)=0$ if and only if $f$ has a repeated root. This criterion holds in every characteristic.

derivations.claim:
For $d\ge1$ interpolate $p$ at $x_j=-1+2j/d$, $j=0,\ldots,d$. The Lagrange basis is $L_j(x)=\prod_{k
e j}(x-x_k)/\prod_{k
e j}(x_j-x_k)$. The numerator's sum of absolute coefficients is at most $\prod_{k
e j}(1+|x_k|)\le2^d$; the absolute denominator is $(2/d)^d j!(d-j)!\ge(2/d)^d$. Therefore each coefficient of $L_j$ has absolute value at most $d^d$, and, since $|p(x_j)|\le1$, every coefficient of $p$ has absolute value at most $A=(d+1)d^d$. This interpolation identity follows because subtracting the interpolant leaves a polynomial of degree at most $d$ with $d+1$ distinct zeros. For $d=0$ use $A=1$. Hence $\log_2(\max(2,A))=O(d\log(d+1)+1)$, independently of any encoding of the original coefficients.

We give explicit coarse separation estimates sufficient for counting subdivisions. For a primitive integer polynomial $U$ of degree $m$ and coefficient magnitude at most $2^J$, every root has $|z|\le C=1+2^J$ by the Cauchy argument: outside that radius the leading monomial strictly dominates the geometric sum of the others. Every primitive integer divisor $V$ of $U$ has leading coefficient dividing that of $U$ and all its roots among those of $U$. Its coefficients, by expanding its linear factors, thus have magnitude at most $2^J2^m\max(1,C)^m$. The assertion that primitive integer divisors may be used here follows from Gauss's lemma: products of primitive polynomials are primitive, since reduction modulo any prime gives a product of two nonzero polynomials over a field; clearing denominators of a rational factorization and comparing contents then gives the integral factorization. Consequently the primitive square-free part, and every gcd with another integer polynomial, has coefficient height $O(m(J+1))$. This is an output coefficient-growth bound; it does not bound the internal Euclidean fractions.

For the root-isolation input $P$, if $n=\deg P=0$, the constant branch in [F1] returns the empty list, which is correct and takes constant work; assume $n\ge1$ below. Put $q$ equal to the square-free part of $P$ and $F(x,y)=\operatorname{Im}q(x+iy)$. This is a nonzero real bivariate polynomial of total degree at most $n$: if $\operatorname{Im}q$ vanished everywhere, its $x$ derivative and its $y$ derivative would force $q^{\prime}=0$ by the coefficient expansion, contrary to nonconstancy. A nonzero bivariate polynomial of total degree $\le n$ vanishes at at most $nN$ points of a product of two $N$-point sets. Indeed, if its leading nonzero coefficient as a polynomial in $y$ has $x$-degree $s$, at most $s$ $x$-values annihilate that coefficient; at every remaining $x$ there are at most $n-s$ $y$-zeros, giving at most $sN+(N-s)(n-s)\le nN$. Each fixed old edge restriction of $F$ is nonzero by admissibility, so it has at most $n$ forbidden new vertex coordinates. There are at most $n$ root real coordinates and $n$ root imaginary coordinates, and at most $n$ coordinates making $F$ vanish identically along a vertical or horizontal line: such a coordinate must annihilate any chosen nonzero coefficient polynomial. The new center-vertex condition excludes at most $nN$ pairs. Old-edge vertex, root-line, and identically-zero-edge restrictions together exclude fewer than $20(n+1)N$ pairs. The analogous four outer-corner polynomials $F(\pm X,\pm Y)$ are nonzero and obey the same bound. Therefore $N=100(n+1)$ gives an admissible pair both outside and inside, so `INTERNAL_ERROR` is unreachable. At most $N^2$ candidate pairs are tested at each node. A univariate nonzero polynomial similarly excludes at most $n$ candidates, proving the one-dimensional bounded search.

Let $\tau=\min(\delta,8)$ and $t=2^{-L}$. The least-$L$ rule gives $t\le\tau/[64(d+1)]$ and, unless $L=0$, $t>\tau/[128(d+1)]$. Since $0<\tau\le8$, the shrink factor $1-\tau/16$ lies in $[1/2,1)$. For each scaled coefficient, binary search over the integer mesh indices in $[-M,M]$, where $M=(A+2)2^L$, finds the lower mesh point and exact comparison with its midpoint resolves the rounding tie. Since the interpolation bound gives $|((1-\tau/16)p)_j|\le A$, this search interval contains the needed cell and takes $O(\log(A+1)+L)$ exact comparisons and rational arithmetic operations, including each integer midpoint division by two. Rounding error per coefficient is at most $t/2\le\tau/[64(d+1)]$, so $\|h-(1-\tau/16)p\|_\infty\le\tau/64$. Thus $\|h-p\|_\infty\le5\tau/64<\tau/8$ and $\|h\|_\infty\le1-3\tau/64$. Parity is preserved because forbidden coefficients remain exactly zero. The integers $2^L h_j$ have length $O(L+\log(A+1))$, and the convolution coefficients of $2^{2L}(1-h^2)$ have length $O(L+\log(A+1)+\log(d+1))$. Minimality of $L$ gives $L=O(\log(d+1)+\log_+(1/\tau)+1)$, proving the claimed height and rounding cost, also when $\delta\ge1$. Zero leading rounded coefficients only lower the actual degree.

Let $V(z)=az^r+\sum_{j<r}v_jz^j$ be the primitive square-free integer part of $U$, of degree $r\ge2$. Define $W(t)=a^{r-1}V(t/a)$. Its leading coefficient is one, and its $j$-th coefficient for $j<r$ is $v_ja^{r-1-j}$, an integer. Its distinct roots are $\beta_i=a\zeta_i$, with $|\beta_i|\le|a|C$. By [F4], $\operatorname{Disc}(W)$ is a nonzero integer and $|\operatorname{Disc}(W)|=\prod_{i<j}|\beta_i-\beta_j|^2\ge1$. If $\Delta_\beta$ is the least separation of its roots, all other pairwise distances are at most $2|a|C$, so $1\le\Delta_\beta^2(2|a|C)^{r(r-1)-2}$. Therefore the separation of the roots of $V$ obeys $\Delta_\zeta=\Delta_\beta/|a|\ge|a|^{-1}(2|a|C)^{-(r(r-1)-2)/2}$. Step 1.2 bounds $\log_2|a|$ by $O(m(J+1))$ and $\log_2 C$ by $O(J+1)$, so $\log_2(1/\Delta_\zeta)=O(m^3(J+1))$. Constants and degree-one polynomials need no separation estimate. This argument uses only the two actual local discriminant suppliers in [F4], with no resultant multiplicativity premise.

Every child side length lies between one third and two thirds of its parent side length. The initial side lengths have logarithm $O(H+1)$, by the original Cauchy bound. By step 2.2, after $D=\operatorname{poly}(n,H,b)$ levels every rectangle has diameter less than both $2^{-b}$ and the least distinct-root separation, and hence has count at most one. At every level at most $n$ positive-count rectangles exist, because their disjoint interiors each contain a root by [F2]. Each is replaced by at most four children, so there are $O(n(D+1))$ tested tree nodes, not $4^D$. A side at level $k$ has length at least its initial length times $3^{-k}$. The least dyadic denominator containing $N+1$ middle-third points therefore has exponent $O(H+k+\log(n+1))$; all coordinates have numerator and denominator length $T=O(H+D+\log(n+1))$. Even if the interval already contains many integers, only its first $N$ grid points are tested. This last restriction is essential: unrestricted lexicographic enumeration of all pairs in a very wide interval has no polynomial bound merely from a finite forbidden-coordinate count.

For root analysis with $n\ge1$ (the constant case is settled in step 1.3), integer parts and grid generation are charged operations rather than free primitives. For a rational operand of numerator/denominator length at most $S$, find its bounding signed powers of two by doubling, then find its floor by binary search through the bounded integer interval, using $O(S+1)$ rational comparisons and additions; compare exactly with the resulting integer to obtain the ceiling and strict open-interval endpoints. Before denominator clearing, normalize the input $P$ by its nonzero leading coefficient in $O(n+1)$ rational field operations. If $U$ is its primitive integer representative with height $H$, each resulting monic coefficient ratio is $U_j/U_n$, whose reduced numerator and denominator lengths are $O(H)$, independently of an arbitrarily large common rational scalar in the original $P$. The product of these at most $n+1$ denominators has length $O((n+1)H)$; using that product as common denominator gives integer coefficients of length $O((n+1)H)$. Their content is found by integer Euclidean gcds. Each division quotient is obtained by the bounded binary search just described, with polynomial-length integer operands. Integer remainders decrease in magnitude; after at most two nonterminal divisions the larger nonzero operand has at least halved (if the first remainder exceeds half the previous divisor, the next is smaller than its complement). Thus the number of divisions per gcd is linear in the initial operand length. Content removal and denominator clearing therefore cost $\operatorname{poly}(n,H)$ rational arithmetic and comparisons. The resulting primitive integer representative has height at most $H$ and is the input used in step 1.2 and step 2.2 and step 1.3 and step 3.1. In particular the outer $B$ is obtained in $\operatorname{poly}(H)$ operations from the original coefficient ratios. To generate a grid, begin with denominator one and double it, recomputing the strict lower/upper admissible integer numerators by this binary search, until their difference gives at least $N+1$ points. Step 3.1 bounds the number of doublings by $O(H+D+\log(n+1))$; every rational tested has polynomial numerator/denominator height in $n,H,b$, because it is a parent coordinate or width times such a dyadic denominator. Each integer-part search therefore costs $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,b)$ operations. Writing the first $N$ consecutive grid numerators costs $O(N)$ further additions. This bound also applies to any one-dimensional bounded grid once its coordinate-height and denominator-doubling bounds are established. The least $L$ in rounding is likewise found by sequential denominator doubling and exact comparison with $\tau/[64(d+1)]$, with $O(\log(d+1)+\log_+(1/\tau)+1)$ iterations; mesh-cell integer selection is the bounded binary search already charged in step 2.1. No floor, ceiling, or denominator selection is treated as unit-cost.

Each rational edge substitution $z=u+vt$ into $q$ has degree at most $n$. Clearing the rational denominators after binomial expansion gives real and imaginary integer polynomials with coefficient height $J_{\mathrm{edge}}=\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)$: each term uses at most $n$ coordinate factors of length $T$ and one $q$ coefficient of height $O(n(H+1))$, and there are at most $n+1$ terms per coefficient. This also applies to all proposed edges, since they use the same bounded-coordinate grids. Products of two such edge polynomials have polynomial degree and height. Their primitive square-free parts and gcds have polynomial output height by step 1.2, and their distinct roots have separation $2^{-\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)}$ by step 2.2. The same facts apply to the gcds used for multiplicity tests, since the $m$-th derivative has coefficient height $O(H+n\log(n+1))$ and its gcd is a divisor of $q$.

Polynomial division of degree-at-most-$n$ rational polynomials takes $O(n^2)$ field operations, and Euclidean and negative-remainder chains have at most $n$ nonzero stages. A Sturm evaluation at rational endpoints thus takes $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ field operations and comparisons, regardless of the rational operand sizes. Square-free reduction and every boundary gcd test have the same polynomial arithmetic bound. Isolate each edge's $I$-roots on $[0,1]$ with the bounded one-dimensional search, first handling endpoint factors. The separation estimate for the square-free product $RI$ proves that $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)$ levels suffice to separate distinct $I$-roots and distinguish each $I$-root from all noncommon $R$-roots. A root $\alpha$ of $I$ on the edge is not a root of $R$ by the certified boundary test. Refinement therefore eventually puts $\alpha$ in an interval containing no $R$-root; [F3] certifies this last fact by zero $R$-root count, and a rational sample gives the nonzero sign of $R$ there. The sign change of $I$ is its two endpoint signs. At every level at most $n$ positive $I$-root intervals are retained (at most $2n$ when isolating the product). For a depth-$K$ interval in $[0,1]$, its length is at least $3^{-K}$ and its endpoints have dyadic height $O(K+\log(n+1))$; the grid denominator therefore requires $O(K+\log(n+1))$ doublings. The grid integer parts, ceilings, and written candidate coordinates are consequently charged by step 4.1 within the same polynomial operation bound. Endpoint handling, bounded-grid cuts, all root counts, and all refinements therefore take $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,T)$ rational arithmetic operations. A nonzero constant $I$ has no crossings; an identically zero $I$ was already excluded by the grid.

Combining $O(n(D+1))$ nodes, $N^2$ candidates per node, polynomial edge costs from step 5.1, and at most $n$ derivative/gcd multiplicity tests per retained root proves $\operatorname{poly}(n,H,b)$ rational arithmetic cost. All accepted boundaries satisfy exactly the conditions in [F2], so its winding, partition, and multiplicity arguments prove correctness unchanged. Substituting $n\le2d$ and $H=O(d\log(d+1)+\log_+(1/\delta)+1)$ from step 2.1 gives the claimed rounded-input root cost. The proof counts field operations; it never bounds Euclidean intermediate operand lengths or the precision required by later algebraic phase calculations, so it makes none of those additional assertions.

Let $d\ge0$ and let $A\in\mathbb R[x]$ be even, of degree at most $2d$, and nonnegative on $[-1,1]$. Then there are $B,C\in\mathbb R[x]$ such that
$$A(x)=B(x)^2+(1-x^2)C(x)^2,$$
where $\deg B\le d$, $\deg C\le d-1$, $B$ has parity $d$, and $C$ has parity $d-1$. The zero polynomial is both even and odd and satisfies every degree bound.

For every integer $d\ge0$, a pair $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ is QSP-admissible of degree bound $d$ if and only if there is a real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix}\quad (x\in[-1,1]).$$
The converse is constructive: a leading-coefficient phase peel reduces the degree at each nonconstant stage. The polynomial identity, determinant signs, product order, and phase convention are exactly those in [[def-qa-23-qsp-admissible-polynomial-pair]] and [[def-qa-23-qsp-signal-sequence]].

Put $s=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, $W_R=\begin{pmatrix}x&s\\s&-x\end{pmatrix}$, $W_S=\begin{pmatrix}x&is\\is&x\end{pmatrix}$, and $C=Z(\pi/4)$. Then
$$CW_RC=iW_S^\dagger,\qquad W_S^\dagger=Z(\pi/2)W_SZ(-\pi/2).$$
For $d\ge1$, define $U_S(\Psi)=Z(\psi_0)\prod_{j=1}^d(W_SZ(\psi_j))$. If $\Psi$ is the SU(2)-convention phase list with $\psi_0=\phi_0+\pi/4$, $\psi_j=\phi_j-\pi/2$ for $1\le j<d$, and $\psi_d=\phi_d-3\pi/4$, then
$$U_R(\Phi)=i^dU_S(\Psi).$$
The affine phase-list map is invertible. The scalar $i^d$ is part of the identity: in a control-first block $\operatorname{diag}(I,U)$ it acts on the active control branch and cannot be discarded as a global phase.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: For an exact algebraic $r=x+iy$ with $x^2+y^2=1$, select one square root by:
If $x=-1$, return $\omega=i$ (then necessarily $y=0$). Otherwise put $s=\sqrt{(1+x)/2}>0$, $t=y/(2s)$, and return $\omega=s+it$.

Given an existing exact real algebraic value $A\ge0$ and a known rational $U\ge\max(1,\sqrt A)$, compare $A$ with zero. If equal, return rational zero. Otherwise initialize $[l,r]=[0,U]$. While $r-l>1/2$, put $m=(l+r)/2$ and compare $A$ with $m^2$ exactly. Equality returns the rational value $m$. If $A<m^2$, put $r=m$; if $A>m^2$, put $l=m$. After the loop, return the tower descriptor consisting of $T^2-A$ over the existing field and the rational isolating interval $[l,r]$, specifying its unique nonnegative root.

Here $-1<x\le1$, so the positive square root exists, is nonzero, and has the root-selection description $S^2-(1+x)/2=0$, $0<S<2$ over the existing real algebraic field. Its two roots are distinguished immediately by sign. One has $t^2=(1-x)/2$ because $y^2=(1-x)(1+x)$, whence $s^2+t^2=1$, $s^2-t^2=x$, and $2st=y$. Therefore $|\omega|=1$ and $\omega^2=r$. The $x=1,y=0$ case returns $1$. No small-denominator numerical approximation is performed; the division is exact. There is no conditioning assumption.

For $A>0$, the roots are $\pm\sqrt A$, distinct, and only the positive root belongs to $[0,U]$. The square function is strictly increasing on this nonnegative interval, so each branch preserves $\sqrt A\in[l,r]$ and excludes the negative root. Every iteration halves the width and uses $O(1)$ rational or exact field operations and one exact comparison. Hence the routine uses $O(1+\log U)$ operations/comparisons and writes a degree-two defining equation plus its rational isolator. A root at the original right endpoint is permitted in the closed isolator; the root is still unique. If open endpoints are required, start with $[0,2U]$; this adds at most one iteration and makes the positive root interior unless a midpoint equality has already returned it rationally.

In a model requiring conversion at every step to a rational defining polynomial and a rational isolator, the quadratic relation has an algebraic coefficient. Converting it to a rational defining polynomial requires elimination, and converting all subsequent values into that representation can be expensive. The descriptor routine does not bound that conversion cost. A tower of $d$ quadratic extensions may have degree $2^d$, even though its construction writes only $d$ degree-two tower equations and rational isolators.

This replaces a generic call ROOTS($z^2-r$,1) by a constant number of field operations and exact comparisons and the explicit quadratic-root descriptor routine below. It may choose the other square root from the existing lexicographic-rectangle rule. Either root gives the leading-term cancellation and an exact factorization: subsequent phases change coherently with that choice. The synthesis algorithm selects this formula in every mode; the efficient-numerical cost bound here uses its known upper bound rather than a bound search.

For the half-angle radicand $A=(1+x)/2$, one has $0<A\le1$ after the $x=-1$ branch, so $U=1$ is known without search. One bisection suffices for a closed width-$1/2$ isolator; at most two suffice with the open-endpoint initialization. This is an actual counted descriptor-construction loop, not a free ROOTS call or a radical oracle. Subsequent field operations and order/equality queries on these tower values remain the explicit charged primitives of the declared exact algebraic comparison/field model. These are ideal exact equality/order resources charged per use; their implementation is not supplied by the descriptor loop.

Suppose the rational completion polynomial $R$ has nonzero coefficient numerators and denominators of absolute value at most $2^H$. A rational Cauchy bound $B\ge1$ can be chosen with $B\le2^{2H+2}$, because the leading coefficient ratio is at most $2^{2H}$. Every classified root coordinate $s,a,b$ then has absolute value at most $B$. The real exterior and imaginary radicands are bounded by $B^2$ and $B^2+1\le2B^2$, so $U=2B$ works. For a quadruple put $D=2(a^2+1)b^2+(a^2-1)^2+b^4$. Then $D\le4B^4+4B^2+1\le9B^4$, so $U=3B^2$ works for $\sqrt D$. The resulting $c=a^2+b^2+\sqrt D$ is at most $5B^2$, so $U=5B^2$ works for $\sqrt{c^2-1}$ once its required nonnegativity is established by the complement supplier. All these descriptor-construction loops therefore use $O(1+H)$ operations/comparisons per radical. They do not require roots to be well separated, and they do not approximate the input algebraic coordinates.

Write $N(B,C)=B^2+(1-x^2)C^2$. Expanding the pair multiplication rule gives $N((B,C)(D,E))=N(B,C)N(D,E)$. The factors $(x,0)$, $(x^2-s^2,0)$, $(\sqrt{s^2-1}x,s)$ and $(\sqrt{b^2+1}x,b)$ have norms respectively $x^2$, $(x^2-s^2)^2$, $s^2-x^2$ and $x^2+b^2$. For a quadruple put $A=a^2+b^2$. The radicand in step 3.3 satisfies $D=(A-1)^2+4b^2$, so $b>0$ gives $c=A+\sqrt D>1$. Also $c^2-2Ac-1=-2(a^2-b^2)$. Consequently the pair $(cx^2-A,\sqrt{c^2-1}x)$ has norm $x^4-2(a^2-b^2)x^2+A^2$, the monic polynomial with roots $\pm a\pm ib$. These identities verify the radicands and the norm factors directly. There is also no uncontrolled reciprocal scale hidden in the final $K$. The squared norms of the unscaled elementary factors are, respectively, $x^2$, $(x^2-s^2)^2$, $s^2-x^2$, $x^2+b^2$, and the monic degree-four root polynomial for a quadruple. For the quadruple, the $x^4$ coefficient is $c^2-(c^2-1)=1$. Thus the product norm $G$ has leading coefficient $+1$ or $-1$. If $R$ is nonconstant, its leading coefficient is minus the square of the leading coefficient of the rounded target, and $\kappa>0$ implies $\kappa=|\operatorname{lc}(R)|$. Hence $\kappa\le2^H$, and one can compute the rational upper bound $U=1+|\operatorname{lc}(R)|\le2^{H+1}$ to construct $K=\sqrt\kappa$; alternatively use the absolute value of the target leading coefficient directly. If $R$ is a nonzero constant, $0<R\le1$ and $U=1$ suffices. The unit-norm parity correction does not alter $G$ or this bound. These estimates count only the quadratic descriptors after the exact root list has already been obtained; they supply no bound for generating that root list.

At a nonconstant peel, comparison of the highest coefficients in $PP^*+(1-x^2)QQ^*=1$ forces $\deg Q=\ell-1$ and $|a_\ell|^2=|b_{\ell-1}|^2$, so $b_{\ell-1}\ne0$ and $r=a_\ell/b_{\ell-1}$ is unit. For either unit square root $\omega^2=r$, the leading terms in $P'$ and $Q'$ below are $\overline\omega a_\ell-\omega b_{\ell-1}=0$ and $\omega b_{\ell-1}-\overline\omega a_\ell=0$; parity lowers the resulting degree bounds by one. Direct expansion preserves the admissibility norm identity. The selected root therefore implements the same exact cancellation used for [F2]. Computing it, selecting the unit root above with its counted tower descriptor, and conjugating the root are $O(1)$ charged operations/comparisons. The simultaneous coefficient-array updates $P'=\overline\omega\,xP+\omega(1-x^2)Q$, $Q'=\omega xQ-\overline\omega P$ take $O(n+1)$ field operations at nominal degree $n$. Degree/parity scans take $O(n+1)$ exact comparisons; there are at most $d$ peels. Thus the peel itself takes $O((d+1)^2)$ field operations/comparisons, including the $O(d)$ quadratic-root descriptor constructions. If every full polynomial coefficient identity is recomputed naively after every peel, budget $O((d+1)^3)$ field operations instead; this remains polynomial. Padding and multiplication by the fixed eighth roots of unity use $O(d+1)$ additional operations and at most one fixed $\sqrt2$ descriptor construction with $U=2$. The base constant is already a unit algebraic scalar and needs no Arg oracle.

There are at most $2d$ roots counting multiplicity and therefore $O(d+1)$ elementary complement factors and quadratic descriptors. Schoolbook polynomial-array pair multiplication and final coefficient-identity checks use $O((d+1)^3)$ field operations in total; root classification and symmetry checks use $O((d+1)^2)$ exact comparisons. Each descriptor writes a degree-two equation whose coefficients reference existing nodes, and an isolator of $O(H+1)$ rational bits from its known bounded endpoint. Every field operation writes one referenced node rather than expanding prior expressions. Thus all certificate equations and operation lists have polynomially many nodes, indices and bits in $d,H$; the supplied root descriptors are referenced. These are arithmetic/descriptor costs, and make no claim about implementing the ideal equality/order tests or field operations.

citations.quote:
Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Write $T^{\dagger}$ for the adjoint $T^*$ characterized by [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]. Fix integers $m,n\ge1$, $a\ge0$, and $d\ge\max(m,n)$. On each coordinate space $\mathbb C^r$ use $\langle x,y\rangle_{\rm root}:=\sum_{q=1}^r x_q\overline{y_q}$, linear in the first argument. Put the ancilla register before the system register in every tensor product, and let $e_0=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ be the first standard basis vector in $\mathbb C^{2^a}$. For $A:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^m$, choose as part of the data padding maps $E_{\rm in}:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^d$ and $E_{\rm out}:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^d$ satisfying $E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}E_{\rm in}=I_n$ and $E_{\rm out}^{\dagger}E_{\rm out}=I_m$. The default padding sends a coordinate vector to the same coordinates followed by zeros. Set $\widehat A:=E_{\rm out}AE_{\rm in}^{\dagger}:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^d$.

Let $J_a:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^{2^a}\otimes\mathbb C^d$ be $J_ax=e_0\otimes x$, where $e_0$ is the all-zero computational basis vector, and let $\Pi_a:=J_aJ_a^{\dagger}$. For a unitary $U$ on $\mathbb C^{2^a}\otimes\mathbb C^d$, its **projected block** is the endomorphism $B_U:=J_a^{\dagger}UJ_a$ of $\mathbb C^d$. It is not asserted to be unitary.

For $\alpha>0$ and $\varepsilon\ge0$, the tuple $(U,a,\alpha,\varepsilon,d,E_{\rm in},E_{\rm out})$ is an **$(\alpha,a,\varepsilon)$ block encoding of $A$** when $\alpha\ge\|A\|_{\rm op}$ and $\|B_U-\widehat A/\alpha\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon$. The exact case is $\varepsilon=0$. For square $A$, take $m=n=d$ and both embeddings equal to the identity. For rectangular $A$, the dimensions and embeddings remain part of the encoding data.

The equivalent projector notation identifies $B_U$ with the restriction of $\Pi_aU\Pi_a$ to $\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_a)$, transported to $\mathbb C^d$ by $J_a$; it does not regard $\Pi_aU\Pi_a$ as a unitary.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: If $H_R=0$, then $A$ is the zero map and its operator norm is zero by [F4]. Otherwise take any unit $x\in H_R$. The decomposition $Ux=\Pi_LUx+(I-\Pi_L)Ux$ has orthogonal terms by [F1], so [F2] gives $\|\Pi_LUx\|^2\le\|Ux\|^2$. By [F3], $\|Ux\|=1$, hence $\|Ax\|\le1$. Taking the maximum over unit $x$ proves $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

In the square block-encoding case, $J_a$ is the isometric identification of the system with $H_R=H_L=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_a)$. The definition of the projected block in [F7] is exactly $J_a^*UJ_a$, and the exact case identifies it with the normalized target. Thus this is the stated special case.

Apply [F5] to the finite-dimensional map $A:H_R\to H_L$. For each positive singular pair, $Av_j=\sigma_j u_j$ and $\|v_j\|=\|u_j\|=1$, so [F4] and step 1.1 give $\sigma_j=\|Av_j\|\le1$. The rank-one terms in the SVD sum have the coordinate action fixed by [F6]. When $r=0$, the positive singular list and the displayed sum are empty; the kernel bases still exist by [F5].

For each $k\le r$ and every $x\in H_R$, the SVD formula, root-linear-first rank-one action [F6], and orthonormality of the $u_j$ give $\langle Ax,u_k\rangle=\sigma_k\langle x,v_k\rangle$; for $k>r$ the same pairing is zero. By [F8]–[F9], $\langle Ax,u_k\rangle=\langle x,A^*u_k\rangle$, so positive definiteness [F11] gives $A^*u_k=\sigma_kv_k$ for $k\le r$ and $A^*u_k=0$ for $k>r$. The SVD formula also gives $Av_k=\sigma_ku_k$ for $k\le r$ and $Av_k=0$ for $k>r$. Since each singular list is a basis, expanding an arbitrary vector in those bases shows that $\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n\}$ and $\ker A^*=\operatorname{span}\{u_{r+1},\ldots,u_m\}$: the positive-index coefficients must vanish because the corresponding singular values are positive and the other basis is orthonormal. The argument includes empty bases and sums.

By [F1], orthogonal decomposition gives $\langle \Pi_LUx,y\rangle=\langle Ux,y\rangle$ and $\langle x,\Pi_RU^*y\rangle=\langle x,U^*y\rangle$ for $x\in H_R$ and $y\in H_L$. The adjoint rule [F8] for $U$ therefore gives $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,\Pi_RU^*y\rangle$. Thus $y\mapsto\Pi_RU^*y$ is an adjoint of $A$, and uniqueness [F9] yields $A^*=\Pi_RU^*|_{H_L}$. Also, [F10] applies to the unitary $U$ and shows that $U^*=U^{-1}$ is unitary.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $U:H\to H$ be unitary, and let $\Pi_R,\Pi_L:H\to H$ be orthogonal projections. Write $H_R=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_R)$ and $H_L=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_L)$. The **projected-unitary encoding** (PUE) of this data is the linear map

$$A:H_R\to H_L,\qquad Ax=\Pi_L Ux.$$

Equivalently, its ambient-space compression is $\Pi_LU\Pi_R$, restricted to $H_R$ and regarded as taking values in $H_L$. The map $A$ is a contraction: $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

Put $n=\dim H_R$, $m=\dim H_L$, and $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. A singular-value decomposition consists of orthonormal bases $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $H_R$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $H_L$, and positive singular values $1\ge\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, such that

$$A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

derivations.claim: For each distinct positive singular value $\sigma$, define $E_\sigma=\ker(A^*A-\sigma^2I)$ in $H_R$ and $F_\sigma=\ker(AA^*-\sigma^2I)$ in $H_L$. The adjoint rule [F4] and adjoint algebra [F5] make $A^*A$ and $AA^*$ self-adjoint, and [F2]–[F3] identify these eigenspaces with the right and left singular subspaces. If $v\in E_\sigma$, then $Av\in F_\sigma$ because $AA^*Av=A(A^*Av)=\sigma^2Av$. Also [F4] gives $\|Av\|^2=\langle v,A^*Av\rangle=\sigma^2\|v\|^2$. Thus $J_\sigma:=A/\sigma$ is an isometry from $E_\sigma$ into $F_\sigma$. For $y\in F_\sigma$, [F5] gives $A^*y\in E_\sigma$, and $J_\sigma(A^*y/\sigma)=y$; hence $J_\sigma$ maps $E_\sigma$ onto $F_\sigma$.

Group the positive singular terms in the odd transform by their common value $\sigma$. In any orthonormal basis $(v_j)$ of $E_\sigma$, the paired left vectors are $u_j=J_\sigma v_j$, so $\sum_{j:\sigma_j=\sigma}|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|=J_\sigma\Pi_{E_\sigma}$, where $\Pi_{E_\sigma}$ is the unique projection from [F6]. The grouped term is therefore $p(\sigma)J_\sigma\Pi_{E_\sigma}$, independent of the basis.

For the even right transform, grouping by positive singular value gives $p(\sigma)\Pi_{E_\sigma}$, and the zero-singular part is $p(0)\Pi_{\ker A}$; both are canonical projections. For the even left transform the corresponding terms are $p(\sigma)\Pi_{F_\sigma}$ and $p(0)\Pi_{\ker A^*}$. The zero right and left singular vectors may be chosen independently, but the even definitions use only these unique subspace projections, while the odd definition omits zero singular pairs. Thus all three transforms are independent of the SVD choices.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. Fix the two signs

$$R_\Pi:=2\Pi-I,\qquad S_\Pi:=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi.$$

Thus $R_\Pi$ acts as $+I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and $-I$ on $\ker\Pi$; $S_\Pi$ reverses those signs. They are not interchangeable inside a controlled block. For a unit vector $\psi$, the rank-one reflection is $R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I$ with the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An access model counts a direct reflection as one primitive call only when that call is explicitly declared. Controlled reflection access is a separate declaration. If $|0\rangle$ is a specified unit input in the same space $H$, the state is prepared as $\psi=U|0\rangle$ for a declared unitary $U$, and a reflection is implemented by conjugating $R_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I$, the construction is $UR_0U^\dagger$ and its cost must include the calls to $U$, $R_0$, and $U^\dagger$. A state vector or matrix description alone implies neither an efficient reflection nor inverse access.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

derivations.claim: Define the ancilla-controlled bit flip $X_\Pi:=H_aC(S_\Pi)H_a$, where $H_a=H\otimes I_H$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$, $S_\Pi=-I$, so [L2] makes $C(S_\Pi)$ act as $Z_a$ on the ancilla; conjugating by $H_a$ gives $X_a$. On $\ker\Pi$, $S_\Pi=I$, so $C(S_\Pi)$ acts as $I$ and $X_\Pi$ is the identity. Thus $X_\Pi$ flips the ancilla exactly on the range of $\Pi$. By [L3], each use of $C(S_\Pi)$ is one supplied call to $C(R_\Pi)$ plus one ancilla $Z_a$ gate.

Apply $X_\Pi$, then $R_z(2\phi)=e^{-i\phi Z_a}$, then $X_\Pi$ again. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$, the ancilla operation is $X_a e^{-i\phi Z_a}X_a=e^{i\phi Z_a}$; on $\ker\Pi$ it is $e^{-i\phi Z_a}$. Acting on $|0\rangle$, these give phases $e^{i\phi}$ and $e^{-i\phi}$, respectively, and both branches return the ancilla to $|0\rangle$. The induced system operation is therefore $e^{i\phi}(\Pi)+e^{-i\phi}(I-\Pi)=e^{i\phi(2\Pi-I)}$.

The construction uses two occurrences of $X_\Pi$, hence two controlled-reflection calls by step 1.1, and one variable $R_z(2\phi)$ rotation. Its Hadamard and ancilla-$Z$ gates have constant count per phase slot. Applying the same construction with $\Pi_R$ or $\Pi_L$ gives the two projector-phase operations used by the QSVT sequence; no direct or controlled reflection cost is inferred from the matrix description alone.

Let $c$ be an external branch qubit. Replace the middle rotation by its controlled version, leaving both occurrences of $X_\Pi$ unchanged. On branch $c=1$, step 2.1 gives $e^{i\phi R_\Pi}$. On branch $c=0$, the middle operation is identity and the two adjacent $X_\Pi$ operations cancel because $X_\Pi^2=I$; the system operation is identity. Thus this is the controlled projector phase. Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

derivations.claim: The loop in [F1] executes once for each integer $j=d-1,\ldots,0$, hence it makes exactly $d$ signal calls. The side starts at $R$, so the first call is $U$ and directions alternate; therefore the counts are $\lceil d/2\rceil$ forward calls and $\lfloor d/2\rfloor$ inverse calls. If $d=0$, the loop is empty.

For a controlled sequence against identity, control each phase rotation. When the outer control is zero, every phase is the identity, so the remaining alternating signal calls cancel in adjacent $UU^*$ or $U^*U$ pairs. If $d$ is even all signal calls pair and cancel. If $d$ is odd, leave one signal call controlled and pair all others; on the zero branch that controlled call is also identity, while the one branch executes the original sequence. Thus this variant requires zero extra controlled signal calls for even $d$ and one for odd $d$, whose availability is explicit by [F3].

For a branch selector between $\Phi$ and $-\Phi$, let control value $0$ select $\Phi$ and value $1$ select $-\Phi$. At a slot with phase $\phi$ about $\Pi$, use the clean-ancilla toggle $X_\Pi$ from step 1.1 of [F2], then unconditional $R_z(2\phi)$, then a control-one-controlled $R_z(-4\phi)$, and then $X_\Pi$ again. The middle rotation is $R_z(2\phi)$ in branch $0$ and $R_z(-2\phi)$ in branch $1$; because $X_\Pi$ flips the ancilla on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and leaves it unchanged on $\ker\Pi$, the system phases are respectively $e^{i\phi(2\Pi-I)}$ and $e^{-i\phi(2\Pi-I)}$. The same unconditioned signal call occurs between each pair of phase slots, so the signal list is shared and this selector adds no controlled signal query.

There is one phase at the initial $R$ side and one after each of the $d$ signal calls, for $d+1$ slots. Their sides alternate beginning at $R$, giving $\lceil(d+1)/2\rceil$ right-projector slots and $\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$ left-projector slots.

Apply [F2] to each slot counted in step 2.2. The total controlled-reflection calls are $2\lceil(d+1)/2\rceil$ for $\Pi_R$ and $2\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$ for $\Pi_L$, unchanged for the paired selector. A single unconditioned sequence has $d+1$ variable rotations; the $\Phi/-\Phi$ selector instead uses $d+1$ unconditional rotations $R_z(2\phi_j)$ and $d+1$ separately charged branch-controlled rotations $R_z(-4\phi_j)$, with constant one-qubit overhead per slot.

The counts above describe only the listed operations. By [F4], the cost of supplied $U$, $U^*$, controlled calls, phase gates, ancilla wires, classical phase generation, and finite-gate compilation are recorded in their applicable separate coordinates; none is inferred from the matrix $A$ alone.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $U:H\to H$ be unitary, and let $\Pi_R,\Pi_L:H\to H$ be orthogonal projections. Write $H_R=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_R)$ and $H_L=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_L)$. The **projected-unitary encoding** (PUE) of this data is the linear map

$$A:H_R\to H_L,\qquad Ax=\Pi_L Ux.$$

Equivalently, its ambient-space compression is $\Pi_LU\Pi_R$, restricted to $H_R$ and regarded as taking values in $H_L$. The map $A$ is a contraction: $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

Put $n=\dim H_R$, $m=\dim H_L$, and $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. A singular-value decomposition consists of orthonormal bases $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $H_R$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $H_L$, and positive singular values $1\ge\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, such that

$$A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

The remaining right basis vectors span $\ker A$ and the remaining left basis vectors span $\ker A^*$. Empty bases and sums are allowed when a dimension or the rank is zero. The pairing in each rank-one map is the root-linear-first Dirac conversion of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An exact square block encoding is a special case: identify the system with the all-zero ancilla subspace and take $\Pi_L=\Pi_R$ equal to that subspace. Under the injection $J_a$ of [[def-qa-22-block-encoding]], the compression is $J_a^*UJ_a$; an exact $(\alpha,a,0)$ block encoding has compressed block $A/\alpha$.

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular pairs $(\sigma_j,v_j,u_j)$. For every $0<\sigma_j<1$, set

$$w_j=\frac{(I-\Pi_R)U^*u_j}{\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}},\qquad \widetilde w_j=\frac{(I-\Pi_L)Uv_j}{\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}}.$$

The vectors $w_j$ form an orthonormal family in $\ker\Pi_R$ and the vectors $\widetilde w_j$ form an orthonormal family in $\ker\Pi_L$. In the input basis $(v_j,w_j)$ and output basis $(u_j,\widetilde w_j)$,

$$U\big|_{\operatorname{span}(v_j,w_j)}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_j&\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}\\\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}&-\sigma_j\end{pmatrix}.$$

For $\sigma_j=1$, $Uv_j=u_j$ and the complementary vector is absent. A right zero-singular vector $v\in\ker A\cap H_R$ satisfies $Uv\in\ker\Pi_L$; a left zero-singular vector $u\in\ker A^*\cap H_L$ satisfies $U^*u\in\ker\Pi_R$. Let $M_R$ be the orthogonal sum of all positive-singular input planes or lines, $\ker A$, and $U^*(\ker A^*)$; let $M_L$ be the corresponding sum of positive-singular output planes or lines, $U(\ker A)$, and $\ker A^*$. Then $U(M_R)=M_L$. The residual ambient subspaces $M_R^\perp$ and $M_L^\perp$ lie in $\ker\Pi_R$ and $\ker\Pi_L$, and $U(M_R^\perp)=M_L^\perp$. Thus each named block is invariant under its corresponding projector, with no implicit pairing of the two kernels.

Let $x\in[-1,1]$, put $s(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ using the nonnegative real square root, and define the Hermitian-reflection signal matrix
$$W_R(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&s(x)\\s(x)&-x\end{pmatrix}.$$
For each real $\phi$, define $Z(\phi)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\phi},e^{-i\phi})$. For an integer $d\ge0$ and real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$, the length-$d$ QSP sequence is the ordered matrix product
$$U_\Phi(x)=Z(\phi_0)\prod_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(W_R(x)Z(\phi_j)\bigr),$$
where the product is written left to right in increasing $j$ and matrix multiplication acts right to left. For $d=0$ this is $Z(\phi_0)$. This definition fixes the sign of the off-diagonal signal entry, both endpoint phases, and the product order.

The phases are in matrix order: when the factors are applied as chronological circuit layers, the rightmost factor acts first, in accordance with [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]]. In the ordered signal basis, if both coordinates are nonzero, applying $Z(\phi)$ multiplies the ratio of the second coordinate to the first by $e^{-2i\phi}$; if either coordinate is zero, that relative phase is undefined, while the displayed matrix action remains defined. This is the relative phase convention fixed by [[def-qc-relative-phase]].

For every $x\in[-1,1]$ and phase list $\Phi$ of length $d+1$, $U_\Phi(x)$ is unitary with determinant $(-1)^d$. There are polynomials $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix},$$
where $P=0$ or $\deg P\le d$ with parity $d$, $Q=0$ or $\deg Q\le d-1$ with parity $d-1$, and $PP^*+(1-x^2)QQ^*=1$ as a formal polynomial identity.

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular-value decomposition $A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|$. Let $p:[-1,1]\to\mathbb C$ be a scalar function.

If $p$ is **odd**, define the odd singular-value transform by

$$p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A):H_R\to H_L,\qquad p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}p(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

If $p$ is **even**, define its right-space transform by

$$p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{R}(A):H_R\to H_R,\qquad p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{R}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}p(\sigma_j)|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|+p(0)\Pi_{\ker A},$$

where $\Pi_{\ker A}$ is the orthogonal projection in $H_R$ onto $\ker A$. The left-space version is

$$p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{L}(A):H_L\to H_L,\qquad p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{L}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}p(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|+p(0)\Pi_{\ker A^*}.$$

The odd transform annihilates the right kernel because oddness gives $p(0)=0$; the even transforms use the canonical kernel projections. The resulting operators are independent of the chosen SVD by [[lem-qa-24-singular-transform-basis-independence]].

For a finite-dimensional PUE map $A:H_R\to H_L$, the odd singular-value transform and both even singular-value transforms of [[def-qa-24-singular-value-transform]] are independent of the chosen singular-vector bases. On a positive singular-value subspace, $A/\sigma$ canonically pairs the right and left eigenspaces; on repeated singular values the transform is scalar on the whole corresponding subspace. The even transforms use the canonical orthogonal projection onto $\ker A$ or $\ker A^*$ with coefficient $p(0)$; the odd transform has no zero-singular cross term.

Let $d\ge0$ and let $p\in\mathbb R[x]$ have degree at most $d$, parity $d\bmod2$, and $|p(x)|\le1$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$. Then there is a QSP-admissible pair $P,Q$ of degree bound $d$ such that $\operatorname{Re}P(x)=p(x)$ on $[-1,1]$. In fact, the completion is exact, so for every $\delta>0$ it also satisfies $|\operatorname{Re}P(x)-p(x)|\le\delta$.

For every integer $d\ge0$, a pair $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ is QSP-admissible of degree bound $d$ if and only if there is a real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix}\quad (x\in[-1,1]).$$
The converse is constructive: a leading-coefficient phase peel reduces the degree at each nonconstant stage. The polynomial identity, determinant signs, product order, and phase convention are exactly those in [[def-qa-23-qsp-admissible-polynomial-pair]] and [[def-qa-23-qsp-signal-sequence]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

Put $s=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, $W_R=\begin{pmatrix}x&s\\s&-x\end{pmatrix}$, $W_S=\begin{pmatrix}x&is\\is&x\end{pmatrix}$, and $C=Z(\pi/4)$. Then
$$CW_RC=iW_S^\dagger,\qquad W_S^\dagger=Z(\pi/2)W_SZ(-\pi/2).$$
For $d\ge1$, define $U_S(\Psi)=Z(\psi_0)\prod_{j=1}^d(W_SZ(\psi_j))$. If $\Psi$ is the SU(2)-convention phase list with $\psi_0=\phi_0+\pi/4$, $\psi_j=\phi_j-\pi/2$ for $1\le j<d$, and $\psi_d=\phi_d-3\pi/4$, then
$$U_R(\Phi)=i^dU_S(\Psi).$$
The affine phase-list map is invertible. The scalar $i^d$ is part of the identity: in a control-first block $\operatorname{diag}(I,U)$ it acts on the active control branch and cannot be discarded as a global phase.

Let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on a finite-dimensional space $H$, with reflection $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi$. Suppose the control-first call $C(R_\Pi)$ is explicitly supplied, together with an ancilla initialized in $|0\rangle$ and exact one-qubit $H$ and $R_z$ gates. Then the unitary $e^{i\phi R_\Pi}$ is implemented exactly by two controlled-reflection calls and one variable phase rotation, with a constant number of additional one-qubit gates, and the ancilla is returned to $|0\rangle$. If an external branch qubit is present and a branch-controlled $R_z(2\phi)$ is supplied, controlling only that rotation implements the controlled projector phase; the two controlled-reflection calls remain unconditional with respect to the external branch. In QSVT the construction is applied separately to $\Pi_R$ and $\Pi_L$; each projector-phase slot uses two controlled calls to the corresponding reflection. The access and gate costs are charged separately.

derivations.claim: Fix $0<\sigma_j<1$. In the input basis $(v_j,w_j)$ and output basis $(u_j,\widetilde w_j)$, [F2] says that $U$ is $W_R(\sigma_j)$, and $U^*$ has the same matrix because it is real symmetric. The right-projector phase is $Z(\phi)$ on the input basis since $2\Pi_R-I$ has eigenvalues $+1,-1$ there; the left-projector phase is the same $Z(\phi)$ on the output basis. Thus the alternating sequence multiplies in the fixed order $Z(\phi_0)W_R(\sigma_j)Z(\phi_1)\cdots W_R(\sigma_j)Z(\phi_d)=U_\Phi(\sigma_j)$, whose upper-left entry is $P_\Phi(\sigma_j)$ by [F3]–[F4].

If $\sigma_j=1$, [F2] gives $Uv_j=u_j$ and the complementary component is zero; the surviving one-dimensional action is the first-coordinate action of $U_\Phi(1)$, namely $P_\Phi(1)$. For $\sigma_j=0$, $Uv_j$ lies in $\ker\Pi_L$ and $U^*(Uv_j)=v_j$. The alternating calls therefore swap this right-kernel vector and its left-complement image exactly as $W_R(0)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ does. If $d$ is odd the final vector lies in $\ker\Pi_L$ and the left compression is zero, equal to $P_\Phi(0)$ because [F4] makes $P_\Phi$ odd. If $d$ is even it returns to $v_j$ with coefficient $P_\Phi(0)$, the prescribed even-kernel term in [F5]. Left-kernel inputs and the residual complement contribute nothing to the stated compression by [F2].

The positive singular planes, the $\sigma=1$ lines, the right zero-kernel lines, and the residual blocks are orthogonal and exhaust the relevant projected spaces by [F2]. Summing the scalar coefficients from steps 1.1–1.2 therefore gives the displayed odd and even compressed-block formulas.

For real $p$ under the stated degree, parity, and interval bounds, [F7] gives an admissible pair $P,Q$ with $\operatorname{Re}P=p$, and [F8] supplies its exact phase list $\Phi$. At each slot with phase $\phi_j$ about $\Pi$, use the clean-ancilla toggle $X_\Pi$ from [F11], then apply unconditional $R_z(2\phi_j)$, then a control-one-controlled $R_z(-4\phi_j)$, and then $X_\Pi$ again. In control branch $0$ the middle rotation is $R_z(2\phi_j)$; in branch $1$ it is $R_z(-2\phi_j)$. Since $X_\Pi$ places the ancilla in $|1\rangle$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and in $|0\rangle$ on $\ker\Pi$, the induced system phases are respectively $e^{i\phi_j(2\Pi-I)}$ and $e^{-i\phi_j(2\Pi-I)}$, and the ancilla returns to $|0\rangle$. The same unconditioned signal calls therefore give full branch operators $U_\Phi$ and $U_{-\Phi}$. Because $W_R(x)$ is real and $Z(-\phi)=\overline{Z(\phi)}$, entrywise conjugation gives $U_{-\Phi}(x)=\overline{U_\Phi(x)}$, and projection of the control from $|+\rangle$ to $|+\rangle$ has block $\frac12(U_\Phi+U_{-\Phi})$. By step 2.1, its coefficient on each positive singular pair is $\frac12(P_\Phi(\sigma_j)+\overline{P_\Phi(\sigma_j)})=\operatorname{Re}P_\Phi(\sigma_j)=p(\sigma_j)$; for an even transform the same identity gives $p(0)$ on $\ker A$. Thus the compressed block is $p^{\mathrm{SV}}(A)$. If the supplied scalar approximation satisfies $\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|\operatorname{Re}P_\Phi(x)-p(x)|\le\eta$, each singular coefficient changes by at most $\eta$, so orthonormality gives operator-norm error at most $\eta$. The proof stays in the reflected convention; [F10]'s scalar is not discarded if a circuit is translated to the SU(2) convention.

$$A:H_R\to H_L,\qquad Ax=\Pi_L Ux.$$

Equivalently, its ambient-space compression is $\Pi_LU\Pi_R$, restricted to $H_R$ and regarded as taking values in $H_L$. The map $A$ is a contraction: $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

Put $n=\dim H_R$, $m=\dim H_L$, and $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. A singular-value decomposition consists of orthonormal bases $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $H_R$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $H_L$, and positive singular values $1\ge\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, such that

$$A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

The remaining right basis vectors span $\ker A$ and the remaining left basis vectors span $\ker A^*$. Empty bases and sums are allowed when a dimension or the rank is zero. The pairing in each rank-one map is the root-linear-first Dirac conversion of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An exact square block encoding is a special case: identify the system with the all-zero ancilla subspace and take $\Pi_L=\Pi_R$ equal to that subspace. Under the injection $J_a$ of [[def-qa-22-block-encoding]], the compression is $J_a^*UJ_a$; an exact $(\alpha,a,0)$ block encoding has compressed block $A/\alpha$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular pairs $(\sigma_j,v_j,u_j)$, and let $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ be the exact phase list in [[alg-qa-24-qsvt]]. Let $P_\Phi$ be the upper-left scalar polynomial of its QSP signal sequence. On every positive two-dimensional singular plane from [[lem-qa-24-pue-svd-invariant-subspaces]], the QSVT sequence is exactly $U_\Phi(\sigma_j)$. Consequently, if $d$ is odd,

$$\Pi_LU_\Phi\Pi_R\big|_{H_R}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}P_\Phi(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|=\bigl(P_\Phi\bigr)^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A),$$

and if $d$ is even,

$$\Pi_RU_\Phi\Pi_R\big|_{H_R}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}P_\Phi(\sigma_j)|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|+P_\Phi(0)\Pi_{\ker A}=\bigl(P_\Phi\bigr)^{\mathrm{SV}}_R(A).$$

The formulas include singular values $0$ and $1$, repeated singular values, unmatched left and right kernels, and zero-dimensional singular spaces. If $p\in\mathbb R[x]$ is zero or has degree at most $d$, has parity $d\bmod2$, and satisfies $|p(x)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, the exact completion and phase-factorization suppliers give a phase list with $\operatorname{Re}P_\Phi=p$. The coherent $\Phi$/$-\Phi$ branch then has compressed block $p^{\mathrm{SV}}(A)$; for a supplied uniform scalar error $\eta$, its block differs from $p^{\mathrm{SV}}(A)$ by at most $\eta$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$
