A **finite expectation-estimation task** consists of a nonempty finite set $X$, a probability law $p:X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in X}p_x=1$, and an exactly encoded real-valued function $g:X\to[a,b]$, where $a\le b$ are finite rationals. Its target is
$$\mu:=\mathbb E_p[g]=\sum_{x\in X}p_xg(x).$$

For rational parameters $\varepsilon>0$ and $0<\delta<1$, an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ estimator is a randomized or quantum procedure that outputs a real number $\widetilde\mu$ satisfying
$$\Pr\bigl(|\widetilde\mu-\mu|\le\varepsilon\bigr)\ge1-\delta.$$
The task specifies the target law and success event only. A particular procedure must state how it accesses samples or coherent state preparation and must charge those resources separately.

A value that approximates an underlying real-valued observable to error $\tau$ defines a different task with target $\mathbb E_p[\widetilde g]$; any claim about $\mathbb E_p[g]$ must add the encoding error $\tau$ to its error budget.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set with probability law $p_x\ge0$, $\sum_{x\in X}p_x=1$, and let the value register contain an exact finite encoding of a real function $g:X\to[a,b]$, where $a\le b$ are finite rationals. A **coherent finite sampler** for $(X,p,g)$ is an explicitly supplied finite-dimensional unitary $V$ on ordered sample, value, and work registers such that
$$V|0\rangle=\sum_{x\in X}\sqrt{p_x}\,|x\rangle|g(x)\rangle|w_x\rangle,$$
where the sample labels $|x\rangle$ are distinct computational-basis vectors and each work state $|w_x\rangle$ has norm one. Zero-probability labels may occur and need no special branch. The registers and their order use [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] and [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]; each output is a pure state in the sense of [[def-qc-pure-state-and-ray]]. The separate item [[lem-qa-29-coherent-sampler-outcome-law]] verifies the induced measurement law.

The access contract lists the actual circuits or oracle interfaces for $V$, $V^\dagger$, controlled $V$ and controlled $V^\dagger$, value decoding, reversible arithmetic, any coherent predicate and controlled rotation, and the reflections used by the chosen estimator. Their availability is explicit under [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]] and [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]]. A forward unitary alone does not grant an inverse or a controlled call.

The resource record follows [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]: charge state preparation, inverse and controlled access, data loading, value comparison and arithmetic, controlled-rotation synthesis and precision, good-state and initial-state reflections, gates, width, ancillas, and classical postprocessing separately. The state-preparation circuit and its costs are inputs; a state description is not a free QRAM or preparation oracle.

For a coherent sampler $V$ with output state $|\psi\rangle=\sum_x\sqrt{p_x}|x\rangle|g(x)\rangle|w_x\rangle$ as in [[def-qa-29-coherent-sampler]], projective measurement of the sample register returns $x$ with probability $p_x$. If the value register is measured too, the pair $(x,g(x))$ has the same probability. The work register is not required to be measured, and work states for different labels need not be orthogonal.

**Input.** A finite expectation-estimation task with an exact encoded observable $g:X\to[a,b]$, a coherent sampler $V$ for its law, rational target $\varepsilon>0$, and rational failure probability $0<\delta<1$. For $a<b$, require $\varepsilon\le b-a$. The supplied access model must include every forward, inverse, controlled, value, predicate, and reflection operation that the chosen QA13 amplitude-estimation circuit invokes.

If $a=b$, return $a$. Otherwise compute the exact affine value
$$q(x)=\frac{g(x)-a}{b-a}\in[0,1].$$
Append a good flag to the coherent sampler. Reversibly compute $q(x)$ in the declared value workspace, apply the supplied one-qubit rotation
$$|0\rangle\longmapsto\sqrt{1-q(x)}|0\rangle+\sqrt{q(x)}|1\rangle$$
controlled by the sample/value registers, and uncompute all scratch used only for $q$. Let $A_q$ denote the resulting state-preparation unitary, including $V$ and the controlled rotation; let $P_{\rm good}$ project onto flag $|1\rangle$. Run the unchanged median-confidence estimator [[alg-qa-13-median-confidence-estimation]] on $(A_q,P_{\rm good})$ with amplitude tolerance $\eta=\varepsilon/(b-a)$ and failure probability $\delta$, and call its estimate $\widetilde q$. Return
$$\widetilde\mu=a+(b-a)\widetilde q.$$

For $a=b$, the exact-return branch has no quantum call. When $a<b$, the input is a costed finite circuit/oracle description. Charge each use of $A_q$, $A_q^\dagger$, controlled versions, the good and initial-state reflections, value decoding, reversible arithmetic and uncomputation, the controlled rotation and its precision, phase estimation, state preparation, gates, width, ancillas, and classical output processing according to [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. No operation is free because it is described by the law $p$ or observable $g$.

Let $g:X\to[a,b]$ be exactly encoded with $a\le b$, let $V$ be the coherent sampler of [[def-qa-29-coherent-sampler]], and let $\mu=\sum_xp_xg(x)$. If $a=b$, the algorithm [[alg-qa-29-quantum-expectation-estimation]] returns $a=\mu$ exactly. If $a<b$, then for rational $0<\varepsilon\le b-a$ and $0<\delta<1$ it returns $\widetilde\mu$ with $|\widetilde\mu-\mu|\le\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. Writing $q=(\mu-a)/(b-a)$ and $M$ for its QA13 phase-register size, the median output also obeys
$$|\widetilde\mu-\mu|\le(b-a)\left(\frac{2\pi\sqrt{q(1-q)}}{M}+\frac{\pi^2}{M^2}\right)$$
with probability at least $1-\delta$ in either declared QA13 access mode. For $a<b$, in repeated controlled-$Q$ access it uses exactly $r(M-1)$ controlled-Grover calls, where $M$ and $r$ are the current QA13 median-interface parameters. In this mode its controlled-sampler/reflection query count is $O\bigl((b-a)\varepsilon^{-1}(1+\ln(1/\delta))\bigr)$ for all $0<\delta<1$, and $O\bigl((b-a)\varepsilon^{-1}\ln(1/\delta)\bigr)$ when $0<\delta\le1/2$. If $a=b$, the algorithm returns $a$ exactly with no quantum query.

For $a<b$, in supplied controlled-power access it instead uses exactly $rm$ controlled-power queries, where $M=2^m$; sum their separately declared costs over all $r$ runs. No $M-1$ constituent-call expansion is inferred for a supplied power.

The query bound is an oracle statement. Every controlled or inverse sampler call, good-state reflection, initial-state reflection, rotation, arithmetic operation, state preparation, and classical order-statistic computation retains its separately supplied cost.

derivations.claim: Here $\mu=(1-p)\cdot0+p\cdot1=p$ by [F1] and the two-point law [F3]. The range is $[a,b]=[0,1]$, so [F4] gives $q(x)=x$.
Conditional on sample $x$, the controlled rotation places good probability $x$. Averaging over the sample law, the total good probability is $(1-p)\cdot0+p\cdot1=p=\mu$.

Thus the QA13 amplitude estimator is estimating the Bernoulli mean itself; [F5] yields additive error $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-\delta$ in either declared access mode. In repeated controlled-$Q$ access it uses $O(\varepsilon^{-1}(1+\ln(1/\delta)))$ controlled sampler/reflection rounds; in supplied controlled-power access its power queries retain their separately declared prices. The circuit costs remain those declared by the supplied sampler.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: Conjugating the diagonal sum in [F5] entry by entry and using [F2] gives $\overline{\operatorname{tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{tr}((AB)^*)$. For $n=0$, both sides are the empty sum $0$.
By [F1] and [F3], $(AB)^*=B^*A^*=BA$. Then [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}(BA)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$, so step 1.1 says $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ equals its conjugate and is real.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Let $R=P^{1/2}$ from [F2] and put $T=RQR$. Since $Q$ is nonnegative by [F1], self-adjointness of $R$ and the inner-product identity [F5] give $\langle Tx,x\rangle=\langle QRx,Rx\rangle\ge0$ for every $x$. Thus every diagonal entry $\langle Te_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal coordinate basis is nonnegative real; summing by [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}(T)\ge0$. This also holds in dimension zero because the trace is the empty sum.
Since $P=R^2$, [F3] applied to $U=R$ and $V=RQ$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)=\operatorname{tr}(R(RQ))=\operatorname{tr}((RQ)R)=\operatorname{tr}(RQR)=\operatorname{tr}(T)\ge0$ by step 1.1.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

For a finite-dimensional unitary $U$, **inverse access** is the explicitly granted operation $U^\dagger=U^{-1}$. Its availability and query or gate charge are recorded separately from forward access, including any controlled access in [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. For a chronological sequence of length $k\ge0$ that applies $U_1$ first and $U_k$ last, the total operator is $W=U_k\cdots U_1$ when $k>0$ and $W=I_H$ when $k=0$. For $k>0$, the inverse sequence applies $U_k^\dagger$ first, then $U_{k-1}^\dagger$, down to $U_1^\dagger$; for $k=0$ it is the empty sequence.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

derivations.claim: If $p=1$, the direct flag outcome is good. If $0<p<1$, put $u=\sqrt{1-p}$, $v=\sqrt p$, $z=u+iv$, and $\xi=z^2=a+i\beta$, so $a=1-2p$ and $\beta=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}$. The orthonormal vectors $|B\rangle=(I-\Pi)|\psi\rangle/u$ and $|G\rangle=\Pi|\psi\rangle/v$ give $|\psi\rangle=u|B\rangle+v|G\rangle$. In this ordered basis the reflection about $|\psi\rangle$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a&\beta\\\beta&-a\end{pmatrix}$ and $I-2\Pi=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, so one Grover iteration has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&-\beta\\\beta&a\end{pmatrix}$. It multiplies the complex coordinate $u+iv$ by $\xi$, hence after $j$ iterations the good amplitude is $\operatorname{Im}(\xi^jz)=\operatorname{Im}(z^{2j+1})$.

If $p_{\rm low}<1/2$, then $K\ge2$ and minimality of $b=\lceil\log_2K\rceil$ gives $K/2^b\ge1/2$. Conditional on $J<K$, the draw is uniform on $0,\ldots,K-1$. For $p\le1/2$, $(\operatorname{Im}w)^2=(1-\operatorname{Re}(w^2))/2$ and the finite geometric sum of $\xi^{2j+1}$ give $$\frac1K\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Im}(z^{2j+1})\bigr)^2=\frac12-\frac{\operatorname{Im}(\xi^{2K})}{4K\beta}\ge\frac12-\frac1{4K\beta}.$$ Here $\beta=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\ge\sqrt{2p}$ and $K\ge1/\sqrt{p_{\rm low}}$, so $K\beta\ge\sqrt2$ and the conditional mean success exceeds $1/8$. Multiplication by $\Pr(J<K)\ge1/2$ gives randomized-branch success at least $1/16$. For $p>1/2$ the direct flag succeeds with probability greater than $1/2$.

If $p\le1/2$, the direct-then-randomized round succeeds with probability at least $1/16$ by step 2.1; if $p>1/2$ or $p_{\rm low}\ge1/2$, its direct flag succeeds with probability at least $1/2$. Independent fresh rounds therefore fail altogether with probability at most $(15/16)^N\le\rho$ by the exact cap test. The comparison loop terminates because $(16/15)^N=(1+1/15)^N\ge1+N/15$ by the binomial theorem, so $(15/16)^N\le15/(15+N)\to0$. The same asymptotic bound holds for $N=1$, so $N=O(1+\ln(1/\rho))$. Since $K=O(p_{\rm low}^{-1/2})$, the stated call bound follows.

Every successful branch is passed through the supplied flag-only instrument, so its returned state is the normalized good projection of that branch's input and no score, label, or work register is measured. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $I_H:H\to H$ denote the identity map $x\mapsto x$. An **effect** on $H$ is an endomorphism $E$ such that both $E$ and $I_H-E$ are non-negative in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. A **finite complete positive family** is a nonempty finite list $(E_1,\ldots,E_n)$ of non-negative endomorphisms with $\sum_{a=1}^n E_a=I_H$. The next lemma proves that every member of such a family is an effect, so the family is a finite complete effect family. This is algebraic data only; it does not assert a measurement law.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$
If $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are positive semidefinite, then $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)\ge0$ for every $n\ge0$.
For Hermitian matrices $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is real.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: Since $M=M^*$, $MM^*=M^2=M^*M$, so [F1] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $Me_k=\lambda_ke_k$. For each unit $e_k$, [F2] and [F3] give $\lambda_k=\langle Me_k,e_k\rangle=\langle e_k,Me_k\rangle=\overline{\lambda_k}$, so $\lambda_k$ is real; [F13] gives $|\lambda_k|=\|Me_k\|\le\|M\|\le1$. Thus the eigenvalues $(1\pm\lambda_k)/2$ of $E_\pm$ and those of $I-E_\pm$ are nonnegative, so both operators are nonnegative and each $E_\pm$ is an effect by [F4] and [F5]. Direct addition gives $E_++E_-=I$, hence the pair is a two-outcome POVM by [F6].

By [F6], the outcome weights are $p_\pm=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_\pm)$; representing endomorphisms in the orthonormal basis from step 1.1, [F9] makes them nonnegative. By [F8], [F11], [F7], and $E_++E_-=I$, their sum is $p_++p_-=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(E_++E_-))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$. Their signed mean is $p_+-p_-=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(E_+-E_-))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho M)=\operatorname{tr}(M\rho)$ by [F8] and [F12], and it is real by [F10]. Thus the outcome law has mean $\operatorname{tr}(M\rho)$.

normal, and write the spectral resolution from
[[thm-spectral-resolution-and-polynomial-spectral-projections]] as

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

where the $\lambda_j$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$ and $P_j$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$. For a function

$$f(T):=\sum_{j=1}^r f(\lambda_j)P_j.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$

Here $X\succeq0$ and $D\succeq0$ mean positive semidefinite in the finite-dimensional quadratic-form sense. By [[lem-qa-30-hermitian-product-trace-real]], all displayed trace objectives and constraints are real. Primal and dual feasibility, boundedness, attainment, trace bounds, sparsity, and normalizations such as $A_1=I,b_1=R$ are separate promises and do not follow from this definition.

The sign convention is maximize for the primal, minimize for the dual, $\le$ for primal scalar constraints, nonnegative dual multipliers, and dual slack $\sum_jy_jA_j-C\succeq0$.
For Hermitian matrices $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is real.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ and let
$x \in X$. Balls are as in [[def-metric-ball]] and open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]]; recall that a real $r$ written as a radius is always
$> 0$.

- $x$ is an **interior point** of $A$ if $B(x,r) \subseteq A$ for some $r$. The
  set of interior points is the **interior** $\operatorname{int}(A)$.
- $x$ is an **adherent point** of $A$ if $B(x,r) \cap A \ne \emptyset$ for every
  $r$. The set of adherent points is the **closure** $\overline{A}$.
- $x$ is a **limit point** (accumulation point) of $A$ if
  $B(x,r) \cap (A \setminus \{x\}) \ne \emptyset$ for every $r$. The set of limit
  points is the **derived set** $A'$.
- $x$ is an **isolated point** of $A$ if $x \in A$ and $B(x,r) \cap A = \{x\}$
  for some $r$.
- The **boundary** of $A$ is $\partial A := \overline{A} \setminus \operatorname{int}(A)$.
- $A$ is **dense** in $X$ if $\overline{A} = X$.

**The interior is open, and it is the largest open subset of $A$.** If
$x \in \operatorname{int}(A)$, fix $r$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq A$; the ball
$B(x,r)$ is itself open ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]), so every
$y \in B(x,r)$ has some $s$ with $B(y,s) \subseteq B(x,r) \subseteq A$, which
puts $y$ in $\operatorname{int}(A)$. Hence $B(x,r) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(A)$
and $\operatorname{int}(A)$ is open. It is contained in $A$, since
$x \in B(x,r) \subseteq A$ for an interior point $x$; and if $V \subseteq A$ is
open then every $v \in V$ has a ball inside $V \subseteq A$, so
$V \subseteq \operatorname{int}(A)$.

**Two descriptions of the boundary agree.** $x \in \partial A$ says that every
ball around $x$ meets $A$ and that no ball around $x$ is contained in $A$; the
second half says exactly that every ball around $x$ meets $X \setminus A$. So

$$\partial A = \{\, x \in X : B(x,r) \cap A \ne \emptyset \text{ and } B(x,r) \cap (X \setminus A) \ne \emptyset \text{ for every } r \,\},$$

from which $\partial A = \partial(X \setminus A)$ is immediate.

**Elementary containments, straight from the definitions.** $A \subseteq \overline{A}$,
because $x \in A$ lies in every $B(x,r) \cap A$; $A' \subseteq \overline{A}$,
because a ball meeting $A \setminus \{x\}$ meets $A$; and
$\operatorname{int}(A) \subseteq A \subseteq \overline{A}$. A point of $A$ is
either isolated in $A$ or a limit point of $A$, and not both, according to
whether some ball meets $A$ only in $x$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\notin C$. Then there are $a\ne0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that $\langle a,z\rangle\le b<\langle a,x\rangle$ for every $z\in C$. Thus a hyperplane strictly separates $x$ from $C$ ([[def-supporting-hyperplane-to-a-convex-set]]).

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, there is one matrix $X$, all traces are zero, and primal nonemptiness implies $b_j\ge0$ for every $j$. The primal singleton is compact with optimum $0$, while every $y\ge0$ is dual feasible and $b\cdot y\ge0$, with equality at $y=0$. The vector $q_1=m+1$, $q_j=1$ for $j\ge2$ is strictly positive and its empty matrix slack is positive definite in the quadratic-form sense, since there is no nonzero vector. Thus all conclusions hold. Henceforth assume $n\ge1$.

Regard the Hermitian matrices $H_n$ as a real space with coordinates the $n$ real diagonal entries and the real and imaginary parts above the diagonal, giving $\mathbb R^{n^2}$. Direct diagonal summation yields $\operatorname{tr}(UV)=\sum_iU_{ii}V_{ii}+2\sum_{i<j}\operatorname{Re}(U_{ij}\overline{V_{ij}})$ for Hermitian $U,V$. This is a real inner product, with norm $\|U\|_F=(\sum_{i,j}|U_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$; all finite linear maps below are continuous in these coordinates. The cone $K=\{X\in H_n:X\succeq0\}$ is convex and closed, being the intersection over $v\in\mathbb C^n$ of the closed real half-spaces $v^*Xv\ge0$.

Direct summation gives $\operatorname{tr}(Dvv^*)=v^*Dv$. For $X\in K$, write $X=\sum_i\lambda_i v_iv_i^*$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis, with $\lambda_i\ge0$. Then $\operatorname{tr}(X)=\sum_i\lambda_i$ and $\|X\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(X^2)=\sum_i\lambda_i^2$, so $\|X\|_F\le\operatorname{tr}(X)$. For $D\in K$, $\operatorname{tr}(DX)=\sum_i\lambda_i v_i^*Dv_i\ge0$. Conversely, a Hermitian $D$ pairing nonnegatively with every $X\in K$ has $v^*Dv\ge0$ by testing $X=vv^*$, so $D\in K$. Thus $K$ is self-dual for the real trace pairing. If $D$ is Hermitian with $\|D\|\le1$, [F4] gives $|v^*Dv|\le\|v\|^2$, whence $-I\preceq D\preceq I$ and $|\operatorname{tr}(DX)|\le\operatorname{tr}(X)$ for $X\in K$.

The first constraint gives $0\le\operatorname{tr}(X)\le R$ for every primal feasible $X$. That feasible set is nonempty, closed by step 1.2 and continuity of its finitely many constraints, and bounded by $\|X\|_F\le R$. Hence [F5] and [F7] give compactness and attainment of the primal maximum. Step 2.1 with $D=C$ gives $|\operatorname{tr}(CX)|\le R$, so $p^*\in[-R,R]$.

Set $q_1=m+1$ and $q_j=1$ for $j\ge2$. Step 2.1 gives $S_0:=\sum_jq_jA_j-C\succeq((m+1)-(m-1)-1)I=I$, so $q$ has strictly positive coordinates and positive definite matrix slack. For primal feasible $X$ and dual feasible $y$, self-duality gives $b\cdot y-\operatorname{tr}(CX)=\sum_jy_j(b_j-\operatorname{tr}(A_jX))+\operatorname{tr}((\sum_jy_jA_j-C)X)\ge0$. Thus $p^*\le d^*\le b\cdot q$, and the dual infimum is finite.

Put $A(X)=(\operatorname{tr}(A_jX))_j$ and $\Phi(X,s,a)=(A(X)+s,\operatorname{tr}(CX)-a)$. The image $S=\Phi(K\times\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R_+)$ is a nonempty convex cone containing $(0,0)$. To prove it closed, fix $z=(u,t)\in\overline S$ and the open neighborhood $V=\{(u',t'):|u'_j-u_j|<1\text{ for all }j,\ |t'-t|<1\}$. For every point of $S\cap V$ and every witness $(X,s,a)$, step 4.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(X)+\sum_js_j+a\le\operatorname{tr}(S_0X)+q\cdot s+a=q\cdot u'-t'\le\sum_jq_j(|u_j|+1)+|t|+1$. With $B=\sum_jq_j(|u_j|+1)+|t|+2$, all these witnesses belong to the closed bounded set $E=\{(X,s,a):X\in K,\ \operatorname{tr}(X)\le B,\ 0\le s_j\le B,\ 0\le a\le B\}$ in $\mathbb R^{n^2+m+1}$. By [F5] and [F6], $\Phi(E)$ is compact and closed, and $S\cap V\subseteq\Phi(E)\subseteq S$. Every neighborhood $U$ of $z$ has $U\cap V$ meeting $S$, so [F8] gives $z\in\overline{S\cap V}\subseteq\Phi(E)\subseteq S$. Thus $S$ is closed; no sequence of witness selections was used.

Fix $\gamma>p^*$. If $A(X)+s=b$ with $X\in K,s\ge0$, then $X$ is primal feasible and $\operatorname{tr}(CX)-a\le p^*<\gamma$ for $a\ge0$. Hence $(b,\gamma)\notin S$. By [F9] there are $w\in\mathbb R^m$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$ with $w\cdot u+\alpha t\le\beta<w\cdot b+\alpha\gamma$ for every $(u,t)\in S$. The points $(0,-a)\in S$ for all $a\ge0$ force $\alpha\ge0$. Fix one primal feasible $X_f$ and set $s_f=b-A(X_f)\ge0$; then $(b,\operatorname{tr}(CX_f))\in S$. If $\alpha=0$, that point gives the contradiction $w\cdot b\le\beta<w\cdot b$. Thus $\alpha>0$, using no strictness of $X_f$ or its scalar inequalities.

The coordinate rays $(s,0)\in S$ force $w_j\le0$. Scaling $(A(X),\operatorname{tr}(CX))\in S$ by arbitrarily large nonnegative scalars forces $\operatorname{tr}((\sum_jw_jA_j+\alpha C)X)\le0$ for every $X\in K$. Self-duality therefore makes $y=-w/\alpha\ge0$ dual feasible. Since $(0,0)\in S$, separation gives $0\le\beta<w\cdot b+\alpha\gamma$, so $b\cdot y<\gamma$. Consequently every $\gamma>p^*$ exceeds some dual feasible objective. If $d^*>p^*$, taking $\gamma=(p^*+d^*)/2$ contradicts the definition of $d^*$. Thus $d^*\le p^*$, and weak duality gives equality. Step 3.1 supplies primal attainment and the interval. An additionally promised optimal dual witness satisfies $b\cdot y^*=d^*=p^*$ and retains its promised norm bound.

citations.quote:
Supply a finite coherent sampler $V$, its inverse, an exactly ordered finite score/label encoding, and a reversible exact comparison circuit. Supply controlled versions when used, the all-zero input reflection $R_0=I-2|0\rangle\langle0|$, and the reflection $R_v=I-2\Pi_v$ for the predicate score strictly smaller than an incumbent $v$. Each preparation retains its value/label work; every named access, comparison, reflection, gate and numerical precision cost is charged. The input quantile parameter is an integer $N\ge1$, with rational confidence $0<\delta<1$.

A trial first samples an incumbent using $V$. Set its charged counter to one. To search for an improvement, use stages $j=0,1,\ldots$, with $K_j=\lceil(3/2)^j\rceil$ and worst-case stage charge $4K_j+4$ for preparation/inverse/reflection calls. Before starting a stage that would exceed $100000\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$ total charge, stop the trial and return its incumbent. Otherwise charge that amount and do the following:

1. Take one fresh direct sample. If its score is strictly smaller, replace the incumbent and restart at $j=0$.
2. If not, draw at most five independent blocks of $\lceil\log_2K_j\rceil$ unbiased bits and use the first resulting integer $q<K_j$. If every draw is out of range, treat this stage as failed and increase $j$. For $K_j=1$ the zero-bit draw is $q=0$.
3. If an index was accepted, prepare a fresh $V|0\rangle$, apply $q$ copies of $-VR_0V^\dagger R_v$, and measure the score/label. Verify the same exact comparison. On improvement replace the incumbent and restart at $j=0$; otherwise increase $j$.

Run $R$ independent trials, where $R$ is the least positive integer for which the exact rational comparison $8^{-R}\le\delta$ holds; find it by repeated rational multiplication and comparison. Return their least measured score and label. The loop is finite because $8^R\ge1+7R$ by the binomial theorem. Integer square-root ceilings use integer squaring comparisons; powers, ceilings, comparisons, and bit generation have their finite classical costs. The query theorem is [[thm-qa-30-generalized-minimum-guarantee]].

Let $V$ be a supplied finite-dimensional unitary preparation, $\Pi$ a supplied success projector, and $|0\rangle$ the declared initial vector. For every unit vector $|\phi\rangle$ on the sampler register, supply a two-outcome flag-only measurement instrument: its good outcome has probability $\|\Pi|\phi\rangle\|^2$ and returns the normalized branch $\Pi|\phi\rangle/\|\Pi|\phi\rangle\|$ when nonzero; its bad outcome returns the normalized $(I-\Pi)|\phi\rangle$ branch when nonzero. It leaves every score, label, and work register unmeasured, and its implementation and cost are declared. Let $p=\|\Pi V|0\rangle\|^2\ge p_{\rm low}>0$, where $p_{\rm low}$ is a supplied positive rational, and let $0<\rho<1$ be a supplied rational failure target. A Grover iteration is $G=(2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I)(I-2\Pi)$, where $|\psi\rangle=V|0\rangle$, using the supplied exact reflections.

Set $K=\lceil1/\sqrt{p_{\rm low}}\rceil$ and let $N$ be the least positive integer for which the exact rational comparison $(15/16)^N\le\rho$ holds. These choices are finite: $K$ is found by integer squaring comparisons, and repeated multiplication by $15/16$ terminates because its powers tend to zero. If $p_{\rm low}\ge1/2$, take at most $N$ fresh preparations and apply the flag-only instrument to each, returning the first good branch or FAIL. Otherwise set $b=\lceil\log_2K\rceil$; in each of at most $N$ rounds, prepare $V|0\rangle$ and measure only the flag. Return its good branch if present. After a bad outcome, draw $b$ fair bits to obtain $J$ uniformly in $\{0,\ldots,2^b-1\}$. If $J<K$, prepare a fresh $V|0\rangle$, apply $J$ Grover iterations, and measure only the flag; return its good branch if present. The events $J\ge K$ and a failed amplified flag count as a failed round. Return FAIL only after the cap. This procedure returns the normalized good projection $\Pi V|0\rangle/\sqrt p$ up to global phase with probability at least $1-\rho$. Its preparation, inverse, reflection, verifier, random-bit, and output costs are charged; the calls to $V,V^*$ and reflections are $O(p_{\rm low}^{-1/2}(1+\ln(1/\rho)))$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

derivations.claim: Write $p=\Pr(\text{score}<v)$ for an incumbent. By the good/bad decomposition in [F2], after $q$ Grover iterations the success probability is $|\operatorname{Im}(z^{2q+1})|^2$ for $z=\sqrt{1-p}+i\sqrt p$; the same exact two-coordinate recurrence as in that lemma applies. The flag-only good branch has the normalized good projection, whose score/label measurement is therefore distributed as the original sampler conditioned on score $<v$. Direct successes have this same conditional distribution. Thus every verified improvement has that conditional distribution, with probability zero of improvement when $p=0$. For $0<p<1$, the finite geometric sum in [F2] also gives the random-iteration average $\frac12-\operatorname{Im}(z^{4K})/(4K\beta)$, where $\beta=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ and $K$ is the current stage cap.

Suppose the sampler preserves a uniform input index $j\in[m]$ and has bad-estimate probability at most $
u$ for each $j$. In analysis only, replace its per-index output by the normalized good projection. The good subspace can depend on the true value; no implementation of that projector is assumed. For each $j$, a two-dimensional rotation takes the actual unit output to its good normalization with operator distance at most $2\sqrt
u$: its angle has cosine $\sqrt{1-p_{bad}}$, so $2\sin(\gamma/2)\le2\sqrt
u$. The direct sum of these rotations over the preserved index gives a unitary sampler replacement with the same operator bound. Inverses and controlled versions have the same bound. For at most $Q$ sampler calls, telescoping products gives output-vector error at most $2Q\sqrt
u$, and any measured event changes by at most $4Q\sqrt
u$. This also covers adaptive classical branches by retaining measurement results as orthogonal history registers.

If $p=0$, no improvement is possible and the incumbent already has strict-lower mass zero. For $0<p\le1/2$, put $\beta=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\ge\sqrt{2p}$, $t=5/(2\beta)\ge5/2$, and let $J$ be the first stage with $K_J\ge t$. For every subsequent stage, step 1.1 gives conditional Grover success at least $2/5$; five bounded bit attempts make the random part accepted with probability at least $31/32$, so stage survival is at most $49/80$. The pre-threshold charge is at most $42t$: use $\sum_{j\le J}(4K_j+4)\le12(3/2)^J+8(J+1)$, $(3/2)^J<(3/2)t$, and $J+1\le3t$. The remaining expected charge is at most $\sum_{h\ge0}(49/80)^h(6t(3/2)^h+8)=960t/13+640/31$. Together these are below $128t$, hence below $256/\sqrt p$. If $p>1/2$, the direct sample alone makes stage survival at most $1/2$, and total expected charge is at most $\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j}(4(3/2)^j+8)=32\le256/\sqrt p$. Thus every verified improvement has expected charge at most $256/\sqrt p$.

For clarity choose dyadic rank bands $[a,2a)$, $a=2^\ell/N$, truncated at one. If an incumbent lies in such a band, the next improvement has probability at least $1/2$ of having rank below $a$. Indeed, under the distribution conditioned below the incumbent, the total mass of scores whose strict lower cumulative mass is less than $a$ is at least $a$; an atom crossing that cumulative threshold is included, so discreteness cannot reduce that mass. The conditional mass is at least $a/q(v)\ge1/2$. Ranks decrease, so each band is entered at most once and has at most two visits in expectation. The expected charge until rank is below $1/N$ is therefore at most $1+512\sqrt N\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^{-\ell/2}<2048\sqrt N$. Markov's inequality at the declared finite cap $100000\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$ gives trial failure below $1/8$. Truncation is coupled to the precharged unbounded procedure: on paths whose hitting charge is within the cap, no precharge check stops the trial before its successful incumbent.

Independent trials each succeed with probability at least $7/8$. Returning their smallest score preserves success whenever one trial succeeds, so the all-failure probability is at most $8^{-R}\le\delta$ by the exact rational cap test in [F1]. If $R>1$, minimality gives $8^{-(R-1)}>\delta$; applying the increasing logarithm and using $\ln(8^{R-1})=(R-1)\ln8$ yields $R-1<\ln(1/\delta)/\ln8$, with $\ln8>0$ since $8>1$. This also gives $R=O(1+\ln(1/\delta))$ when $R=1$. A cutoff with $q(v)<1/N$ is at or below any score whose cumulative mass is at least $1/N$; this proves the minimum specialization. No probability of an exact score atom is assumed beyond the stated quantile/minimum promise.

Run the quantile algorithm with $N=m$ and confidence $\delta/2$ on that ideal cleaned sampler, and choose $\nu\le(\delta/(16Q))^2$. The ideal output is good and has less than $1/m$ strict-lower score mass. Thus no index can have every good output score strictly below the returned score: that one index alone would contribute probability $1/m$. The hybrid bound transfers this good-output/nondomination property to the implemented sampler with failure at most $\delta$. It does not require the selected score atom to have probability $1/m$, does not union-bound unmeasured branches as classical samples, and does not infer a simultaneous deterministic table of all estimates. $$\sup\{\operatorname{tr}(CX):X\in\mathbb C^{n\times n},\ X\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}(A_jX)\le b_j\ (1\le j\le m)\},$$
and its declared **dual program** is
$$\inf\{b\cdot y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ y_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=1}^m y_jA_j-C\succeq0\}.$$
Here $X\succeq0$ and $D\succeq0$ mean positive semidefinite in the finite-dimensional quadratic-form sense. By [[lem-qa-30-hermitian-product-trace-real]], all displayed trace objectives and constraints are real. Primal and dual feasibility, boundedness, attainment, trace bounds, sparsity, and normalizations such as $A_1=I,b_1=R$ are separate promises and do not follow from this definition.

The sign convention is maximize for the primal, minimize for the dual, $\le$ for primal scalar constraints, nonnegative dual multipliers, and dual slack $\sum_jy_jA_j-C\succeq0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$
If $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are positive semidefinite, then $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)\ge0$ for every $n\ge0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
normal, and write the spectral resolution from
[[thm-spectral-resolution-and-polynomial-spectral-projections]] as

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

where the $\lambda_j$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$ and $P_j$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$. For a function
$f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C$ on the spectrum of $T$, define

$$f(T):=\sum_{j=1}^r f(\lambda_j)P_j.$$

This is the **spectral functional calculus** of $T$. For the identity function
$\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}$, one has $\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}(T)=T$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]), let
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with powers as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. **Signs.** If $a \ge 0$ then $a^n \ge 0$, and if $a > 0$ then $a^n > 0$.
2. **Strict monotonicity in the base.** If $0 \le a < b$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n < b^n$. Consequently, for $a, b \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$: $a < b \iff a^n < b^n$ and $a \le b \iff a^n \le b^n$, and $x \mapsto x^n$ is injective on $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with the base.** If $a \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a \ge 1$; if $a > 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a > 1$; and if $0 \le a \le 1$ then $a^n \le 1$.
4. **Monotonicity in the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^m < a^n$ whenever $m < n$ in $\mathbb{N}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^n = 1$ for all $n$; and if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^m > a^n$ whenever $m < n$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Fix integers $n\ge0$ and $m\ge0$, Hermitian matrices $C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The **primal semidefinite program** is
$$\sup\{\operatorname{tr}(CX):X\in\mathbb C^{n\times n},\ X\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}(A_jX)\le b_j\ (1\le j\le m)\},$$
and its declared **dual program** is
$$\inf\{b\cdot y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ y_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=1}^m y_jA_j-C\succeq0\}.$$
Here $X\succeq0$ and $D\succeq0$ mean positive semidefinite in the finite-dimensional quadratic-form sense. By [[lem-qa-30-hermitian-product-trace-real]], all displayed trace objectives and constraints are real. Primal and dual feasibility, boundedness, attainment, trace bounds, sparsity, and normalizations such as $A_1=I,b_1=R$ are separate promises and do not follow from this definition.

The sign convention is maximize for the primal, minimize for the dual, $\le$ for primal scalar constraints, nonnegative dual multipliers, and dual slack $\sum_jy_jA_j-C\succeq0$.

derivations.claim: Put $u=-\eta x$, so $|u|\le1$. From [F5] and $2!=2$, induction gives $k!\ge2^{k-1}$ for $k\ge2$: if it holds at $k\ge2$, then $(k+1)!=(k+1)k!\ge3\cdot2^{k-1}>2^k$, so the bound is strict for $k\ge3$. Thus [F6] gives $\sum_{k\ge2}1/k!\le1/2+1/6+\sum_{k\ge4}2^{-(k-1)}=1/2+1/6+(1/8)\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j}=11/12<1$. If $u=0$, [F4] gives $\exp(u)=1=1+u+u^2$. If $0<u\le1$, then $u^k=u^2u^{k-2}\le u^2$ for $k\ge2$ by [F5], so [F4] gives $\exp(u)=1+u+\sum_{k\ge2}u^k/k!\le1+u+u^2\sum_{k\ge2}1/k!<1+u+u^2$. If $u=-v\le0$ with $0\le v\le1$, the absolute convergence in [F4] allows consecutive grouping because the partial sums after each pair are a subsequence of the ordinary partial sums and hence have the same limit; each pair after the quadratic term is $-v^{2j+3}/(2j+3)!+v^{2j+4}/(2j+4)!=-\frac{v^{2j+3}}{(2j+3)!}(1-\frac{v}{2j+4})\le0$ for $j\ge0$. Hence $\exp(-v)\le1-v+v^2/2\le1-v+v^2$. In every case, $\exp(u)\le1+u+u^2$.

The scalar bound in step 1.1 gives $\exp(-\eta x)\le1-\eta x+\eta^2x^2\le1-\eta x+\eta^2$. Since $M=M^*$, it is normal, so [F1] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $Me_k=\lambda_ke_k$. citations.quote: For $n\ge1$, a round count $T\ge1$, and Hermitian losses $M_1,\ldots,M_T\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $-I\preceq M_t\preceq I$, choose $0<\eta\le1$. Define $S_0=0$, $S_t=\sum_{s=1}^tM_s$, $W_t=e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}$, and $\rho_t=W_t/\operatorname{tr}(W_t)$. The round cost is $\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)$. The exponential is the finite-dimensional Hermitian spectral functional calculus. Loss matrices, access to them, and the classical or quantum work to construct them are input costs.

For $0<\eta\le1$ and $x\in[-1,1]$,
$$\exp(-\eta x)\le1-\eta x+\eta^2.$$
Consequently, if $M=M^*$ and $-I\preceq M\preceq I$, then $\exp(-\eta M)\preceq I-\eta M+\eta^2I$.

For Hermitian matrices $H,K\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$ with $p\ge1$,
$$\operatorname{tr}\exp(H+K)\le\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\exp(H)\exp(K)\bigr).$$
Here $\exp(A)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}A^j/j!$ is the norm-convergent finite-matrix exponential series. No commutativity assumption is imposed.
If $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are positive semidefinite, then $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)\ge0$ for every $n\ge0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.
For Hermitian matrices $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is real.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

derivations.claim: Put $Z_t=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\eta S_t})$ and $m_t=\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)$. By [F5], write $M_t=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^*$; the loss bounds imply $\lambda_k\in[-1,1]$. The matrix $\sigma=U^*\rho_tU$ is positive with trace one by [F1] and [F7]. Thus $q_k=\sigma_{kk}\ge0$ and $\sum_kq_k=1$. Trace cyclicity and the diagonal-sum formula give $m_t=\sum_k\lambda_kq_k\in[-1,1]$, consistently with [F6]. Hence $1-\eta m_t+\eta^2\ge1-\eta+\eta^2=(\eta-1/2)^2+3/4>0$. Since $S_t$ is Hermitian, Golden–Thompson [F3] gives $Z_t\le\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}e^{-\eta M_t})$. By [F2], $(I-\eta M_t+\eta^2I)-e^{-\eta M_t}\succeq0$; [F4] compares its trace product with the positive matrix $e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}$, and [F9] expands the result as $Z_t\le Z_{t-1}(1-\eta m_t+\eta^2)$. Put $s=-\eta m_t+\eta^2$, so $s\ge\eta^2-\eta\ge-1/4$. If $s\ge0$, the series [F8] gives $\exp(s)\ge1+s$. If $s=-v$ with $0<v\le1/4$, absolute convergence [F8] permits pairing the tail after its linear term as $\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{v^{2j+2}}{(2j+2)!}(1-\frac{v}{2j+3})\ge0$, so again $\exp(s)\ge1+s$. Therefore $Z_t\le Z_{t-1}\exp(-\eta m_t+\eta^2)$.

Iterating step 1.1 from $Z_0=n$ gives $Z_T\le n\exp(-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T)$. If $S_T$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, [F5] gives $Z_T=\sum_ke^{-\eta\lambda_k}\ge\exp(-\eta\lambda_{\min}(S_T))$. Since $n>0$, [F10]–[F11] give $n\exp(-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T)=\exp(\ln n-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T)$. Strict increase of $\exp$ and the inverse relation in [F10] therefore imply $-\eta\lambda_{\min}(S_T)\le\ln n-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T$. Rearranging and dividing by $\eta>0$ proves the inequality.

Fix integers $n\ge0$ and $m\ge0$, Hermitian matrices $C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The **primal semidefinite program** is
$$\sup\{\operatorname{tr}(CX):X\in\mathbb C^{n\times n},\ X\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}(A_jX)\le b_j\ (1\le j\le m)\},$$
and its declared **dual program** is
$$\inf\{b\cdot y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ y_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=1}^m y_jA_j-C\succeq0\}.$$
Here $X\succeq0$ and $D\succeq0$ mean positive semidefinite in the finite-dimensional quadratic-form sense. By [[lem-qa-30-hermitian-product-trace-real]], all displayed trace objectives and constraints are real. Primal and dual feasibility, boundedness, attainment, trace bounds, sparsity, and normalizations such as $A_1=I,b_1=R$ are separate promises and do not follow from this definition.

The sign convention is maximize for the primal, minimize for the dual, $\le$ for primal scalar constraints, nonnegative dual multipliers, and dual slack $\sum_jy_jA_j-C\succeq0$.

For $n\ge1$, a round count $T\ge1$, and Hermitian losses $M_1,\ldots,M_T\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $-I\preceq M_t\preceq I$, choose $0<\eta\le1$. Define $S_0=0$, $S_t=\sum_{s=1}^tM_s$, $W_t=e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}$, and $\rho_t=W_t/\operatorname{tr}(W_t)$. The round cost is $\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)$. The exponential is the finite-dimensional Hermitian spectral functional calculus. Loss matrices, access to them, and the classical or quantum work to construct them are input costs.

Let $n\ge1$, $T\ge1$, $0<\eta\le1$, and let $M_1,\ldots,M_T$ be Hermitian with $-I\preceq M_t\preceq I$. For the update of [[def-qa-30-mmw-game]],
$$\sum_{t=1}^T\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)\le\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^TM_t\right)+\eta T+\frac{\ln n}{\eta}.$$

derivations.claim: By $\|A_j\|,\|C\|\le1$ and $\|y_t\|_1\le r$, the triangle inequality gives $\|M_t\|\le(r+1)/w=1$, so the regret bound applies. The trace-estimate assumptions and $\sum_jy_{t,j}\le r$ give $\left|\sum_jy_{t,j}\widetilde a_{t,j}-\widetilde c_t-\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\left(\sum_jy_{t,j}A_j-C\right)\rho_t\right)\right|\le(r+1)\theta=w\theta.$ Together with the shifted-oracle inequality, this implies $\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)\ge-2\theta$.

Sum the lower bounds from step 1.1 and combine them with [F3]. Writing $S=\sum_tM_t$, we get $-2\theta T\le\lambda_{\min}(S)+\eta T+\ln(n)/\eta$, hence $\lambda_{\min}(S/T)\ge-(2\theta+\eta+\ln(n)/(\eta T))$.

The dual slack of $\bar y$ is $\sum_j\bar y_jA_j-C=\gamma I+(w/T)S$, because the identity coefficient contributes $\gamma A_1=\gamma I$. Step 2.1 and the lower bound on $\gamma$ make this matrix positive semidefinite. Also $\bar y\ge0$ and $b\cdot\bar y=\gamma R+T^{-1}\sum_tb\cdot y_t\le\gamma R+\alpha$. These are exactly the dual feasibility and objective claims in [F1].
