citations.quote:
A **promise problem** is a pair $(Y,N)$ of disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$. Its promise is $Y\cup N$. A deterministic solver must accept every word of $Y$ and reject every word of $N$, with either answer allowed elsewhere. The pair belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseP}$ if such a solver has a polynomial time bound on every input.

It belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseNP}$ if there are a polynomial $p$ and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate $V(x,w)$ such that every $x\in Y$ has some $w$ with $|w|\le p(|x|)$ and $V(x,w)=1$, whereas for every $x\in N$ every such $w$ has $V(x,w)=0$. The promise need not be decidable; either side or both sides may be empty. When $Y\cup N=\{0,1\}^*$, this is the ordinary language decision convention.

For every fixed deterministic Turing machine $M$ that halts in polynomial
time, there is a polynomial-size logspace-uniform Boolean circuit family
$(C_n)$ such that $C_n(x)=1$ exactly when $M$ accepts
$x\in\{0,1\}^n$.

Let $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a polynomial-size Boolean circuit family generated in the indexed-gate, logspace sense of [[def-logspace-uniform-circuit-family]]. Assume a fixed polynomial $q$ bounds the number of non-input nodes of $C_n$ by $q(n)$. There is one deterministic polynomial-time machine which, on unary input $1^n$, writes a complete self-delimiting topological gate list for $C_n$, including its input count, all node records and its designated output. The resulting list describes the same circuit and therefore computes the same Boolean function.

Let a finite Boolean DAG in the basis of [[def-boolean-circuit-size-depth-fanin-and-basis]] have $n$ ordered input bits, $m$ ordered output ports, $S$ non-input nodes and $E$ input-port uses counted with multiplicity. There is a deterministic compiler which, from its explicit topological list, emits a valid QC14 circuit over exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ with the first $n$ wires as data, $m$ zero-initialized target wires, at most $S+E$ clean value wires and one additional clean scratch wire. For every $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and $y\in\{0,1\}^m$, its unitary satisfies

$$ |x,y,0^{S+E+1}\rangle\longmapsto |x,y\oplus f(x),0^{S+E+1}\rangle, $$

where $f(x)$ is the ordered Boolean output. It uses at most $27(6S+4E+m)$ QC14 gate occurrences, and the full self-delimiting circuit list is produced in time polynomial in the Boolean-DAG description length. The same action holds on superpositions by linearity.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{EQP}$ in the QC14 model if there is a full-list uniform family $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ and a polynomial-time total acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], using the exact gate and cost conventions of [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]] and [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]], such that

$$ p_{C_{|x|}}(x)=1\quad(x\in Y),\qquad p_{C_{|x|}}(x)=0\quad(x\in N). $$

No condition is imposed on $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The finite output law is normalized by [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]].

In this page, $\mathrm{ZQP}$ denotes the following bounded-failure zero-error promise class. A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{ZQP}$ if there are a full-list uniform QC14 family $(C_n)$, a polynomial-time total label decoder $D_n(x,z)\in\{\mathrm{YES},\mathrm{NO},?\}$, and the finite output law of [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], such that for every $x\in Y$ the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is zero, while for every $x\in N$ the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is zero. All output strings receive one of the three labels, so the remaining probability is the allowed failure label $?$; the output law is normalized by [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]]. No promise condition is imposed off $Y\cup N$.

This explicit fixed-circuit, bounded-failure convention is sufficient for the containments proved on this page. No equivalence with an expected-time quantum zero-error model or with $\mathrm{BQP}\cap\mathrm{coBQP}$ is asserted.

A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to **BQP in the QC14 model** when there exist a full-list uniform family $(C_n)$ and a polynomial-time acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]] and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] such that, for every $x\in Y$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\ge\frac23,$$
and for every $x\in N$,
$$p_{C_{|x|}}(x)\le\frac13.$$
By [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]], $p_{C_n}(x)$ is the probability of the specified acceptance event and lies in $[0,1]$. No condition is imposed for $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The gate alphabet is exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$; its matrix entries lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$ as specified by [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]. This definition does not assert a BQP-versus-classical separation, nor does it assert an unproved equivalence with another circuit-uniformity convention.

For every finite promise computation, every length $n$, and every classical input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, the output weights $p_{C_n}(z\mid x)$ from [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] are nonnegative and sum to one over $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$. The acceptance probability is the probability of the event $\{z:A_n(x,z)=1\}$, lies in $[0,1]$, and agrees with the finite computational-basis POVM outcome law on the named output register.

derivations.claim: Let $\Pi=(Y,N)\in\mathrm{PromiseP}$ and choose its deterministic polynomial-time decider $M$ from [F1]. The Boolean circuit family of [F2] computes $M$; [F3] gives a polynomial-time full-list generator, and [F4] compiles each list into a QC14 family whose one-bit target is $1$ exactly when $M$ accepts. The two polynomial-time stages compose to one fixed deterministic multitape generator $G$ on input $1^n$: it emits the Boolean list and compiles that list to the complete QC14 description. Its intermediate list length and total running time are polynomial in $n$. Convert $G$ to one tape by storing the finitely many simulated tape contents in aligned tracks of a finite product alphabet, with one head marker per tape. During a computation of at most $P(n)$ steps, each track uses at most $n+P(n)+O(1)$ cells; a constant number of sweeps across this interval simulates each transition, so the one-tape time is $O(P(n)(n+P(n)))$. Write the generated circuit description on an output track starting at cell $0$; at halt, a cleanup sweep replaces each product symbol by its output-track component, leaving the exact binary description followed by blanks on the final tape. This is one fixed deterministic one-tape polynomial-time generator as required by [F5]. Use the target bit as the acceptance predicate. For every $x\in Y$ the acceptance probability is $1$, and for every $x\in N$ it is $0$, so $\Pi\in\mathrm{EQP}$.

If $\Pi\in\mathrm{EQP}$, take its witnessing family and define $D_n(x,z)=\mathrm{YES}$ when its acceptance predicate accepts and $D_n(x,z)=\mathrm{NO}$ otherwise. This is a total polynomial-time decoder. The exact probabilities in [F5] make the wrong definite label have probability zero and the correct definite label have probability one on each promised side; therefore the same family witnesses $\Pi\in\mathrm{ZQP}$.

If $\Pi\in\mathrm{ZQP}$, keep its full-list family and define the BQP acceptance predicate to accept exactly when $D_n(x,z)=\mathrm{YES}$. On $Y$ this event has probability at least $2/3$. On $N$ it has probability zero, since a wrong definite YES label is forbidden. By [F8] these event probabilities are normalized, and [F7] gives $\Pi\in\mathrm{BQP}$.

Let $\Pi=(Y,N)$ be a promise problem, so $Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ are disjoint ([[def-promise-problem]]). We say $\Pi$ belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseBPP}$ if there are one fixed probabilistic Turing machine $M$ and one positive integer polynomial $p$ such that every random branch halts within $p(|x|)$ transitions and

$$ \Pr[M(x)\text{ accepts}]\ge \frac23\quad(x\in Y),\qquad \Pr[M(x)\text{ accepts}]\le \frac13\quad(x\in N). $$

The probability is over the uniform finite tape $\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}$ of independent fair bits; after the machine halts, unused suffix bits are ignored, as in [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. The pair has no correctness requirement outside $Y\cup N$. For total promise pairs this is the ordinary BPP acceptance convention of [[def-rp-corp-zpp-bpp-and-pp-classes]].

A probabilistic Turing machine (PTM) is a fixed multitape machine with two total ordinary transition tables. At each nonhalting transition a fresh independent fair bit selects the table. It is polynomial time if one fixed integer polynomial p bounds the number of transitions on every random branch on every input x by $p(|x|)$. This is a worst-case branch bound, using [[def-polynomial-time-verifier-and-reduction-interface]], not an expected-time bound.

For an input of length n, probabilities may be defined on the finite space $\Omega_n=\{0,1\}^{p(n)}$, giving every word mass $2^{-p(n)}$. A deterministic simulator uses bit j for transition j and ignores unused suffix bits after halting. Acceptance probability is the sum of masses of words giving acceptance. Independence has the finite-variable meaning of [[def-independence-of-finite-random-variables]]. The finite probability space is not itself storage charged to the machine.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Fix a length-$n$ finite promise computation from [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], with input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, zero-initialized auxiliary register $|0^{a(n)}\rangle$, circuit unitary $U_{C_n}$, and ordered output-wire tuple $O_n$. Let $P_{O_n}$ be the tensor-factor permutation that moves $O_n$, in its declared order, to the front, and let $W_n$ be the ordered tuple of all remaining wires ([[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]). Set
$$\psi_x:=U_{C_n}(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle),\qquad v_x:=\operatorname{coord}(P_{O_n}\psi_x).$$
Here coordinates are in the ordered computational basis, and the root inner product is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$ and $w\in\{0,1\}^{|W_n|}$, write $e_{z,w}$ for the corresponding product-basis vector and define
$$p_{C_n}(z\mid x):=\sum_{w\in\{0,1\}^{|W_n|}}\left|\langle P_{O_n}\psi_x,e_{z,w}\rangle_{\rm root}\right|^2.$$
The acceptance probability is
$$p_{C_n}(x):=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}\\A_n(x,z)=1}}p_{C_n}(z\mid x).$$
Equivalently, if $E_{A,x}$ is the diagonal projection onto the basis vectors $(z,w)$ with $A_n(x,z)=1$, then $p_{C_n}(x)=\operatorname{Tr}(E_{A,x}v_xv_x^\dagger)$; the matrix adjoint is conjugate transpose in an orthonormal basis ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]]).

These are finite sums. The definition itself does not assert normalization, positivity of the resulting operator expression, or a probability bound; those consequences are the purpose of [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]]. No Dirac bra convention is used here: every amplitude uses the root pairing displayed above.

For every finite promise computation, every length $n$, and every classical input $x\in\{0,1\}^n$, the output weights $p_{C_n}(z\mid x)$ from [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]] are nonnegative and sum to one over $z\in\{0,1\}^{|O_n|}$. The acceptance probability is the probability of the event $\{z:A_n(x,z)=1\}$, lies in $[0,1]$, and agrees with the finite computational-basis POVM outcome law on the named output register.

derivations.claim: If $\Pi\in\mathrm{PromiseP}$, run its deterministic decider as a PTM that ignores all random bits. Its acceptance probability is $1$ on $Y$ and $0$ on $N$, so it satisfies [F2]. Thus $\mathrm{PromiseP}\subseteq\mathrm{PromiseBPP}$.

Now let $\Pi\in\mathrm{PromiseBPP}$ be witnessed by a PTM $M$. Choose a strictly increasing positive integer polynomial $R(n)$ that bounds both its run time and the number of fair bits it can use on length-$n$ inputs. By [F3], using a uniform $R(n)$-bit string and ignoring its unused suffix preserves every acceptance probability.

For a binary word $w$ of length $m$, define one deterministic polynomial-time machine $M^\sharp$ as follows. Search for an $n$ with $m=n+R(n)$; strict increase makes it unique if it exists. If none exists, output $0$. If it exists, split $w=x\|r$ with $|x|=n$ and $|r|=R(n)$, simulate $M$ on $x$ using $r$ as its fair random tape, and output its accept bit. The search and simulation take polynomial time in $m$, since $n\le m$ and $R$ is a fixed polynomial. Whenever a fixed multitape stage in this construction or its later composition runs for at most $P(m)$ steps, a one-tape simulator stores its finitely many tape contents in aligned tracks of a finite product alphabet, with one head marker per tape. Each track uses at most $m+P(m)+O(1)$ cells, and a constant number of sweeps simulates each step in $O(m+P(m))$ time. Put the binary output on a designated track starting at cell $0$; a final cleanup sweep replaces each product symbol by its output-track component, leaving the exact output word followed by blanks on the final tape. Thus the construction has a one-tape polynomial-time implementation whenever that convention is needed.

Apply [F4] to $M^\sharp$, then [F5] to emit the Boolean gate list at length $m(n)=n+R(n)$. Compose this generator with the polynomial-time map $n\mapsto m(n)$. Apply [F6] to that list. In the resulting QC14 family on input $x$, designate the next $R(n)$ auxiliary wires as the random register, apply $H$ to each from its initial zero state, and then run the reversible compiler on the $x$ and random registers with a zero target and clean work. Starting from the compiled list with $g$ gates, prefix Hadamard records on wire indices $n,\ldots,n+R(n)-1$, change the unary input-wire count to $n$, and rewrite the self-delimiting gate count to $g+R(n)$; retain the same total-wire count, target tuple and compiled gate records. The fixed composition of these list operations runs in polynomial time in $n$ because all intermediate Boolean and QC14 descriptions have polynomial length. The one-tape simulation described in step 2.1 therefore yields one fixed deterministic one-tape generator that leaves the complete QC14 description as its final tape word, as required for the full-list family.

By [F8]–[F9], the Hadamards prepare $2^{-R(n)/2}\sum_{r\in\{0,1\}^{R(n)}}|r\rangle$ on the zero-initialized random register. For each basis $r$, the reversible circuit writes exactly the bit $M(x;r)$ into the target and returns its work to zero. Distinct $r$ values remain in orthogonal computational-basis states of the unmeasured random register. The one-tape generator from step 3.1 satisfies the full-list uniformity condition in [F7]. Therefore, by [F10], the target's acceptance probability is $2^{-R(n)}\#\{r\in\{0,1\}^{R(n)}:M(x;r)\text{ accepts}\},$ which is exactly the PTM acceptance probability in [F3]. Fix $n\ge1$ and put $V_n=\{0,1\}^n$, with coordinatewise addition $\oplus$ over $\mathbb F_2$ and cardinality $N=2^n$. For $s,y\in V_n$, define the dot product $s\cdot y=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}s_jy_j\pmod 2$. A table code consists of a unary header $1^n0$ followed by the $n$-bit words $f(x)$ in lexicographic order of $x\in V_n$; this identifies function instances with binary strings as in [[def-promise-problem]], [[def-finite-field-and-its-order]], and [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]].

The YES promise set $Y_n$ consists of table codes of injective maps $f:V_n\to V_n$. The NO promise set $N_n$ consists of codes for which there is a nonzero $s\in V_n$ such that, for every $x,y\in V_n$,

$$ f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=x\ \text{or}\ y=x\oplus s. $$

The sets are disjoint: every NO function has a collision between the distinct inputs $x$ and $x\oplus s$. Its mask is unique, since two different nonzero masks would give a third distinct input in the same fiber. Classical query access returns $f(x)$ at a chosen address. Quantum query access is the coherent XOR oracle $U_f|x,z\rangle=|x,z\oplus f(x)\rangle$ of [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], which is unitary and involutive by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Each call is one query; query charges remain separate from ordinary gate costs by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. In the query model the table is not supplied as gate data; the table code fixes the promised function only.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$
Probability zero need not imply that an event is empty.

derivations.claim: Consider the finite input distribution that chooses YES or NO with probability $1/2$. In the YES case choose a uniform permutation of $V_n$. In the NO case choose a uniform nonzero mask $s$, then a uniform injection from the $N/2$ cosets $\{x,x\oplus s\}$ into the $N$ output labels. Every valid NO function has a unique mask, and each mask has the same number of such injections, so this is uniform over valid NO functions.

It suffices to bound every deterministic query strategy: any randomized strategy has finitely many possible histories and actions up to depth $T$, so its conditional action choices can be represented as a finite distribution over deterministic decision trees. Repeated queries can be removed by caching their earlier answer, so assume every queried address is fresh.

Fix a deterministic strategy and a query index $k\le T$. Since $N\ge16$, the premise $T\le\sqrt N/8$ implies $k\le N/2$. Suppose its first $k-1$ distinct query addresses $x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}$ have produced distinct outputs. Under a NO mask, this transcript is possible exactly when $s\ne x_i\oplus x_j$ for every $i<j<k$. Thus at most $\binom{k-1}{2}$ of the $N-1$ nonzero masks are excluded. For every remaining mask, the queried addresses lie in distinct cosets; the number of injective assignments of output labels to the unqueried cosets is $\frac{(N-k+1)!}{(N/2)!},$ independent of the mask. Hence, conditioned on this transcript, the mask is uniform among at least $N-1-\binom{k-1}{2}$ candidates.

The next address $x_k$ is determined by the transcript. At most $k-1$ candidate masks, namely $x_k\oplus x_j$ for $j<k$, make its output collide with a previous output. Therefore $\Pr[\text{first collision at query }k\mid\text{no earlier collision}] \le \frac{k-1}{N-1-\binom{k-1}{2}}.$ If there is no collision, $x_k$ belongs to a new coset whose output label is uniform among the $N-k+1$ unused labels, exactly as the next output of a uniformly random permutation. Couple the two oracle transcripts to use the same unused label until a Simon collision occurs; the adaptive address choices then also agree up to that time.

For $T\le\sqrt N/8$ and $N\ge16$, each denominator in step 3.1 is at least $N-1-T^2/2>N/2$. Summing the conditional first-collision bounds gives $\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[\text{a collision by query }T] \le \sum_{k=2}^T\frac{2(k-1)}N =\frac{T(T-1)}N\le\frac1{64}<\frac13.$ This also bounds the probability that the coupled transcripts differ.

Let $D$ be the deterministic decision bit, with $1$ meaning YES. Under the coupling, its outputs in the two cases differ with probability at most $1/64$, so $\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]-\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=1]\le\frac1{64}.$ Its average success under the equal mixture is $\frac12\bigl(\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]+\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=0]\bigr) =\frac12\left(1+\Pr_{\mathrm{YES}}[D=1]-\Pr_{\mathrm{NO}}[D=1]\right) \le\frac{1+1/64}{2}<\frac23.$ By step 1.2 the same bound holds for every randomized algorithm. A worst-case error bound of $1/3$ would imply average success at least $2/3$, a contradiction. Therefore at least $\sqrt N/8$ queries are required for all sufficiently large $n$, which is $\Omega(2^{n/2})$.

Input: an integer $n\ge1$ and oracle access to a promised function $f:V_n\to V_n$ from [[def-qa-32-simon-decision-oracle-promise]]. Set $m=n+2$. For each of $m$ independent runs, initialize two ordered $n$-qubit registers $X,Y$ to $|0^n\rangle|0^n\rangle$, apply $H^{\otimes n}$ to $X$, and query the coherent XOR oracle $U_f$ once on $X,Y$. Apply the computational-basis instrument on $Y$ from [[lem-qa-32-simon-function-register-instrument]], record and discard its classical outcome, apply $H^{\otimes n}$ again to $X$, and measure $X$ in the computational basis using the same instrument. Record the resulting $y_j\in V_n$.

Form the $m\times n$ binary matrix with rows $y_1,\ldots,y_m$. Set the next pivot row to $r=1$ and scan columns $j=1,\ldots,n$ from left to right. In column $j$, search rows $r,\ldots,m$ for the first row with a $1$ in that column. If there is no such row, leave the column without a pivot and continue to the next column. Otherwise swap that row with row $r$, XOR row $r$ into every other row with a $1$ in column $j$, and increase $r$ by one. Accept (declare injective) exactly when the number of pivots is $n$.

This procedure uses exactly $n+2$ oracle queries, $2n(n+2)$ ordinary Hadamard gates, two finite measurement readouts per run, and $O(n^3)$ classical bit operations for elimination. A query is charged separately from an implementation of $f$ by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. It makes no gate-time separation claim.

Let $\omega=e^{i\pi/4}$. The one-qubit generators and exact matrices in the
ordered computational basis are

$$H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\omega^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$

On basis vectors, $H|q\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^q|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and
$T^k|q\rangle=\omega^{kq}|q\rangle$ for $q\in\{0,1\}$.

Write $S=T^2=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ and
$Z=T^4=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. Pauli $X,Y,Z$ are as in
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]. On two ordered wires,
$\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,b\mathbin\oplus a\rangle$; the first wire
is control and the second target. A circuit is a finite chronological word of
these gates at stated wire positions; its matrix is the product with later
gates on the left. No extra wire or controlled-$T$ operation is implicit.

The scalar phase $\omega I$ is an allowed Clifford phase in the one-qubit
matrix-word convention. Its scalar factor is retained in exact matrix products;
the convention that an overall scalar does not affect a resource count is
stated separately from matrix equality. It does not grant a controlled-$T$
operation or allow a scalar on a target wire to be discarded under control.

The exact one-qubit H/T algebra is generated by $H,T,T^\dagger$; $S$ and $Z$
are aliases for the displayed powers. The distinction between exact matrix
equality and [[def-qc-global-phase-equivalence|global-phase equivalence]] is
maintained. Resource costs are supplied by
[[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]] and remain separate from this matrix
definition.

Let $A,B$ be nonzero finite-dimensional registers with ordered orthonormal bases $(e_a)_{a\in\Lambda}$ and $(g_b)_{b\in\Gamma}$. Define $P_a e_{a'}=\delta_{a,a'}e_a$ and $Q_b g_{b'}=\delta_{b,b'}g_b$; tensor products of these maps use [[def-qc-tensor-map]]. The maps

$$ \mathcal I_a(R)=(P_a\otimes I_B)R(P_a\otimes I_B),\qquad \mathcal J_b(R)=(I_A\otimes Q_b)R(I_A\otimes Q_b) $$

form finite instruments on $A\otimes B$. If $\psi=\sum_{a,b}c_{a,b}e_a\otimes g_b$ is a unit vector, then their outcome probabilities are

$$ p_A(a)=\sum_b|c_{a,b}|^2,\qquad p_B(b)=\sum_a|c_{a,b}|^2. $$

For a positive-probability outcome, the conditional state is the rank-one density operator on the normalized projected vector. This applies to measuring either register of the Simon state after its coherent XOR query.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

The weights in every finite product of finite probability spaces are nonnegative and sum to $1$. For events $A_i\subseteq\Omega_i$, the coordinate events
$$C_i:=\{\omega\in\prod_{j\in I}\Omega_j:\omega_i\in A_i\}$$
are mutually independent, and for every $J\subseteq I$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j\right)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P_j(A_j).$$

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$
Probability zero need not imply that an event is empty.

derivations.claim: By the factorwise tensor rule [F5], $H^{\otimes n}|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y\in V_n}(-1)^{x\cdot y}|y\rangle$. In particular the first Hadamards prepare $N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in V_n}|x,0^n\rangle$. After one query the state is $|\psi_f\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x\in V_n}|x,f(x)\rangle.$ For each function-register result $z$ in the image of $f$, [F4] gives probability $|f^{-1}(z)|/N$ and the conditional input superposition that is uniform on that fiber.

If $f$ is YES, every fiber is a singleton $\{x\}$. The conditional input state is $|x\rangle$, and the second Hadamards give amplitude $N^{-1/2}(-1)^{x\cdot y}$ at every $y\in V_n$. By the first-register instrument law [F4], its squared modulus is the conditional output probability $1/N$, independent of the measured function-register value; hence the unconditional sample is uniform on $V_n$.

If $f$ is NO with mask $s\ne0$, a positive-probability fiber has the form $\{x,x\oplus s\}$. Its conditional input state is $(|x\rangle+|x\oplus s\rangle)/\sqrt2$. After the second Hadamards the amplitude at $y$ is $\frac{(-1)^{x\cdot y}}{\sqrt{2N}}\bigl(1+(-1)^{s\cdot y}\bigr).$ It is zero when $s\cdot y=1$ and has squared modulus $2/N$ when $s\cdot y=0$. By [F4], these squared moduli are the conditional output probabilities. Pairing $y$ with $y\oplus e_j$ for a coordinate $j$ with $s_j=1$ shows that exactly $N/2$ strings lie in $s^\perp$. The conditional law is therefore uniform on $s^\perp$ and independent of the measured fiber label, so the unconditional law is the same.

In the NO case every sample lies in $s^\perp$, which is proper because $e_j\notin s^\perp$ when $s_j=1$. The span of the samples is proper, so its rank is less than $n$ and the algorithm rejects. The elimination procedure preserves row span under row swaps and row XORs; at termination its nonzero rows have distinct pivot columns and are linearly independent. They still span the original rows, so the pivot count is the matrix rank. At most $n$ pivots each inspect and update $O(n+2)$ rows of $n$ bits, giving $O(n^3)$ bit operations.

Each run reinitializes both registers and uses no earlier outcome as an input. Thus the conditional law of the next sample given any previous transcript is the same one-run law; induction on the number of runs gives the product law, and [F7] identifies the coordinates as independent. In the YES case each sample is uniform on $V_n$ by step 2.1. Their matrix has rank below $n$ exactly when some nonzero $t\in V_n$ satisfies $t\cdot y_j=0$ for every row $j$: Gaussian elimination uses invertible row operations and produces fewer than $n$ pivot columns, so a free variable can be set to $1$ and the pivot variables solved backwards to give a nonzero solution of the homogeneous system. Conversely, if such a $t$ exists, every row lies in its kernel; a coordinate vector $e_k$ with $t_k=1$ is outside that kernel, so the rows cannot span $V_n$.

Fix $t\ne0$ and choose $k$ with $t_k=1$. The involution $y\mapsto y\oplus e_k$ pairs vectors with opposite values of $t\cdot y$, so a uniform sample satisfies $t\cdot y=0$ with probability $1/2$. Independence gives probability $2^{-m}$ that all $m$ samples are orthogonal to $t$. Pointwise, the indicator of the union over the $N-1$ nonzero $t$ is at most the sum of their indicators; summing over the finite probability space yields $\Pr[\operatorname{rank}<n]\le (N-1)2^{-m}=(2^n-1)2^{-(n+2)}<\frac14.$ The procedure makes exactly $m=n+2$ oracle calls.

$$ f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=x\ \text{or}\ y=x\oplus s. $$

The sets are disjoint: every NO function has a collision between the distinct inputs $x$ and $x\oplus s$. Its mask is unique, since two different nonzero masks would give a third distinct input in the same fiber. Classical query access returns $f(x)$ at a chosen address. Quantum query access is the coherent XOR oracle $U_f|x,z\rangle=|x,z\oplus f(x)\rangle$ of [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], which is unitary and involutive by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Each call is one query; query charges remain separate from ordinary gate costs by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. In the query model the table is not supplied as gate data; the table code fixes the promised function only.

Let $t,s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$.

For nonnegative resource functions $a,b$, the notation $a(n)=O(b(n))$ means that some constants $c>0$ and $n_0$ satisfy $a(n)\leq c b(n)$ for every $n\geq n_0$. Every resource bound below uses constants fixed for the machine, uniformly over all its inputs and branches. Time counts transitions; space counts all cells visited on all tapes, including the input tape, with each distinct tape/cell pair counted once. No constructibility assumption on $t$ or $s$ is needed to define these classes.

A language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ belongs to **DTIME$(t(n))$** when there exists
a deterministic multitape Turing machine deciding $L$ in time $O(t(n))$.

A **nondeterministic $k$-tape Turing machine** is obtained from the deterministic
$k$-tape model of [[def-multitape-and-nondeterministic-machines]] by replacing
its transition function with a finite-valued transition map
$$\Delta_k:(Q\setminus\{q_{\mathrm{acc}},q_{\mathrm{rej}}\})\times\Gamma^k\longrightarrow\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fin}}(Q\times\Gamma^k\times\{L,R\}^k).$$
One branch chooses one instruction from the finite set at each step.

A language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ belongs to **NTIME$(t(n))$** when there exists
such a nondeterministic $k$-tape machine $N$ for which:

- every branch of $N$ on every input of length $n$ halts within $O(t(n))$
  steps, and
- some branch of $N$ accepts exactly on the words of $L$, in the same
  existential sense as [[def-nondeterministic-accepting-computation]].

A language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ belongs to **DSPACE$(s(n))$** when a
deterministic multitape decider uses worst-case space $O(s(n))$. It belongs to
**NSPACE$(s(n))$** when a nondeterministic multitape machine accepts exactly the
words in $L$, every branch halts, and the maximum number of visited cells over
all branches and inputs of length $n$ is $O(s(n))$.

Let $M$ be a deterministic $k$-tape Turing machine. For an input word $w$, let
$\operatorname{time}_M(w)$ be the number of steps in the computation of $M$ on
$w$ when that computation halts, and let $\operatorname{space}_M(w)$ be the
total number of tape cells that are ever visited during that computation across
all $k$ tapes.

If $M$ halts on every input of length $n$, its **worst-case time complexity**
and **worst-case space complexity** at that length are
$$ \operatorname{Time}_M(n):=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{\operatorname{time}_M(w):|w|=n\}\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{Space}_M(n):=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{\operatorname{space}_M(w):|w|=n\}\bigr). $$
Thus both values are $0$ when the input alphabet has no words of length $n$.

For a nondeterministic machine $N$, a **maximal branch** either is infinite,
ends in an accepting or rejecting state, or ends at a nonhalting configuration
with no allowed transition. Suppose that every maximal branch on $w$ ends in
an accepting or rejecting state. Since the computation tree is finitely
branching, it then has finitely many nodes: if it had arbitrarily large depth,
repeatedly taking the first child with descendants at arbitrarily large depths
would produce an infinite branch. Define $\operatorname{time}_N(w)$ and
$\operatorname{space}_N(w)$ as the maxima over these finitely many halting
branches. The worst-case values $\operatorname{Time}_N(n)$ and
$\operatorname{Space}_N(n)$ use the same input maxima with $0$ adjoined as
above, provided the branch condition holds for every input of length $n$.

We say that a machine **runs in time at most $t(n)$** when its worst-case time
is bounded by $t$, and **runs in space at most $s(n)$** when its worst-case
space is bounded by $s$.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

derivations.claim: Let $N=2^n$ and $L=nN+n+1$, the length of the unary-header table code. For each of the $\binom N2$ distinct address pairs, scan the table to retrieve both $n$-bit outputs and answer NO if they coincide; answer YES if no pair collides. On a promised table this is correct, since YES functions are injective and every NO function has a collision.

One table scan and output comparison take $O(L)$ transitions, so the $\binom N2$ pairs take $O(N^2L)$ time. Since $N\le L$, this is $O(L^3)$; the explicit-table promise problem is therefore in deterministic polynomial time under [F4].

The oracle bounds in [F1] and [F2] charge calls to $f$ or $U_f$, whereas the explicit-input algorithm charges table scans and ordinary computation as required by [F5]. The deterministic $O(L^3)$ algorithm in step 2.1 contradicts the asserted absence of a polynomial-in-$L$ algorithm. Thus this oracle-query separation does not imply superpolynomial classical running time in the explicit-input length. This comparison does not refute an $\Omega(2^{n/2})$ time bound measured in $n$: the explicit table already has length $L=n2^n+n+1$.

For every $n\ge1$, the sample in [[alg-qa-32-simon-query-rank-test]] is uniform on $V_n$ when $f$ is YES, and uniform on $s^\perp=\{y:s\cdot y=0\}$ when $f$ is NO with mask $s\ne0$. The rank test rejects every NO instance. On YES its error probability is at most

$$ (2^n-1)2^{-(n+2)}<\frac14. $$

It uses exactly $n+2$ queries and $O(n^3)$ classical bit operations.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

derivations.claim: The dot product with $s=01$ is the second coordinate, so $s^\perp=\{00,10\}$. Its span is itself and has rank one. Hence four NO samples cannot have rank two, and the algorithm rejects with probability one.

In $V_2$, the three one-dimensional subspaces are $\{00,10\}$, $\{00,01\}$, and $\{00,11\}$. Four vectors fail to span exactly when all four lie in one of these three subspaces. Each corresponding set of four-tuples has $2^4=16$ elements; every pairwise intersection and the triple intersection consist only of $(00,00,00,00)$. Inclusion-exclusion therefore gives $3\cdot16-3\cdot1+1=46$ failing tuples out of $4^4=256$.

The exact failure probability is $46/256=23/128$. The union bound is $3\cdot16/256=3/16$, agreeing with [F1] and strictly below $1/4$. There are exactly four oracle runs by the algorithm's definition.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For all $x,y\in R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,

$$ (x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^ky^{n-k}.$$

The natural-number coefficients act by repeated addition. The formula includes $n=0$.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Regard the nonnegative weights $p_j=\binom djx^j(1-x)^{d-j}$ as a finite distribution. [F1] gives $\sum_jp_j=1$. Reindexing the first count in [F2] gives $\mathbb E K=\sum_jjp_j=dx$. For $d\ge2$, reindexing the second count gives $\mathbb E[K(K-1)]=\sum_jj(j-1)p_j=d(d-1)x^2$; for $d=1$ this expectation is $0=d(d-1)x^2$ directly. Since $K^2=K(K-1)+K$, it follows that $\mathbb E(K/d-x)^2=x(1-x)/d\le1/(4d)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

Since $|\sqrt{u}-\sqrt{v}|\le\sqrt{|u-v|}$ for $u,v\ge0$, [F3] gives $\mathbb E\sqrt{|K/d-x|}\le\sqrt{\mathbb E|K/d-x|}$ and $\mathbb E|K/d-x|\le\sqrt{\mathbb E(K/d-x)^2}$. Therefore $|B_d(x)-\sqrt{x}|\le\bigl(\mathbb E(K/d-x)^2\bigr)^{1/4}\le(4d)^{-1/4}.$ The bound is uniform in $x$, and solving $(4d)^{-1/4}\le\eta$ gives the stated degree choice.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

derivations.claim: For every vector $v$, $\|Mv\|\ge\|Uv\|-\|(M-U)v\|\ge(1-\varepsilon)\|v\|$. Thus $M$ is injective and hence bijective in finite equal dimension. The eigenvalues of $M^*M$ are $\sigma_j^2$, where each singular value obeys $1-\varepsilon\le\sigma_j\le1+\varepsilon$ by the triangle inequality and [F2].

By [F1], define $(M^*M)^{-1/2}$ by applying the positive scalar inverse-square-root to its positive eigenvalues. Then $Q^*Q=I$, so $Q$ is unitary; moreover the singular-value decomposition, obtained by diagonalizing $M^*M$, gives $\|Q-M\|=\max_j|1-\sigma_j|\le\varepsilon$. Consequently $\|Q-U\|\le\|Q-M\|+\|M-U\|\le2\varepsilon$. Finally, $X=M^*M-I$ has norm at most $2\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2\le17/64<1/2$; the binomial series for $(I+X)^{-1/2}$ converges absolutely in operator norm, and its geometric tail bound gives effective truncations from effective entries of $M$.

derivations.claim: Set $K=\|H_1\|$. By [F1], the Hermitian compression $H_1|_S$ has a unit eigenvector $u\in S$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_S$. Since $H_2u=0$, its Rayleigh quotient for $H_1+H_2$ is $\lambda_S$, so $\lambda_{\min}(H_1+H_2)\le\lambda_S$.

If $S^\perp=\{0\}$, then $S=H$ and $H_2=0$, so the conclusion is equality. Otherwise both $S$ and $S^\perp$ are nonzero. For a unit vector $x\in H$, write $x=\alpha u+\beta w$ with $u\in S$, $w\in S^\perp$ unit and $\alpha,\beta\ge0$, $\alpha^2+\beta^2=1$; absorb the phases into $u,w$. If either component of $x$ is zero, choose any unit vector in its nonzero subspace for the unused direction. Self-adjointness of $H_2$ and $H_2|_S=0$ make its cross terms zero, so $\langle H_2x,x\rangle\ge J\beta^2$. Also $\langle H_1u,u\rangle\ge\lambda_S$, $\langle H_1w,w\rangle\ge-K$, and $|\langle H_1u,w\rangle|\le K$.

Expanding the quadratic form and using $\lambda_S\ge-K$ gives $\langle(H_1+H_2)x,x\rangle\ge\lambda_S+(J-2K)\beta^2-2K\beta.$ Indeed the $S$-diagonal term is $\alpha^2\langle H_1u,u\rangle\ge\alpha^2\lambda_S=\lambda_S-\beta^2\lambda_S\ge\lambda_S-K\beta^2$, the $S^\perp$ term is at least $-K\beta^2$, and $\alpha\le1$ bounds the cross term below by $-2K\beta$.

The scalar quadratic $(J-2K)\beta^2-2K\beta$ has minimum $-K^2/(J-2K)$ by completing the square. Thus every unit Rayleigh quotient is at least $\lambda_S-K^2/(J-2K)$; [F1] identifies the least eigenvalue with the minimum Rayleigh quotient. This proves the lower bound.

Use the Pauli matrices $X,Y,Z$ and exact gates $H=(X+Z)/\sqrt2$ and
$T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})$ from
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and
[[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]]. Write $PU(2)$ for the
quotient of $U(2)$ by its unit-modulus scalar matrices, equipped with the
quotient topology. Their normalized lifts $h=iH$ and
$t=e^{-i\pi/8}T$ lie in $SU(2)$ and generate a dense subgroup of $SU(2)$;
therefore the projective classes of $H,T$ generate a dense subgroup of
$PU(2)$.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

derivations.claim: Direct determinants give $\det(iH)=i^2\det(H)=1$ because $\det(H)=-1$, and $\det(e^{-i\pi/8}T)=e^{-i\pi/4}e^{i\pi/4}=1$. Unitarity is preserved by unit-modulus scalars, so $h,t\in SU(2)$.

Density of the group generated by $h,t$ is [F1]. For any fixed finite word, replacing each normalized generator by its physical gate multiplies the whole word by the product of the corresponding scalar phases, which is a single scalar on the entire one-qubit subcircuit. Such a scalar does not affect any outcome probability when the subcircuit is applied unconditionally. If the word is controlled, this scalar acts only on the active control block and is therefore not irrelevant; the statement explicitly excludes that use without correction.

A finite-dimensional complex matrix input of dimension $d$ is **effectively encoded** if its complete binary description specifies $d$ and conforms to one fixed deterministic entry-approximation machine. Given the description, an entry index, and unary precision request $1^p$, that machine returns rational real and imaginary parts within $2^{-p}$ of the exact entry in time bounded by one fixed polynomial in the total description length plus $p$, uniformly over all valid encodings. Rational entries use their exact binary numerator and denominator; algebraic entries use a finite encoding compatible with this same evaluator and bound. A **uniform matrix family** supplies one polynomial-time description-generation procedure for each member. Hermiticity, dimensions, and norm bounds are promises on the exact matrices, not conclusions inferred from a finite approximation.

This interface includes finite output size and all approximation bit costs. It does not supply a matrix oracle, exact comparisons on arbitrary computable reals, or a free unitary implementation.

Use the exact one-qubit matrices $H$ and $T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})$ of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]]. The matrices $h=iH$ and $t=e^{-i\pi/8}T$, together with their inverses, are determinant-one representatives in $SU(2)$. Their generated subgroup is dense in $SU(2)$. Replacing each normalized letter in a word by its underlying physical $H,T,T^\dagger$ letter changes the product only by one scalar phase, so an unconditional one-qubit circuit can approximate every $SU(2)$ target up to an irrelevant global phase. A normalized letter must not be placed under a control without correcting its scalar phase.

Fix a finite inverse-closed dense $G\subset SU(2)$ whose real and imaginary
gate-entry coordinates are algebraic numbers supplied by their minimal
polynomials over $\mathbb Q$ and rational isolating intervals with opposite
endpoint signs and exactly one real root, and fix a
rational certified base-net radius
$0<\eta_0<64^{-2}$. Let the finite base-net certificate be fixed. Suppose
$U\in SU(2)$ is given by a Cauchy name whose query on unary input $1^b$ takes
at most $(b+1)^c$ bit operations for a fixed integer $c\ge1$. Given rational
$0<\varepsilon\le\eta_0$ encoded as $\varepsilon=p/q$ by positive binary
integers $p,q$ with a fixed delimiter (not necessarily reduced), there is a
deterministic Turing implementation of the Solovay–Kitaev recursion that outputs a gate word $W$
with $\|U-W\|\le\varepsilon$ and length
$O(\log^{\log_{3/2}5}(1/\varepsilon))$. If $s_\varepsilon$ is the binary
encoding length of $\varepsilon$ and
$N=\lceil\log_2(2/\varepsilon)\rceil$, its bit time, including reading
$\varepsilon$ and printing the expanded word, is
$$O\bigl((N+s_\varepsilon)^{c+10}\bigr).$$
Here $s_\varepsilon$ is the total bit length of this numerator/denominator
encoding. The constants depend on $G$, the fixed base-net certificate, and the fixed
algebraic descriptions. This is distinct from the exact-real arithmetic
count in [[thm-qc-solovay-kitaev-error-and-resource-bound]].

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Use the rotation convention of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] and define $R_y(\theta):=R_{(0,1,0)}(\theta)$:
$$R_z(\alpha)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\alpha/2}&0\\0&e^{i\alpha/2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_y(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta/2)&-\sin(\theta/2)\\\sin(\theta/2)&\cos(\theta/2)\end{pmatrix}.$$
For every $U\in U(2)$ there are real $\delta,\alpha,\theta,\beta$ with
$$U=e^{i\delta}R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta).$$
If $\det U=1$, the scalar factor is unnecessary and $U=R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta)$.

In the ordered two-qubit basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the controlled-NOT with first wire control and second wire target is

$$\operatorname{CNOT}_{1\to2}|a,t\rangle=|a,t\mathbin{\oplus}a\rangle,\qquad a,t\in\{0,1\}.$$

Equivalently, it is the control block $C(X)=\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]], where $X$ is the Pauli bit-flip matrix. The wire order is part of the definition.

Fix a positive matrix dimension $d$ and an integer $c\ge1$. A dyadic interval is a
closed interval with dyadic-rational endpoints; a complex matrix interval
stores one such interval for every real and imaginary entry. Suppose each
input is given by a Cauchy procedure which, on unary request $1^q$, returns a
rational approximation to each real and imaginary entry with error at most
$2^{-q}$ and uses $O((q+1)^c)$ bit operations. Suppose exact scalar and
matrix inputs have entries of modulus at most $3$. Each fixed algebraic real
constant is supplied by a rational polynomial and an open rational interval
with nonroot endpoints on which the polynomial has opposite endpoint signs
and exactly one real root.
When each scalar divisor
and each norm used for normalization has modulus at
least $2^{-B}$, the following routines return dyadic intervals of diameter at
most $2^{-p}$ containing the exact answer, using
$O((p+B+1)^{\max(c,3)})$ bit operations:

- any fixed finite composition of sums and products;
- quotient by a scalar whose modulus is at least $2^{-B}$;
- the nonnegative square root of a real in $[0,1]$;
- normalization $v/\|v\|_2$ of a real vector with $\|v\|_2\ge2^{-B}$;
- the matrix exponential $e^A$ when $\|A\|\le1$; and
- the matrix logarithm $\log(I+E)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j+1}E^j/j$
  when $\|E\|\le1/2$.

Here $d$ and the number of scalar operations in the fixed composition are
constants. The exponent $B$ is needed only for divisions and normalization;
the square-root routine also works at input zero. The constants in the
complexity bound may depend on the fixed dimension, routine, and Cauchy-time
constant.

Let a finite ordered register have an orthonormal computational basis $(|z\rangle)_{z\in\mathcal X}$, using the root convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. For distinct labels $x,y\in\mathcal X$, choose $V\in U(2)$, where $U(2)=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=MM^*=I_2\}$. The **two-level unitary** $T_{x,y}(V)$ acts by the matrix $V$ in the ordered basis $(|x\rangle,|y\rangle)$ and acts as the identity on $\operatorname{span}\{|x\rangle,|y\rangle\}^{\perp}$. Its action is exact matrix equality: any scalar phase contained in $V$ is retained.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

Use the rotation convention of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] and define $R_y(\theta):=R_{(0,1,0)}(\theta)$:
$$R_z(\alpha)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\alpha/2}&0\\0&e^{i\alpha/2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_y(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta/2)&-\sin(\theta/2)\\\sin(\theta/2)&\cos(\theta/2)\end{pmatrix}.$$
For every $U\in U(2)$ there are real $\delta,\alpha,\theta,\beta$ with
$$U=e^{i\delta}R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta).$$
If $\det U=1$, the scalar factor is unnecessary and $U=R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta)$.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

derivations.claim: If $D=1$, output the empty circuit: the scalar $1\times1$ unitary is immaterial up to the allowed whole-circuit phase. Assume $D\ge2$. Every Pauli-$X$ requested anywhere in this construction is emitted as the QC14 word $HT^4H$: the exact matrices in [F9] give $T^4=Z$ and $HZH=X$. First construct exact computational-basis transpositions for row pivoting. For bit strings $x,y$, flip their differing positions in order to form a Gray path $g_0=x,\ldots,g_d=y$. The adjacent swap $g_j\leftrightarrow g_{j+1}$ is an $X$ on their differing bit, controlled on the other $q-1$ fixed bits; for each control required to be $0$, apply the same exact $HT^4H$ word to that control wire before computing the control conjunction (or before the one-control gate), then undo it after the controlled operation and any conjunction uncomputation. A conjunction of at least two controls is computed into clean bits by a chain of Toffoli gates, the target $X$ is applied under the last conjunction bit, and the chain is reversed; with no controls use the same $HT^4H$ word, and with one positive control use CNOT. Toffoli is exact over the gate alphabet: for bits $a,b,c$, $4abc=a+b+c-(a\oplus b)-(a\oplus c)-(b\oplus c)+(a\oplus b\oplus c).$ Compute each parity into a clean bit by CNOTs, apply $T$ for positive terms and $T^\dagger$ for negative terms, and uncompute; the resulting phase is $(-1)^{abc}$. Conjugating the third bit by $H$ gives Toffoli. The product of swaps along the path except its last edge, followed by the last swap and the reversed prefix, is exactly the transposition of $x,y$. In column $j$, earlier columns have already been made zero below row $j$, so the remaining tail has norm one by unitarity. Approximate its entry magnitudes to error at most $1/(8D)$ and choose the least row among those with largest approximate magnitude as pivot; the selected exact magnitude is at least $1/\sqrt D-1/(4D)\ge1/(2\sqrt D)$. Move that row to $j$ by the exact transposition just constructed, which preserves earlier zeros. For each lower entry $b$ and pivot $a$, use the determinant-one Givens block $r^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\bar a&\bar b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$, $r=(|a|^2+|b|^2)^{1/2}$; direct multiplication sends $(a,b)^T$ to $(r,0)^T$. The pivot remains bounded below, so every division is conditioned and no exact zero test is needed. Fixed dimension, [F7], and the pivot lower bound give polynomial-time Cauchy names for the Givens factors and a diagonal unitary remainder. If the recorded left multipliers are $Q_1,\ldots,Q_s$, the terminal upper-triangular unitary is $\Delta=Q_s\cdots Q_1U$; its first column has only a unit-modulus first entry, orthogonality forces the rest of the first row to vanish, and induction on the trailing principal block shows $\Delta$ is diagonal. Hence $U=Q_1^{-1}\cdots Q_s^{-1}\Delta$, an exact factorization in reverse chronological application order. [F1, F4, F6, F7, F8, F9, algebra]

Each Givens factor from step 1.1 is an $SU(2)$ block on two basis strings $x,y$, in the two-level sense of [F8]. Flip their differing bit positions in order to form a Gray path $g_0=x,\ldots,g_d=y$. Controlled-$X$ gates on the other fixed bits swap $g_j,g_{j+1}$ for $j<d-1$; the final controlled one-qubit block acts on $(g_{d-1},y)$, and reversing the swaps gives the exact two-level action. Every intermediate controlled-$X$ is implemented by the conjunction and target construction of step 1.1, including the exact $HT^4H$ expansion for its target $X$. With middle block $X$, the same path conjugation is the exact basis transposition used in step 1.1. When $q=1$, the Givens block is itself an unconditional one-qubit $SU(2)$ gate. For $q\ge2$, reduce each multi-control to one control by computing its $q-1$-bit conjunction into clean bits with the exact Toffoli gates from step 1.1 and then uncomputing. For a one-controlled $SU(2)$ block, choose $R_z(\alpha)R_y(\beta)R_z(\gamma)$. For $R=R_z$ or $R_y$, the chronological sequence “apply $R(\theta/2)$ to the target, CNOT, apply $R(-\theta/2)$ to the target, CNOT” has denotation $\operatorname{CNOT}(I\otimes R(-\theta/2))\operatorname{CNOT}(I\otimes R(\theta/2)).$ On control $0$ the two rotations cancel; on control $1$, $XR(-\theta/2)X=R(\theta/2)$ by the exact $R_y,R_z$ matrices in [F9], so the active block is $R(\theta)$. This proves the controlled Euler product using only unconditional one-qubit rotations and CNOTs. The closed forms from [F9] give $R_z(\theta+4\pi)=R_z(\theta)$ and $R_y(\theta+4\pi)=R_y(\theta)$; reduce each Euler angle modulo $4\pi$ to a representative in $[0,4\pi)$. For a candidate mesh angle $\theta\in[0,16]$ and $a\in\{y,z\}$, write $R_a(\theta)=e^{A_a(\theta)}$ with $A_a(\theta)=-i\theta\sigma_a/2$. Since $\|A_a(\theta)/9\|\le8/9<1$, the interval routine [F7] evaluates $e^{A_a(\theta)/9}$ in its stated domain; multiplying nine such matrices evaluates $R_a(\theta)$, with guard precision chosen so each three-rotation product and target has certified Frobenius error at most $\eta/(100C_D)$. Put $M=\lceil1600C_D/\eta\rceil$ and use the rational mesh $\{16j/M:0\le j\le M\}$ in each coordinate. Since $4\pi<16$, each reduced Euler angle is within $16/M\le\eta/(100C_D)$ of a mesh point. The exact rotation formula gives $\|R_a(u)-R_a(v)\|\le|u-v|/2$, so the product at one such mesh triple is within $\eta/(8C_D)$ of the target. For each candidate, compute a certified Frobenius-distance upper bound from the entry intervals; its square-root input is scaled by $1/9$, since the squared distance between two $2\times2$ unitaries is at most $8$, and then rescaled by $3$. Select the first mesh product whose upper bound is at most $\eta/(4C_D)$; the guaranteed nearby mesh point passes because its true Frobenius distance is at most $\sqrt2\,\eta/(8C_D)$ and the interval error is at most $\eta/(100C_D)$. Every selected product therefore has operator error at most $\eta/(4C_D)$. Here $C_D\ge1$ is a fixed upper bound for the total number of rotation factors requiring approximation, including the recursive diagonal construction described below; for example, for $q\ge1$ take $C_D=\max\{1,3D(D-1)+(D-1)(2q-1)\}$. The search uses $O((C_D/\eta)^3)$ candidates and only rational interval comparisons, not an exact-real branch test.

Factor the diagonal remainder as $\Delta=d_0\operatorname{diag}(1,(d_z/d_0)_{z\ne0})$. Since $|d_0|=1$, every ratio $\widetilde d_z=d_z/d_0$ is a unit scalar with a polynomial-time Cauchy name by [F7]: the denominator has the uniform lower bound one. For each $z\ne0$, choose a bit position where $z$ is one, compute the condition that all other bits match $z$, and apply $\operatorname{diag}(1,\widetilde d_z)$ to the chosen bit controlled by that condition; this phases $|z\rangle$ and leaves its partner with chosen bit zero unchanged. If $q=1$ the condition is empty and the phase is unconditional. The common factor $d_0$ is the single global scalar for the complete diagonal remainder. Approximate each $\widetilde d_z$ by scanning an $M$-point rational angle grid, with $M\ge16\pi D/\eta$, and accept a grid point whose certified chordal distance is at most $4\pi/M$; a nearest grid point is within $\pi/M$, so a valid one is found after $O(M)$ evaluations using [F7]. Write its phase as $e^{i\theta}$. Implement a phase on a pattern of $k$ original data bits by induction on $k$. For $k=1$, use $\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\theta})=e^{i\theta/2}R_z(\theta)$ on that data bit (conjugated by exact $X$ gates for pattern zero), retaining its scalar as a whole-circuit scalar.
